units.la: VIROS principes & magistratum gerentes, literis operam navare, & tetricis ac difficilibus Reipublicæ negotiis, otium illud honestum blandum interponere, magna semper laus fuit; utinam hodie non tam rara foret! Nam quotusquisque jam ex isto numero, veteres illos Reipublicæ Romanæ proceres & heroës æmulatur? qui, quantum eis ab officiis & publico munere superabat temporis, tantum in pulcerrimas doctissimasque commentationes impendebant: quarum etiamnum partem aliquam (nam injuriâ temporis intercidêre potiora) magno cum fructu voluptate terimus : Capi interim nos admiratio non mediocris, cum perpendimus, id in hac Musarum palæstra præstitisse viros, domi militiæque, mari atque terrâ occupatos, quod ab umbratico quocunque, sedentario, & jugiter chartis impallescente literatore spe- rare non auderes. Te intuens, hæc dico, Nobilis & Amplissime Vir, qui succi- sivas & subsecundarias horas perire non pateris, nec à luxu vel desidiâ, mentis avocamenta camenta petis; sed quod otium à cura publica & re familiari datur, id omne confers in hæc studia doctrinæ: Testes mihi fuerunt, præteralia monimenta, Versus, in quos incidi, latinè àte & venustissimè compositi; tales fundis occasione datâ, facilis & extemporalis poeta. units.tr: It has always been great praise for men who are princes and hold office to devote themselves to letters, and to set a pleasant and honourable leisure against the grave and difficult affairs of the commonwealth. Would that it were not so rare today! For how few of that number now emulate those old nobles and heroes of the Roman commonwealth, who devoted to the most elegant and learned studies as much time as their duties and public service left them? Part of those writings we still enjoy with great profit and pleasure (for the greater works have perished through the injury of time). Meanwhile I am not a little amazed when I consider that men occupied at home and in war, on sea and on land, achieved in this school of the Muses what no shady, sedentary scholar, grown pale over his papers without ceasing, would dare to hope for. It is with you in view that I say these things, Noble and Most Distinguished Sir, you who do not allow your spare and leftover hours to be lost, and who do not seek distractions of the mind in luxury or idleness; but whatever leisure is granted you from public care and your family affairs, you devote entirely to these studies of learning. Witness to this for me are the other memorials, the verses I came upon, composed in Latin very elegantly and charmingly; you pour out such verses, a ready and extemporaneous poet, whenever the occasion is given. units.tr: (which I have experienced myself) far removed from pride and disdain; gravity, candour; besides these, force of judgement, sharpness, maturity. None of these virtues in you is ordinary; all are of the highest degree. Those last ones I have listed are more striking and rare at your age, which has not yet reached forty; but of course this is the fruit of History, of which you are a constant and most diligent reader. It makes young men and mature men equal to the old in prudence. Therefore I congratulate the Fatherland and the Republic of the Belgians, and I congratulate it even in these waves and storm, that, together with the other most skilled pilots, it has summoned you to its helm and now summons you again, since virtue and men are required. When the winds are silent and the sea is calm, even an oarsman may sit at the tiller and remain harmless, and even hold the right course for some time. units.tr: all his virtues. So you shape yourself after his example: Rule your mind. This is your family motto. Rule it by reason, for you know that the mind is not ruled by the bit or spur of desires and passions, but only broken or made wild. Therefore take up the second motto, which the Roman sage (I meant to say the poet) impresses on you: Many kings. For he says: You will be many kings, if reason rules you. Following these footsteps of yours and of his illustrious parents also walks the most noble and promising young man, Mr. Cornelius de Jonghe, lord of Osterlant, S'heer-Janslant, etc., son of your sister, now for more than three years my pupil and fellow boarder, and by his merit far the dearest to me. So I gladly applaud him: Brave men are born of brave and good men.

units.la: EN Oratiunculas aliquot, quas juvenis & penè adolescens Lovanii, ubi Philosophiae Professorem agebam, ab hinc annos tredecim lusi, dixi, edidi: Et lusi, inquam: videor enim hîc interdum Poëta, videor entheo quodam spiritu instin-ctus, anhelare subinde verius, quam perorare: Hoc tunc juvabat, hoc sors tunc & aetas ferebat: Legeram mihi genus aliquod dicendi arduum, abruptum, & (quod vitio mihi vertebant adversarii mei) Afrum, quod velut è Pythia quadam specu per intervalla detonaret; & tamen plus in sinum reconderet (quod acutos tunc & perspicaces censere memini) quam fronte promitteret: solito meo stylo & modulatione vocis abdicaveram: nec meorum, sed eorum etiam quae ab aliis hauseram, conabar oblivisci; Eos tantum modos orationis, & velut metricas leges, quas ipse mihi dixeram, tenax & animosus observabam: Itaque nihil ab aliis mutuabar, ne à me ipso quidem: quidquid depromebam, erat ex penu illa quam mihi recens comparaveram. De aliorum judiciis non laborabam: qui si boni essent, boni consulturos, quæ bono dixissem animo; sin mali, altè contemnendos mihi & despiciendos arbitrabar. Hunc ego, qui dictas Declamationes animat spiritum & ardorem, evitare nondum aut suffiaminare constitui: vivat ibi, & glíscat ibi; Castigavi tamen eum, ne me conniventem patrem, & prolibus meis justo plus indulgentem dicas: crudiora digessi, austeriora mitigavi, quæ luxuriare videbantur, recidi: ad extremum etiam, nullâ aliâ caussâ, solùm pro meo jure hinc inde quædam addidi, dempsi, mutavi; sed totum id modicè feci, aut etiam intra modum;
units.tr: I have published and given to the press a few little speeches that I delivered at Louvain, where I was professor of philosophy, when I was a young man and nearly an adolescent, thirteen years ago. I say I played at them, because here I often seem a poet, seem to be stirred by some divine spirit, and to gasp out my words rather than deliver a speech. That was my pleasure then, and my age and situation allowed it. I had chosen a kind of style that was difficult, abrupt and (as my opponents blamed me for) African, which thundered at intervals like a priestess from some Pythian cave, yet hid more in its bosom than it promised on its brow (I remember that the sharp and discerning men of the time judged so). I had put aside my usual manner and tone of voice. I tried to forget not only my own style but also whatever I had borrowed from others. I kept firmly and boldly to those modes of speaking and, as it were, to those metrical laws which I had set for myself. So I borrowed nothing from others, nor even from myself: whatever I brought out came from that store which I had lately acquired. I did not worry about the judgments of others. If they were good, I thought they would take in good part what I had said in good faith; if bad, I considered they should be utterly scorned and despised. I decided not to tone down or stifle this spirit and fire which animates these declamations: let it live and grow there. Yet I did correct it, so that you could not call me an indulgent father, too lenient towards my own children. I rearranged the cruder parts, softened the harsher ones, and cut out what seemed to grow too lush. In the end, for no other reason than my own right, I added, removed and changed some things here and there; but I did all this with moderation, or even within bounds.

units.la: Nisi quod fortè primum Actum hujus fabulæ (Orationem, quam in auspiciis dixi) studiosè magis & accuratè recognovi: Et erat operæ pretium: Cum enim enim perversa Scholarum Dogmata (à quibus hodie tantum in Ecclesiis & Republica turpitudinis & turbarum) non è Philosophia (à qua equidem nihil, nisi beneficum & salutare) sed è perversè Philosophantium affectibus (quos ibi Geniorum nominibus insignivi) scaturire videamus: promptum jam & expeditum erit unicuique, sive veterum, sive recentium Philosophemata pervolventi, permixtos cum iis errores certis & indubitatis criteriis deprehendere, & delirantes à Rationis lira sententias, suis quasque Geniis, à quibus dimanant, assignare: atque adeo iis ipsis Geniis, Cave canem inurere: Genii enim tres, aut potius quatuor (Pantomimus, Mango, Dogmatistes & Gerro) quos nostra illa exagitat & insectatur Oratio, illiserè sunt, qui Equum Trojanum infarciunt, quem jam diu fatalem & inauspicatum intra Scholam aspeximus.
units.tr: Except that perhaps I went over the first act of this play (the oration I gave at the opening) more carefully and accurately. And it was worth the effort. For since we see the perverse doctrines of the schools (from which today there flows nothing but shame and turmoil in the Churches and the commonwealth, not from philosophy, from which I expect nothing but what is beneficial and wholesome, but from the passions of those who philosophise perversely, which I have marked there with the names of the Genii), it will be easy for anyone who turns over the philosophical teachings of the ancients or the moderns to detect the errors mixed in with them by certain and indubitable criteria, and to assign each opinion that strays from the line of reason to the Genius from which it flows. And indeed to those very Genii I would apply the warning "Beware of the dog" to brand them. For the three, or rather four, Genii (Pantomimus, Mango, Dogmatist and Gerro) whom that oration of ours harasses and hunts down, are those who stuff the Trojan horse, which we have long seen inside the school as fatal and ill-omened.

units.la: Insuper hac secundâ editione, Libello meo lucernam geminam accendi, Para-phrasim & Commentationem; sed has in limine tantùm habeo: Nam quid erat opus faculas illas omnibus locis interpo-nere, & ubique lychnuchos ex fornice sus-pendere? si rectè putas, non fuisset hoc aliud, quam oleum & operam perder. non prodest, inquam, ea res, sed obest: per-stringit oculorum aciem, obtundit & confundit. Tu igitur sume tibi, quem dixi, ardentem in vestibulo dimixum, ut videas ubi pedem ponas. & gressum di-rigens eâ luce, penetra jam securus in adyta Libelli.
units.tr: Moreover, in this second edition I have lit a twin lamp for my little book, a paraphrase and a commentary; but I have them only at the threshold. For what need was there to place those torches in every spot and hang lamps from the vaulted roof everywhere? If you think rightly, that would be nothing but wasted oil and effort. I say such a thing does not help but hinders: it dazzles the sight of the eyes, dulls and confuses them. So take up, as I said, the burning lamp left at the entrance, so that you may see where to set your foot; and, directing your step by its light, now enter the sanctuary of the book without fear.

units.la: Sicut enim generosos & itineribus aptos ac assuetos equos, tantisper quidem fræno ducimus, calcar etiam interdum addimus, donec viam illam, quam conficere decrevimus, insistant; quam simul atque instiiterunt, illi alacres & sponte properant, nec deflectunt, sed institutum iter, si non aliud jussi fuerint, perpetuò & rectâ prosequuntur: sic etiam prudens & cordatus Lector satis habet bet per primas aliquot Librorum paginas Annotationibus dirigi, Commentario sensum & mentem Authorum edoceri; cætera, quid sibi velint, inter legendum suo marte conjicit & assequitur.
units.tr: For just as we guide well-bred horses, suited and accustomed to journeys, with the bridle for a while and sometimes add the spur, until they set out on the road we have decided to travel; and as soon as they have set out, they go eagerly and of their own accord, and do not turn aside, but keep to the chosen path straight on without ceasing, unless they are ordered otherwise: so the prudent and sensible reader thinks it enough to be directed by notes through the first few pages of the book, and to be taught the meaning and intention of the authors by a commentary; the rest, what they wish to say, he grasps and works out by his own effort as he reads.

units.la: Tandem ad calcem, Orationem subjeci, quam dixi Lugduni Batavorum à duobus plus annis, cum in illa Academia publicas in Logicam Lectiones auspicarer. units.tr: Finally, at the end I have appended the oration which I delivered at Leiden more than two years ago, when I began my public lectures on logic in that academy. If, having read this oration through, you weigh its argument carefully in your mind, you will recognise that this last oration is a supplement to that first one. For the Gerro who, according to the judgment attributed to him in that first tragedy, slipped away secretly (as you can see in this book on p. 156), is here taken up and beaten; but he is beaten in a different figure and under a different mask. For his Gerros are not viewed as Gerros now, but as sewers (and what else are they?), fouling the philosophical Hippocrene. In that same passage four of these sewers are uncovered: the Prologue,

units.tr: QUESTIONS

units.la: ORATIO Quam dixit in auspicio Quæstionum Quodlibeticarum.
units.tr: ORATION Which he delivered at the opening of the Quodlibetical Questions.

units.la: Textus I.
units.tr: Text I.

units.la: Continet Actionem in Seductores Genios, Pantomimum præsertim, Mangonem & Dogmatistam: Qui omnes ad Philosophiæ tribunal citantur: Fraudis, seductionis & stellionatus rei aguntur
units.tr: Contains an action against the Seducing Genii, especially the Pantomimus, the Mango and the Dogmatist. All of them are cited before the tribunal of Philosophy, and are tried as defendants for fraud, seduction and swindling.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Genii isti sunt persuasiones quædam, quæ increbuerunt, vel potius instinctus & proclivitates persuadendi sibi aliquid præter dictamen Rationis.
units.tr: These Genii are certain persuasions that have taken hold, or rather impulses and propensities to persuade ourselves of something beyond the dictate of Reason.

units.la: A Pan-
units.tr: The Pan-

units.la: Pantomimus est instinctus quidam atque proclivitas, Metaphoram cum Proprietate confundendi, seu ita capiendi, quod metaphorice dicitur, ac si id etiam in proprietate sermonis obtineret: Unde Pantomimi praecipua pars est proclivitas cogitandi, res omnes sensu nobis ac vita similes esse, & in actionibus motuque suo, sud se cognitione dirigere: plurima enim a nobis ad res inanimas, per Metaphoram & similitudinem translata sunt: Hinc Pantomimus, ab ista tantum parte agitatur in Oratione nostra.
units.tr: The Pantomimus is a certain impulse and propensity to confuse metaphor with proper meaning, or to take in its proper sense what is said metaphorically, as if it also held good in the literal use of speech. Hence the chief part of the Pantomimus is the propensity to think that all things are like us in feeling and life, and direct their actions and motions by their own knowledge; for very many things have been transferred from us to inanimate things through metaphor and likeness. Hence the Pantomimus is driven by this part alone in our discourse.

units.la: Mango est instinctus ornandi, ordinandi, concinnè disponendi. Cum illum ornatum ac ordinem rebus adscribimus, quem Ratione ducti deprehendimus, bene habet: res enim omnes, procul dubio, concinnè elegan- terque dispositæ sunt ab Auctore suo; Cum ex libidine tantum & instinctu ornandi, ornandi, ornatum illum rebus attri-buimus, qui imaginationem nostram capit ac demulcet, hoc vero Mangoni debemus.
units.tr: The Mango is the impulse to adorn, arrange and dispose neatly. When we ascribe to things that ornament and order which we perceive when led by Reason, it is well; for without doubt all things have been neatly and elegantly disposed by their Author. But when from mere lust and the impulse to adorn we attribute to things that ornament which captures and soothes our imagination, we owe this to the Mango.

units.la: Dogmatistes denique est instinctus & proclivitas, generatim statuendi, Regularum & Axiomatum formu-las tradendi, Artium & Scientiarum Systemata condendi. Et in Dogma-tista considera, quomodo in Mangone: Licet profecto generatim concludere, licet Axiomata, Regulas & Syste-mata ponere; sed ductu & auspiciis u-nicæ Rationis: Ex impetu tantùm, in-stinctu spirituque ponendi, ea ponere, hoc vero & Rationi inimicum est, & fœdi in eo hærent ac perniciosi er-rores.
units.tr: Finally, the Dogmatist is the impulse and propensity to lay down generally, to deliver formulas of rules and axioms, to construct systems of arts and sciences. And consider the Dogmatist in the same way as the Mango: it is certainly permissible to conclude generally, to lay down axioms, rules and systems, but under the guidance and auspices of Reason alone. To posit these things merely from impulse, from the urge and spirit of positing, is hostile to Reason, and foul and pernicious errors cling to it.

units.la: Sic igitur affecti sunt isti Genii: eodem aliquando ducunt, quo Ratio; nunquam eadem: Atqui non modo, qui non ivit, quò eundum erat; sed & qui ivit, quà eundum non erat, aberravit. Mango ducit ad ornatum; ad Regulas Dogmatista: eodem sæpe Ratio tendit; sed alia vid: hæc per lucem; per calignem illi.
units.tr: So these Genii are affected: sometimes they lead to the same place as Reason, but never by the same way. For not only does one who has not gone where he ought to go err, but also one who has gone where he ought not to go has strayed. The Mango leads to ornament, the Dogmatist to rules. Reason often tends to the same end, but by another road: this one by light, those by darkness.

units.la: Textus II.
units.tr: Text II.

units.la: QUam tetris errorum fumis involuta, Mentis Humanæ fax est! Quam spissis difficultatum fustibus subjicitur: Obruta, suffocata (quid multa?) exstincta: Restat tantum tremula, quæ fungum elychnii perrerrat scintilla.
units.tr: How the torch of the human mind is wrapped in the black smoke of errors! How it is pressed down under the thick clubs of difficulties: overwhelmed, suffocated, (why say more?) extinguished. Only a trembling spark remains, wandering over the fungus of the wick.

units.la: Paraphrasis.
units.tr: Paraphrase.

units.la: RAtio ratio, illa supremi Ducis indubitata tessera, tot adulteratur erroribus, tot in Veritatis investigatione difficultatibus infringitur, vix ut ipsa sibi constare, & Ratio, iam ratio non amplius esse videatur.
units.tr: Reason, that undoubted token of the supreme Leader, is so corrupted by so many errors and broken by so many difficulties in the search for truth that it scarcely seems able to remain consistent with itself, and reason no longer seems to be reason at all.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: RAtio (quod Textus innuit) lucerna nostra: qua, cum destituimur, obscura sunt omnia: caligo cæca, spissæ tenebræ, nox horribilis: quilibet etiam è vulgo, conscientiæ suæ testimonio convictus, id agnoscit, & verbis palam præfert. Ratio etiam (quod Paraphrasis innuit) tessera divinitatis, qua nutum summi ducis (Dei) & imperium persentiscimus. Sed, proh dolor! Ratio in nobis magnam partem corrupta est, tum per Errores (qui Rationis, si lucerna est, fumi atri, & involvunt eam; si tessera, adulteria, deflorant & inducunt eam) tum per Difficultates (quæ Rationis, si ea igniculus est, dura cruda robora, & obruunt illam; si tessera, obviæ spinæ, discerpunt & infringunt gunt illam). Errores illi, Difficultates illæ sic affligunt Rationem, ut illa velut intercluso spiritu exstincta dici possit, & jam non nisi creperam aliquam scintillam, ellychnio lucernæ depastam ostentare.
units.tr: Reason (as the text hints) is our lamp: when we are deprived of it, all things are obscure, a blind murk, thick shadows, a dreadful night. Anyone at all from the common people, convinced by the testimony of his own conscience, recognises this and openly declares it in words. Reason too (as the paraphrase hints) is the token of divinity, by which we perceive the nod and command of the supreme Leader, God. But, alas! Reason in us is for the most part corrupted, both by errors (which, if reason is a lamp, are black smokes that wrap it round, and if it is a token, are adulterers that deflower and debase it) and by difficulties (which, if reason is a little fire, are hard, raw logs that overwhelm it, and if it is a token, are thorns in the way that tear and break it). Those errors and those difficulties so afflict reason that it may be said to be extinguished, as if its breath were cut off, and now shows only some faint spark, fed on the wick of the lamp.

units.la: Textus III.
units.tr: Text III.

units.la: LUdibrium quoddam su-mus, quamdiu hic fumus, scopus quidam sumus, in quem collineant innumerabiles impostura: Hæremus, cespitamus, inter salebras & vepres, inter confragosa caligamus sine duce.
units.tr: We are a sort of laughing-stock while this smoke lasts; we are a target at which countless deceptions aim. We stumble and fall among the ruts and brambles, and we grope about in the rough places without a guide.

units.la: Paraphrasis:
units.tr: Paraphrase:

units.la: NNon mirum igitur, si inducta & obliterata tesserâ, socios & exploratores non internoscimus, mus, si confundimur, si ludibrium debemus hosti.
units.tr: It is no wonder, then, that once the token is covered over and blotted out, we do not recognise our allies and scouts, and that we are confused and become a laughing-stock to the enemy.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: SIc affectâ Ratione, si lucerna ea, necessum est, nos in via, qua gradimur ad Veritatem, miserum in modum offendere, impingere ac labi; si verò tessera sit Ratio, in expeditione, qua contendimus ad Palladium extrema arce Naturæ diripiendum, turbari nos oportet, & inter summa pericula versari, signa hostium, ac Imperatoris nostri non rectè dispicientes: adeoque salutares sæpe cogitationes, ut infestas refutare; pestiferas, ut auxiliares copias amplecti.
units.tr: When Reason is in such a state, if it is the lamp, we must necessarily stumble wretchedly on the way by which we advance towards Truth, strike against things and slip; but if Reason is the token, then in the campaign by which we press on to plunder the Palladium in the outermost citadel of Nature, we must be thrown into confusion and live amid the greatest dangers, not rightly discerning the signals of the enemy or of our Commander. Hence we often reject wholesome thoughts as hostile, and embrace pestilent ones as auxiliary troops.

units.la: Textus IV.
units.tr: Textus IV.

units.la: Hoc deteriore conditione, quod nihilominus, & avidi ad pergendum & cre-
units.tr: Under this worse condition, that we are at once both eager to press on and too credulous,

units.la: A creduli, unius vicem ducis, varios amplectamur sedustores.
units.tr: we embrace, as if they were a single leader, a variety of deceivers.

units.la: Paraphrasis.
units.tr: Paraphrasis.

units.la: Sed & hisce malis (o pudor!) nos ipsi caussam damus, tum impotentiâ, tum credulitate nostrâ: Impotentiâ quidem, quia reductâ, & se in suam caliginem abdente Ratione, quod receptui signum nobis esse debebat, excurrimus tamen avidi, nescio quam fortuitam Veritatis prædam, animo agitantes: Credulitate vero, quia cuilibet ductum directionemque pollicenti acquiescimus: Unde fit, ut loco unius Ducis, cui in verba juravimus, multis & variis nos temere committamus seductoribus.
units.tr: But we ourselves (O shame!) give cause for these evils too, both by our powerlessness and by our credulity. By powerlessness, because Reason, withdrawn and hiding itself in its own darkness, which ought to have been for us the signal to retreat, nevertheless we rush on eagerly, turning over in our minds some chance prey of Truth, I know not what. By credulity, because we submit to whoever promises guidance and direction. Hence it comes about that, instead of the one Leader to whom we swore allegiance, we rashly entrust ourselves to many and various seducers.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Aviditas & credulitas duo mala importunissima & exitialia iis, qui quando satis a consilio firmi non sunt, inter insidiantes etiam versantur: Nascuntur hi morbi ex confidetia, quam homines in fortuna collocatam habent: vident enim hanc aliquando præter spem aspirare rebus afflictis, & quibus, nec consilium, nec res suppetebat, iis tamen ex sententia nonnunquam eventum procedere; Sed esto, id in fortunæ bonis (quæ hinc etiam fortunæ vocantur) obtineat: hæc enim, seu casu, seu ratione parta sint, idem valent: imo nescio quo pacto, plus valent, magisque quod sunt, esse videntur, cum ea temere, & aliud agenti casus injecit. At in animi bonis, inter quæ primas tenet Veritas, nihil juris habet fortuna: non enim reperit Veritatem, qui imprudens eam reperit, qui rit, qui sortis uncum in illam impegit: Ambas, ambas se manus praestat sola Ratio: haec sola Veritatem attingere, capere, tenere potest: quia Veritas, nisi sui agnitione non tangitur; & vero agnoscit illam sola Ratio. Planius rem ob oculos ponam: Sit idiota quispiam: & hic forte incidat in Librum Elementorum Euclidis: Amplam sane Veritatem nactus est (singula enim Effata, singulae Veritates sunt) Sed non capit illas (id ipsus ingenue fatetur) tunc demum capiet, cum ratio ex demonstrationibus accesserit. Idem ille idiota videat ferrum ad Magnetem accedere: videat aurum cum aere libratum in aere, praeponderare in aqua: videat, quae magis obvia sunt, noctium & dierum, hyemis & aestatis vicissitudines, incrementa ac decrementa luminis in Luna, aquarum in mari fluxus ac refluxus: Haec omnia, cum videat, nihil horum capit: quia rationem, ob quam ita sint, ignorat, id est manu, qua capiat ista, destituitur. Quo igitur isti mihi in scientiis avidi, creduli, prurientes? Avem illam, Veritatem, aucupantur: & manibus, quibus eam præhendant, truncati, somniis illam captant, & possident in aëre: Nota nobis paræmia, o Belgæ, Avem in cælo habere, nihil habere est.
units.tr: Greed and credulity are two most troublesome and deadly evils for those who, when they are not firm enough in judgment, still move among snares. These diseases arise from the confidence that people place in fortune. They see that fortune sometimes favours people in distress, and that things sometimes turn out as they wished for those who had neither plan nor resources. But grant that this holds for the goods of fortune (which are therefore also called fortune's goods): whether they are acquired by chance or by reason, they have the same worth. Indeed, somehow they seem to have more worth, and to be more what they are, when chance throws them at us carelessly, while we are busy with something else. But over the goods of the mind, of which Truth holds first place, fortune has no right. For a person does not find Truth if he finds it without thought, if he strikes it by chance, as one who throws a hook at random into a lot. Reason alone offers both hands: reason alone can touch, grasp and hold Truth, because Truth is not touched except by being recognised, and reason alone recognises it. I will set the matter before your eyes more plainly. Suppose some unlearned man happens to come upon the Elements of Euclid. He has come upon a wealth of Truth (for each proposition is a truth), but he does not grasp them (he frankly admits this himself). He will grasp them only when reason comes in through demonstrations. Let the same unlearned man see iron drawn to a magnet; see gold weighed against bronze in air, and then outweigh it in water; see the more obvious things, the alternations of night and day, of winter and summer, the waxing and waning of the moon's light, the ebb and flow of the sea's waters. Though he sees all these things, he grasps none of them, because he does not know the reason why they are so; that is, he lacks the hand with which he could grasp them. Why, then, do these men, greedy, credulous and itching for knowledge, chase me? They hunt after that bird, Truth, and, with hands too maimed to hold it, they catch at it with daydreams and possess it in the air. We know the Dutch proverb: to have a bird in the sky is to have nothing.

units.la: Textus V.
units.tr: Text V.

units.la: Sensus nostros non sugillo: Circumscriptores illi quidem; sed, & singuli stolidi, & universi malè fœderati: mutua consilia non rarò, mutuos astus eludunt: Patent, tenentur: Jam pridem iis dica scripta, & palam fraudis mendaciisque convictis, fides abrogata.
units.tr: I do not disparage our senses. Those deceivers are indeed cheats, but each of them is also foolish, and all together they are badly allied. They often thwart one another's plans and one another's tricks. They are exposed and caught. Long ago their writings were condemned, and once they were convicted of fraud and lying in public, their credit was withdrawn.

units.la: Paraphrasis.
units.tr: Paraphrase.

units.la: Cum seducto̅res dico, Sensus nostros, Auditum, Aspectum, Tactum, Gustatū, Odoratum, & si qui alii sint, non moror. Sunt verò etiam illi seductores; at non ita callidi, non ex astutiorum illorum & versipellium genere, quos insectari mox & agitare decrevi: Quilibet enim Sensus, cum alii suppetias non veniunt, stolidior est, quam ut capiat eos, qui teretem mentem habent intelligensque judicium: Ecce enim Aspectus hominem procerum, si modo is turrim conscendat, in pumilionem subito decrescere testatur, quasi jam gentilis sit eorum, qui cum gruibus pugnant,
units.tr: When I speak of seducers, I do not dwell on our senses: hearing, sight, touch, taste, smell, and any others there may be. Yet these too are deceivers, but not so clever, not of the kind of those crafty and shifty tricksters whom I have resolved to hunt down and harass shortly. For each sense, when the others do not come to its aid, is too dull to catch those who have a clear mind and sound judgment. Consider: sight testifies that a tall man, if he climbs a tower, suddenly shrinks into a dwarf, as though he were already a kinsman of those who fight with cranes,

units.la: Ubi tota cohors pede non est altior uno:
units.tr: Where the whole troop is not a foot taller than one.

units.la: Quis credat Aspectui tam impudenter denter mentienti. Auditus nuper balatrones in specubus & puteis delitescere dejerabat, qui loquentibus obstreperent, & extrema dictionum importuni regererent: Credant hoc Philosophi illi, quos Manducus vesperi ad cunas abigit invitos. Et denique Tactus (mirum, quantum hic sibi sumpserit præ fratribus suis) nunquid urinatoribus sæpius jam suasit, & persuasit forte, nullum maris, etiam classibus constrati pondus esse? Hæc & id genus alia mendacia innumera, aperta, splendida satis arguunt, quemlibet de quinque illis fratribus, si suas tantum tendiculas objecerit, frustra fore, nec decepturum eorum quemquam, qui mediocriter sapiunt. Quod si tamen conspirare possent Sensus, & facta manu nos adoriri, nullus dubito, quin facilè circumvenire quem-
units.tr: Who would believe Sight, which lies so shamelessly? Hearing lately swore that buffoons hide in caves and wells, shouting down those who speak and annoyingly repeating the last words of what is said. Let those philosophers believe this whom Manducus drives off to the cradle against their will in the evening. And finally Touch (remarkable how much he has claimed for himself before his brothers): has he not often persuaded people, and perhaps convinced them, that the sea has no weight, even for fleets of decked ships? These and countless other lies of this kind, plain and clear enough, show that whichever of those five brothers sets out only his own snares will fail and will not deceive any of those who have moderate wisdom. But if the Senses could conspire and attack us with united hand, I have no doubt that they could easily surround and entangle any one of us.

units.la: Catchword: quemquemvis nostrûm & illaqueare possent: Sed ipsi odiis inveteratis inter se dissident: unde fit, ut sæ-penumero, quas hic nobis insidias struxerat, has ille, vel evertat, vel prodat: Videndi sensus remum, qui pars in aëre consistit, pars sub aqua conditur, fractum esse cla-mat; Tactus id ipsum constanter negat: Tactus e contrario, situlam ex fune demissam in cisternam, ubi aquam subiit, a fune solvi testatur; id autem Oculorum acies explo-dit: Aspectus item & Auditus, emi-nus forte hominem ligna finden-tem nacti, quemadmodum non ambiguntinter se? quemadmodum non altercantur? Auditus jam fe-rire censet, jam securim illidi; As-pectus insiciatur, & securim jam in aërem attolli, ac alterum ictum minari confirmat: Et ita passim isti
units.tr: ...any one of us and ensnare him. But they are divided among themselves by long-standing hatreds, so that often the trap that one has set for us is undone or betrayed by another. Sight cries out that the oar of vision, part of which stands in the air and part is hidden under water, is broken; Touch steadily denies this very thing. Touch, on the other hand, testifies that a bucket lowered into a cistern on a rope is loosed from the rope when it goes under the water; but the keenness of Sight explodes this. Likewise, when Sight and Hearing have caught sight of a man chopping wood from a distance, do they not disagree among themselves? Do they not quarrel? Hearing thinks he has already struck, that the axe has now come down; Sight denies it and insists that the axe is already lifted into the air and threatens a second blow. And so everywhere these

units.la: Terrigenæ (facinus miserabile!) fratres.
units.tr: Earth-born brothers (a wretched crime!)

units.la: In se constrictas conseruere manus.
units.tr: They have joined their hands, locked against one another.

units.la: Hoc amplius, quod Sensus in Philosophorum ubique pulpitis, ceu tribunalibus quibusdam, sceleris jam pridem accersiti perfidiæque condemnati, cassâ sint apud Sapientes omnes existimatione. Jam Cartesius Rationis ille vindex & Sensuum acris insectator pessumdedit & abolevit, quidquid illis ex unanimi, quod subinde depromunt, constantique testimonio, reliquum erat apud incautos quosdam Philosophos auctoritatis: nec minus suspectum & sublestum esse decrevit, quod stabiles concordesque, quam quod vagi dissonique profiterentur.
units.tr: Moreover, the senses have long since been summoned, like criminals, before the tribunals that the philosophers set up everywhere from their pulpits, and condemned as treacherous; among all the wise they have lost all credit. Now Descartes, that champion of reason and fierce persecutor of the senses, has ruined and abolished whatever authority remained to them among some unwary philosophers, namely the unanimous and constant testimony they regularly give. He also decreed that what is stable and in agreement is no less suspect and unreliable than what wanders and disagrees.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Tres igitur occurrunt caussæ, quæ Sensuum fallaciam enervant, & vim seducendi, quâ pollerent alioqui, vehementer obtundunt: Et eædem tres caussæ adferuntur in Oratione, cur hîc, ubi stelliones tantum & coryphæi seductorum accusantur, Sensus in numerum aliquem venire non mereantur: Prima caussa est, quod Sensus singuli in valde multis negotiis, fatui sint, stupidi, stolidi: Altera caussa, quod et si juncti aliquid possent, ægrè tamen jungantur & conspirent, quin potius mutuas fraudes sæpe prodere ac detegere soleant. Tertia caussa, quod Sensus sint infames, & jam per omnium Philosophorum Scholas tamquam seductores traducantur.
units.tr: There are therefore three causes that weaken the deceptiveness of the senses and greatly blunt the power to seduce which they otherwise possess; and these same three causes are advanced in the Oration as to why here, where only the charlatans and ringleaders of seducers are accused, the senses do not deserve to be counted at all. The first cause is that the senses, taken singly, are foolish, dull and stupid in very many matters. The second is that, even if joined together they could accomplish something, they are hard to join and to agree, and rather often tend to betray and expose each other's mutual frauds. The third cause is that the senses are infamous, and are now held up in every school of the philosophers as seducers.

units.la: Textus VI.
units.tr: Text VI.

units.la: Sunt seductores alii, versi-pelles quidam Genii, ad fallaciam & technas nati: Hi non in cute substitêre, quo-modo Sensus; sed percolati, & medullam subeuntes, ad Animum penetrarunt: His utitur Animus, his ut charissi-mis convictoribus, totum se credidit:his non ducitur jam; sed agitur, trahitur,raptatur: hos necessarios ei, hos ei dominos fecit longafamiliaritas.
units.tr: There are other seducers, certain shape-shifting spirits, born for deceit and trickery. These have not settled on the skin, as the senses do; they have seeped through and entered the marrow, and penetrated to the mind. The mind uses them, and has entrusted itself wholly to them as its dearest companions; it is no longer led by them but driven, dragged and hurried along by them. Long familiarity has made them necessary to it, and has made them its masters.

units.la: Paraphrasis.
units.tr: Paraphrase.

units.la: Sunt igitur præter Sensus, seductores alii, iique spiritus, instinctus, Genii, majoris longè, quam Sensus nostri fallaciæ: Cumque que Sensus, ut hostes abarceri, atque ad ambitum corporis propelli videamus, tum hos aditu dignatur Animus: Dicas eum consuetudine sibi hos Genios & familiaritate velle devincire; Sed qui familiares fuerant, paulo post necessarii, & ex necessariis non duces, quos se ferebant, sed agasones facti, flagris Animum, ceu inertem pecudem, huc illuc agunt impelluntque pro sua libidine.
units.tr: Besides the senses, then, there are other seducers, namely those spirits, impulses and genii, whose deceptiveness is far greater than that of our senses. And since we see that the senses are kept off like enemies and driven back to the perimeter of the body, the mind admits these others to its approach. You would say that it wishes to bind these genii to itself by custom and familiarity; but those who were once familiars soon became necessary companions, and from being necessary they have become not the guides they claimed to be but drivers of oxen, who with whips drive and push the mind, like a sluggish beast, hither and thither at their own pleasure.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentarius.

units.la: Genii isti Pantomimus, Mango, Dogmatistes, plane videntur esse de illorum genere, quos Affectus, & vulgo Passiones vocamus: Quibus unicum pabulum, quo & nutriuntur & crescunt, obsequium est: Cupiditatibus suis morem gerere, earum impulsu facere quidpiam aut omittere, non est eas sedare, sed irritare: flammae sunt, næ sunt, & oleo isto affuso; crescunt quidem, sed non satiantur. Et certè solus ad decipiendum Cupiditas, quam Sensus valet: imo nihil hic ad præstiorias valet sine cantu istius Sirenis: Quidvis enim Sensus exhibeat, non decipiemur, nisi stimulet nos & inducat proclivitas quædam & velut libido credendi; Atqui hæc non aliò referri, quam ad Cupiditatem potest. Proclivitas hæc impotentia quædam est, luxuries & animi profusio, qua quod nostrum est, jactamus, & in alios temerè prodigimus: Dnquam, Sensuum nostrorum perceptiones, quæ nobis propriæ sunt, in causas a quibus excitantur, transferimus: Et, cum v.g. paries iste sic affectus, talem in nobis sensum causet, quo, cum fruimur, album colorem nos videre dicimus, ipsum illi parieti seusum ascribentes, id eum in se habere judicamus, quod in nobis, ut haberemus, effecit: Sic etiam in sole lumen, in igne calorem, in corporibus collisis, aut prope ab illis, sonum esse judicamus; cum extra nos illorum modo causae, intra nos illa ipsa sint: Similiter ergo facimus ac si loca maritima, quod famem avant, fame infecta, & gladium, quo sauciet, imbutum dolore, & postem in quem oculo forte per tenebras errabundi incurrimus, scintillare putaremus. Sensus, hac fascinatione sublata, integri sunt, incorrupti, nunquam fallunt aut falluntur. Cavendum igitur, ne quas nobis sensus exhibet imagines, earum rerum esse putemus, quarum formandis occasionem praebuerunt, neu, quid extra nos illis imaginibus simile cominiscamur: hoc enim nulla suadet ratio; si vero hoc sine arte sumpserimus, etiamsi forte verum esset, erravimus tamen: quid quod contrarium non suadeat modo, sed & convincat Ratio? Sed non omnia huc promenda sunt.
units.tr: Those spirits, Pantomimus, Mango and Dogmatistes, plainly seem to belong to the kind we call the affects, or in common speech the passions. Their only food, by which they are both nourished and grow, is compliance: to humour one's desires, to do or leave undone something at their urging, does not calm them but provokes them. They are flames, and when this oil is poured on they grow but are never satisfied. Desire alone has the power to deceive, and the senses have none without it. Indeed, nothing here works as an illusion without the song of that Siren. For whatever the senses present, we will not be deceived unless some inclination and, as it were, a desire to believe stirs us and leads us on. This inclination can refer to nothing but Desire. It is a kind of intemperance, a luxury and prodigality of mind, by which we boast of what is ours and rashly squander it on others. Moreover, we transfer the perceptions of our senses, which belong to us, to the causes by which they are excited. For example, when a wall so disposed produces in us the sensation by which, while we look at it, we say we see a white colour, we ascribe that sensation to the wall itself and judge that it has in itself what it produced in us. So too we judge that light is in the sun, heat in the fire, and sound in bodies struck together or near them, when outside us those are only causes and the things themselves are within us. We do the same as if we thought that seaside places, which crave hunger, were infected with famine, that a sword which wounds were steeped in pain, or that a doorpost, against which we happen to strike in the dark while wandering with eyes shut, were sparkling. Once this fascination is removed, the senses are sound and uncorrupted; they never deceive or are deceived. We must therefore take care not to think that the images the senses present to us are of the things whose forms they occasioned, nor to invent anything outside us resembling those images. No reason suggests this. And if we accept it without skill, even if by chance it were true, we would still have erred. What is more, Reason not only does not suggest the contrary but actually proves it. But not everything should be brought forward here.

units.la: Textus VII.
units.tr: Textus VII.

units.la: Tandem tamen aliquando manifestis indiciis deprehensi: ad igniculum Raonis, afflictum illum quiem, eluctantem tamen exinervallo, & irradiantem clarius, detecta perfidia, ad jUlices etiam delata nomina; Acerrimos habent propugnatores. Boni duces videntur ranis quibusdam & prurientibus ingeniis, quod interlum sine offensa seducant longius: suspenso gradu dum obsecuti, præstolantur Eventum; at eventus ille, non nisi scrobs aut obex: interea nicant ancipiti spe, & ipsâ peripericuli trepidatione gestiunt. Quosdam longa majorum duces hos sequentium caterva, patronos fecit: Superstitiosum hoc genus, cui ne manifestus quidem Antiquitatis Error sine sacrario est: Novitatum Osores audiunt. His accedit Philosophorum vulgus, vecors illud cæcæ consuetudinis mancipium: Hi communia, quotidiana, pervagata, quæ passim apud populum increbuêre, cujusmodicumque illa sint, ferunt; Ea, quorum insolentes sunt, exibilant, explodunt, sarcasmis exagitant & dicteriis proscindunt.
units.tr: Yet at last, caught by clear evidence, in the small light of Reason, that sick mind, struggling though at intervals and shining more brightly, has had its treachery exposed and its names carried even before the judges. They have most fervent defenders. Good leaders seem to some frogs and itching wits, because they sometimes lead them further astray without offence. Stepping cautiously, they follow and wait for the outcome; but that outcome is nothing but a ditch or a barrier. Meanwhile they strive with doubtful hope, and rejoice in the very trembling of their danger. A long line of followers has made some leaders of the ancients into patrons: this superstitious kind, for whom even a plain error of antiquity has its sanctuary, is called haters of novelties. To these is added the crowd of philosophers, that senseless slave of blind custom. They accept whatever is common, daily, and widely spread, which has taken hold among the people, whatever its kind; what is unfamiliar to them they hiss at, explode, harass with sarcasm and tear apart with taunts.

units.la: Paraphrasis.
units.tr: Paraphrasis.

units.la: Verum enim vero appetente jam crepusculo Rationis, pu-lere cæpit Animum ignominiosæ servitutis suæ: Atque adeo hos Ge-nios, hos sub ducum exuviis tene-briones, judicum, id est Philoso-phorum sententiis exauctorare constituit. Sed illi habent sui stu-diosissimos patronos, qui rebus eo-rum (sic præ se ferunt) aderunt ut difficillimis. Horum alii vano, superstitioso alii, alii denique cani-no ingenio sunt. Vani quidem illi, quos periculum, quos anceps even-tus juvat, etiamnum post tot erro-res & lapsiones experiri volentes, quorsum Evadent (si tamen eva-dent) cæci cæcos duces insecuti. Superstitiosi vero, quibus a majo-rum vestigiis vel latum unguem declinare, religio est: quibus hæc una bene firma videtur ad sta-tuendum ratio, statutum esle jam dudum, etiam sine ratione.Hi ve-lut heri sunt, hos catelli comitan-tur: qui,quod dici solet,non min-gunt nisi ad illum, quem alii ante perminxerint, parietem:His assen-tiunt, quibus asluevêre, his velut caudâ blandiuntur; insolitum o-mne vago discursu latratuque per-turbant, rictibus tandem etiam & morsibus infestant.
units.tr: But truly, as the twilight of Reason now begins to approach, the mind has begun to shake off the shameful servitude that was its own. And so it has resolved to deprive these Genii, these shadowy beings that hide under the cloaks of leaders, of their office, that is, by the judgements of the philosophers. But these have their most zealous patrons, who, as they put it, take up their cause as the most difficult. Some of these are vain, some superstitious, and some, finally, of a dog-like temper. The vain ones, whom danger and an uncertain outcome delight, want to try it even now after so many errors and falls: whither they will come out (if they come out at all), blind men who have followed blind leaders. The superstitious, however, for whom it is a religious scruple to deviate even a finger's breadth from the footsteps of their ancestors, think this one reason sufficiently firm to settle the matter: that a thing was decided long ago, even without reason. These are like old dogs, and the puppies follow them. They do not piss except against the wall that others have pissed on before: they agree with those to whom they are accustomed, fawn on them as if with a tail, and with wandering runs and barking they disturb everything unfamiliar, and at last attack it with snapping and biting.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentarius.

units.la: CErtè tribus his hominum generi-bus, præcipui continentur erro-rum tutores & patroni: Et pri-mum quidem, qui recensiti, auctores sunt,hi concipiunt & gignunt Erro-res: Qui deinde notati, alumni sunt, nutriunt Errores, & tempestivè, quidquid eis nociturum videtur, ab-arcent:Nam qui aliquâ forte de Na-tura tura rerum cogitatione, velut navi, qua per mare Philosophicum feratur, oblata, cursum dirigit non ad Cyno- suram Rationis, sed ad Erraticam Eventus, longiusque provehitur, & gratulatur sibi, quamdiu obvia con- sentiunt, & institutum errorem, nec remorantur, nec produnt; donec quasi tempestate aliquâ, ad inopinatam & votis non respondentem Experien- tiam, tamquam ad saxum adhære- scat, is profectò in hac Erronum clas- se, familiam ducit, & prætoriam quasi navim gubernat; Cæteri lint- ribus ac phaselis passim insecuti, dum numero inter se ac turbâ confidunt, consuescunt cum erroribus, solitos eos ac familiares reddunt, & (si opinio- nes præjudicatæ præstare periculum possent) etiam tutos: cum, aut non er- rare penitus, aut non imperitè vi- deantur errare qui tam frequentes er- rant.Breve dicam, Sors parit errores, Mos nutrit : Rationem enim, ceu lucernam aliquam, mentibus nostris accendit Deus; Sortem nobis cæcam esse voluit & meram noctem: Cum igitur non ratiocinari jam, quod nati sumus; sed, quod Sortis est, conjicere, divinare, suspicari lubet, etiam cum sic in Veritatem incidimus, tamen aberravimus: Errores, quos sic alii peperêre, fovent alii, cum eorum primo, qui præeunt, ac dein mutuâ contemplatione, easdem conjecturas & opiniones amplectuntur : Hoc jam moris est; illud sortis erat.
units.tr: Certainly, the chief guardians and patrons of error are contained in these three classes of men. First, those who have been listed as authors: they conceive and beget errors. Then those who have been noted as foster-children: they nourish errors and in good time keep away whatever seems likely to harm them. For whoever, by some thought about the nature of things that has come to him, as into a ship sailing across the philosophical sea, directs his course not by the compass of Reason but by the wandering of Chance, and goes on further, and congratulates himself as long as things he meets agree with him, and neither delays nor betrays the error he has adopted, until, as if by some storm, he runs aground on experience, which is unexpected and does not answer to his wishes, as on a rock: he, certainly, in this class of errors, leads a family and steers what is, as it were, the flagship. The others, following him about in boats and skiffs on all sides, while they trust one another in number and crowd, grow used to errors, make them familiar and customary, and, if preconceived opinions could guarantee safety, even safe. For either not to err at all, or not to err in an unskilled way, seems to belong to those who err so often. In short, chance produces errors, custom nourishes them. For God kindled reason in our minds like a lamp, but he willed that chance should be blind to us and pure night. So when we do not reason, which is what we were born for, but prefer to guess, divine and surmise, which belongs to chance, then even if we fall upon the truth in this way, we have still gone astray. The errors that others have thus begotten, others cherish, first those who go before, and then, through mutual regard, embrace the same conjectures and opinions. This is now a custom; that was a matter of chance.

units.la: Textus. VIII.
units.tr: Text. VIII.

units.la: HIs freti patronis impostores, quem fraude sibi arrogarant, etiamnum staude gerunt & administrant ducatum, & porro seducunt impudenter: Præeunt passim in PhiPhilosophicis viretis, credulum illud & sequax ovile: Et sicut Sensus olim, adipati cliens Epicuri, ridiculam suos asseclas devolvit in foveam, dum meridiano Sole, orientem occidentemque Solem, majorem fateri cogit, quia majorem oculi testarentur: Ita & hi pudendis æquè quos ducunt, imo turpioribus circumveniunt modis, nisi frontem illaqueatis perfricuisset publicus ille ganeo & corruptor, Mos.
units.tr: Relying on these patrons, the impostors who have seized leadership by fraud still hold and exercise their command, and they continue to mislead shamelessly. Everywhere in the philosophical pastures they lead that gullible and servile flock. Just as Sensus once, the client of the fat Epicurus, plunged his ridiculous followers into a pit, forcing them to admit that the rising and setting sun is larger than the midday sun because their eyes testified that it was, so these men also entangle those they lead in shameful ways, or rather in even baser ones. Only that public pimp and corrupter, Custom, has hardened their brows enough to let them do so.

units.la: Paraphrasis.
units.tr: Paraphrase.

units.la: Horum in Cimmeria Republica tam potentium patronorum clientes, cum se sentiant Genii nostri, Ducatu, quem malis artibus sibi sumserant, abire nondum decreverunt: Quin potius in Academiis, ubi magno passim apparatu, magnâ pompâ, iter instruitur ad Veritatem, Doctores se ambitiosè Ductoresque profitentur; Sed ampla quædam polliciti, deludunt credulos: &, cum sponte suâ cupidam juventutem, tum speciosis promissis vehementer illectam, abducunt in Laqueos & in avia. De Sensu quidem accepimus: olim eum Epicuro patrono, ridiculos in casses impulisse, quem pascebat gregem: Dicebant Epicurei, nunquam Sensum fallere; sæpe Rationem delirare: proinde, si quid certi vellemus amplecti, abeundum a Ratione, & standum esse cum Seusu: Interrogati, num igitur Sol in ortu major esset, minor in meridie (id enim Videndi Sensus perhibebat) non dubitabant affirmare: Instabant qui rogaverant: Atqui, inquiebant, Sol, cum aliis oritur, tum aliis meridiem facit; simul igitur, & tanto major, & tanto minor Sol est: Hîc irretitos se senserunt Epicurei: cumque non esset, quod aptè responderi posse videretur, irridebantur. Sic Sensus suum gregem; Sed Genii nostri turpius longe, longe scelestius fallunt credulos & incautos suos sectatores, absque velut abrupto repente filo, in Philosophico Labyrintho destituunt, a confusionum Minotauro devorandos: Et hæc eorum non obscura prævaricatio, explorata satis cum helluone collusio; nisi Mores nos, quibus ceu fœdere quodam obstricti nefando monstro tenemur, fascinarent: Moribus effectum, ut errare non pudeat, ut irriti laboris non
units.tr: In the Cimmerian Republic, the clients of such powerful patrons, though they perceive that our Genius's rule, which they seized by wicked arts, is failing, have not yet resolved to give it up. Rather, in the academies, where a great show of preparation and a grand display is everywhere arranged for the journey toward Truth, they openly profess themselves teachers and eager guides. But by promising grand things they deceive the credulous, and having drawn in a youth that was already eager of its own accord and was strongly enticed by splendid promises, they lead it into snares and pathless places. We have heard of Sensus: once, with Epicurus as his patron, he drove his ridiculous followers into nets, though he was the shepherd of their flock. The Epicureans used to say that the senses never deceive, while reason often goes astray; therefore, if we wished to embrace anything certain, we had to abandon reason and stand with the senses. When they were asked whether the sun was therefore larger at rising and smaller at midday (for this was what the sense of sight reported), they did not hesitate to affirm it. Those who had asked pressed on: "But," they said, "the sun, as it rises for some, makes midday for others; so at the same time the sun is both so much larger and so much smaller." Here the Epicureans felt themselves caught, and since there was no answer that seemed apt to give, they were mocked. Thus Sensus led his flock. But our Genii deceive their credulous and incautious followers far more basely and far more wickedly. Without warning, as if the thread had suddenly been cut, they abandon them in the philosophical labyrinth to be devoured by the Minotaur of confusion. This is not an obscure betrayal of theirs, a collusion with the glutton that is clear enough. Yet we are bewitched by Customs, to which we are bound as by a certain covenant with that unspeakable monster. By custom it has come about that we are not ashamed to err, not sorry for fruitless labour, and that we now seem to owe what has been wrung from us by wrong so often. For just as the Athenians, under a covenant with the man-eating tyrant, were forced to hand over their children to be devoured, so most people by custom give up their good hours to trifles and nonsense.

units.la: [The continuation of this sentence follows on the next page.] non pæniteat, ut jam debere videamur, quod sæpius per injuriam extortum est: Sicut enim Atheniensès Antropophago Tyranno ex fœdere suos liberos commessandos objiciebant: sic ex more plerique nugis & ineptiis bonas horas.
units.tr: [The continuation of this sentence follows on the next page.] not to repent, so that we now seem to owe what has so often been extorted by wrong; for just as the Athenians used to hand over their children to be devoured by the man-eating tyrant in accordance with a treaty, so by custom most people squander their good hours on trifles and nonsense.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Constat eum, qui utique (si fieri possiet) Ratione repudiatâ, totus cum Sensu facere decrevisset, concinnius erraturum nec perinde multa turbaturum, ut hos, qui Geniis illis Pantomimo, Mangoni, Dogmatistæ dirigendos se dederunt: Cum enim Epicurei, aut quicumque illi (non mor or enim si in numero Fabularum reponatur ista narratio) de industria Sensum audirent, obstreperent Rationi, poterant in ea, quam induxi, disputatione, adversariis suis scitè respondere: Rationi quidem ineptum ac absurabsurdum accidere, si dicas idem simul & majus & minus esse; non vero Sensui: qui memorare poterat, idem cominus ac eminus visum objectum, majorem etiam ac minorem sui speciem in animo signare; Se vero de Ratione, cui res suas habere jusserant, non laborare; æqui bonique consulendum, si Sensui probarentur, quæ censerent: Sic illi cum ratione aliquâ, universè contra Rationem (si constare sibi hoc dissidium posset) ire satis lepidè viderentur; Sed qui Geniis se manciparunt, & imperitius errant, & errorum nulla gratia; turpis squallor & inficeta barbaries: Quod cum exemplis, tum rationibus, Oratio, in quam commentamur, comprobatum dabit.
units.tr: It is agreed that a man who had resolved, rejecting Reason where that is possible, to go wholly with Sense, would err more neatly and would not throw things into such confusion as those who have given themselves over to be directed by those Genii: Pantomimus, Mangon, and the Dogmatist. For when the Epicureans, or whoever they were (for I do not linger over whether this story is counted among the fables), deliberately listened to Sense and shouted down Reason, they could, in the disputation I have introduced, answer their opponents cleverly. They could say that it is absurd and ridiculous for Reason to hold that the same thing is at once both larger and smaller, but not so for Sense, which could recall that the same object seen near and far leaves in the mind a sign of its appearance as both larger and smaller. As for Reason, to which they had told it to look after its own affairs, they need not trouble themselves about it; it should be accepted calmly and kindly if the senses approve what they judge. Thus they would seem to act quite gracefully, with some reason, and altogether against Reason, if this disagreement could be reconciled with itself. But those who have surrendered themselves to the Genii err both more clumsily and without any excuse for their errors: a foul squalor and a dull barbarism. The Oration on which we are commenting will show this to be so, by examples as well as by arguments.

units.la: Textus IX.
units.tr: Textus IX.

units.la: Seductores hos hodiernâ die reos ago: Amor-sapientiæ (partes hæ tuæ sunt) sedeto pro tribunali: Adsisti-te, quibus a præjudicatis opinionibus vacuum pectus, & justam judicum facite decuriam: Vobis judicibus pedum iis extorquebo de manibus: intensum ad viam indicem, cæteris digitis æquabo, & flectam in pugnū: insidiosam dexteram, usque & usque aventem inseri axillæ, religabo post tergum: Ducis illa insignia, Ducis hæc munia: soli debentur Rationi: soli vindicabo Rationi.
units.tr: Today I bring these seducers to trial. Love of Wisdom, the role of presiding judge is yours: take your seat on the tribunal. Come forward, you whose breasts are free of prejudiced opinions, and make up a just bench of judges. To you as judges I will wrench the staves from their hands. I will level the index finger, stretched out toward the way, with the other fingers and bend them into a fist. I will bind behind their backs the treacherous right hand, always reaching to thrust itself into the armpit. Those are the insignia of a leader, and these are his duties. They are owed to Reason alone, and I will claim them for Reason alone.

units.la: Paraphrasis.
units.tr: Paraphrasis.

units.la: Ausus, o Amor Sapientiæ, ad te tuosq; candidos collegas, Veritatis intaminatos sacerdotes, in jus adire: ausus ego perfidos illos, & se patronis suis necquidquam efferentes veteratores, capitis anquirere: Te ipso adductus pulcerrimo judice, fretus optimâ caussâ, eorumque, quos in consilium adhibes, summâ sanctimoniâ.
units.tr: I dare, O Love of Wisdom, to summon before you and your fellow judges, the bright colleagues, the unstained priests of Truth. I dare to seek the death penalty against those treacherous charlatans who puff themselves up in vain under their patrons. You yourself are the most beautiful judge who leads me on, and I trust in the best of causes and in the utmost holiness of those whom you take as your counsel.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentarius.

units.la: (1.) Pedum (id est baculus pastoralis) insigne pastoris est, qui dux quidam suarum ovium: (2.) Indicem (id est digitum pollici proximum) ad viam intendere, & insigne ducis est, & etiam munus: (3.) Dexteram manum axillæ inserere, & ita sustentare gressum ejus, quem dirigas, ducis item officium est: Cum igitur, & munia hæc (3. & 2.) & insignia illa (2. & 1.) Genii nostri involaverint subdolè, usurpent injustè, cum summis eorum, quos ducunt, opprobriis, periculis, damnis, deturbandi sunt competentium & legitimorum judicum sententiis & auctoritate ab injusta istorum insignium & officiorum possessione. Quam in rem, ego quidem mihi partes Accusatoris depošco; Amor Sapientiæ (sic enim decet) judicis officio fungetur: Assessores erunt, quotquot verè doctos, & verè candidos, nullisque velut opinionum muneribus corruptos, totos, totos, purus ille puræ Veritatis Amor incessit: Et hos quidem Assessores, Textus innuit; Paraphrasis autem (forte quod tales aliquos in humano cœtu, repertum iri dissideret) Cælum adiit, & inde divo judici (Amori-Sapientiæ) divos collegas adscivit: Nitorem, Ordinem, CanCandorem, denique Fas & Æquum, Veritatis (quam solam spectant, cui se jugiter consecrant, & sua omnia semper immolant) devotissimos antistites. Ego igitur hac mea in Seductores Genios Actione (quid enim talibus judicibus, & tali causâ non sperem?) illis ipsis Geniis Pantomimo, Mangoni & Dogmatistæ (1.) baculum pastoralem extorquebo de manibus: (2.) digitum vero secundum à pollice, quem ad viam jugiter intendunt ac porrigunt, cæteris digitis, qui in volam inclinantur (hoc enim gestu viam demonstrare solemus) æquabo, id est etiam inclinabo, ut tota manus jam sit in pugnum contorta, adeoque ad dirigendum inepta: nam clausâ manu commonstrare non solemus:(3.) Tandem dexteram manum, qua tamquam fortiori, eorum quos ducunt, axillas suffulciunt, inde retractam, revinciam Geniis nostris post
units.tr: (1.) The staff (that is, the pastoral crook) is the mark of a minister, who is a kind of leader of his sheep. (2.) To aim the index finger (that is, the finger next to the thumb) at the way is both a mark and a duty of a leader. (3.) To place the right hand under the armpit and so support the step of the one you are guiding is likewise the office of a leader. Since, then, our Genii have stealthily seized these duties (3 and 2) and these insignia (2 and 1) and unjustly usurp them, they must be thrown out of their unlawful possession of these insignia and offices, with the greatest disgrace, dangers and losses for those whom they lead, by the sentence and authority of the proper and lawful judges. For this purpose I, for my part, demand the role of prosecutor. The Love of Wisdom (for so it is fitting) will perform the office of judge. The assessors will be all those who are truly learned and truly upright, not corrupted by any gifts of opinions, and that pure Love of pure Truth will enter wholly, wholly into them. The Text hints at these assessors, but the Paraphrase, perhaps because it doubted that such men could be found in the human assembly, has gone up to heaven and from there has enlisted divine colleagues for the divine judge (the Love of Wisdom): Brightness, Order, Candour, and in short Right and Equity, the most devoted ministers of Truth (whom alone they regard, to whom they are constantly consecrated, and for whom they always sacrifice all things). So in this my action against the seducing Genii (for what should I not hope from such judges and in such a cause?), I will wrench the pastoral staff from the hands of the Genii themselves, the Pantomime, the Mangonist and the Dogmatist. (1.) (2.) I will level the second finger from the thumb, which they constantly aim and stretch out toward the way, with the other fingers, which are bent into the palm (for this is the gesture we usually use to show the way). That is, I will also bend it, so that the whole hand is now twisted into a fist and so unfit for pointing; for we do not usually show the way with a closed hand. (3.) Finally, the right hand, with which they prop up the armpits of those they lead, as though it were the stronger, I will draw back and bind behind the backs of our Genii.

units.la: (1.) Pantomimo, Mangoni & Dogmatistæ: the words are printed as in the main text; the note reference is not visible on this scan. post tergum: Tum verò, & insignia illa, & munia, Genii erepta, transcribam Rationi, cui debentur soli. Pedum illa gerat, & nos sola pascat, quae satiare nos sola potest ( inanem tantum speciem propinant Genii, quae deludit oculos; mentem non explet ) sola monstret viam, quae sola videt (Genii omnes caeci sunt) sola gressum nobis firmet, quae sola sana, sola viget & constat sibi (vix artubus haerent Genii, languidi, flaccidi, laceri)
units.tr: (1.) Pantomime, Mangonist and Dogmatist: the words are printed as in the main text; the note reference is not visible on this scan. behind the back: Then indeed, and those insignia, and duties snatched from the Genii, I will hand over to Reason, to whom alone they are owed. Let Reason bear the staff, and let it alone feed us, which alone can satisfy us (the Genii offer only an empty show, which deceives the eyes; it does not fill the mind). Let it alone show the way, which alone sees (all the Genii are blind). Let it alone steady our step, which alone is sound, alone is vigorous and consistent with itself (the Genii scarcely cling to their limbs, being weak, flabby, torn).

units.la: Textus X.
units.tr: Textus X.

units.la: Sic adversariis, antequam jure cum iis experimur, in sultamus: sic causse confidimus & judici. Habeant sibi sane ad iniqua Vanitatis, Superstitionis, Inscitiæ tribunalia, gratiosos patronos; At SupreSupremo hoc Judice, non sperent, nisi ferale Theta.
units.tr: Thus we assault our adversaries before we proceed against them by law, and thus we trust in our cause and in the judge. Let them, by all means, keep their favoured patrons at the unjust tribunals of Vanity, Superstition and Ignorance. But before this Supreme Judge they should expect nothing except the deadly Theta [Θ].

units.la: Paraphrasis.
units.tr: Paraphrasis.

units.la: Sint in foro Vanitatis, nugatoribus illis, quales merentur patroni: ubi Sors cæca cognoscit caussas, vitilitigant & altercantur inter se discordes Experientiarum rabulę, avida sibi litem addicit exspectatio, anceps eventus comperendinat, & tandem casu vel tempore detectus error pronunciat sententiam. Habeant in Superstitionis tribunali, qui suâ caussâ plurimum velint: ubi ex tripode jus dicit Auctoritas: ubi quod majoribus placuit, imo non placuit subinde, sed aliud agentibus excidit, decretum, lex & oraculum est: ubi laborant sub verborum involucris perplexa mysteria: ubi de mente unius aliquando Scriptoris, diffusæ fusæ rixantur Notæ, cavillantur Interpretationes & Commentaria. Gratiâ etiam valeant in Consuetudinis regno præpostero: ubi non fit, quod faciendum est; sed faciendum esse, quod passim fit, summa lex est: ubi Mos canino rictu disceptat controversias, tumultuantur Opiniones communiter receptæ: in novum quodcumque latrant & calumniantur Adagia popelli, Poëtarum versiculi, Sensa vulgi: & contra Rationem, longi temporis præscriptionem objicit, gregatim ipsa se, pecudum ritu secuta Multitudo. Ast in hac Curia, in hoc templo sanctitatis, amplitudinis, mentis: ubi tu præsides & leges exerces, o salutaris Amor-Sapientiæ: ubi latus tuum cingunt religiosissimi pontifices, in hoc judicio, collegæ & socii tui, Nitor, Ordo, do, Candor, Recti tenor, & Æ-quitatis splendor: ubi Rationi advocatum veniunt cana Fides, genuina Simplicitas, & pacata Modestia: circumstant alacres Attentiones, Studia in Veritatem & alta Silentia: Foris excubant vigiles Industriæ, Constantia, Sedulitas, & latè vulgi curas ac celebritatẽ abarcens Solitudo, & improbus cum nocturnis Lucubrationibus Labor. Sed ecce tibi! Hoc tam austero satellitio perterritos, procul aufugisse sentio delicatos & imbeles Geniorum nostrorum patronos, & ne quidem ad vestibulum hujus arcis, clientes suos comitari sustinuisse: Quid si in hæc adyta bubones, in hanc tantam lucem & decus involassent? Prorsus nihil abfuisset, quin adverso fulgore perstricti, consternati, attoniti corruissent, egissent animam. Igitur præpræsidio destituti Seductores, vano quidem illo & fatuo, tum apud hosce judices invidioso, detestabili, caduco, viderint ipsi, qua se ratione contra Rationem defendent. Hoc tantum superest. Arma petant a Ratione, quibus ipsam jugulent contra rationem: quæ si impetrare se posse diffidant (quid enim Rationem in furias agat? quid ipsam Mentem dementet?) præsentiant jam nunc, quę Fabulam hanc maneat catastrophe.
units.tr: Let them be in the forum of Vanity, with those trifling fellows, such as the patrons they deserve. There a blind Chance hears the causes. The quarrelsome lawyers of Experience wrangle and bicker among themselves. Eager expectation awards them the dispute, the uncertain outcome is postponed, and at last an error, detected by chance or by time, pronounces the sentence. Let those who most wish to have their cause heard keep to the tribunal of Superstition, where Authority delivers judgment from the tripod, where what pleased the elders, or rather did not please them at times but slipped out while they were doing something else, is decreed, becomes law and oracle, where obscure mysteries labour under the wrappings of words, where the marks and interpretations and commentaries, scattered in all directions, quarrel over the mind of some single writer. Let them also flourish with favour in the perverse kingdom of Custom, where what ought to be done is not done, but what is commonly done is held to be the supreme law. Here the Custom of the dog's snarl settles disputes, and commonly received opinions riot. Proverbs of the common people, verses of the poets, the notions of the crowd bark and slander against anything new. Against Reason, the long prescription of time is brought forward by the Multitude, which, in the manner of cattle, follows itself in herds. But in this court, in this temple of holiness, greatness and mind, where you preside and exercise your rule, O salutary Love of Wisdom, where your side is surrounded by your most devout pontiffs, your colleagues and companions in this judgment: Brightness, Order, Candour, the steadiness of what is right, and the splendour of Equity. Where grey-haired Faith, genuine Simplicity and calm Modesty come to plead for Reason. Eager Attentions stand around, with Studies directed at Truth and deep Silences. Outside keep watch the vigilant Diligence, Constancy and Assiduity, and Solitude, which keeps far away from the cares and crowds of the common people, and toil that is hard with nightly Lucubrations. But look! I perceive that these delicate and feeble patrons of our Genii, terrified by this so austere guard, have fled far away, and have not been willing even to accompany their clients to the threshold of this citadel. What if the owls had flown into these sanctuaries, into this so great light and splendour? Nothing would have been lacking for them to fall, struck down by the opposing brilliance, dismayed and stunned, and to breathe their last. So the seducers, deprived of their protection, shall see for themselves, before these judges, how they will defend themselves against Reason, by that empty and foolish defence, hateful, detestable and fallen. Only this remains: let them seek arms from Reason with which to slaughter Reason itself, against reason. If they despair of being able to obtain these (for what would Reason do to drive itself mad? what would it drive Mind itself out of its wits?), let them now foresee what catastrophe awaits this drama.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Perversi & stolidi homines illi, qui Rationem rejicere, aut ei anteferre aliquid (velut Experientiam, Auctoritatem, Enthusiasmum: aut in usu vitæ, commoda, voluptates, honores) quoquo modo videri volunt: Interrogati enim, cur ita censeant, conantur illico suæ sententiæ rationē alialiquam comminisci: Atque adeo, quod palam profiteri, quod verbis ast-ruere videbantur, re ipsâ, ipso suo fa-ƈto demoliuntur & evertunt: Quomodo enim Ratione potior & antiquior Auctoritas, Experientia, aut aliud hujus generis quodcumque, si cur ita sit, dicenda est ratio? Certè quod ratione aliquâ suaderi probariq; debet, totum id sub Ratione est. Primum igitur, ô homo, Ratio est; aut si quid eâ prius est, sine ratione prius est: nam si rationem dederis, ob quam prius sit, jam necessum est, non illud, sed rationem illam priorem esse fateâre: In eo autem, quod sine ratione est, jubet Ratio, rationem non quærere: igitur, ne hîc quidem manu mittit te Ratio: ɛtiam, cum extra fines ejus ditionemque concesseris, tu tamen in imperio ejus & potestate permanes: Tibi igitur, ô homo, primum est Ratio.
units.tr: Those perverse and foolish men who wish to reject Reason, or to set something above it in any way (such as Experience, Authority, Enthusiasm, or, in the conduct of life, convenience, pleasures, honours), when they are asked why they think so, at once try to devise some reason for their opinion. And so, what they seemed to profess openly and to assert in words, they in fact undo and overturn by their own deed. For how can Authority, Experience, or anything else of this kind be prior to and greater than Reason, if one must still give a reason why it is so? Surely whatever must be persuaded and proved by some reason is wholly under Reason. First, then, O man, there is Reason; or if anything is prior to it, it is prior without reason. For if you give a reason why it is prior, then you must necessarily admit that it is not that thing but that reason which is prior. But in regard to what is without reason, Reason commands that one not seek a reason; so not even here does Reason release you: even when you have withdrawn beyond its borders and its territory, you still remain in its dominion and power. To you, then, O man, Reason comes first.

units.la: Textus XI.
units.tr: Textus XI.

units.la: {a}Prodi huc primum pantomime, Allegoriæ, Similitudinum & Fabularum Genie: judicibus te sistę: Quid? In gremio Charitum educatus, inter Parnassi flosculos lascivire solitus, amœnis Rhetorum spatiis inambulare, ludere natus eras speciosę puer: Quæ te vesana compulit ambitio, munia Ducis, quibus fungendis, par non es, affectare? Viam pręire vis ad Veritatem: Sed quid ad teneros istos pedes, inaccessa Naturæ tesqua, spinosa Philosophiæ nostræ dumeta?
units.tr: Come forward here first, you pantomime, you genius of allegories, similes and fables. Stand before the judges. What is this? Raised in the lap of the Graces, accustomed to frolic among the little flowers of Parnassus, born to play in the pleasant grounds of the rhetoricians, you were a handsome boy. What mad ambition has driven you to aim at the duties of a leader, for which you are not equal? You want to go before us on the way to Truth. But what have those tender feet to do with the untrodden wastes of Nature, the thorny thickets of our Philosophy?

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentarius.

units.la: Pantomimus ejusdem fermè naturæ est cum Cupidine, carnis impudico illo Genio: Pueri quidem ambo; cæterum simplicitatis & innocentiæ nihil: personati ambo, & sub puerili habitu circumferunt astutissimos veteratores: Molles sunt, sed virorem omnem roburque consopiunt: Humiles iidem & pusilli, sed quidquid in animo surgit & elatum est, dejiciunt, inter nugas & crepundia sua contorquent: Pueri tamen merito censentur, quia blandicias tantum & voluptatem curant; qua trahi, pasci, demulceri, puerile est: quomodo videmus pueros, saccharis ac bellariis (quæ viris nauseam movent) supra modum inescari: Hinc etiam Philosophi, Intemperantiam, cum deliniri animus & voluptatum illecebris pellici se sinit, puerile vitium esse censuerunt.
units.tr: The pantomime is much the same sort of character as Cupid, that shameless genius of the flesh. Both are boys, but there is nothing of simplicity or innocence in either. Both are masked, and under a boyish appearance they carry about the most cunning old schemers. They are soft, but they lull to sleep all vigour and strength. They are humble and puny, but whatever rises up and is lofty in the mind they cast down, and they wear it out with their trifles and rattles. Yet they are rightly judged to be boys, because they care only for coaxing and pleasure; to be drawn, fed and soothed by these is childish, just as we see boys greatly enticed by sweets and cakes, which turn men's stomachs. Hence the philosophers too have judged intemperance a childish vice, when the mind allows itself to be softened and lured by the enticements of pleasures.

units.la: Pantomimus igitur cum voluptate facit, Heliconis Genius, & Poëtarum deliciæ: Omnis enim Poëtarum à Metaphoris & Allegoriis leposi hæc, (quod in Logica notabam) ubi latius, quam par est, excurrunt, & animi gratiâ, diffusius luxuriant, in Fabulas faceßunt: Et certè, quæ passim Fabulæ à Poëtis descriptæ circumferuntur, non aliud sunt, quam Alegoriæ sic amplificatæ: Quo etiam nomine à Poëtis eorumque fautoribus, aut excusantur, aut commendantur: quod nempe sub cupediis & aurato cortice, salutarem aliquam medicinam continent, quam adolescentium animis, non nisi lascivire & catillare volentium, furtim instillent: adeoque non sentientes sanent, & , quod verè divinum est, per impostu-ram conferant beneficium. Ego Pantomimum ita sobrium, ita frugi, non arguo; sed ambitiosum eum petumetulantemque compesco, interponen- em serebus non suis, turbantem, fi- ‹ta cum seriis & vera cum falsis pro- miscua ducentem, excutio, insector, exagito.
units.tr: Pantomime, then, works with pleasure, the genius of Helicon and the darling of the poets. For nearly all the metaphors and allegories of the poets, which (as I noted in logic) run on further than is fitting, and luxuriate more widely for the sake of delight, turn into fables. And indeed, the fables described by the poets and passed about everywhere are nothing other than allegories so enlarged. For this reason the poets and their supporters either excuse or commend them, because they contain, under sweetmeats and a gilded rind, some wholesome medicine, which they slip into the minds of young people who want only to frolic and nibble; and so they heal without the youths noticing, and, what is truly divine, they bestow a benefit through deception. I do not accuse a pantomime so sober and so thrifty; but that ambitious and petulant fellow, puffed up, I rebuke.
