He meddles in matters not his own, he mixes fictions with serious things and truths with falsehoods, and I shake him off, pursue him and harass him.

units.la: Textus XII.
units.tr: Text XII.

units.la: Genius hic, judices, cum ad omnem Metamor- phosim inclinat propendetque, tum inanima in animata transformandi longè cupidissimus est: Ipse lapides, ipse silvas, montes, urbes, fluvios, ventos, & quaevis tandem adscisicit in humanam societatem & jubet homines nobiscum esse: queri ea sæpe, sæpe lætari facit, modò dolore percita, modo spe elata, modo metu perculsa, tum amore, tum miseratione, o dio aliisque impulsa cupidi tatibus inducit.
units.tr: This genius, judges, when it inclines and leans toward every metamorphosis, is also most eagerly inclined to change inanimate things into animate ones. It itself takes stones, forests, mountains, cities, rivers, winds, and whatever else there is into human society and bids them be with us. It often makes them complain, often makes them rejoice, now stirred by grief, now lifted up by hope, now struck by fear, and now driven by love, now by pity, now by hatred and other desires, it brings them on.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: VIs mira nobis, homines, indole mira: Ita complexu & conjunctione gaudemus, tam sumus sociales, ut ea etiam in societatem nostram vocare videamur, quae fera, quae bruta, quae sensus omnis expertia, nulla teneri societate possunt: Potentiorum viribus oppressi, muta, surda testantur, caelos, mare, sidera: Absentium desiderio languentes, annulum, vestes, arrham, in lacrymas soluti osculantur: Ira perciti, injurias suas persequuntur in calices, in sedes, in vitra fenestrarum: Quo spectant etiam phrases, quas frequentamus & loquendi formulae: nam veteres aedes ruinam minari, prata verna ridere, laetas Ætas segetes, sævum mare, bibulam arenam, pedem montis, & sexcenta quotidie similia, inter confabulandum effundimus: quæ clarè arguunt, nos personam nostram rebus inanimis, in scena vehementiorū affectuum ac familiarium sermonum sæpe admodum imponere. Hoc amplius: Simias, bubones, ranas, deformes & turpes animantes esse, passim asseveramus: quid ita? cur potius hac infamiæ notâ inuruntur, quam equi, oves, galli? Nimirum propter majorem nobiscum in figura similitudinem, tum etiam (quod præsertim in similis valet) propter similes quasdam gesticulationes, facilius quam animantes aliæ in humanum genus adoptantur, intra quod imaginationis ope consistentes deficiunt, & conspicuo formæ ab hominibus, cum quibus componebantur, recessu, fiunt monstrosæ: quo utique probro non laborarent, si in familia sua perpermanere, & id modò quod sunt apparere potuissent. Iam totum illud Metamarphoseon opus, illud Phæbi corculum non alio spiritu salit: crebræ illæ hominum in feras & aves, in arbores, fontes, & saxa, commutationes, undique spirant Pantomimum: & Ovidius, qui ipsissimus ille Genius sub humanis exuviis videri potest, tam hîc festivè lusit, tam non cecinit, sed pinxit ad vivum, ut in ipso conversionis puncto, quo vestigium veteris & rudimentum novæ formæ commiscentur, in lupis, equis, bobus, arboribus, ipsos homines, quos in ea transformari narrat, non animo tantum, sed oculis videre videare.
units.tr: Wondrous is our nature, we men, and wondrous our disposition. We so delight in embracing and joining together, and we are so sociable, that we seem to call into our society even things that are wild, brutish, and without any sensation, which cannot be bound by any society. Those crushed by the might of the powerful bear witness, dumb and deaf: the heavens, the sea, the stars. Those wasting away with longing for the absent kiss a ring, a garment, a pledge pressed into tears. Those stirred by anger pursue their wrongs against cups, seats, and window glass. To this also point the phrases we use and our turns of speech: for we commonly say that old buildings threaten collapse, spring meadows laugh, the joyful summer crops, the savage sea, the thirsty sand, the foot of the mountain, and countless similar things every day in our conversation. These clearly show that we often attribute our own persona to inanimate things on the stage of more vehement emotions and familiar talk. Moreover, we constantly assert that monkeys, owls, frogs are deformed and foul creatures. Why so? Why are they branded with this mark of infamy rather than horses, sheep, or cocks? Surely because of their greater resemblance to us in form, and also (which holds especially for the similar ones) because of certain similar gestures, they are more readily adopted into the human race than other animals; and, staying within it by the power of imagination, they fall short, and by departing from the human form in which they were placed, they become monstrous. They would not suffer this disgrace if they could have remained in their own family and appeared only as what they are. Now that whole work of the Metamorphoses, that darling of Phoebus, leaps with no other spirit: those frequent changes of men into beasts and birds, into trees, springs, and rocks, breathe pantomime on every side. And Ovid, who may seem that very Genius under human cast-off skin, played so wittily here, and did not so much sing as paint from life, so that at the very moment of transformation, where the trace of the old form and the beginning of the new mingle, you seem to see with your mind, and not only your mind but your eyes, the men themselves whom he tells of being changed into wolves, horses, oxen, and trees.

units.la: Textus XIII.
units.tr: Text XIII.

units.la: Dum animi gratiâ, dum dicis ergo, inter Poëtas ista suos comminiscitur, remitto, nitto, concedo, æqui boni- que facio;dum pro seriis ven-ditat, malas artes! malas ar-res! vel me tacente, res ipsa clamat: Nec est, quod ambi-gat de crimine: Si inficias i-verit, convincam. Age: Cum olim in Gindo fluvio, equus aliquis, qui Cyro in deliciis erat, submersus periisset, nun-quid flumini necem illam assi-gnasti Pantomime? Nunquid credulo regi persuasisti Gin-dum lacessere, & injuriis ul-tro læsam majestatem provo-care? Adeo enim Cyrus faci-ous tuis exarsit in iras, ut con-tinuo jusserit Gindum in cen-tum sexaginta rivulos, quo nobilis quondam fluvius exa-resceresceret, dissecari: Ha nimis fero corde! Xerxes etiam immanis ille κύκλωπ⁠ς, qui maria pedibus & classibus montes peragravit, eodem Genio in similem actus est furorem: Nam, cum Helle-spontū contabulasset,& Asiæ Europam ponte junxisset;hic vero fluctibus insurgens, sto-lidam illam compagem excussisset, ruinasque ejus inter undas suas volveret, trecentos mari colaphos infringi jussit, ferreas etiam compedes, ne qua liberè vagaretur, sed arctis intra litora sua carceribus detineretur, injecit. Mussitat Pantomimus, nictat oculis, nutat capite, gesticulatur. latur manibus, vacillat pedi- ous, totus in gestum abivit Genius: Videtur aliquid vel- le innuere: Quidlibet; Modo ne nobis imponat vastas illas oceani genas, alapis, quas ei Xerxes incussit, livorem suum debere. Sed leve sit sin- gulos aliquos homines dece- pisse; quod subjiciam, populi delirium est, & ejusdem il- lius Genii impostturis ac in- stinctui ascribendum est uti- que. Psyllorum gens, quæ propter majores Africæ Syr- tes, sedem habuit, crebris ab Austro vento, damnis & cla- dibus accepti: nunc obtriti domorum arborumque stra- ge, nunc arenarum, velut in flufluctus quosdam se efferentium, procellis hausti & demersi (siccum enim mare Syrtes exhibent, quod ventis agitatum, pro fluctibus arenarum cumulos versat) Horum tandem malorum impatientes, ad arma conclamare, turmatim concurrere, in Austrum, quasi in hostem (agilem illum, & ordines intercurrere subtilem) saxis & telis irruere: Sed ita furentes, & (quod hic vere dixeris) aërem verberantes, adverso turbine violentior ventus occupat, & dicto citius, universos cum omnibus copiis armisque, collibus arenarum involvit & sepelit. Silet hic
units.tr: While he invents these things among the poets for the sake of amusement, and as they say, "by way of a joke," you retract, you wink, you concede, and you make it all right and good. While you pass these off as serious matters, what bad arts! What bad arts! Even if I say nothing, the thing itself cries out. There is no doubt about the crime. If he denies it, I will convict him. Come now: when once, in the river Gindes, a horse that was a darling of Cyrus drowned and perished, did you not, Pantomimus, assign that death to the river? Did you not persuade the credulous king to attack the Gindes and, by injuries, provoke a majesty that had been wronged? For Cyrus flared up in such rage at your doings that he immediately ordered the Gindes to be split into one hundred and sixty channels, so that the once noble river would be dried up. Ah, what a savage heart! Xerxes too, that monstrous Cyclops [κύκλωψ], who crossed seas on foot and with fleets and mountains, was driven into a similar fury by the same Genius. For when he had bridged the Hellespont and joined Asia to Europe with a bridge, the waves rose up, shook off that foolish structure, and rolled its ruins among their own billows. He then ordered three hundred lashes to be dealt to the sea and put iron fetters on it, so that it would not wander freely but be held in narrow prisons within its own shores. Pantomimus mutters, blinks, nods his head, gestures with his hands, and sways on his feet. The Genius has gone over entirely into gesture. He seems to hint at something: whatever it is, let him not impose on us the notion that the vast cheeks of the ocean owe their bruises to the slaps Xerxes gave them. But let it be a small matter to have deceived some individual men. What I will add is the madness of a whole people, and this too must certainly be ascribed to the impostures and urgings of that same Genius. The Psylli, who lived near the greater Syrtes of Africa, were often struck by losses and disasters from the south wind: at times crushed by the destruction of houses and trees, at times swallowed up and drowned by storms of sand rising like waves (for the Syrtes present a dry sea which, stirred by the winds, heaps sand into billows). At last, impatient of these evils, they cried to arms, ran together in troops, and rushed with stones and weapons at the South Wind as though at an enemy, one nimble and skilled at darting between their ranks. But raging thus, and (as you may rightly say here) beating the air, a stronger wind from the opposing whirlwind seized them, and quicker than a word it wrapped and buried them all, with all their forces and arms, in hills of sand. Here our Genius falls silent.

units.la: Genius noster; Sed si staret ad plebejum inscitiæ tribunal, jam Catastrophen illam mordicus rapuisset, in suas partes: Senßit, inquit, qui injurias suas persecutus est ventus, qui ultus est rebelles; At coram hoc judice nostro, de nugis istis, ne hiscit quidem: Pudor vetat. Quid? Idem ille Genius, Barbaros dicam? imo Romanos, viros illos: imo Græcos, cultos illos, tamquam pueros, tamquam fatuos induxit, ut Lunæ laboranti (sic enim hi loquuntur) id est noctem nostram offendenti, curationem aliquam adhiberent: Et quidem contra sideris lethargum, præsens hoc remedium præscripsit: inconditos clamores tollerent, tubas clangerent, pelves & tintinnabula colliderent, fragoribus complerent omnia. Aniles intemperiæ, vix Christianos purioribus sacris abstractos demiserunt; hodie Sinas adhuc & Turcas agitant.
units.tr: But if he stood before the tribunal of common ignorance, he would already have snatched that catastrophe eagerly for his own side: "The wind," he would say, "which pursued its injuries, felt it, and took vengeance on rebels." But before this judge of ours he does not so much as open his mouth about these trifles; shame forbids it. And what of that same Genius? Shall I call them barbarians? No, Romans, those men; no, Greeks, those cultivated ones. He led them on like boys, like fools, so that they would apply some remedy to the Moon when she was suffering (for so they speak), that is, when she is struck by our night. And indeed, against the lethargy of the heavenly body, he prescribed this very remedy: let them raise confused shouts, sound trumpets, clash pans and tinkling bells, and fill everything with din. Old women's follies, scarcely dismissed by Christians who had been drawn away from purer rites, and today they still harass the Chinese and the Turks.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Quamvis cum omni vehementiori affectu, seu passione, facile consuescat Pantomimus; præcipuè tamen irâ gaudet: & constat eos, qui vindictæ cupidine distenduntur, ipsi etiam spiritu plerumque turgere: Id etiam historiæ probant, quæ in Textu afferuntur: Tres enim priores, Pantomimum in ira ac furore nidulantem lantem inducunt; sola postrema est, quæ illum benevolentiæ, vel sollicitudini alicui adhærentem exhibeat. Iræ igitur & stomachi familiaris convictor Pantomimus; sed in trivio: Nam in Schola factiones alias sequitur, Desidiam & mollitiem, Rationis austeram semitam formidantes, Pruritum & Veritatis fortuitò consequendæ præposteram aviditatem, Superstitionem, Mores: Interdum etiam, nullâ singulariter caussâ stimulatus, merè pro libidine sua, Scholam infestat.
units.tr: Although the Pantomimus readily grows accustomed to every more vehement affection or passion, he especially delights in anger; and it is established that those who are swollen with desire for vengeance are for the most part themselves puffed up with spirit. The histories cited in the Text also prove this. For the first three bring Pantomimus in, nesting in anger and fury; only the last shows him clinging to some goodwill or concern. Pantomimus is therefore the familiar companion of anger and bile, but at the crossroads. For in the School he follows other factions: he fears Idleness and softness, the austere path of Reason, the itch and the perverse eagerness to reach truth by chance, Superstition, and Manners. Sometimes too, goaded by no particular cause, merely at his own pleasure, he infests the School.

units.la: Textus XIV.
units.tr: Text XIV.

units.la: Dies me deficiat, si porro enarrare pergam præstigias, quibus Genius ille nos ludit & fascinat, in oppro- brium Humanæ Mentis & sannas: Non negat hæc: pa- lam
units.tr: Day would fail me if I went on to relate the tricks by which that Genius deludes and bewitches us, to the disgrace and mockery of the human mind. He does not deny these things; openly

units.la: At enim non decepit Philosophos; sed plebem multo. Iam sunt; Habet tamen quod loquatur: Audiamus: Plebem decepi: Quid ad hoc forum? Philosophos non circumveni: Et cur insulsam istam ac turbulentam multitudinem elusisse, crimini sit? Repagulum ponimus, dum scite imponimus: Frœnum & flagellum sunt illi, quos suggerimus, instinctus: apprehendat hos prudens rector, utatur his: & domet, & agat quo vult, debili Rationi, vanis Legibus obluctantem semper & recalcitrantem feram.
units.tr: But indeed he did not deceive the philosophers; he deceived the common people, and by far. Well, so be it; yet he has something to say. Let us hear it: "I deceived the common people; what has that to do with the forum? I did not get around the philosophers. And why should it be a crime to have fooled that dull and turbulent crowd?" We set up a barrier while we cleverly impose. The bridle and whip are the impulses we suggest to them. Let the prudent driver take hold of these and use them, and tame and drive wherever he wishes that wild beast, always straining and kicking against feeble Reason and vain Laws.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Equidem Actor ipse, quæ domige- rit Pantomimus, in bonam partem accipiebat (Tex. 13.) confabulantem cum Poëtis suis, ludentem cum ludionibus, dummodo sana, seria, ria, non defloraret, non vitiaret, æ-quo animo ferebat. Alteram excusa-tionem Pantomimus pro se moliebatur (Tex. cod. post historiam de Xer-xe) apparebat enim ex gestu, aliquid dicturum; Sed ibidem, quantum conjicere possumus, salso, nec opinato sarcasmo, ab Actore repressus, obmutuit. Hic tandem prorumpit in illas voces, quæ Exceptionem, Adulationem, & Purgationem aliquam continere videantur: Exceptio id agit, ne coram hoc judice (Amore Sapientiæ, seu Philosophiâ) de illis criminibus accusandus videatur Pantomimus, quæ in Philosophos non commiserit. Adulatio tecta, astuta: Palpat Philosophos (præsertim politicos illos, & regnandi avidos: quibus hoc jugiter in ore: Beata Respublica, in qua Philosophi regunt, aut reges Philosophantur.) primum quidem, quod omnes, qui hactenus in Textus decepti leguntur, censeat cum plebe; cum tamen inter eos sint potentissimi reges, Cyrus & Xerxes: in eo Philosophos ipsos secutus, qui promiscuè omnes, cujuscumque in Republica dignitatis aut meriti, si modo Philosophorum Albo ascripti non sint, in ordinem redigere solent, üsque vulgi vel Plebis notam inurere: Iterum adulatur, cum hoc ipso Philosophos occultè rectores rerum moderatoresque profitetur (velut memor ejus, quod de se canunt Philosophi, Sapiens natura rex est) Quibus etiam in domando populo industriam & artes suas offert. Purgatio tandem in eo versatur, quod usu jam satis edocti simus: Rationem imbelle populo continendo vinculum esse: felicius longè regimen stare, si, qui in imperio & potestate sunt, cum decipi omninò velint, instinctibus & cupidini suae relinquantur: Ipsos illos tacitos instinctus, stinctus, qui à Pantomimo & reliquis Geniis proficiscuntur, frænum subministrare, quo sustineri, & flagellum, quo agi possit mala illa bestia, Populus.
units.tr: Indeed, the Actor himself took in good part what the Pantomime did (Tex. 13.) when he chatted with his poets and joked with his jesters, so long as he did not corrupt or spoil what was sound and serious, and he bore it with an even mind. The Pantomime made a second excuse for himself (Tex., same passage, after the story about Xerxes); for it was clear from his gesture that he was about to say something. But there, as far as we can guess, he was checked by the Actor with a witty and unexpected jibe and fell silent. At last he bursts out with those words, which seem to contain an exception, a flattery and a kind of purgation. The exception aims to ensure that before this judge (the Love of Wisdom, or Philosophy) the Pantomime should not appear to be accused of those crimes which he has not committed against the Philosophers. A veiled and crafty flattery: He strokes the Philosophers (especially those political ones, greedy for ruling, with the constant phrase on their lips: Happy the commonwealth in which the Philosophers govern, or the kings philosophize). First, in that he judges all who are read of as deceived in the Textus up to now to be on a par with the common people; yet among them are the most powerful kings, Cyrus and Xerxes. In this he follows the Philosophers themselves, who usually reduce everyone, of whatever dignity or merit in the commonwealth, to the rank of the crowd, and brand them with the mark of the common people, unless they have been enrolled on the Philosophers' Roll. Again he flatters, since by this very thing he secretly declares the Philosophers to be the rulers and governors of affairs (as if mindful of what the Philosophers sing about themselves: the wise man is by nature a king). To them he also offers his zeal and skills in taming the people. Finally, the purgation consists in this: that we have now learned from experience well enough that reason is a weak bond for restraining the people, and that government stands far more happily if those who hold power and authority, since they wish to be deceived altogether, are left to their instincts and their desires. Those very silent instincts, which come from the Pantomime and the other Geniuses, supply the bridle by which that evil beast, the People, can be held in, and the whip by which it can be driven.

units.la: Textus XV.
units.tr: Text XV.

units.la: Nihil de ista Politica dicam, qua callidos illos, qui soli Politicorum nomine censentur hodie, callidè pelexit in suas partes ista vulpes: nihil, inquam, de ista Politica dicam: Aut potius, hoc solum dicam: Probrosam esse Majestatem, quæ Populi se tuetur erroribus: quæ cives suos, pecudes facit: & bubulcum mavult agere, quam Principem. Principem ego mihi serium totum, syn-
units.tr: I shall say nothing of that Politics by which this fox has cunningly enticed into her party those shrewd men who today alone are counted as the politicians. I shall say nothing, I repeat, of that Politics. Or rather, I shall say only this: that a Majesty which protects itself by the errors of the people is shameful, one which makes its citizens into cattle and prefers to be a herdsman rather than a Prince. I picture to myself a Prince wholly serious, sin-

units.la: Imo vero Philosophos potius, quam plebem. syncerum totum suspiciente imaginatione repræsento, & velut humani conventus sanctissimum aliquem gravissimumque præsulem: Fugiant! fugiant! Machiaveli noctuæ ad illustrem hanc & pulcerrimam boni Principis notionem. Nunc Purgationi, Pantomime, respondebo tuæ: Plebem decepisse te dicis; non Philosophos: Imo, inquam, Philosophos decepisti, non plebem: In Scholis montes tuarum fraudum; in triviis verucæ tantum.
units.tr: Nay, rather philosophers rather than the common people, wholly sincere, and I set before my imagination, as it were, some most holy and most dignified president of the human assembly. Let them flee, let them flee, Machiavelli's owls, from this illustrious and most beautiful notion of the good Prince! Now, Pantomime, I shall answer your Apology. You say that you have deceived the common people, not the philosophers. Nay, I say, you have deceived the philosophers, not the common people. In the schools, the mountains of your frauds; in the crossroads, only warts.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Tres partes in oratione Pantomimi observatæ nobis fuerant; Actor duabus tantum respondet, Adulationi lationi & Purgationi; Exceptioni, nihil; Non quod hanc remittat concedat ve (nam judex hic non in Schola tantum, quæ regni ejus metropolis est; sed universe in humana gente caussas cognoscit: cui dies noctesque consulit) verum, quod Actor ipse sponte sua properet ad eam partem, in qua summa hujus judicii totag₃ caussa consistit: ubi cum Pantomino fraudis & injuriarum agendum est, quas in Philosophos, qui judicis nostri curiales & aulici sunt, quotidie machinatur. Omissâ igitur Exceptione, Adulationi, quæ perversissimam aliquam Politicam celat, perfunctorie, sed generose respondet Actor: Quantum hodie a simplici & generoso discessum! Nobis illi libri teruntur (ut recentes pestes omittam) qui Tiberios exhibent, Caligulas, Neriones, & reliqua illa non Principum, sed scelerum nomina: Ex his acroamata legunleguntur, quæ quo magis vafra, tor-ta, ficta, hoc arcana magis & politica videntur: Itaque altum inculcantur juventuti, quæ in spem administrandæ Reipublicæ succrescit: his generosum omne strangulare, futilia tutari sciet: His scilicet artibus, & Tyranni illi pulcerrimum imperium à majoribus acceptum, res florentissimas perdidère: & Christiani Principes jam a tot sæculis Oriente toto cedunt: & quo tandem cedent? Seditiosi, discordiosi assuescunt Barbari Latronis nutum observare, minas expavescere: Vah degeneres! Tandem quod Actor ad ipsam Purgationem respondet, breve est, sed continet summam totius accusationis: nempe Pantomimum decepisse Philosophos, & magis hos turpiusque decepisse, quam plebem; Quod sequentibus in Textu argumentis probandum est.
units.tr: We had noted three parts in the Pantomime's speech. The Actor replies to only two of them, Flattery and Apology, and says nothing to the Exception. This is not because he concedes it or lets it pass (for this judge takes cognizance of causes not only in the School, which is the metropolis of his kingdom, but throughout the whole human race, for whose welfare he cares day and night). Rather, the Actor himself hastens of his own accord to that part in which the whole weight of this judgment and cause rests: where the Pantomime is to be charged with the fraud and injuries he daily plots against the philosophers, who are the courtiers and attendants of our judge. Therefore, passing over the Exception, the Actor answers the Flattery, which conceals some most perverse politics, in a perfunctory yet noble manner: How far today we have departed from simplicity and nobility! Those books are worn in our hands (to omit recent plagues) which set forth Tiberiuses, Caligulas, Neros, and those other names not of princes but of crimes. From these are read the lectures, which the more crafty, twisted and feigned they are, the more secret and political they seem. Thus they are deeply impressed upon the youth who grow up in hope of administering the Republic. By these they will learn to strangle all that is noble and to protect what is frivolous. By these very arts, surely, those tyrants lost that most splendid empire received from their ancestors, and most flourishing affairs were ruined. And Christian princes for so many centuries now yield the whole East; and where will they finally yield? Seditious and quarrelsome men grow accustomed to watch the nod of a barbarian brigand and to dread his threats. Alas, degenerate men! Finally, as to the Apology itself, the Actor's reply is brief, but it contains the sum of the whole accusation: namely, that the Pantomime has deceived the philosophers, and deceived them more shamefully than the common people. This is to be proved by the arguments that follow in the Text.

units.la: Textus XVI.
units.tr: Text XVI.

units.la: Vin' tibi Stoicos produ- cam? qui Iustitiam, Clementiam cæterasque virtutes animalia quædam esse censuerunt: Vin' Pytagoras olim & Platones? Vin' nostrâ memoriâ Klepperos & Campanellas? Quorum alii sideribus & telluri, plantis alii, alii etiam elementis, lapidibus & metallis sensum impertiti: Quin horum aliquis calorem, frigus, lucem, tenebras non sentire modò, verum etiam ratiocinari nobis narrat: nec imperitè ratiocinari, sicut plerique nostrum, sed accuratè: hæc talia Geometriam triam callere, Staticam exer-cere deprehendit.
units.tr: Shall I bring forward for you the Stoics, who held that justice, clemency and the other virtues are certain animals? Shall I bring forward Pythagoras and Plato of old? Shall I bring forward in our own memory Klepperos and Campanella? Some of these have given sense to the stars and the earth, others to plants, others again to the elements, stones and metals. Indeed, one of them tells us that heat, cold, light and darkness not only sense but also reason, and not poorly, as most of us do, but accurately; he finds that such things understand geometry and practise statics.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Mirum est homines intelligentes & doctos, ad hanc Philosophandi rationem injectos fuisse, ut illis, quæ passim inanima vocantur, lapidibus, lignis, igni, aquæ sensum aliquem intelligentiamque tribuerent: Cum enim ipsi, qui credi illa volunt, nunquam fuerint, aut lapides, aut metalla, aut aliud hujus generis quodcumque, utique, num hæc cognitione sensuque censeantur, coguntur ignorare: Adeoque, cum hîc scientiæ locus non sit, reliquum est, ut Hypothesim aliquam afferre se fateantur; At Hypothesis in Disciplinis huc tota refertur, ut declaret & facem præferat rebus obscuris: Quam vero lucem cem speres ab Hypothesi, quæ tota caligo, tota nox est. Constat equidem, nos multos membrorum nostrorum motus, nostrâ cognitione & intelligentiâ moderari; Sed totum id mutuæ, quæ inter corpus & mentem intercedit, actioni referimus acceptum. Quippe corpus in mentem, & vicissim hanc in illud agere, conscientiâ notum est: cum enim corpus in oculi pupilla certo modo vibratur, lumen & colores consequuntur in mente: cum corpus in aure, in linguâ vel palato, in cute, ac alibi concutitur, resultant in mente soni, sapores, odores, calor, frigus, dolor, & id genus affectiones innumeræ: Rursum, cum mens nostra vult, pedes in corpore moventur, & imus, linguâ movetur, & loquimur, manus moventur, & apprehendimus. Igitur animum in corpus agere, & vicissim ab hoc accipere & quasi pati, est in confesso, fesso; Modus vero, quo agit & patitur, abstrusissimus & penitus inef-fabilis est humanae menti: Quid e-nim opus est, vibratis certo modo nervis, obversari animo lucem, colores, sonos, sapores? Quid item opus est, cum animus aliud atque aliud voluerit, alium atque alium motum manare in corpus? quis consequen-tiam illam capit? quis tam lynceus est, qui hic aliquid videat? Cum igi-tur modus rei tam sit obscurus nobis, qui rei ipsius intimam habemus cla-rissimamque conscientiam, quantae nebulae, quanta nos opacabit nox, u-bi res & rei modus (quod in his, quae pridem commemoravimus, usu ve-nit) pariter & ex aequo fuerint ob-scura? Plerique vero, qui dictis re-bus intelligentiam ascribunt, hanc suam assertionem, non quidem per se notam esse volunt, nec etiam ut Hy-pothesim afferunt, sed ut Conclu-sionem, fionem, multis eam indiciis & argumentis comprobantes: Videntur, inquiunt, stellæ suas orbitas, gravia terram, chalybs Magnetem novisse: nam gravia sublime posita, simul ac integrum datur, brevissimâ viâ terram repetunt: stellæ ab orbitis, quas institère, nunquam deflectunt: & chalybs in amplexum Magnetis, renitente corporis sui pondere, quantocyus ascendit. Sed reputent illi secum, hæc talia, quamvis mente prædita forent, atque perspicerent, unde recedendum sibi, & quo tendendum esset, tamen hanc suam scientiam exerere nunquam posse, nullum cognitionis istius exercitium aut usum fore: non est enim iis corpus aptum quo quod mente conceperint, exsequantur; Nos quidem manum, pedes, linguam movemus; sed sunt nobis idonea motus instrumenta, musculi, nervi, denique spiritus qui muscumusculis illapsi, motum musculis, pro mentis arbitrio dispensent; Quibus nihil simile respondet in silice (ut unum illum de inanimis capiam inanimum valde) quo descensum moliatur; Sed etsi forte silex generatim è sublimi discedendum sibi, decrevisset; tamen cum in sublime datus fuerit, unde resciet hanc sortem suam? oculis & alio quocunque sensus instrumento, quo id persentiscat, destituitur. Tandem ponamus nobis ob oculos cribrum, atque id, si lubet, sensu præditum dicamus, ut furfures ac pollinem internoscat: Dic, age, quoniam id jam poni placuit, quid ad secernendos ac separandos a farina furfures conferet illa cognitio, si non corpus cribro multis minutisque foraminibus pertusum detur? hoc vero corpore in cribrum collato, quid jam ei opus est mente vel sensu? manibus nostris, ut solet, variè quassum & agi& agitatum, tenebit recrementa trajiciet farinam, sive interim compos, sive (quod est profecto) mentis sit impos: Atqui item, inquam, quid gravibus, quo deorsum vergant, quid stellis, quo in orbem ferantur, quid ferro, quo Magnetem adeat, mens sensusque proderit, nisi corpus iis aptum (quod ex poris & figura, definiendum est) obtingat, ut vicinorum corporum impulsu, vel deorsum agi, vel in gyrum ferri, vel aliò denique protrudi queant: quod simul ac nacta sunt, jam satis habent: labi, circuire, sequi possunt, etiamsi non cognoscant.
units.tr: It is remarkable that intelligent and learned men were drawn into this way of philosophizing, so as to attribute some sense and understanding to those things commonly called inanimate: stones, wood, fire, water. For since those who want these things to be believed have never been stones, metals or anything of this kind whatever, they are bound to admit that they are ignorant whether such things are endowed with knowledge and sense. And so, since there is no place here for science, it remains that they confess they are offering some hypothesis. But in the disciplines a hypothesis is referred wholly to this end: that it may declare things obscure and carry a torch before them. What light, however, you may hope for from a hypothesis that is all darkness and all night! It is certainly agreed that we govern many motions of our limbs by our knowledge and understanding. But we refer all of that to the reciprocal action that passes between body and mind. Indeed, it is known through consciousness that the body acts upon the mind, and in turn the mind upon the body: when the body is vibrated in a certain way in the pupil of the eye, light and colours follow in the mind; when the body is struck in the ear, on the tongue or palate, on the skin, or elsewhere, sounds, tastes, odours, heat, cold, pain and countless affections of this kind arise in the mind. Again, when our mind wills, the feet are moved in the body and we walk, the tongue is moved and we speak, the hands are moved and we grasp. Therefore that the mind acts upon the body and in turn receives from it, and as it were suffers, is admitted. But the manner in which it acts and suffers is most abstruse and wholly ineffable to the human mind. For what need is there, when the nerves are vibrated in a certain way, for light, colours, sounds and tastes to present themselves to the mind? Likewise, what need is there, when the mind wills one thing and another, for one motion and another to flow into the body? Who grasps that sequence? Who is so lynx-eyed as to see anything here? Since, then, the manner of the thing is so obscure to us, who yet have the most intimate and clearest consciousness of the thing itself, how great the clouds, how great the night that will darken us, where the thing and its manner (as happens in those things we have mentioned before) are equally and alike obscure? Most of those, however, who ascribe understanding to the things mentioned do not want this assertion to be known through itself, nor do they put it forward as a hypothesis, but as a conclusion, supporting it by many signs and arguments. The stars, they say, know their orbits; heavy bodies know the earth; the loadstone knows the magnet: for heavy bodies, placed on high, as soon as they are free, return to the earth by the shortest way; the stars never deviate from the orbits they have entered; and the iron, resisting the weight of its own body, climbs more quickly into the embrace of the magnet. But let them consider this with themselves: even if such things were endowed with mind and perceived whence they must withdraw and whither they must tend, they could never exercise that knowledge; there would be no exercise or use of that cognition, for they do not have a body fit to carry out what they have conceived in mind. We indeed move our hands, feet and tongue; but we have suitable instruments of motion, muscles, nerves, and finally the spirits that, insinuated into the muscles, distribute motion to the muscles at the mind's pleasure. Nothing similar corresponds in flint (to take that one inanimate thing, very inanimate) by which it might effect its descent. But even if perhaps the flint had decided that it must withdraw from on high, yet when it has been placed on high, from where will it learn this its lot? It is deprived of eyes and of any other organ of sense by which it might perceive this. Finally, let us set a sieve before our eyes, and let us say, if you like, that it is endowed with sense, so that it may distinguish bran and fine meal. Come now, since it has pleased us to posit this, what would that knowledge contribute to separating and dividing the bran from the flour, if the body, pierced with many small holes, were not placed in the sieve? But once this body has been brought to the sieve, what need has it now of mind or sense? Shaken and agitated in various ways by our hands, as is customary, it will hold back the refuse and let the flour pass through, whether it be in its right mind or, as is indeed the case, out of its mind. And so, I say, what will mind and sense profit heavy bodies, that they may tend downward; or the stars, that they may be carried in an orbit; or iron, that it may approach the magnet, unless a body suited to these ends (which must be defined by its pores and figure) is at hand, so that by the impulse of neighbouring bodies they may be driven downward, or carried in a circle, or finally thrust elsewhere? Once they have obtained this, they are already satisfied: they can slide, circle and follow, even if they do not know it.

units.la: Textus XVII.
units.tr: Text XVII.

units.la: Sed missos faciamus hos Pantomimi studiosos, hos Volones, qui ultro eum & dedità operà sequuntur: in quo, quo, ut jam sit in eo culpa, qui circumvenit, non minor est in iis, qui circumveniri se sivêre: Ad illos potius orationem convertamus, quos aliud agentes, aliò spectantes & invitos impulit, elusit, induxit. Nos, nos (apertè dico) Peripatetici defecimus, nos, qui Rationis triarii ferebamur, nos, o pudor! transfugæ, nos Mimo illo imperatore meruimus, antequam scivimus.
units.tr: But let us set aside these devotees of the pantomime, these Volones, who follow him of their own accord and on purpose. In that case, although the blame lies with the one who deceives, it is no less with those who allowed themselves to be deceived. Let me rather turn my speech to those whom he drove, enticed and led on while they were doing something else, looking elsewhere and unwilling. We, we (I say it openly) Peripatetics have given way; we, who were carried as the spearmen of Reason; we, shame on us, have deserted, and we earned that pantomime as our commander before we knew it.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.

units.la: Quibus Philosophis (si modò Philosophi illi, & non verius Poëtæ) nativo vultu Pantomimus placuit, imbelles illi debent sibi, quod levi fraude (blanditiis) capti, multis deindeinceps errorum laqueis implicentur: Pantomimus enim suam à se natu-ram expellere non potest: lepidus est, blandus est, ludit: Eorum erat, animum obfirmare & crepundia hæc ex alto despicere. Si quibus vero sic affectis, ut Pantomimum serio traducant, palam execrentur, cum his etiam, qui signa ejus sequuntur, internecinum bellum gerendum sibi putent; Pantomimus tamen ita temperet negotium & refingat, ut iidem illi clam & re ipsa stent a partibus ejus, & toti faciant cum ipso, hæ profecto non artes jam, non fraudes; sed præstigiæ sunt istius Genii: Peripateticos dico, quos volentes, nolentes prevaricatores sibi apposuit præstigiator ille: Negant illi palam & conceptis verbis, elementa, sidera, metalla, lapides cognoscere; re vero & tacitâ quadam ac interiore, quam ipsi met non satis capiunt, animi sui sententiâ, tentiâ, non aliud clamant, id unum profitentur, cunêta cognoscere, & in suis actionibus suâ se cognitione dirigere: Hæc ferè sola Philosophiæ istius elementa, hæc prima lineamenta, quæ ut variis postea coloribus induVcantur, peritis tamen pictoribus non latent: Quod deinceps in Textu vide: quem huc usque Commentario prosecuti sumus: Cui, quando jam domum venit, & res suas agere ingreditur, bene agere & valere.
units.tr: To those philosophers (if indeed they were philosophers and not rather poets), the pantomime pleased by his natural look. Those feeble men owe it to themselves that, caught by a slight deceit (flattery), they are then entangled in many snares of error. For the pantomime cannot drive out his own nature: he is charming, he is flattering, he plays. It was their task to steel their minds and to look down from on high on these baubles. But if some who are so disposed that they openly curse the pantomime, yet hold that they must wage a war to the death against those too who follow his signs, while the pantomime so manages the business and reshapes it that these same men stand, secretly and in fact, on his side and wholly act with him, then these are surely no longer arts or frauds, but the juggling tricks of that Genius. I mean the Peripatetics, whom that trickster has placed as his unwilling or willing prevaricators. They deny openly and in so many words that they know the elements, the stars, the metals, the stones; yet in fact, and by a certain silent and inward judgement of their mind, which they themselves do not fully grasp, they cry out nothing else, and profess only this one thing: that they know all things, and that in their actions they are guided by that knowledge of their own. These are almost the only elements of that philosophy, these its first outlines, which later are to be filled in with various colours, though they are not hidden from skilled painters. Look to what follows in the Text, which we have so far pursued in this Commentary. To him, now that he has come home and begins to attend to his own affairs, may all go well and may he be well.

units.la: Lectori
units.tr: To the Reader

units.la: Lectori meo S. D.
units.tr: To my reader, greetings.

units.la: Quia deinceps perpetuus Textus est, operæ pretium facturus videor, si & eam partem Textus, quæ præcessit, reproducam : ut ita magis una & continua sit Oratio. Vale.
units.tr: Since the text from now on runs continuously, I think it worthwhile to reproduce also the part of the text that came before, so that the discourse may be more unified and continuous. Farewell.

units.la: Oratio quam dixit in auspicio Quæstionum quodlibeticarum.
units.tr: Speech delivered at the opening of the Quodlibetical Questions.

units.la: Continet actionem in Seductores Genios: Pantomimum præcipue, Mangonem & Dogmatistam, qui omnes ad Philosophiæ tribunal citantur. fraudis, seductionis & stellionatus rei aguntur.
units.tr: It contains the action against the Seducing Geniuses, chiefly the Pantomime, Mangon and the Dogmatist, who are all summoned to the tribunal of Philosophy and are being tried for fraud, seduction and swindling.

units.la: Quam tetris errorum fumis obvoluta Mentis Humanæ fax næ fax est! quam spissis difficultatum fustibus subjicitur! Obruta, suffocata (quid multa?) exstincta : non restat nisi tremula, quæ fungum ellychnii pererrat scintilla. Ludibrium quoddā sumus, quamdiu hic sumus, scopus quidam sumus, in quem collineant innumerabiles imposturæ: Hæremus, cespitamus, inter salebras & vepres, inter confragosa caligamus sine duce: hoc deteriore condicione, quod nihilominus, & avidi ad pergendum, & creduli, unius vicem ducis, varios amplectamur seductores. Sensus nostros non sugillo: circumscriptores illi quidem; sed, singuli stolidi, & universi male foederati, mutua consilia non raro, mutuos actus eludunt: patent, tenentur: iam pridem iis dica scripta, & palam fraudis mendaciique convictis, fides abrogata. Sunt seductores alii, versipelles quidam Genii, ad fallacia & technas nati: Hi non in cute substituere, sicut Sensus; sed percolati, & medullam subeuntes, ad Animum penetraverunt: his utitur Animus; his, ut charissimis convictoribus, totum se credidit; his non ducitur jam; sed agitur, trahitur, raptatur: hos necessarios ei, hos ei dominos fecit diuturna familiaritas. Tandem tamen men aliquando manifestis indiciis deprehensi: ad ignicu- lum Rationis, afflictum illum quidem; eluctantem tamen ex intervallo & irradiantem clarius, detecta perfidia: tum etiam ad judices delati, acerrimos habent propugnatores. Boni duces videntur vanis quibusdam & prurientibus ingeniis, quod interdum sine offensa seducant longius: suspenso gradu ductum obscuri, præstolantur eventum; at eventus ille, non nisi scrobs aut obex: interea micant ancipiti spe, & ipsâ periculi trepidatione gestiunt. Quosdam longa majorum duces hos sequentium caterva, patronos tronos fecit: superstitiosum hoc genus: cui ne manifestus quidem Antiquitatis error sine sacrario est: Novitatum osores audiunt. His accedit Philosophorum vulgus, vecors illud cæcæ consuetudinis mancipium: hi communia, quotidiana, pervagata, quæ passim apud populum increbuêre, cuiusmodicumque illa sint,ferunt; Ea, quorum insolentes sunt, exibilant, explodunt, sarcasmis exagitant & dicteriis proscindunt. His freti patronis seductores, quem fraude sibi arrogarant, etiamnum fraude gerunt & administrant Ducatum, & porro seducunt impu-
units.tr: How the torch of the human mind, wrapped in the foul smoke of errors, is almost no torch at all! How it is trampled under the thick clubs of difficulties! Overwhelmed, choked, extinguished (why say more?), nothing is left but a trembling spark that wanders over the fungus of the wick. We are a kind of plaything while we are here, a kind of target at which countless deceits take aim. We stumble and trip among the thorns and brambles, and we grope blindly through the rough places without a guide, and in a worse condition, because, eager to press on and credulous, we embrace various seducers in place of one leader. I do not disparage our senses: they are deceivers indeed, but each is foolish and all are badly allied, so they often thwart one another's plans and actions. They are exposed and held; long ago their written claims were refuted, and once they were openly convicted of fraud and lying, their credit was withdrawn. There are other seducers, shifty geniuses born for tricks and wiles. These do not stop at the skin as the senses do; they filter through, enter the marrow, and penetrate to the mind. The mind uses them; it has entrusted itself wholly to them as its dearest companions. It is no longer led by them but driven, dragged and hurried along. Long familiarity has made them necessary to it and made them its masters. Yet at length they are caught by clear signs: the deception is exposed to the flame of Reason, which is weakened indeed but struggles back and shines more brightly after an interval. Then they are brought before the judges and have very fierce defenders. They seem good guides to certain vain and itching wits, because they sometimes lead them astray without offence. With cautious step the blinded followers await the outcome, but that outcome is nothing but a ditch or a barrier, and meanwhile the guides glitter with doubtful hope and rejoice in the very trembling of danger. The long line of ancestors has made some of these leaders of their followers and patrons of the ruling party: this superstitious kind, to whom even a plain error of antiquity has its sanctuary. They are called haters of novelties. To these is added the common herd of philosophers, that mindless slave of blind custom. They accept whatever common, everyday and widely spread opinions have taken root among the people, whatever their nature; whatever is unfamiliar to them they hiss at, explode at, harass with sarcasms and tear apart with jibes. Relying on these patrons, the seducers still carry out, by fraud, the leadership they arrogated to themselves by fraud, and go on seducing

units.la: impudenter : præeunt passim in Philosophicis viretis credulum illud & sequax ovile: Et sicut Sensus olim adipati cliens Epicuri, ridiculam suos asseclas devolvit in foveam, dum meridiano sole, orientem occidentemque solem, majorem fateri cogit, quia majorem oculi testarentur: ita & hi, pudendis æque, quos ducunt, imo probrosioribus circumveniunt modis; nisi frontem illaqueatis perfricuissetpublicus ille ganeo & corruptor Mos. Seductores hos, hodierno die, reos ago: Amor-Sapientiæ (partes hæ tuæ sunt) sedeto pro tribunali: Assistite, quibus bus à prejudicatis opinioni-bus vacuum pectus, & justam judicum facite decuriam: Vobis judicibus pedum iis extorquebo de manibus, intensum ad viam indicem, cæteris digitis æquabo & flectam in pugnum, insidiosam dexteram usque & usque aventem inseri axillæ, religabo post tergum: Ducis illa insignia, Ducis hæc munia: soli debentur Rationi, soli vindicabo Rationi: Sic adversariis, antequam jure cum iis experimur, insultamus, sic caussæ confidimus & judici: Habeant sibi sanè ad iniqua Vanitatis, Superstitionis, Infscitię tribunalia, gratiosos pa-trotronos; at supremo hoc judi- ce, non sperent, nisi ferale Theta.
units.tr: shamelessly. Throughout the philosophical pastures they go before that credulous and following flock. Just as Sensus, once the flatterer and client of Epicurus, tips his deluded followers into a ridiculous pit when he compels them, under the noonday sun, to confess that the setting sun and the rising sun are larger, because their eyes testify that they are larger, so these also deceive with methods as shameful as those they lead, or rather more disgraceful, unless that public debauchee and corrupter, Custom, had made their foreheads shameless. I summon these seducers to trial today. Love of Wisdom, this part is yours: sit as the tribunal. Stand by, you whose breasts are free of prejudiced opinions, and form a just jury of judges. From these seducers I shall wrench the feet out of their hands, straighten the index finger pointed at the road, level the other fingers and bend them into a fist, and bind behind their backs the treacherous right hand that always reaches to be thrust into the armpit. These are the badges of a leader, these are his duties; they are owed to Reason alone, and to Reason alone I shall claim them. So we insult our opponents before we contend with them by right, so we trust in our cause and in the judge. Let them, to be sure, have their favourite patron-advocates before the unjust tribunals of Vanity, Superstition and Ignorance; but before this supreme judge let them hope for nothing but the deadly Theta.

units.la: Prodi huc primum Pan- tomime, Alegoriae, Similitudinum & Fabularum Genie: judicibus te siste. Quid? In gremio Charitum educatus, inter Parnassi floscculos lascivire solitus, amoenis Rhetorum spatiis inambulare, ludere natus eras, speciose puer: quae te vesana compulit ambitio, munia Ducis, quibus fungendis, par non es, affectare? Viam praeire vis ad Veritatem; Sed quid ad teneros istos pedes, inaccessa Naturae tesqua, spinosa Philosophiae nostrae dumeta? Genius nius hic, judices, cum ad omnem Metamorphosim inclinat propendetque, tum inanima, in animata transformandi longe cupidissimus est: Ipse lapides, ipse silvas, montes, urbes, fluvios, ventos, & quævis tandem adsciscit in humanam societatem, & jubet homines nobiscum esse: queri ea sæpè, sæpè lætari facit, jam dolore percita, jam spe elata, jam metu perculsa, jam amore, jam miseratione, iam odio, aliisque impulsa cupiditatibus inducit: Dum animi gratia, dum dicis ergo, inter Poëtas ista suos comminiscitur, remitto, concedo, æqui bonique facio dum pro seriis venditat, malas artes! malas artes! vel me tacente, res ipsa clamat: Nec est, quod ambigat de crimine; Si inficias iverit, convincam. Age: Cum olim in Gindo fluvio, equus aliquis, qui Cyro in deliciis erat, submersus periisset, nunquid flumini necem illam assignasti, Pantomime? nunquid credulo regi persuasisti, Gindum lacessere, & injuriis ultro, laesam majestatem provocare? Adeo enim Cyrus facibus tuis, exarsit in iras, ut continuo jusserit Gindum in centum sexaginta rivulos, quo nobilis quondam fluvius exaresceret, dissecari: Ha, nimis fero corde!. Xerxes etiam immanis ille κύκλωτ⊙, qui maria pedibus, & classibus montes peragravit, eodem Genio, in similem actus est furorem; Nam cum Hellespontum contabulasset, & Asiæ Europam ponte junxisset; hic vero fluctibus insurgens, stolidam illam compagem excussisset, ruinasque ejus inter undas suas volveret, trecentos mari colaphos infringi jussit, ferreas etiam compedes, ne qua liberè vagaretur; sed arctis intra litora sua carceribus detinereretur, injecit. Mussitat Pantomimus, nictat oculis, nutat capite, gesticulatur manibus, vacilvacillat pedibus, totus in ge-stum abivit Genius, Videtur aliquid velle innuëre, Quidlibet; Modo ne nobis impo-nat, vastas illas oceani ge-nas, alapis, quas ei Xerxes incussit, livorem suum debere. Sed leve sit singulares homines decepisse, quod subdam, populare delirium est, & ejusdem illius genii imposturis ac instinctui ascriben-dum est utique. Psyllorum gens, quæ circa majores Africæ Syrtes, sedem habuit, crebris ab Austro vento, damnis & cladibus accepti, nunc obtriti domorum arborumque strage, nunc arenarum, velut in fluctus quosdam se esseefferentium, procellis hausti & demersi (siccum enim mare Syrtes exhibent, quod ventis agitatum, pro fluctibus arenarum cumulos versat) Horum tandem malorum impatientes, ad arma conclamare, turmatim concurrere, in Austrum, quasi in hostem (agilem illum, & ordines intercurrere subtilem) saxis & telis irruere: Sed ita furentes, & (quod hîc verè dixeris, aërem verberantes, adverso turbine violentior ventus occupat, & dicto citius, universos cum omnibus copiis armisque, collibus arenarum involvit & sepelit. Silet hic Genius noster; sed si staret ad plebeplebeium Inscitiæ tribunal, jam catastrophen illam, mordicus rapuisset in suas partes: Sensit, inquit, qui ultus est rebelles, qui injurias suas persecutus est ventus; At coram hoc judice, de nugis istis ne hiscit quidem : pudor vetat. Quid? Idem ille Gemus, Barbaros dicam? imo Romanos, viros illos, imo Græcos, cultos illos, tamquam pueros, tamquam fatuos induxit, ut Lunæ laboranti (sic enim hi loquuntur) id est noctem nostram offendenti, curationem aliquam adhiberent; Et quidem contra sideris lethargum, præsens hoc remedium præscripsit, psit ; inconditos clamores tollerent, tubas clangerent, pelves & tintinabula collide-rent, fragoribus complerent omnia: Aniles intemperiæ vix Christianos purioribus sacris abstractos demiserunt; hodie Sinas adhuc & Turcas agitant. Dies me deficiat, si porro enarrare pergam præstigias, quibus Genius ille nos ludit & fascinat, in opprobrium Humanæ Mentis & sannas: Non negat hæc : palam sunt; Habet tamen jam pridem (quantum ex gestibus & inquieto vultu conjecisse videor) quod loquatur : Audiamus : Plebem decepi : Quid ad hoc forum? Philosophos non circumcircumveni: Et cur insulsam illam ac turbulentam multitudinem elusisse, crimini sit? Repagulum ponimus, dum scitè imponimus: frænum & flagellum sunt illi, quos suggerimus, instinctus: apprehendat hos prudens rector, utatur his: & domet, & agat, quo vult, debili Rationi, vanis legibus obtuentem semper & recalcitrantem feram. Nihil de ista Politica dicam, qua callidos illos, qui soli Politicorum nomine censentur hodie, callide pellexit in suas partes ista vulpes: nihil, inquam, de ista Politica dicam; aut potius hoc solum dicam: Probrosam esse majestatem, quæ populi se tuetur erroribus. bus, quæ cives suos, pecudes facit, & bubulcum mavult agere, quam Principem: Principem ego mihi serium totum, syncerum totum, suspiciente imaginatione repræsento, & velut humani conventus sanctissimum aliquem gravissimumque præsulem: Fugiant! Fugiant! Machiavelli noctuæ, ad illustrem hanc & pulcerrimam boni Principis ideam. Nunc purgationi, Pantomime, respondebo tuæ: Plebem decepisse te fateris; non Philosophos? Imo, inquam, Philosophos decepisti, non plebem. In Scholis montes tuarum fraudum; in triviis verucæ tantum; Vin' tibi Stoicos producam, qui Justitiam, Clementiam cæte-rasque virtutes, animalia quędam esse censuerunt? Vin' Pytagoras olim & Platones? Vin' nostrâ memoriâ Klep-peros & Campanellas? Quo-rum alii sideribus & telluri, plantis alii, alii etiam ele-mentis, lapidibus & metallis sensum impertiti; Quin ho-rum aliquis calorem, frigus, lucem, tenebras, non sentire modò, sed etiam ratiocinari nobis narrat; nec imperite ra-tiocinari, sicut plerique no-strûm, sed accuratè; hæc ta-lia Geometriam callere, Sta-ticam exercere deprehendit. Sed missos faciamus hos Panto-
units.tr: Come forward here first, Pantomime, you Genius of allegories, similitudes and fables, and present yourself to the judges. What? Reared in the lap of the Graces, accustomed to frolic among the little flowers of Parnassus, born to wander in the pleasant walks of the rhetoricians and to play, beautiful boy, what mad ambition has driven you to aspire to the duties of a leader, for which you are not equal? You want to lead the way to Truth; but what has that to do with those tender feet, with the untrodden wildernesses of Nature, the thorny thickets of our philosophy? This Genius, judges, is inclined and prone to every metamorphosis, and above all he is most eager to turn inanimate things into animate ones. He himself admits stones, woods, mountains, cities, rivers, winds, and whatever else you like into human society, and orders them to be with us. He often makes them complain, often makes them rejoice, now stirred by grief, now lifted by hope, now struck by fear, now moved by love, pity or hatred, and drives them on by other passions. While for the sake of amusement, of mere saying, he invents these things among the poets, I let it pass, I concede, I count it fair and good. But when he peddles bad arts as serious matters! Bad arts! Even if I kept silent, the thing itself cries out, and there is no doubt about the crime; if he denies it, I shall convict him. Come now. When once in the river Gindes a horse that was a darling of Cyrus drowned and perished, did you assign that death to the river, Pantomime? Did you persuade the credulous king that the Gindes had provoked him and injured his majesty of its own accord? For Cyrus was so inflamed to anger by your torches that he at once ordered the Gindes to be cut into a hundred and sixty little channels, so that the once noble river might dry up. Ah, too savage a heart! Xerxes too, that huge Cyclops [κύκλωψ] who traversed seas on foot and mountains with fleets, was driven into a similar madness by the same Genius. For when he had bridged the Hellespont and joined Europe to Asia with a bridge, the waves rose, shattered that foolish structure and rolled its ruins among the waves; so he ordered the sea to be struck with three hundred lashes and also put on iron fetters, so that it should not wander freely but be held in narrow prisons within its own shores. The Pantomime mutters, blinks, nods his head, gestures with his hands, wavers on his feet; the whole Genius has turned into gesture. He seems to want to hint at something, anything at all; only let him not impose on us that the vast cheeks of the ocean owe their bruises to the slaps Xerxes gave it. But let it be a small thing to have deceived single individuals; what I add is a popular madness, and it must certainly be ascribed to the same Genius's impostures and promptings. The Psylli, a people who had their seat near the greater Syrtes of Africa, were often hit by losses and disasters from the south wind, now crushed by the wreckage of houses and trees, now swallowed and sunk by storms of sand, which rise like waves (for the Syrtes present a dry sea, which, stirred by the winds, churns heaps of sand in place of waves). At last, impatient of these evils, they called to arms, ran together in troops, and rushed with stones and weapons against the South Wind as against an enemy, nimble and subtle at darting between the ranks. But raging thus, and, as you may truly say here, beating the air, a stronger wind met them with a whirlwind from the opposite quarter and, quicker than a word, buried and entombed them all, with their forces and arms, under hills of sand. Our Genius is silent here; but if he stood at the tribunal of common Ignorance, he would at once have seized that catastrophe with his teeth for his own side: "The wind felt it," he would say, "it avenged the rebels, it pursued its injuries." But before this judge he does not even open his mouth about such trifles; shame forbids it. What of it? The same Genius, shall I say, led barbarians, or rather Romans and those men, or rather Greeks, cultivated people, like boys and fools, to apply some cure to the labouring moon (for so they speak), that is, to our night when it is being troubled. And indeed, against the lethargy of the star, he prescribed this ready remedy: they were to raise uncouth shouts, sound trumpets, clash basins and little bells, and fill everything with din. Such old-wives' follies barely let go of Christians, drawn away from purer rites; today they still harass the Chinese and the Turks. The day would fail me if I went on to recount the tricks by which that Genius mocks and bewitches us, to the disgrace and derision of the human mind. He does not deny these things; they are plain. Yet he has long had something to say (as far as I can conjecture from his gestures and restless face). Let us hear it. "I deceived the common people. What has that to do with this forum? I did not circumvent the philosophers. And why should it be a crime to have fooled that foolish and turbulent crowd?" We place a bar when we cleverly put one in place: the impulses we supply are the bit and whip for those who take them up; let a prudent ruler seize them, use them, and tame and drive wherever he wishes the weak Reason, the wild beast that always looks back and kicks against vain laws. I shall say nothing of that Politics by which this fox has cleverly drawn into its party those shrewd men who alone are counted as politicians today. I say nothing of it, or rather I say only this: that majesty is disgraceful when it protects itself with the errors of the people, which makes its citizens cattle and prefers to drive oxen rather than to rule a prince. I picture a prince to myself, wholly serious, wholly sincere, and, with my imagination looking up, as some most holy and most grave president of the human assembly. Let the Machiavellian owls flee, flee from this illustrious and most beautiful idea of a good prince! Now, Pantomime, I shall answer your defence. You confess that you deceived the common people; not the philosophers? On the contrary, I say, you deceived the philosophers, not the common people. In the schools lie the mountains of your frauds; in the crossroads, only the warts. Shall I bring forward for you the Stoics, who thought that justice, clemency and the other virtues were certain living creatures? Shall I bring forward Pythagoras and the Platos of old? Shall I bring forward, in our own time, the Keplers and Campanellas, some of whom gave feeling to the stars and the earth, others to plants, others even to elements, stones and metals? Indeed one of them tells us that heat, cold, light and darkness not only feel but also reason, and not clumsily reason, as most of our people do, but accurately; he shows that these things know geometry and practise statics. But let us dismiss these Pantomimes

units.la: Pantomimi studiosos, hos Volones, qui ultro eum & dedità operà sequuntur; in quo, ut jam sit in eo culpa, qui circumvenit, non minor est in iis, qui circumveniri se sivêre: Ad illos potius orationem convertamus, quos aliud agentes, aliô spectantes & invitos impulit, elusit, induxit: Nos, nos (apertè dico) Peripatetici defecimus, nos qui Rationis Triarii ferebamur, nos, o pudor! transfugæ, nos Mimo illo imperatore meruimus, antequam scivimus. Pantomimi illa sunt, pro quibus hactenus, tamquam pro aris & focis contra Rationem dimicavimus, vimus: Fugæ Vacui & Impedimenta Vacui, Appetitiones naturales & Aversationes naturales, Sympathiæ & Antipathiæ, Formæ substantiales & Intelligentiæ, Facultates & Potentiæ, sunt, inquam, illa omnia Pantomimi propria, mancipio & nexu, usu & fructu: Quibus adde manubias & prædas, quas, agrum Rationis, contra jus & fas depopulatus, asportavit. Principio: Pantomimus Fugas & Impedimenta Vacui Corporibus injunxit: Nam si forte vasi pleno, epistomium detraxerit promus condus, Vinum suspicere Pantomimus jubet, & dolii sui fornicem, num qua pertupertusus sit rimâ, deligenter explorare, quæ si nulla pateat supernè, væ tibi Bacche, si effluis infernè, sustine, inquam, frænos injice ponderi tuo, non discede de stationė; si vero vel tantilla rimula detecta sit, eja! jam integrum est erumpere, &, ni cantharus adsit, qui te maturè excipiat, pessum ire potes, & in cellæ pavimento, ut Liber es, liberè volutari. Interea exercet Aërem jus quoddam rigidum, & (audeo dicere) iniquum: hic enim genio suo indulgente Baccho, & infrâ per apertum Syphunculum dilabente, genium suum defraudare cogitur, descendere, inre, inquam, cum sit naturâ levis, elarus, amplus, perque spiraculi fauces penetrare in vas, quo sit vicarius, & locum repleat, quem liquor liquerat; Quod equidem praestare non valet Aër, sine corporis sui, ad oras istius angustiae, quam subtilis, exilis, & (pene dixeram) exenteratus perlabitur, allisione, divulsione: itaque duram illam legem indignabundus exsequitur, & saepe (quod prominorunt) cum fremitu. Ast omnes hae Corporum curae, studia, tormenta, quorsum? Nimirum, ne inter dolii fornicem & auxiliis infra dilapsis, subsidens Vinum, prodeat
units.tr: Let us set aside the pantomime's enthusiasts, those Volones who follow him of their own accord and on purpose. In their case, though the one who deceives is at fault, those who allowed themselves to be deceived are no less so. Let us rather turn our speech to those whom he drove on, enticed and led along while they were doing something else, looking elsewhere and unwilling. We, we (I say it openly) Peripatetics have deserted. We, who were borne forward as the triarii of Reason, we, for shame, have turned deserters, and earned the favour of that Mime as our commander before we knew it. These are the pantomime's things, for which until now we have fought against Reason as for altars and hearths: Flights and Impediments of the Void, Natural Appetites and Natural Aversions, Sympathies and Antipathies, Substantial Forms and Intelligences, Faculties and Powers. These, I say, are all the pantomime's own property, held by purchase and bond, by use and fruit. Add the spoils and booty which he carried off after ravaging the field of Reason against right and law. First, the pantomime has yoked Flights and Impediments of the Void to bodies. For if perchance the cellarer draws the stopper from a full jar, the pantomime bids you look up at the wine and carefully examine the vault of his cask for any crack through which it might be pierced. If none is open above, woe to you, Bacchus, if you leak below! Hold on, I say, put reins on your weight, do not leave your station. But if even the tiniest crack is discovered, aha! then it is free to burst out, and unless a cup is at hand to catch you promptly, you may go to ruin and roll freely on the cellar floor, as free as you like. Meanwhile a harsh and (I dare say) unjust law vexes the air. For when Bacchus slips down below through the open siphon, the air, indulging its own nature, is compelled to cheat that nature and descend, I say, though by nature it is light, rare and broad, and to penetrate through the throat of the vent into the vessel, where it serves as a substitute and fills the place the liquid has left. The air cannot manage this without great harm to its own body, by collision and tearing, as it slips through the narrow mouth, subtle, slender and (I nearly said) disembowelled. So, indignant, it obeys that hard law, and often (as they grumble) with a roar. But all these cares, struggles and torments of bodies, to what end? Surely lest, between the vault of the cask and the wine settling on the parts that have slipped below, there should emerge

units.la: deat aliquando monstrum illud vecors, ridiculum, nugax, sine mente, sine corpore, re, Vacuum, inane, nihil: quod horret jure meriro Natura: sicut Manducum.
units.tr: at some time that senseless, ridiculous, trifling monster, without mind, without body, a Void, empty, nothing, which Nature rightly abhors, just as the bugbear is abhorred.

units.la: In gremio matris formidat rusticus infans.
units.tr: The country infant trembles in its mother's lap.

units.la: Ad hæc: Pantomimus vim quamdam vitalem per omnes res pertinentem, Appetitionem & Aversationem induxit: Ipso igitur instigante, non-esse res omnes horrent; esse suum, velut vitam & salutem amant medullitus, nihil eo carius, nihil (ut verum dicam) antiquius habent: mox qualiscumque illius vitæ subsidia quædam parant, & abarcent noxia, postremo res meliores quærunt & de his sibi prospiciunt, quæ sunt ad commodum & voluptates: Sic aqua, quæ incaluit, igne sublato, paulatim excutit calorem, & cudit sibi tacitis malleis, novum frigus: calor enim infestus Aquæ id agit, ut in fumum ac vapores resoluta dispereat, imo, quod horrendum est magis, dispareat, ne residuo quidem cadavere. Sed hic mihi jam, Pantomime, injicitur scrupulus, cur Aquæ frigus affectandum potius, quam calorem putes : ambo, cum modum excesserunt, ex æquo noxia sunt: calor eam in vapores, frigus in glaciem ververtet: At enim glacies in Aquam facile liquescit; Et verò vapores quoque in Aquam facile coguntur: ecce par ratio: Quapropter auctor ego sum Lymphæ (quod memini prudentiores inculcare mihi sæpius: & gratias ago)
units.tr: Moreover, the Pantomime introduced a certain vital force reaching through all things, Appetition and Aversion. Under his urging, therefore, all things shudder at non-being; they love their being from the marrow, as if it were life and safety, and they hold nothing dearer or (to speak truly) more ancient than it. Soon they prepare whatever supports they can for that life, and they ward off what is harmful. Finally they seek better things and provide for themselves those things that serve convenience and pleasures. Thus water that has been heated, when the fire is removed, gradually shakes off its warmth and, with silent hammers, forges for itself a new coldness. For heat, being hostile to water, aims to dissolve it into smoke and vapour so that it perishes, or rather (what is more dreadful) so that it passes away, leaving not even a remaining corpse. But here, Pantomime, a doubt now occurs to me: why do you think water should aim at cold rather than heat? Both, when they exceed the measure, are equally harmful: heat turns it into vapours, cold into ice. Yet ice melts easily into water, and vapours too are easily condensed into water. Here is an equal reckoning. Therefore I am a champion of moderate water (as I remember the wiser men often urging on me, and I thank them),

units.la: Auream servet mediocritatem: Si modo nomen Aquæ, & usus, quos nobis præbet, lavandi, rigandi, navigandi, integros & salvos esse velit. Denique aliàs Aqua in nubes coācta depluit, alias è fontibus scaturit in rivulos, è rivulis in fluvios, & ex his in mare, post multas ambages se devolvit: Quæ omnia tam sedu-
units.tr: Let it keep the golden mean, if only the name of water and the uses it offers us, for washing, watering and sailing, are to remain whole and safe. Finally, water at one time, gathered into clouds, falls as rain; at another it bubbles from springs into streams, from streams into rivers, and from these into the sea, after many twists and turns it rolls on. All these things it does with such diligence

units.la: E sedulò molitur Aqua, ut aucto numero firmior, & adversus hostium insidias tutius, & cum suì similibus degat suavius: Sic mollis ille latex, cum sua sponte infirmus, & aliorum libidine sit infestus, prudenter & catè se tuetur. Sed avos nostros, lapides, inquam, silices, marmora, genus illud durum, & adversus hostium suorum incursiones perpetuò cataphractum, nescio, quæ tanta teneat impotentia: Tutum illis sublime versari; imo sublime, quam humi, securius agent: non situm contrahent, non obterentur, plaustris, non urentur in calcem; Verum enim nim verò, surdis ea canimus: tantum abest, ut his adducti rationibus, ipsi se in altum subvehant, ut manibus nostris in aërem projecti sexcenties, sexcenties recidant, & ne punctum quidem temporis subsistant loco tam aprico, tam salubri: Quin è domorum & turrium fastigiis, quam primum soluti sunt, præcipitant, & devolvunt se in ima, libidine tam effrænatâ, ut infra ad platearum incolas, fraterculos suos appulsi dissiliant in partes, & integritatem suam miseri, velut animulam aliquam exhalent: O interim immites cognatos illos, & verè saxeos! qui hospitem, & fratrem, in amplexus suos tam avidè ruentem, non accipiant molliore culcitrâ. At,at! E vicino Peripato, contenta vox, cum iracundia & stomacho: Inepta sunt ista, quæ Peripateticorum sensis, passim interponis epiphonemata: tute fabulas istas habe tibi: Peripatetici hæc talia non dicunt. Fateor, non dicunt: Sed, ò quisquis es, qui vocem illam animas, incola Peripati: Populares tui glossas faciunt; ego interpretem ago, commentarium adfero: estne, quod mihi jure succensèas? Illi lineamenta ducunt; ego lineamentis istis vivos & convenientes colores induco: Filum illi neverant rant, & opus erat acu. Sed, o bone vir, etiam in Circo vestro,nonprimos tantum actus, sed integras etiam saltant fabulas (quamquam, quæ laus est mutilare, & supremum actum precidere?) Materiâ habere se ad instar fœminæ; formam esse velut marem, eas inter se diligere, concupiscere, num aliud sapiunt? Hinc verò nascuntur longè lateque diffusæ quæstiones triobolares: An Materia Formam appetat, quam amisit? Dicas eos quærere, an Materia lugeat maritum vitâ jam defunctum: An Forma, quâ fruitur Materia, appetitum ejus expleat? ita ut novis nuptiis memoriam exuat veteris connubii: An plures simul Formas appetat? & omnibus se pervulget: An vero nobiles, prae ignobilibus ambiat? Tum vero fescennina illa, de Dispositionibus requisitis in Materia, ut à Forma iniri possit: De copula seu Vnione Physicâ inter Materiam & Formam; si quis appellet, honos praefandus sit. Hæc & cætera de genere hoc, quæ longum est persequi, cum Peripatetici obviis ulnis, in Philosophiam receperint, præstent etiam & tueantur, necessum est, si hasce meas commentationes, & infinitas, quas otiosus comminiscar similes, Philosophica civitate donavero. vero. Scimus igitur ( & quis id ignorat? ) his, quæ sensu & cognitione carent, boni nihil aut mali esse: sint, non sint, nihil pensi habent lapis, aqua, terra; Sed appetitū, inquis, affingo per Metaphorā, similitudine ab animantibus desumptā: Belle: Abi igitur in patriam Pantomimi, ad Parnassum, inquam, te confer, & Castalia bene potus unda, finge somnia, quot volueris: quid ad indaginem veritatis istæ lyræ?. Verum ab hoc parumper abeamus: Communes quasdam Notiones, ceu opima spolia, Rationi detracta, Peripati tholis appendit Pantomimus: velut Ea quæ movenmoventur, naturaliter ad quietem tendere, quod eo spiritu instincti canebamus, qui suis quaeque motibus, ut nos cursu & ambulatione defatigari suggesserat. Alterum, Nihil agere in se ipsum, quia unumquodque (sic nos comparati sumus) amicissimum sibi videbatur; Cum tamen sciamus, homines quosdam mortem non operiri, sed manu facere: cur Pantomimus nonquid simile transtulit ad Res Naturales? statuitque earum aliquas furere, & velut desperabundas, necem sibi conscisc'ere? Et vero, si memini recte, id ipsum, quod ridemus, de igne censet Peripatetiteticorum recentium non nemo, Denique Cessante fi-ne, cessare media, quo mari suadere solebamus, ne premeret in fundo suo, margaritas quærentem urinatorem: Cum enim pondus & premendi vis, eo fine data sit aquæ, ut locum naturalem, si quando de illo deturbaretur, repeteret; locum verò illum, quæ ad mare pervenit, feliciter & ex animi sui sententiâ consecuta sit æqua, non est, quod ibi premat adhuc & fatiget se gratis: Sic Rationis moneta illa proba recuditur, & Pantomimi signis deformata, deinceps non facit ad quæstum Veritatis. Tandem vero, cum etiam Intelligentiæ nobis suppetias venerunt, hæ nos in Pantomimi castra totos abduxerunt: Quid enim aliud sunt Intelligentiæ sideribus aut cælis affixæ, infixæ, quam id ipsum, quod nos sumus, mentes cum corpore? Sed lepidum hoc, & Pantomimum etiam spirat, quod Intelligentiis illis, non nisi ampla & magni momenti officia demandemus; Quæ verò non tanti ponderis negotia videntur, ea Formis substantialibus commisimus; quæ quidem ipsæ, ut eas commenti sumus, non nisi Intelligentiæ quædam sunt; licet illas hac nondum compellatiolatione dignemur : Ne sol aliquando exorbitet ab E-cliptica, directricem ei, & viæ istius peritissimam Intelli-gentiam adjunximus; Lapidi verò de simili comite non prospicimus, nihil veriti, ne forte dum labitur, à perpen-diculo deliret; hujus tamen error, errore solis non minus pernicios𝑢s, & exitiosus ef-set: non vitra fenestrarum, quid dico? non capita nostra tuta sunt, si lapides oblivi-scuntur viæ suæ, si sursum rue-re, aut huc illuc in transver-sum palari statuunt, Asenim, ars major in motu siderum, indu-stria plus: Eà re sideribus assi-stentes Intelligentiæ dantur: Bo-nam nam in partem accipietis, qui-qui de sideribus ita mugina-mini : Videor mihi Phœbum (sic enim sol inter polyony-mos illos vocari mavult) quotidiani operis & pensi sui difficultates, Phaëtonti suo inculcantem audire :
units.tr: ...diligently, so that, multiplied in number, it may be stronger, safer against the ambushes of enemies, and may live more pleasantly with its like. So that soft liquid, weak in itself and vulnerable to the lust of others, guards itself prudently and cautiously. But our grandfathers, the stones, I mean flints, marbles, that hard kind, always armoured in mail against the assaults of their enemies, I do not know what great powerlessness holds them. It is safer for them to dwell on high; indeed they would act more securely on high than on the ground: they would not shrink or be crushed by carts, nor be burned to lime. But truly we sing to deaf ears. So far from being moved by these arguments to raise themselves aloft, when thrown by our hands into the air they fall back six hundred times, six hundred times, and they do not stay for a single moment in so sunny, so wholesome a place. Indeed, as soon as they are released from the gables of houses and towers, they plunge down and roll themselves to the bottom with such unbridled lust that, arriving among the dwellers of the streets, their little brothers, they burst apart, and wretched, they breathe out their integrity like a little soul. Oh, those cruel kinsmen, truly stony, who do not receive the guest and brother rushing so eagerly into their embrace on a softer mattress! But hark! From the neighbouring Peripatos a voice rings out, with anger and spleen: Those absurdities which you pass off as the opinions of the Peripatetics, with your constant exclamations, are nonsense: keep those fables to yourself. The Peripatetics do not say such things. I grant that they do not say them. But, o whoever you are, dweller of the Peripatos, who utter that voice: your fellow-countrymen make glosses; I act as interpreter and bring a commentary. Is there something for which you may justly be angry with me? They draw the outlines; I bring living and harmonious colours into those outlines. They had spun the thread, and the work needed a needle. But, o good sir, even in your Circus they dance not only the first acts but whole plays (though what praise is it to mutilate, and to cut off the final act?). That Matter behaves like a woman, that Form is like a man, and that they love and desire one another: do they think of anything else? From this there arise the widely spread questions worth three obols: Does Matter desire the Form it has lost? You would say they ask whether Matter mourns a husband who has already died. Does the Form which Matter enjoys satisfy its appetite? so that by a new marriage it puts off the memory of the old union. Does it desire several Forms at once and surrender itself to all? Does it court the nobler ones before the baser? Then indeed there are those Fescennine questions: On the dispositions required in Matter so that it can be wedded by Form; on the physical copula or union between Matter and Form; if anyone calls for these, honour must be shown beforehand. These and the other things of this kind, which it would be long to pursue, since the Peripatetics have embraced them with open arms and admitted them into Philosophy, they must also defend and maintain, if I bestow Philosophical citizenship upon these commentaries of mine, and the countless similar ones which I shall idly invent. We know therefore (and who does not know it?) that for things devoid of sense and cognition there is no good or evil: whether they are or are not, stone, water and earth are not concerned. But, you say, I attribute appetite to them by metaphor, borrowed from animate beings. Fine. Go then to your Pantomime's homeland, betake yourself to Parnassus, I say, and drinking well of the Castalian spring, invent as many dreams as you like.
