What have those lyres to do with the search for truth? But let us leave this for a moment. The Pantomime hangs on the Peripatetic columns certain common Notions, like rich spoils stripped from Reason: for example, things that are moved naturally tend to rest, which we used to sing under the same impulse that had suggested to us weariness from running and walking. Another, nothing acts upon itself, because each thing (so we are constituted) seemed most friendly to itself. Yet since we know that some men do not wait for death but bring it about by their own hand, why has the Pantomime not transferred something similar to natural things? Why does he decree that some of them rage and, as if in despair, bring about their own destruction? And indeed, if I remember rightly, some of the more recent Peripatetics hold the very thing we laugh at about fire. Finally, when the end ceases, the means cease, which we used to urge on the diver seeking pearls, lest he weigh down the sea, which was at its bottom. For since weight and the power of pressing down were given to water so that, if it were ever driven from its natural place, it might recover it; and since it has reached that place by the sea, happily and as its spirit desired, there is no reason for it to keep pressing and exhausting itself for nothing. So that sound coin of Reason is restamped with the Pantomime's marks, and from then on it is of no use for the profit of Truth. At last, when even Intelligences came to our aid, they drew us entirely over into the Pantomime's camp. For what else are Intelligences fixed and attached to the stars or heavens, than the very thing we ourselves are, minds with bodies? But this is charming, and breathes the Pantomime too: that we entrust to those Intelligences only tasks of great scope and weight, while we have committed to substantial Forms the affairs that seem of less weight. Yet these, as we invented them, are nothing but certain Intelligences, though we do not yet deign to address them by that name. Lest the sun ever stray from the ecliptic, we have joined to it an Intelligence as its director, most skilled in that course; but for a stone we make no such provision of a similar companion, fearing nothing lest, as it falls, it should swerve from the perpendicular. Yet its error would be no less ruinous and deadly than the sun's error: are not our windows, what am I saying? are not our very heads safe, if stones forget their way, if they decide to rush upward, or to wander crosswise here and there? For the greater art is in the motion of the stars, the greater effort; therefore Intelligences are given to stand by the stars. You will take this in good part, you who mutter such things about the stars. I seem to hear Phoebus (for so the sun prefers to be called among his many names) urging on his Phaethon the difficulties of his daily work and task.

units.la: Ardua prima via est, & qua
units.tr: The first stretch is steep, and it is the stretch on which

units.la: vix mane recentes
units.tr: the fresh horses can scarcely make their way even in the morning.

units.la: Eniituntur equi : Medio est
units.tr: from where I often look down on the sea and lands myself,

units.la: altissima cælo :
units.tr: and fear grips me, and my trembling heart beats with dread.

units.la: Vnde mare & terras, ipsi mihi
units.tr: From there I myself often see sea and lands,

units.la: sæpe videre
units.tr: and yet

units.la: Sit timor, & pavida trepidet
units.tr: fear comes over me, and my trembling heart

units.la: formidine pectus :
units.tr: beats with a fearful dread.

units.la: Vltima prona via est, & eget
units.tr: The last stretch runs steeply downward and needs a steady hand on the reins.

units.la: moderamine certo :
units.tr: Then, too, the sea that receives me beneath its waves

units.la: Tunc etiam, quæ me subjectus
units.tr: gives me pause,

units.la: excipit undis,
units.tr: and

units.la: Neferar in præceps, Thetis solet ipsa vereri:
units.tr: I am carried headlong: Thetis herself is wont to fear it.

units.la: Ut ovum ovo, sic fabula hæc, isti simillima Philosophiæ: Obsequendo confutemus insaniam, &, quod dici solet, clavum clavo pellamus: Ajo ego, in lapidis descensu, tantum artis elucere, quantum elucet in solis circuitu: Notasti lapidem è quocumque fastigio demissum, ad terram recta contendere, idque etiam densissimis tenebris, quando lynces non melius vident, quam talpæ? Notasti lapidem pro mora lapsionis, impetum & vires augere, motum accelerare justissimâ proportione? Notasti lapides, des, majorem alterum, alterum minorem, si interjecto baculo conjuncti, è fenestra domus simul solverint, præcurrere majorem, & primò subjectam aream contingere, sequi minorem; si verò soluti fuerint, comitari inter se, & eodem ambos momento ad terram allidi? Notasti item lapides, majorem alterum, alterum minorem, si quod ad terram è turris apice stadium est, decurrant, mediam propè curriculi partem æquis passibus metari, inde subitò majorem antevertere, & longo minorem intervallo, post se relinquere? * Notasti lapidem in aqua, ita ut nulla pars ejus fundum aut latera tangat. Videbis lapidem A. attolli in aqua; plumbum B. deprimi. dem æquali pondere cum plumbo libratum in aëre, si stateram sub aqua demergas, ascendere, plus tamen ponderis hunc lapidem, quam istud plumbum (quod item ad trutinam examinare potes) in fundum aquæ derivare? Cedo, solaris circuitionis prærogatiuas: si vel unam dederis, dabo victas manus. Satis est, Amor-sapientiæ, ferendæ sententiæ, silentium poscit.
units.tr: Just as one egg is like another, so this fable is very like that philosophy. Let us refute madness by humouring it, and, as the saying goes, drive one nail out with another. I say that in the fall of a stone there shines as much art as shines in the revolution of the sun. Have you noticed that a stone let fall from any height drops straight to the earth, even in the thickest darkness, when lynxes see no better than moles? Have you noticed that a stone, the longer it falls, gathers force and momentum and quickens its motion in the most exact proportion? Have you noticed that two stones, one larger and one smaller, if they are tied together with a stick in between and let go together from a window, the larger runs ahead and strikes the ground first, the smaller following; but if they are released loose, they fall together and strike the ground at the same instant? Have you also noticed that two stones, one larger and one smaller, if they run down the distance of a stadium from the top of a tower to the ground, keep pace with equal steps through about the middle of the course, then suddenly the larger pulls ahead and leaves the smaller far behind? Have you noticed a stone in water, so that no part of it touches the bottom or the sides? You will see stone A rise in the water, and lead B sink. Balance them with equal weight in air; if you plunge the scale under water, this stone rises, yet can you not also weigh that lead, which likewise you can test on the balance, and see that it drags more weight down to the bottom of the water than this stone does? Come, name me the privileges of the solar circuit: if you give me even one, I will surrender. It is enough, Lover of Wisdom; a verdict is due, and silence is required.

units.la: & F. simul cum aquis, quas continent, aquiponderent: Cape prædictum lapidem B., eumque ex fune ligatum & suspensum, demerge in situlam E.: ita manu funem tene, ut quidem lapis B in aqua situla E., penitus demersus sit; sed nec fundum nec latera situla E. contingat. Sit etiam alius tecum, qui plumbum C eodem modo ex fune suspensum, eodem modo demergat in situlam F.: Videbis illam lancem statera D., quæ continet situlam E, cui immergitur lapis B., deprimi; oppositam vero lancem ejusdem staterae D., quæ continet situlam F., cui immergitur plumbum C. attolli. Horum nobis in promptu quidem ratio; sed hîc non promenda. poscit. Pantomime Scholas nostras deserito: Commenta, quae intuleras, efferto: In patriam, ad Parnassum quantocyus remigrato. Habet: Abitum maturat, & excerpit, quibus abundè libros nostros infarserat, paginas: Quanta struesjam nunc! ut, cum loquimur, accessione perpetuâ crescit! ut porro crescet! Itaque bajulos conducat sibi, aut agitatorem cum plaustro: ne si ipse humeris subeat, sarcinae suae succumbat tenebrus. Interea, cum haec parantur,
units.tr: ...and F together with the water they contain balance one another. Take the stone B, tie it to a cord, hang it up, and lower it into the bucket E, holding the cord in your hand so that stone B is wholly submerged in the water of bucket E, yet touches neither the bottom nor the sides of bucket E. Let someone else with you do the same with lead C, hung in the same way from a cord and lowered into bucket F. You will see that pan D of the balance, which holds bucket E into which stone B is immersed, sinks; but the opposite pan of the same balance, which holds bucket F into which lead C is immersed, rises. The reason for these things is ready to hand for us, but it is not to be brought out here. Pantomime, leave our schools; take up the inventions you have brought in, and hurry back homeward to Parnassus. He has it: he hastens his departure and picks out the pages with which he had stuffed our books in abundance. What a heap he has piled up now, growing by constant additions as we speak! And it will grow further! So let him hire porters for himself, or a carter with a wagon, lest, if he shoulders the load himself, he sink beneath his own baggage. Meanwhile, while these things are being prepared,

units.la: Prodeat in judicium Mango, ornatus & harmoniae Genius. Adest ecce: Minio ei & fuco infecta facies: in graciles arcus accuratissimè detonsa supercilia: in pariles utrimque cincinnos, cunctante calamistro, divisa caesaries: Collum & brachia inter byssum & vittas circumludunt monilia: Ex utroque humero, in alterna femora pertinentes, pectus & tergum decussant bullatę torques: Acu-picta vestis, mille meandris in se revoluta, mille fimbriis praetexta, mille striis intorta, centum-coloribus laciniis, digitos pedum lambit, & longo secundum calcem exundat in terram syrmate: Gestus ei, nutus, incessus, elocutionis accentus, tussis, sputum, & his quæ-cumque, aut paria, aut etiam minora, omnia sunt perpetuum artificium, omnia affectata, studio compósita, germanum nihil: Patria hujus Genii, plumariorum & Phrygionum tabernæ: Educatus est in mulierum gynæceis, inter puparum mundos, inter nundinarum crepundia, inter conchyliata aulæa, inter belluata tapetia, inter cælaminum pampinos & thyrsos, inter Corinthiorum operum crobylos & corimbos; &, si quæ his similia, in quibus Artis libidine penitus deflorata Natura est. Cum tetuamque supellectilem con-temtemplor, o Mango, non possum, quin interpellem, ecquid tibi venerit in mentem? quamobrem ad inamœnos illos, & tam tui dissimiles sophistas abieris? Quibus à diurna incubatione, situs: à nocturna lucubratione, tabes: à rimandis minutiis & argutiis, conniventes oculi, distorti & introrsum acti: ab obstructis hypocondriis, squallor, caperata frons, impexum cappillitium, neglecta barba: ab oleo fœda, fœtidaque, à vetustate detrita, ab egestate pannosa lacerna: In eorum Scholis nudi parietes, diffracta vitra, araneisob ducta tabulata, ignotum tum sub pulveribus pavimen- tum, iisdem oppleta scamna cathedrae, pulpita, nisi qua- parte natibus & cubito ver- runtur. Ita sanè austeros illos incultosque viros, fuco, bul- lis & phaleris istis perstrinxi- sti, fascinasti, ut quidquid ae- dibus alibi, quidquid templis & cænaculis & vestibus inest mangonii, totum hoc eorum cerebro transcripsisse videa- re: Toti sunt in smegmate, i- maginariis distorquent o- mnia perfectionibus: si pulcri concinnive quiddam, otium suggesserit aut somnium, id Naturae rerum obtrudunt li- beraliter & plena manu: Pa- lam vociferantur : Mundo nihil [illegible, ~10 letters]ihil abesse potest: hic aptus undi-que, perfectus, expletus est omni-um numeris: Quod ad ornatum & harmoniam ejus facit, nisi sensus ad ravim usque recla-mnet, extemplo concedendum est: Hoc in Philosophiæ funda-mento reponunt, hoc velut iusiurandum, quo Mangoni se obstringunt, non Philoso-phi jam, sed Philomangones. Aliquot fraudes tuas, o Man-go, proferemus in medium, quibus devotum istum gre-gem deludis: omnes prose-qui, voluminis opus erat. Tu eos tot ambientium inter se, & aliarum alias implicantium Sphærarum capsis inclusisti, ut spes nulla suppetat expe-diendiendi, & in communen eos, qua cæteri mortaliun fruuntur libertaté, vindican di: Nam principio quiden terram & aquam, in unum globum conflatas, Centro dedisti: huic aërem orbicula- tim afflas: aërem incrustas igne: ignem orbe Lunari complecteris: Lunarem Mer- curiali, Mercurialem Vene- reo, Venereum Solari, Sola- rem Martio, Martium Jovia- li, denique Jovialem, orbe Saturnio coërces: Hosce Pla- netarum cælos, magnâ im- pensâ, magno Excentrico- rum Epicyclorumque instru- mento tueris: hosce, quo dif- fidentes inter se gyros & at- tritritiones constantius ferant, poliisti jam pridem & solidasti: Spissum opus & operosum! Planetarum cælos, majoribus gremiis complectitur Firmamentum: hoc Sphærâ crystallinâ: hæc Primo Mobili continetur: Et aliquot adhuc fortè cælis interjectis, tandem, tandem Empyrei peristromatis clauduntur omnia: Ultra hæc, nihil; Sed nihil illud, non nihil est, imo verò ingens circum Palatium illud area, quam Mundorum, qualem hunc Mango finxit, myriades quotquot, nunquam expleverint, Spatium, inquam imaginarium, quaquaversus sine fine vastum, desodesolatum, ab omni corpore; sed magis mente vacuum. Euge Mango! Euge! Belle! Καλῶς! tua sunt hæc omnia, & inventa, & commenta præclara. Verum inter hasce faustas acclamationes, aliquid est, quod frontem feriat: Exleges in tellure nostra tubères & colles male te habent: reconcinnare velles, si liceret, complanare terram, eamque in perfectum globum tornare, atque adeo nos omnes superfluis aquis demergere: nam tersa sic & limpida & politula in Mundi meditullio staret res: O igitur, si id liceret! Non licet: Per Sensum, inquam, non licet: Olym-
units.tr: let Mango come forward to judgement, the genius of ornament and harmony. Here he is: a face stained with red lead and rouge; eyebrows plucked very carefully into thin arches; hair parted and curled in matching ringlets on both sides, with the curling iron lingering. Around his neck and arms necklaces play among the fine linen and ribbons; from each shoulder, hanging down to alternate thighs, chains with bosses cross over his chest and back. His embroidered garment, folded upon itself in a thousand windings, edged with a thousand fringes, twisted with a thousand stripes, with a hundred colours of tassels, licks his toes and spills over the ground in a long train down to the heel. His gestures, nods, gait, the accents of his speech, his cough, his spitting, and whatever else is alike or even lesser, are all a constant artifice, all affected, all put together with effort; nothing in him is genuine. His homeland is the shop of the feather-workers and the Phrygian embroiderers. He was brought up in the women's chambers, among dolls' trinkets, among the rattles of the fair, among purple hangings, among beast-patterned tapestries, among the tendrils and thyrsi of embossed work, among the knobs and clusters of Corinthian carvings, and among whatever is like these, in which Nature has been wholly deflowered by the lust of Art. Whenever I contemplate all this trumpery, O Mango, I cannot help asking you: what has come into your head, that you should go away from those unlovely sophists, so unlike yourself? From their daily brooding come filth; from their nightly lucubration, decay; from their hunting after trifles and quibbles, eyes squinting, twisted and turned inward; from obstructed hypochondria, squalor, a wrinkled brow, unkempt hair, neglected beard; from oil, foul and stinking, from age worn-out, from poverty a ragged cloak. In their schools are bare walls, broken glass, shelves hung with cobwebs, a floor unknown beneath the dust, benches and a lectern worn smooth by buttocks and elbows wherever they rub. Such austere and unkempt men, indeed, you have dazzled and bewitched with that paint, those bubbles and those trappings, so that whatever finery there is elsewhere in houses, temples, dining rooms and clothes, all of it seems to have been copied into their brains. They are wholly given over to the cosmetic; in their imaginations they twist everything into perfections. If some beautiful or neat thing has been suggested to them by idleness or a dream, they lavishly and with full hands thrust it upon the nature of things. Openly they cry out: Nothing can be lacking to the world; here everything is fitted on every side, perfect and complete in all its proportions. As far as it contributes to its ornament and harmony, unless the senses cry out to the point of hoarseness, it must at once be conceded. This they place in the foundation of philosophy, this they swear as an oath by which they bind themselves to Mango; they are no longer philosophers, but Mango-lovers. We will bring forward some of your tricks, O Mango, by which you deceive that devoted flock; to pursue them all would require the work of a whole volume. You have shut them up in the boxes of spheres that surround one another and entangle one another, so that no hope remains of extricating them and reclaiming them for that liberty which other mortals enjoy. For first you have made earth and water, fused together into a single globe, the centre; around this you wrap air in circles; you encrust the air with fire; you embrace the fire with the lunar orb; the lunar with the Mercurial, the Mercurial with the Venereal, the Venereal with the Solar, the Solar with the Martial, the Martial with the Jovial, and finally you confine the Jovial within the Saturnian orb. These heavens of the planets you guard at great expense, with the great apparatus of eccentrics and epicycles; these you have long since polished and made solid, so that the wheels and frictions, which disagree among themselves, may be borne more steadily. A heavy and laborious work! The Firmament embraces the heavens of the planets in its wider bosom; this is contained by the crystalline sphere, and this by the Primum Mobile. And perhaps with some further heavens interposed, at last, at last, everything is shut in by the canopy of the Empyrean. Beyond these, nothing; but that nothing is not nothing, indeed it is a vast courtyard around that palace, which the myriads of worlds, such as this Mango has fashioned, would never fill: imaginary space, I say, boundless without end on every side, desolate, empty of every body, but still more empty of mind. Well done, Mango! Well done! Splendid! Well said! [Καλῶς!] All these things are yours, both the discoveries and the splendid inventions. But amid these auspicious acclamations there is something that strikes the forehead: the swellings and hills of our earth, which are out of joint, trouble you. You would like, if it were allowed, to reshape and level the earth, and turn it into a perfect globe, and so to drown us all beneath superfluous waters; for then the thing would stand clean and smooth and neatly polished in the middle of the world. Oh, if only that were permitted! It is not permitted: by the senses, I say, it is not permitted. Here Olympus...

units.la: Olympos hic nobis, & Pindos exhibet, & Immanes scopulos Acroceraunia:
units.tr: Here Olympus and Pindus present themselves to us, and the Immanes scopulos of Acroceraunia.

units.la: Ergo conclamatum est, quando invito Sensu, nihil potes, o Mango: Sed hem! Sensui intercedunt Theologi quidam, caperatâ fronte, male feriati: nam magnâ curâ magnas nugas tuentur: Hi terram olim (non ita multo post Diem judicii) abraso montium rupiumque scabro, reformandam in globum concinnissimum; post hæc, æquali circumquaq; profundo involvendam præscribunt: Proinde, Mango, exspecta cum patientia, & hoc tantantisper utere solatio. Sed ab hoc parumper abeamus: Entium etiam Rempublicam quamdam commentus est Mango, quam dignitatum & officiorum insignibus eleganter distinxit: Nam inter Entia, Substantiæ præstant Accidentibus: Inter Substantias, Spirituales nobiliores sunt Corporeis: Inter has, quæ essentialiter incompletæ sunt, velut Materia prima & Forma Substantialis, ultimo censentur loco: Quarum illa vix in aliquem numerum venit: tota deses, nihil agit, omnia patitur, parvo intervallo distat a muto illo & penitus penitusque mortuo Non ente: Inter Substanstantias corporeas completas patricii sunt Cæli, eorumque Stellæ, tum etiam Ignis: Aër nobilium ultimus, citimus plebi: Plebs ipsa, Aqua, Terra, & hi Terræ filii, Silices, argillæ, Rudera, Quisquiliæ: non enim omnes gigantum fraterculi, plebeii sunt in hac Republica: quidam, quando admodum opulenti sunt, jus sibi & insignia Nobilitatis coëmerunt, ut Aurum, Argentum, Gemmæ: quorum ideo in sanandis & exspoliandis ægris, virtutes & potestates miræ, notæ sunt Archiatris & Pharmacopæis. Omnibus sic inter se communiter constitutis &
units.tr: So it is settled: since Sense is against you, you can do nothing, O Mango. But look! Some Theologians step in against Sense, with furrowed brows and in a bad way, for they guard great trifles with great care. They prescribe that the earth, once the rough places of mountains and cliffs have been scraped away (not long after the Diem judicii), is to be reshaped into the most finely turned globe, and afterwards wrapped in a uniform depth of water all round. So, Mango, wait patiently and take this comfort for the time being. But let us leave this for a moment. Mango has also devised a certain commonwealth of Entia, which he has neatly marked out with the insignia of ranks and offices. Among the Entia, the Substantiae stand above the Accidentibus. Among the Substantiae, the Spirituales are nobler than the Corporeis. Among these, those which are essentialiter incompletae sunt, such as Materia prima and Forma Substantialis, are counted in the last place. Of these, the first hardly comes into any count at all: wholly idle, it does nothing and suffers everything, and it is only a short distance from that dumb and utterly, utterly dead Non ente. Among the Substantiae corporeae completae the patricians are the heavens and their stars, and also fire. Air is the lowest of the nobles and the nearest to the plebs. The plebs themselves are water, earth, and these sons of earth, flints, clays, rubble and sweepings; for not all the little brothers of the giants are commoners in this commonwealth. Some, when they are very wealthy, have bought for themselves the rights and insignia of nobility, such as gold, silver and gems; and so their marvellous powers and virtues in healing and draining the sick are well known to the physicians and apothecaries. With all these thus arranged among themselves in common and squared off, our Genius goes about hawking each thing.

units.la: quadratis, Genius noster mangonizatum vadit singula: & Cæli quidem Physicè simplices, id est, Materiæ primæ & Formæ substantialis expertes ponuntur: Spectat enim ad Mundi ornatum & complementum, ut corpus tale aliquod complexu suo teneat: mutila videri posset, si hoc Gradu entis destitueretur Rerum Universitas: Ex simili delirio, corpora cælestia non generantur, non corrumpuntur, non crescunt, non decrescunt, non gravia sunt, non levia. Post hæc, potestatibus miris donantur sidera, influentiis & qualitatibus, à nomine, occultis: à re tam notis, quam quæ vulgo notissimæ putantur, Gravitas Levitasque. Elementa sic ornantur: duæ dantur singulis qualitates ex quatuor primis: Ignis summè calidus & excellenter siccus: Aër summè humidus & excellenter calidus: Aqua summè frigida & excellenter humida: Terra summè sicca & excellenter frigida. Textus perquam amœnus est & versicolor! Quò exemplo, in quatuor Humoribus, Bile, Sanguine, Pituitâ, Melancholiâ: in quatuor anni tempestatibus, Vere, Æstate, Autumno, Hyeme: in quatuor vitæ ætatibus, Pueritia, Juventute, Ætatis Ætate consistente, Senectute, ac in multis aliis eadem illa tela texitur: Hinc etiam Elementa quædam Symbola dicuntur, quæ nempe in eadem qualitate prima conveniunt: ut Ignis & Aër in Calore: Aër & Aqua in Humore: Aqua & Terra in Frigore: Terra & Ignis in Siccitate (hæc inter se orbem saltatorium versant) Quædam Assymbola: ut Ignis & Aqua: Aër & Terra (hæc disjuncta tripudiant) His momentis examinant Elementorum aliorum in alia faciles ac difficiles commutationes: in his observantur præterea multa ficta, frivola, ad quæ longum gum est abire: Sensus interpellat subinde, & alia testatur? non credunt, ne jurato quidem: obstrepit importunius? os ei batuunt, conspuant, improperant omnes, quas aliquando machinatus est impostruras: Conticescat ocyus: quia lubet, & decet, & debet esse, quidquid adeo speciosum est. Hæc de Cælis & Elementis', quæ Mangoni Corpora simplicia dicuntur; Reliqua ei corpora sunt Mixta, quæ hic in Terrestris globi superficie, aut propè ab illa generantur, Metalla, Lapides, Stirpes, & Animalia: quibus conveniunt quatuor qualitatum primarum variis modis inter se temperatarum complexiones variæ: Igitur marmor calorem habet, etiam dum gelidâ plus urit glacie: & humor est in pumice; cui ne guttam quidem unam exprimas sub artissimo torculari. Inter hæc, & id genus alia, à quorum longius persequendo catalogo, deterreor nauseâ, nulla ratiocinantium sensa; omnia sic volentium placita sunt: Ac miror Placitorum etiam nomine censeri ab iis, quibus oraculorum instar sunt: Nempe quæstionem gravem in mendaces habet Veritas: & quæ rebus nomina conveniunt, ea nihil ejusmodi cogitantantibus, & alia prorsus agentibus extorquet: Sic auritum illud animal, quod ad clavum subinde sedet in Republica, & sub leonis adorandum est exuviis, etiam tunc, fortè per oblivionem, audit vetus suum verumque nomen, asinus. Fateor equidem in hac Rerum Universitate reperiri quamplurima, quæ humanum animum, ordinis ac elegantiæ cupidissimum, specie suâ delectent, & mirum in modum rapiant: In his etiam tam industria sunt quædam, & ad meram quasi, pompam elaborata, ut Natura, quæ Artis exemplar esse solet, reciproco lusu capta, pta, videatur Artem imitari voluisse: Quomodo minimas aliquas nivium quisquilias, in elegantissimas stellulas crenat & circinat, mille gyris & spiris marinas conchas exsculpit, mille modis Tulipa-rum flores, pavonum caudas, colla columbarum distinguit.
units.tr: The heavens are set down as Physicè simplices, that is, free of Materiae primae & Formae substantialis; for it belongs to the adornment and completion of the world that a body of some such kind should hold it together, and the universe of things would seem maimed if it lacked this Gradu entis. By a similar delirium, the heavenly bodies are not generated, do not corrupt, do not grow, do not diminish, are neither heavy nor light. After this, the stars are endowed with marvellous powers, influentiis & qualitatibus, called occultis by name; and heaviness and lightness, things as well known as anything that is thought most commonly known. The elements are adorned in the same way: each is given two qualitates out of the four first ones. Fire is most hot and excellently dry; air is most moist and excellently hot; water is most cold and excellently moist; earth is most dry and excellently cold. A most pleasing and many-coloured fabric! By the same pattern the same web is woven in the four Humoribus (blood, phlegm, yellow and black bile), in the four seasons of the year (spring, summer, autumn, winter), in the four ages of life (boyhood, youth, the age of settled manhood, old age), and in many other things. Hence some elements are called Symbola, that is, they agree in the same qualitate prima: fire and air in heat, air and water in moisture, water and earth in cold, earth and fire in dryness (these whirl round one another in a dance). Some are Assymbola: fire and water, air and earth (these dance apart). By these considerations they work out the easy and difficult changes of the elements into one another. In these there are also observed many fictions and frivolities, which would take too long to pursue. Sense now and then interrupts and bears witness to other things; they do not believe it, not even on oath. Does it clamour too importunately? They beat its mouth, spit on it, and reproach it with all the impostures they have ever contrived. Let it hold its tongue quickly, because it pleases them, and it is fitting, and it must be so, whatever is so specious. So much for the heavens and the elements, which Mango calls Corpora simplicia. The remaining bodies are Mixta, which are generated here on the surface of the terrestrial globe, or near it: metals, stones, plants and animals. To these belong various complexions, mixed in various ways from the four qualitatum primarum. Thus marble has heat, even while it burns more with icy cold; and there is moisture in pumice, from which you could not squeeze a single drop under the tightest press. Among these and other things of this kind, from which I am deterred from pursuing the catalogue at greater length by nausea, there are no thoughts of reasoning men; all are the opinions of those who want things to be so. And I wonder that they are called by the name of Placitorum by those for whom they serve as oracles. Truth, indeed, holds a grave question against liars; and it extracts from things the names that fit them, even from men who think nothing of the kind and are busy with quite other matters. So that long-eared animal, which now and then sits at the helm in the commonwealth and must be worshipped under the lion's hide, even then, perhaps through forgetfulness, hears its old and true name: ass. I admit that in this universe of things there are very many things which delight the human mind, which is eager for order and elegance, by their appearance, and ravish it in a marvellous way. Among these, some are so industrious and so elaborated for mere display that Nature, which is wont to be the pattern of Art, seems to have been caught in a playful rivalry and to have wished to imitate Art: as she crimps and compasses some tiny trifles of snow into most elegant little stars, carves sea shells with a thousand whorls and spirals, and marks the flowers of tulips, the tails of peacocks and the necks of doves in a thousand ways.

units.la: At vero, si animum attendi-mus, sunt alia non pauciora, quæ tumultuariâ quadam confusione & maligna specie terrent nos & turbant: Sunt cancri & araneæ, sunt fœto-res tetri, sunt horribiles ulu-latus, sunt noctypni lemures, qui diro mentem nostram percellunt phantasmate: Cur igitur Naturam Rerum egregiè giè comprehendisse nos exi-stimamus, si eam pulcritudi-ne, quæ nobis arrideat, & concinnitate definivimus? si limatula, si politula cuncta confinximus? Ultra sepem istam ludit, & (si genium ejus percipis) rudi interdum, incondito ac robusto delectatur magis. Hoc amplius: Multa sunt, quæ magis ad regulam exigere posset, si genio nostro morem gerere Natura vellet: Quid si serenis noctibus, pensiles illos sub cæli camera lychnuchos, confusos jam eos, & nimis temerè dispersos, ita redigeret in quadrum, ut Deorum formas & signa, quæ Poëtæ paripariter ac Astrologi notant, repræsentarent ad vivum? Non defigendus esset obtu-tus, non vis adhibenda Phantasiæ: primo statim in fornicem illum conjectu oculorum, perspicuè notaremus
units.tr: But if we pay attention, there are others no fewer, which terrify and disturb us with a certain tumultuous confusion and a malign appearance: there are crabs and spiders, there are foul stenches, there are horrible howlings, there are nocturnal lemures, which strike our mind with a dreadful phantasm. Why, then, do we think we have grasped the nature of things excellently, if we have defined it by a beauty and neatness that pleases us, if we have fashioned everything smoothly and prettily? It plays beyond that hedge, and (if you perceive its genius) it sometimes delights more in the rough, the unshaped and the robust. Moreover, there are many things which it could bring more into line with a rule, if Nature wished to humour our genius. What if, on clear nights, it reduced those hanging lamps under the vault of heaven, now scattered and too randomly dispersed, into a square, so that they represented to the life the forms and signs of the gods which poets and astrologers alike note? The eye would not need to be fixed, nor would any effort of the imagination be needed: at first glance on that vault we would clearly note

units.la: Pleiadas & Hyadas, claramque Lycaonis Arcton Æmoniosq; arcus, violentique ora Leonis,
units.tr: Pleiadas & Hyadas, claramque Lycaonis Arcton Æmoniosq; arcus, violentique ora Leonis,

units.la: Sævaque circuitu curvantem brachia longo Scorpion, atque aliter curvantem brachia Cancrum.
units.tr: The savage Scorpion curving his arms in a long circuit, and the Crab curving his arms in another way.

units.la: Quod si Lunæ nostræ sororem dedisset Natura, tum vero rem, & visu pulcram, & humanis usibus oppidò fecisset commodam: Tunc inter se pari forte nocturnas stationes partitæ, altera semper pharum ægris mortalibus extulisset: nunquam ferales illas, & tetras, & tam germanas morti, in hibernis interluniis ire svivissent noctes: alterius in interlunio silentium & feriias, alterius in plenilunio compensasset sedulitas & vigilia: simul dividuæ, vesper-tinas illa, hæc matutinas tenebras diluisset: deinceps illa crescendo, plus; hæc decrescendo, minus excubuisset: sequens vices & onera mutasset mensis: Id si ita esset, post homines natos, nihil aptius, nihil pulcrius esset: cur autem ita esse, confirmat nemo?
units.tr: If Nature had given us a sister to our Moon, then indeed the thing would be both fair to see and very convenient for human uses. The two would divide the nightly watches between them by some fair arrangement, and the one would always hold up a torch for sickly mortals. The nights of winter, in the interlunar periods, would never have gone by so gloomy, so savage and so akin to death; the silence and the rest of the one in the interlunar period would have been balanced by the diligence and watchfulness of the other at full moon. Shining together, the one would have dispelled the evening shadows, the other the morning ones; the one would have kept watch more as it waxed, the other less as it waned; the month would have changed the duties and burdens in turn. If it were so, after men were born nothing would be more fitting and nothing more beautiful. But why it should not be so, nobody explains.

units.la: Quia sensus reclamat: potis ille est Philomangones exolvere sacramento: At vero adversum clamores ejus aurem obturabant alibi, cur hic non item? Quia hic vocalis nimium est, & ingenti, quidquid aures opplet, pertundit boatu: Si ergo non altum, increpet, si non stentori is clamoribus objurget ille Censor, putant rem salvam esse, bene geri omnia? Alias raucus est, diutinâ cum surdastris vociferatione, alias hebes, alias caecutit & delirat ipse: Quid ergo? Capio: Errare non recusant: quin immo formosos istos errores suaviari cupiunt, ita dulces videnvidentur; si liceat impune, si absit reprehendentium stomachus & irridentium ciconia. Ita est: amabili quadam deludimur insaniâ, dum posthabitâ Ratione ac Naturæ phænomenis, marte nostro Mundum digerimus: & sicut fabulam qui legunt, initio quidem fabulam esse, satis meminerunt: ideoq; non tam ea, quæ narrantur expendunt, quam narrandi modum, narrantisque indolem, affectus, ac studia; Longius autem provecti & inescati, totâ mente atque omni animo pendent: sperant modo, & modo metuunt, tum gemunt, & seriò tragicis illis nugis illacry-
units.tr: Because the senses cry out against it: and they could bind the Philomangones to an oath to renounce it. But against their clamours they stopped their ears elsewhere, why not here too? Because here it is too loud, and with its huge bellowing it pierces whatever fills the ears. If, then, it does not raise its voice high, if that Censor does not rebuke it with stentorian shouts, do they think the matter is safe and everything is going well? Elsewhere sense is hoarse from prolonged shouting with the deaf, elsewhere dull, elsewhere it grows blind and raves itself. What then? I grasp it: they do not refuse to err; indeed they wish to relish those beautiful errors, since they seem so sweet, provided it is allowed with impunity, provided the spleen of the critics and the mockery of the scoffers is absent. So it is: we are deceived by a certain pleasant madness, while, setting aside Reason and the phenomena of Nature, we arrange the world by our own strength. And just as those who read a fable at first remember well enough that it is a fable, and so they weigh not so much the things that are told as the manner of telling, the character of the teller, his feelings and his zeal; but those who have advanced further and are enticed hang on it with their whole mind and every feeling: now they hope, now they fear, then they groan, and in earnest they weep over those tragic trifles.

units.la: lacrymantur: Ita etiam Philosophi, quod præ opinandi libidine, dogma condiderant, id usu, disputationibus, altercationibus, frequenti docentium inculcatione, flagitiosâ discentium credulitate, superstitiosâ vulgi, de Philosophorum placitis imaginatione, tandem vertunt in fatale & inconcussum Elementum: Sic vis adhibetur Veritati: Hac deinde ligamur, & per errores trahimur catenâ, cujus omnes hamos & annulos, humana procudit stoliditas & vecordia. At tibi repentè! (de via decedite) Amor-sapientiæ depellit Mangonem ab ansa istius, quæ nos tamdiu compedivit, catenæ: Ita enim invehitur: Exi de ambulacris nostris: ocyus, inquam, te proripe, fucate, adulterate Mango, cum intolerabili redundantia, cum typho, quo cives meos infatuas, & fumis, & apparatu: Loco cede genuinæ, nudæ, simplicique Rationi. Stupet ad hoc tonitru leno: & correptâ temerè sub axillis cosmetice, discedit titubante passu: quàque gradum incertum facit, dissipat, quæ brachio non satis astrinxerat, crotala, mitras, redimicula, fibulas: Ponè cum scopis, Amoris-sapientiæ satelles: & everrit: ne quid nudam Rationem, mox præsto futuram. ram, ad pedes offendat.
units.tr: So too the philosophers: whatever they had established as a doctrine out of their lust for opinion, they gradually turn, through use, disputations, quarrels, the constant drumming-in by teachers, the shameful credulity of pupils, and the superstitious imagination of the crowd about the philosophers' opinions, into a fatal and unshakeable element. In this way violence is done to Truth. Then we are bound by it and dragged through errors on a chain, every link and ring of which human stupidity and madness have forged. But suddenly, (make way, you there!) the Lover of Wisdom drives the Mango away from the handle of that chain which has shackled us so long. For he attacks him thus: Get out of our promenades! Off with you quickly, I say, you painted, adulterated Mango, with your intolerable excess, your pride, with which you befool my citizens, with your smoke and your show! Give way to genuine, bare, simple Reason. The pimp is stunned by this thunderclap; and, having hastily seized his cosmetics under the arm, he withdraws with a faltering step. And as he walks unsteadily, he scatters the rattles, mitres, headbands and brooches that he had not gripped tightly enough under his arm. Behind him comes the Lover of Wisdom's attendant with a broom, and he sweeps, lest anything should trip up bare Reason, who will soon be at hand.

units.la: Video, judices, ejecto Pantomimo, exterminato Mangone, evulsis simul eorum de libris nostris, dictatis, commentis, & placitis, Scholasticam pene totam cum illis abiisse Philosophiam, & de turgentibus illis in Bibliotheca volumi-nibus, non nisi exiguam superesse faraginem :, Vix quidquam comperio reliquum, præter Axiomata quædam (ut præ se ferunt) Communes Notiones, & Generales Regulas: In his tamen etiamnum aliquid, quod à Ratione non est: Genius iterum aliquis subolet mihi: exerat se dele latebris suis, prodeat in medium. Hem ! quam venerabilis ille est ! à formoso Pantomino, à compto Mangone, quam diversus ! Talis species in religionem veniat populo: In vestitu nihil, præter depexam togam corpori, & capiti, insigne Magisterii, cucullum: erecta facies & plana, nutus nullus: reducta palpebræ, fortes oculi, fixus obtutus: inflatæ buccæ, sesquipedalium verborum ampullæ: Gestus unicus, quo primoribus digitis in summum pollicem coëuntibus, paulatim cum sententia attollitur manus, & in obliquum recidiva, cum emphasi conconcludit effatum: Natus est hic Genius Delphis, sub Apollinis Tripode: educatus autem apud Sphingem, inter Gryphos & Ænigmata: Singula ejus verba, singula mysteria, singuli verborum ambitus, singula decreta, singula sunt oracula, miro instinctu & afflatu edita, miris modis perplexa: Ipsummet audiamus: Conjugatorum sunt conjugata consequentia: Propter quod unumquodque est tale, ipsum est magis tale: Quidquid recipitur, ad modum recipientis recipitur: Nullum violentum est perpetuum: &c. Si sensum exquiras horum glossematum, aut rationem qua nitantur, in [?]n promptu responsio : Abi ad Pedanos ( sic Philosophiæ [?]yrunculos, contemptim appellat præcellentissimus Magister ) & disce : Quid ni? Fundamenta sunt, Principia sunt ; At ubi rudimenta ipsa [?]radit Dogmatistes, si quis-piam præ condiscipulis suis [?]ardelio, magnorum istorum crepituum petat aliquam ratiunculam, Tu, inquit, tace puer : Tu asinus ad lyram es : Aristotelis scitum est ( etiamsi Aristoteles id scisçat nusquam ) Discentem debere credere: O dolosum circulum! provectos ad rudimenta mittit ; rudimentum ex profectu suspendit : His igitur Principiis piis proveniunt nobis impo- sterum falsa multa, involut- quam plurima, quia Princi- piis commentitiis contortis- que proveniunt. Sed ecce aliud quiddam in commodum studiosæ juventutis meditatus est Magister Noster: rem hercule compendio facilem! Tene hæc pauca, tyruncule, & te deinceps, te, inquam, Naturæ consultior erit nemo: Intelligentias, formas substantiales, Causam primam, Influentias & Qualitates occultas, Vapores & exhalationes: Percepistin' hæc puncta? Euge! his expedies omnia: Intelligentias quidem non applicabis, nisi ad res magni momenti nenti magnique moliminis, quæ in valto & patente, quasi ad pompam fiunt: velut ad crusatiles cælorum molas circumagendas, & aquas in marina mactra, quo statis horis intumescant subigendas: Cavesis, ne arboribus, aut herbis, aut lapidibus Intelligentiam ullam adjunxeris, ne Magneti quidem: licet enim hujus operatio, mirabilis valde, plena sit industriæ: at in angulo exercetur, non ita palam, nec in theatro: unde is Influentiâ, quæ de minorum gentium Diis est, contentus sit. Formis substantialibus abutendum tibi erit, ad mutandum corpora, sive intrinsecus, cùs, quod ipsis eorum formis attribues, sive extrinsecùs, quod formæ corporis vicini imputabis; si nulla sit ad manum, cui negotium hoc committi posse videatur, ad asylum commune, ad Influentias cælestes confugies. Causâ primâ opus tibi est in formandis & producendis Formis substantialibus, exceptis tamen formis Elementorum, quibus speciatim concessum est sobolescere, & stirpem suam in vicinia propagare; Cæteræ formæ cælibes sunt & viduæ: & introductis in Materia Dispositionibus, ut plurimùm, à cælorum occultis [virtutibus], Auctor Naturæ supplet eas de suo penu. Tandem, ne longior sim, Vapores & exhalationes habe tibi ad omnem Antiperistasim, omniaque Meteora & Imperfectè mixta discutiendum. I jam, ascende Cathedram, resolve magistraliter,
units.tr: I see, judges, that with the pantomime cast out and the Mango banished, and with their dictates, commentaries and opinions torn out of our books at the same time, almost the whole of Scholastic philosophy has departed with them, and of those swollen volumes in the library only a small heap remains. I can scarcely find anything left except certain axioms (as they call them) common notions and general rules. Yet even among these there is something that does not come from Reason. Some genius, I sense, is again stirring: let him come out of his hiding place and step forward into the open. Ah! How venerable he is! How different from the handsome pantomime and the elegant Mango! Let such a figure come before the people in religious guise: in his dress nothing except a combed-out toga over his body and, on his head, the badge of the teacher's office, a hood. His face is stiff and flat, with no nod; his eyelids drawn back, his eyes fierce, his gaze fixed; his cheeks puffed out, bubbles of words a foot and a half long. His only gesture: with the first fingers joined to the thumb, his hand is gradually raised with the sentence, and then, bent back obliquely, he closes the pronouncement with emphasis. This Genius was born at Delphi, beneath the tripod of Apollo, but was brought up among the Sphinx, the Gryphons and the riddles. Each of his words is a mystery, each circuit of words is a puzzle, each decree is an oracle, uttered by a wonderful impulse and inspiration, and wonderfully tangled. Let us hear him himself: Conjugates have conjugate consequences; for which reason each thing is such, it is itself more such; whatever is received is received according to the mode of the receiver; no violent thing is perpetual; etc. If you ask for the meaning of these glosses, or the reason on which they rest, the answer is ready at hand: Go to the pedants (so the most excellent Master contemptuously calls the little wranglers of philosophy) and learn. Why not? They are foundations, they are principles. But when the Dogmatist scrapes the very rudiments, if some busybody among his fellow pupils seeks some small reason from those great rumblings, Be quiet, boy, he says, you are a donkey at the lyre. It is a rule of Aristotle (although Aristotle nowhere said so) that the pupil must believe. O deceitful circle! He sends the advanced back to the rudiments, and suspends the rudiment on progress. So from these pious principles there arise for us many false doctrines, very many entangled ones, because they arise from twisted and fictitious principles. But look, our Master has devised something else for the benefit of studious youth, a thing easy indeed by a short cut! Hold these few things, little tyro, and after this, I say, no one will be more skilled in Nature than you: Intelligences, substantial forms, the First Cause, occult Influences and Qualities, vapours and exhalations. Have you grasped these points? Splendid! With these you will explain everything. Intelligences you will apply only to matters of great importance and great effort, which are done in the open and in full view, as if in a procession: for example, to turn the crystalline mills of the heavens, and to set in motion the waters in the sea's engine so that they swell at fixed hours. Take care not to attach any Intelligence to trees, herbs or stones, nor even to the magnet: for although its operation is very wonderful and full of industry, it is carried on in a corner, not so openly nor on a stage; so let it be content with the Influence that belongs to the lesser tribe of gods. You will have to misuse substantial forms for changing bodies, either internally, by attributing it to the very forms of those bodies, or externally, by imputing it to the form of a neighbouring body; if no body is at hand to which the business seems able to be entrusted, you will flee to the common refuge, the heavenly Influences. You need the First Cause in forming and producing substantial forms, except the forms of the Elements, to which it is specially granted to breed and to propagate their stock in their neighbourhood; the other forms are celibate and widowed. And once dispositions have been introduced into matter, for the most part the Author of Nature supplies them from his own store, from the hidden [virtues] of the heavens. Finally, not to be too long, keep vapours and exhalations ready for every antiperistasis and for dispelling all meteors and imperfectly mixed bodies. Now go on, ascend the chair, resolve magisterially.

units.la: —— Sume superbiam quæsitam meritis.
units.tr: Take the pride that your merits have won.

units.la: Quis ineptias istas ferat? quis cordatus homo est, qui se scire aliquid in Natura rerum existimet, cum ista sciverit? Quid enim? si quis te miraculi alicujus caussam interroget; tu vero Intelligentiam adferas, aut Influentiam, aut occultas rerum Sympathias & Antipathias, quid ista summatim continet responsio, nisi simplex illud, quod quilibet è plebe responderet, Nescio? Hoc tantum inter te, & illos interest, quod hi quidem humeros adducant, & ignorantiam suam fateantur ingenuè; tu streperis quibusdam verbis fucum facias, & dissimules: Et vero si quæratur, cur aqua, quæ inferbuit, ab igne semota, refrigescat: Cur adductæ, & in arcus sinuatæ virgulæ, si remittantur, in rectum se porrigant: Cur rugatum ab igne corium, si in cella recondatur, explicet se denuo: Respondebis Formam substantialem talium corporum, aut Potentiam aliquam in iis resi-dendentem, hæc omnia machinari? Nugæ! Scopæ dissolutæ! Fili istius, quo res omnes pulcerrimè cum Principiis & primis Notionibus Natura copulavit & vinxit, abruptio manifesta! Non inclementius dico, quam par est: ponam exemplum, ut videas: Sit in Geometria rudis quispiam & idiota, stylo Dogmatistæ docebo eum hac horâ (& equidem non indigeo totâ) ut tam peritus sit Geometriæ, quam deponatus aliquis Philosophus, Phisicæ peritus est: Hoc igitur primum positum sit, Triangulum esse aliquid ad instar Corporis naturalis: Materiæ teria vicem supplebit Magnitudo (hæc enim indifferens est circa varias Formas, nempe (Circuli, Parallelogrammi, &c.) In Formæ loco habebimus, trium rectarum linearum, extremis inter se punctis tagentium, cohærentiam: His igitur ita positis, Geometricæ institutionis incipit mihi initium: Tres anguli in Triangulo simul simpti, duobus rectis angulis simul sumptis sunt pares: Sit enim triangulum quodcumque: tum altero pede circini in ejus apice defixo, altero pede portionem circuli, summo angulo, à latere ad latus, quibus utrimque stringitur, subtende: idem fac duobus reliquis, qui ad basim sunt, angulis, circini cruribus eodem semper intervallo divaricatis: collige jam tres istos arcus, tribus istis angulis subtentos, & in unum arcum dispone: semicirculum habebis, tantam scilicet circuli portionem, quanta duobus rectis angulis subtendendis sufficiat: Eo igitur ventum est, ut tres angulos in triangulo, duobus rectis angulis æquales esse, perinde compertum sit, & experientiâ notum, atque aquam ad frigus se reducere, vel ferrum ad Magnetem tendere. Restat (quod in Disciplinis utramque paginam facit) ut Ratio promenda sit, cur in triantriangulo, omnes anguli, sint æquales duobus rectis: Hanc in promptu habet Dogmatistes: & accipe: Quia Forma trianguli per naturalem resultantiam tres angulos suos cum duobus rectis angulis adæquat. Pergo: In triangulo, angulus externus, interno opposito major est: Id etiam circino expende: si enim unum latus trianguli deinceps producatur, majorem arcum ei subtendes, quam angulo intra triangulum consistenti subtendi possit: illud igitur sic esse, rursum experimento certum habemus: Ratio petitur? Eadem illa, quæ Formam trianguli caussatur, adferri quiquidem poterat (nam in omnem pedem quadrat iste cothurnus) sed grata varietas: Aliud igitur Dogmatistæ nostro emungamus oraculum: Exclusa, conclusis ampliora sinuntur: angulus igitur exclusus, & extra triangulum positus, inclulo angulo major erit: & quamvis hoc argumento, angulum externum, non minus interno apposito, quam interno opposito, majorem esse, efficiatur; Dogmatistes tamen decernit, ut tum modò valeat Regula, cum de angulo externo & interno opposito sermo est: nam, inquit, cum de angulis appositis loquimur, non semper locum cum habet ista Regula: & quid mirum? Omnis Regula patitur exceptionem. Porro pergo: Si duae rectae lineae inter se secuerint, angulos ad verticem aequales facient: Hîc pro ratione, Naturalis quædam Sympathia istorum angulorum adferri poterit: In triangulo rectangulo, quadratum lateris, quod recto angulo opponitur, reliquorum laterum quadratis, aequale est: Hîc jam in consilium adhibere possumus Intelligentiam unam & alteram: est enim hoc Theorema maximi momenti & Pythagoras (ut nobis narrant) cum id invenisset, tantum accepit subitò lætitiæ, ut hecatombem facefaceret. Dixi : Pergat jam quisque isto tenore, & suo marte Mathemata omnia resolvat & pandat : Quid ais Euclides bone, de extempora-libus hisce meis Mathematicis? num te pænitet jam operosæ Demonstrationis, & longæ solicitæque tuorum Effatorum ad Principia deductionis? Ridete Mathematici, & scitote hos meos Geometras-tros, & hodiernos Physicos iisdem cæpis vesci. Satis est: Amor-sapientiæ ad pronunciandam sententiam accingitur : Quid agat? exilio multet Dogmatistam? Mitior quidem ista sententia feri in Pantomimum & Mangogonem potuit, quibus alibi res suæ, nec teuues, erant; ambitio (ut fit) compulerat in aliena; At monstrum hoc nulli bono est, extra, quam intra Scholam perniciosius: Alibi inter veneficos characteres deformat & immurmurat carmina: alibi cum perspicillis ad nasum, legit Sybillam, & interpretatur, & ponderat, & superstitionem injicit popello: Inter haruspices alibi secat animalia, exta consulit, observat avium volatus, & hominum steruntamenta: Alibi inter Physiognomos ex fatalibus in fronte manibusque lineis, præsagia sumit eventuum & fortunæ: Alibi cum judiciariis Astrologis notat Planetarum Domos & Aspectus, Rhumbos facit & Horoscopos: Totum illud atræ bilis plasma squallidum, tetrum, nullâ caussâ, nullâ ratione fundatum, totum ex Phantasiæ ludibrio susceptum, totum se debet huic Genio infesto, perverso, prœposters. Præstat igitur, ut hîc oportunè deprehensus, tradatur lictoribus exurendus: Pyram dabunt tot chartarum in bibliothecis nostris paginæ, impofturis ejus deformatæ. Annuit Amor-sapientiæ: & jubet, ut lictores sui, Zelus-veri & Contemptus-falsi, sententiam tentiam istam quantocyus exsequantur. Tantà judicis severitate deterriti, prori- piunt se è Schola quam plu- rimi pusiones Genii, quos nominare mihi in promptu non est; Antesignanum tamen novi: Gerro est: qui pridem ex trivialibus Scholis, ex Grammatica & imâ Diale- ctícâ huc appellens, gerras multas nobis contexuit, ver- borum tricis detinuit, sylla- bis anxiè discutiendis exer- cuit, proposuit quæstiuncu- las multas exiles, frivolas, rancidas, auctaria, corollaria, parerga: Esto: Fugâ sibi con- sulant: Acuratâ in abjectam illam plebeculam accusatione, sacræ judicis nostri aures nonerant obtundendæ.
units.tr: What man of sense could put up with such nonsense? What thinking person would believe he knows anything about the nature of things because he has learned these? Suppose someone asks you the cause of some marvel, and you bring forward Intelligence, or Influence, or the hidden Sympathies and Antipathies of things. What does such an answer amount to in short, except that simple word any common man would give, I don't know? The only difference between you and them is that they shrug their shoulders and frankly admit their ignorance, whereas you bluster with certain words, put on a show, and hide the truth. Or if someone asks why water, taken off the fire after boiling, cools; why twigs bent into arcs spring straight again when released; why leather shrivelled by fire unfolds again when put away in a cupboard: you will reply that a substantial form of such bodies, or some power residing in them, brings about all these things. Trifles! Loose brooms! A plain breach in that thread by which Nature has beautifully joined and bound all things to their principles and first notions! I say no more harshly than is fitting. I will give an example so you may see. Suppose there is some rude and untaught fellow in geometry. I will teach him, in the manner of a Dogmatist, (and I do not need the whole hour for this) so that he becomes as skilled in geometry as some deposed philosopher is in physics. Let this be laid down first: a triangle is something like a natural body. Magnitude will take the place of matter (for this is indifferent to the various forms, namely circle, parallelogram, etc.). In place of form we shall have the cohesion of three straight lines touching one another at their extremities. With these things so laid down, the beginning of my geometrical instruction starts. The three angles of a triangle taken together are equal to two right angles taken together. For let there be any triangle whatever. Then, with one leg of the compass fixed at its apex, and the other leg, at the largest angle, from side to side, you stretch an arc of a circle which is bounded on either side. Do the same for the two remaining angles, which are at the base, keeping the legs of the compass always opened to the same interval. Now gather these three arcs, subtended by these three angles, and set them together into one arc: you will have a semicircle, that is, precisely that portion of a circle which suffices to subtend two right angles. So it has come about that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles is found in just the same way, and is known by experience, as water is reduced to cold, or iron is drawn to a magnet. What remains (which fills both pages in the textbooks) is that a reason must be given why in a triangle all the angles are equal to two right angles. The Dogmatist has this ready: take it. Because the form of the triangle, by a natural result, makes its three angles equal to two right angles. I go on. In a triangle, the exterior angle is greater than the interior opposite angle. Weigh this also with the compass. For if you extend one side of the triangle in a straight line, you will subtend with it a larger arc than can be subtended by the angle lying within the triangle. We therefore hold, again by experiment, that this is so. Do you want a reason? The very same thing that causes the form of the triangle could indeed be brought forward (for this buskin fits every foot), but variety is pleasing. So let us wring another oracle from our Dogmatist: Things shut out are allowed more room than things shut in. Therefore the excluded angle, placed outside the triangle, will be greater than the enclosed angle. And although by this argument it is established that the exterior angle is no less greater than the interior adjacent angle than the interior opposite one, the Dogmatist nevertheless rules that the rule holds only when we speak of the exterior angle and the interior opposite one. For, he says, when we speak of adjacent angles, this rule does not always apply. And what wonder? Every rule admits of an exception. Further I proceed: If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal. For the reason here, some natural sympathy of these angles may be cited. In a right-angled triangle, the square of the side which is opposite the right angle is equal to the squares of the other sides. Here we may now call in one or another intelligence to help: for this theorem is of the greatest importance, and Pythagoras (as they tell us), when he had found it, was so overcome with sudden joy that he sacrificed a hecatomb. I have spoken. Let everyone now proceed in this vein, and by his own strength resolve and unfold all the mathematics: What do you say, good Euclid, to these extempore mathematics of mine? Do you not now regret your laborious demonstrations and your long and anxious deduction of your propositions to first principles? Laugh, mathematicians, and know that these my little Geometers, and today's physicists, feed on the same scraps. Enough. The Love-of-wisdom gets ready to pronounce sentence. What shall he do? Shall he fine the Dogmatist with exile? That sentence might have been milder, sent off to the pantomime and Mangogo, where their affairs, not slight, were elsewhere; ambition (as happens) had driven them into other men's business. But this monster is harmful to no good end, more pernicious outside the School than within it. Elsewhere he traces out and mutters incantations among the characters of poisoners; elsewhere, with spectacles on his nose, he reads the Sibyl, and interprets, and weighs, and throws superstition upon the common folk. Among the soothsayers he cuts up animals elsewhere, consults entrails, watches the flights of birds and the droppings of men. Elsewhere among the physiognomists he takes omens of events and of fortune from the fateful lines on the forehead and palms. Elsewhere, with the judicial astrologers, he notes the houses and aspects of the planets, makes rhumbs and horoscopes. That whole squalid, foul clay of black bile, founded on no cause and no reason, wholly taken up from the mockery of fancy, owes everything to this hostile, perverse and preposterous Genius. It is therefore best that he, caught here at the right moment, be handed over to the lictors to be burnt. The pages of so many papers in our libraries, deformed by his impostures, will supply the pyre. The Love-of-wisdom nods, and orders that his lictors, Zeal-for-truth and Contempt-for-falsehood, carry out this sentence as quickly as possible. Terrified by the judge's severity, very many of the little boys of the Genius dash out of the School, whose names I have not ready to hand. I know one forerunner, however: Gerro. He, having come here some time ago from the trivial schools, from grammar and the lowest dialectic, wove many a chatter for us, held us in the snares of words, kept us busy with anxious scrutiny of syllables, put forward many slight, frivolous, rancid little questions, addenda, corollaries, sidelines. Very well: let them look to their own safety by flight. With a careful accusation of that abject little crowd, the ears of our sacred judge must not be deafened.

units.la: Erasis jam, excisis & abolitis, cæcis istis Geniorum nostrorum commentis, paucula supersunt, quæ sola Ratio dictat Principia: exposita in propatulo, cunctis nota, purissimo liquidæ Veritatis radio conspicua: Dives inopia! immensus in parvo scrinio thesaurus! Eliciemus illum & expromemus; sed sensim & sine sensu: Præcipites hîc, prurientes, inconsideratos esse non decet: Gemmas istas tener ordo devinxit, si avidè, si temerè manum injicis, turbantur, excidunt, & cum spuriis,
units.tr: With these blind inventions of our Genii now erased, cut out and abolished, a few things remain, which Reason alone dictates as principles: set out in the open, known to all, visible in the purest ray of clear Truth. Rich in poverty! An immense treasure in a small chest! We shall draw it out and bring it forth, but gradually and without noticing it. It is not fitting to be hasty here, eager or thoughtless. A delicate order binds those gems together; if you lay hands on them greedily and rashly, they are thrown into confusion, fall out, and among the spurious things

units.la: quæ humi jacent, confusæ, suspeẜtæque, non satis internoscuntur. Et hinc ordine murato, quem tradendis scientiis majores nostri præscripserunt, expediret iis primum Disciplinis excolendam dare juventutem, quæ sine ulla Hypothesi, meræ ex CommunibusNotionibus demonstrant suas Propositiones: quales sunt Geometria & Arithmetica. Ante tamen Scientiam Consequentiarum, quæ est in Logica, percepe-rint: sine qua Apodixes Mathematicæ non satis feliciter procedunt, & cujus ope compendium in illis non exiguum fieri potest: Quæ quidem scienscientia non ita ex tempore & sparsim (ut hodie fit) velut sylva quædam & rhapsodia tradatur; sed ordine ac tenore Geometrico; Hanc autem, quam dico, Consequentiæ scientiam ita corrigi, & in apicem illum evidentiæ subvehi posse, cum jam ante certum haberem ex ratione, ipso etiam eventu, & successu, quem nuper publici juris feci, edoctus sum. Tribus his, Logicæ, Geometriæ, Arithmeticæ, Metaphysicam subnectant, sed probe repurgatam, Mentis & Corporis essentiam ac Proprietates apodictice perhibentem. Dein ad rerum naturalium Historiam applicentur: tur: Hanc voco congeriem ex diversis Naturæ Phænomenis experimentisque certis & indubitatis; purâ narratione sine conjectura rationis, ob quam ita se habere videantur, propositis: Hæc Historia à docentibus in communia quædam capita digeretur: hanc tyrones non Legent in libris dumtaxat, aut ex pulpito audient; sed oculis ac manibus usurpabunt: tantisper suspecta sint, quæ ab his vel illis Physiologis arcana jactantur: Constat enim res obviâ facillimâque experientiâ tentandas, totam retro Vetustaten fefellisse: velut plumbum celerius labi per aëra.
units.tr: which lie on the ground, jumbled and suspect, they cannot be sufficiently distinguished. Hence, with the order walled round which our elders have prescribed for handing down the sciences, it would be useful first to give young people to those disciplines which demonstrate their propositions without any hypothesis, from common notions alone: such as geometry and arithmetic. Yet before that, they should learn the science of consequences, which is in logic, without which the mathematical demonstrations do not proceed happily enough, and by whose help a not small shortcut can be made in them. This science, I say, should not be taught extemporaneously and scattered (as is done today), like some forest or patchwork, but in a geometric order and sequence. I have long been sure from reason, and have since been taught by the outcome and success itself, which I lately made public, that this science of consequence can be corrected in this way and raised to that summit of evidence. To these three, logic, geometry and arithmetic, let them add metaphysics, but properly purged, setting out apodictically the essence and properties of mind and body. Then let them be applied to the history of natural things. I call this a collection of various phenomena of Nature and certain and indubitable experiments, set forth by plain narrative without conjecture of reason for why they seem to be so. This history should be arranged by teachers under certain common headings; students will not read it in books only, or hear it from the pulpit, but will use it with their eyes and hands. Meanwhile, whatever secrets this or that physiologist boasts of should be held in suspicion. For it is established that things which are to be tested by plain and easy experience have deceived all antiquity: for example, that lead falls through the air more quickly than wood, a fact unknown to the ancients, and a experiment now exploded even by the street boys.

units.la: æra, quam lignum, indubi-ratum Antiquis; explodit ho-die ipsis etiam triviis non ignotum experimentum. Et hinc Academiarum supellex non erunt vasta illa volumina, inepti centones, in quibus cæci disputant de coloribus, & pecorum ritu, in Veterum sententias abeunt Minores; sed telescopia, quibus è cælo remotissima quævis adducun-tur, nova sidera deteguntur, aliorum cornua, aliorum asperitates, quas longo intervallo dissimulant, veniunt, in conspectum, insuper herbarum & fruticum horti, Anatomica Theatra, Alembici, fornaces, Magnetes, aliaque id genus, quæ Natura voluit suorum miraculorū acervos, illices & exploratores esse. Intelligentia jam à scientiis cultâ, ab Experientiis firmâ ac maturâ, Hypothesis Physica proponatur, quæ Sensum cum Ratione, Experimenta cum Scientiis ad amussim conciliet. Tandem agmen hoc claudat Ethica
units.tr: ...for the lead falls faster through the air than wood, a fact the ancients never doubted and which is now refuted by a test not unknown even to the common street. Hence the furniture of the Academies will not be those vast volumes, those clumsy patchworks in which the blind dispute about colours and, like sheep, pass over into the opinions of the ancients as lesser men. Instead there will be telescopes, through which the most distant objects of the heavens are brought close, new stars are discovered, and the horns and roughnesses of others, which they hid at a great distance, come into view; in addition, the gardens of herbs and shrubs, anatomical theatres, alembics, furnaces, magnets, and other things of that kind, which Nature wanted to be heaps of her wonders, lures and testers. Let a Physical Hypothesis now be put forward, one informed by the sciences, firm and mature through experience, which will bring sense into exact agreement with reason and experiments with the sciences. At last let Ethics close this procession.

units.la: Eja Amor sapientiæ, in sublime te tolle: desere nos hîc tantisper cum plebe, æternum equidem tibi jurejurando devinctos: Incesse summorum Magistratuum & Principum Virorum pectora: opus est eorum robusto brachio, ut Genus Humanum in sutiutilitatem & indignas nugas iam altè demersum eruatur: Hæc restat, & si modò capiant, sola penè restat ad Divinitatem via: Bellis istis & cladibus, quibus ferarum ritu in mutam necem sævimus hodie, non gloriam, sed proborum rependet æqua posteritas: & magna forte, quæ nunc veneramur nomina, audient olim ( quod sunt ) cruentæ belluæ & Humani Generis lanii. I, Amor sapientiæ: supple quæ subticeo: &, si visum fuerit, adde etiam acriora: Audes enim: A me quidem dicta, & frustra ferent, & non tuta.
units.tr: Come, Love of wisdom, lift yourself up on high. Leave us here for a while with the common people, though we are bound to you forever by oath. Penetrate the hearts of the highest magistrates and the leading men of princes; their strong arm is needed to drag the human race out of its filth, its useless trifles, and its unworthy follies, into which it has sunk deep. This is the one way left, and if they will but take it, it is almost the only way left to the Divine. Fair posterity will not reward with glory but with the name of good men those wars and slaughters in which today we rage like beasts of prey in a dumb killing; and the great names we now revere will one day be heard for what they are: bloody beasts and butchers of the human race. Go on, Love of wisdom, supply what I pass over in silence, and, if you think fit, add even sharper things. For you dare; what I have said will be fruitless and not safe.

units.la: DIXI.
units.tr: I HAVE SPOKEN.

units.la: Quæstio I.
units.tr: Question I.

units.la: An mutuæ per plateas & templa, Salutationes approbandæ?
units.tr: Whether greetings exchanged in the streets and temples are to be approved?

units.la: Nosci omnes appetunt Non notum fuisse, fermè est non natum fuisse: Ii ipsi, qui Cynico quasi stupore perculsi, in dolium se abdidère, familiares salutationes & celebriora commercia dedignantes, id unum agunt ut facti raritas, oculos in se defigat intuentium, dum cæteri consueta tractantes, levi oculorum conjectu transmittuntur. Quid ni igitur Salutationes illæ inter amicos passim obvios, sint approbandæ? quibus solis, & nosci se à multis, & amari videt & coli, cui illæ frequentiores obtingunt. Adde, hoc pacto futuræ amicitiæ fundamenta commodissilissimè jaci: dum qui primus salu-at, aut parem, aut majorem, il-ius erga se animum explorat & sentat, qui in resalutantis nutu vel gestu, manifesto plerumque se prodit indicio: Dum interea qui æpè jam salutavit ac resalutatus est, ad colloquium & familiares sermones, & prorumpit fidenter, & admittitur facilè: in his, & animi sui sensa studiaque significat, & obsequia desert, &, quod amare perspiciatur, redamatur: fitque jam subitò necessarius & intimus, qui paulò ante totus erat præter rem & extraneus. Quin etiam veteri & radicatæ amicitiæ, fomentum suppeditant & succum, blandi illi amicorum sibi occurren-rium applausus, suaves arrisiones: quibus nihil aliud, quam mutuos mores & genium novisse se fatentur & approbare: Estque usu experientiâ quam notissimum nubilam curis & mœrore mentem vel uno benevolo arridentis oculi radio, sæpe detergi ac defæcari. Quin etiam leviter interdum sus-cepti simultatum igniculi, irarum tamen & inimicitiæ incendia, n[?]i ocyus provisum fuerit, meditantes, hac arte commodè præfocantur, & animi ad lenitatem dantur, ut, si quid jurgii & offensiuncularum inter amicos obortum sit ( sic enim vivitur ) salutet prior, qui ansam dedit indignandi, aut visus est dedisse. Denique his ultro citroque salutantium officiis constat publico vigor & vita: dum in platearum compitis obviam facti, catervatim inter se inclinant, festivo ritu capita nudantes, & in templorum atriis, stridente plantarum ad pavimentum affrictu, nescio quid solenne exhibentes
units.tr: Everyone longs to be known; not to have been known is almost the same as never having been born. Even those who, struck as it were by Cynic astonishment, have shut themselves in a tub, scorning familiar greetings and the more common forms of social intercourse, have one aim: that the rarity of their conduct should fix the eyes of onlookers upon them, while the others, going about their customary business, are passed over with a slight glance. Why, then, should those greetings between friends who meet one another everywhere not be approved? By these alone a man sees that he is known and loved and honoured by many, if such greetings come to him more often. Add that by this means the foundations of future friendship are very conveniently laid. The one who greets first, whether an equal or a superior, tests and perceives the disposition of the other towards himself, which for the most part reveals itself plainly in the nod or gesture of the one returning the greeting. Meanwhile, the one who has greeted often and been greeted in return then speaks freely and is readily admitted into conversation and familiar talk. In these he shows the feelings and inclinations of his mind, offers his services, and, since he is seen to love, is loved in return; and he who a little before was altogether a stranger and an outsider soon becomes a necessary and intimate friend. Indeed, the warm welcomes that friends give one another when they meet, and their sweet smiles, provide nourishment and sap to an old and rooted friendship. By these they confess that they have come to know and approve one another's manners and temperament; and, as experience shows, a mind clouded by cares and sorrow is often cleared and refined by the single ray of a kindly smiling eye. Even the small sparks of enmity that sometimes arise, but would threaten to kindle the fires of anger and hatred unless quickly dealt with, are smothered in good time by this art, and minds are brought to gentleness, so that if any quarrel or little offence has arisen between friends (for that is how life goes), the one who gave cause for indignation, or seemed to have given it, greets first. Finally, it is by these mutual services of greeting that public vigour and life are maintained: when people meet at the crossroads of the streets, they bow to one another in crowds, uncovering their heads in festive ritual, and in the courts of the temples, with the scraping of feet on the pavement, they perform I know not what solemn rite.

units.la: His argumentis tamen multum derogat perversa & indigna quorundam ambitio: hoc officii genus, quod amicorum candor protulit, in fastum & fastidium præposterè detorquentium: Dum grandi elatoque supercilio obambulantes & nescio quid luridum ac torvum tuentes, obsequiorum & salutationum vectigalia jure suo exigere videntur: Quæ si quandoque prætereuntium, vel simplicitas, vel candor pendat, idem tamen illis, qui ante, stat silens ac feralis aspectus: Ac non nisi post justam moram, manus gravatè ad pileum ascendit, eumque transversum vix unguem à capite tollit, & fastidium illico reponit: Erubescente interea officioso salutatore, & anxio, quibus cæremoniis infesto illi & malè ominato numini deinceps supplicandum sit. Sed quod hi affectant (& non ferendum est) hoc Philomusi illi & mortuorum socii, præter animi sui sententiam patiuntur (& ignoscendum est) ut nimirum distractâ sæpè atque in museio plusquam semirelictâ mente, in publicum prodeuntes, amicorum occursus non percipiant, eosque velut ignotos prætereant, aut impensè officiosis tantum frigidè respondeant: Itaque in sermonem incidunt & vapulant: nam habet ista suspicio neglecti officii, acre quid & mordax, quod acerbam ex intervallo vellicat, nec sopiri patitur memoriam: scilicet turpis repulsæ speciem habet, si quem ambibat salutans, is resalutâdo non deferatur honos: Atqui à tam futili caussa sæpè compertum est provenire, ut boni doctique viri, ubi pro meritis amari se putant, maledicorum quiquidem linguis (quod solet) exagitentur; sed nec amicorum (quod par erat) favore subleventur. Denique compositis his salutationum gestibus, quibus in dies adolescentum vanitas addit demitque, inest virilis animi quædam effæminatio & fucata lascivia: quæ per simulationem humanitatis, libidinis caussam agit: Venustarum mulierum ac juvenum occursus salaci blanditiâ, fora plateasque infamat, & in Ecclesiis sacra Divis musica profanatur: dum ad ejus modos, puellaris gressus & pellex corporis demissio se confingunt, cum illecebris & lubrico spiritu oculorum, cernuas procorum turmas lacessente.
units.tr: Yet this good argument is much weakened by the perverse and unworthy ambition of some people, who turn this kind of courtesy, which friendly candour brought forth, into arrogance and disdain. Strutting about with a haughty and lofty brow, and gazing at I know not what sallow and grim thing, they seem to exact the tribute of attentions and salutations as their right. If at any time the simplicity or good nature of passers-by pays it, their look remains silent and gloomy as before; and not until after a due pause does the hand reluctantly rise to the hat, lift it barely a finger's breadth from the head, and at once put back their disdain. Meanwhile the obliging greeter blushes and is anxious as to what rites must be offered to that hostile and ill-omened deity. But what these men aim at (and it is not to be tolerated), those lovers of the Muses, companions of the dead, suffer against their own judgement (and it is to be pardoned): namely, that, with their minds often distracted and nearly half-abandoned in their study, they go out in public and fail to notice their friends who meet them; they pass them by as though they were strangers, or give only a cold reply to those who are most attentive. And so they fall into talk and are battered by it. For such a suspicion of neglected courtesy has something sharp and biting, which pricks painfully after an interval and does not allow the memory to be lulled to sleep. Indeed, it looks like a shameful rebuff if the honour is not returned to one whom the greeter had sought out. And yet it has often been found that from so trivial a cause good and learned men, when they think themselves loved for their merits, are harassed by the tongues of slanderers (as usually happens), but are not relieved by the favour of their friends (as would be fitting). Finally, in these gestures of greeting, which the vanity of young people daily adds to and takes away from, there is a certain effeminacy of manly spirit and a painted wantonness, which, under the pretence of courtesy, serves the cause of lust: with alluring flattery they disgrace the markets and the streets by meeting beautiful women and young men, and in the churches sacred music is profaned by its melodies, while the girlish steps and the lowered bodies of harlots shape themselves to those tunes, with enticements and a slippery look of the eyes that provoke the bowing crowds of suitors.

units.la: Commentarius.
units.tr: Commentary.
