units.la: SAlutationis seu reverentiæ, quam adversus alios adhibemus, ritus vatus varii, variae veluti cæremo- niæ: Omnes in eo conveniunt, quod prosternant & supplicem faciant eum, qui salutat: nam cernui plerique salutantium, corpus antrorsum inclinant: mulieres rigido quidem pectore, flectunt poplites: Viri inter Christianos galerum, quem ex lanis coactis cum aliquanto apice, gestare solent, à capite tollunt: quo ritu, minores jam, & subsidisse quodammodo videntur. Omnes hosce gestus idem aliquis Genius animat: omnes enim, ut vidimus, dejiciunt salutantem, & hoc ipso quasi efferunt salutatum, sublimen eum ac cælo propiorem faciunt: Quia enim importunum erat, si quem salutatum venires, manibus levare & sursum agere deberes, hinc alia id via tentandum erat: nam quasi idem assequeris, cum te ipse prosternis sternis aut quoquo pacto diminuis: sic enim salutatus attollitur, & te humili sublimis est. Cælum hic nobis in corpore versantibus pulcherrima res visa est: quæ magni facimus, omnia hæc in cælum aut ad cælum ferimus, si non re, saltem animo, verbis, laudibus; Sed ecce! cum Genium istum studiose inspicio, corripior ipso Genio: nam Magni facere, quod dixi, ab ejus æstro fuit: magna siquidem appropinquant cælo. Huc faciunt reliquæ phrases, quibus, quæ laudare volumus, Alta dicimus, Ingentia, Sublimia, & Eminere; quæ contemnimus, Demissa, Abjecta, Humilia, & Jacere. Huc & mores faciunt: nam principes in solio, judices in tribunali, professores in cathedra, ut magni facimus, ita in eminenti locamus.
units.tr: Of the greeting, or of the reverence which we show towards others, there are various customs and various ceremonies. All agree in this, that they prostrate or abase the one who greets: for most greeters bow the body forward with head lowered; women, with stiff bodies, bend the knees; men among Christians take off from the head the hat, which they are accustomed to wear, made of pressed wool with a little point. By this rite they seem already to be made smaller and to have sunk down in some way. Some one genius inspires all these gestures; for all, as we have seen, cast down the one who greets, and by this very act as it were raise up the one greeted, make him lofty and nearer to heaven. For since it would be inconvenient, if you were to greet someone, to lift him with your hands and carry him upward, another way had to be tried: for you achieve the same thing as if you prostrate yourself or in some way lower yourself: for so the one greeted is raised up, and you are made low while he is lofty. Heaven seemed to us, while we dwell in the body, the most beautiful thing; whatever we value highly, we carry all these things up to heaven or toward heaven, if not in deed, at least in mind, in words, in praises. But see! When I study this genius closely, I am seized by the genius himself: for to hold in high regard, as I said, came from his inspiration; for great things are near to heaven. Other phrases also agree with this, by which we call the things we wish to praise high, great, sublime, and eminent; and those we despise low, cast down, humble, and lying. Manners also agree: for princes on the throne, judges on the bench, professors in the chair, as we hold them in high regard, so we place them on a raised position.

units.la: Quæstio II.
units.tr: Question II.

units.la: An tradentem audientemque Scientias, recentibus, quam antiquis Auctoribus, operam dare, sit satius?
units.tr: Whether it is better for those who teach and those who learn the sciences to devote their effort to recent authors rather than to ancient ones?

units.la: Rude Scientiarum Artiumque principium: eas Longævus usus perpolivit, & in fastigium educuit: & minores, majorum suorum erroribus sapiunt, supraque molem illam, quæ Veterum vires exhausit, parvo negotio evecti, eique de suo rursum inædificantes, aliquanto longius prospiciunt. His itaque speculatoribus tutius te committas, quibus ex tam edito datum est despicere, sententiarum suarum adversarias Rationes, iisque procul adventantibus, viam obsepire. Huic accedit Veterum pleplerorumque magna credulitas: qui receptis suo tempore, & nescio unde depromptis fabellis, sine maturiori examine fidem adhibentes, ingenia sua miserum in modum torserunt: dum falsa cum veris feliciter sæpe deprehensis, anxiè conciliant, collectoque ex his absurdo dogmate, in plura (quod necesse est) dilabuntur absurda;
units.tr: The beginnings of the sciences and arts are rough. Long experience has refined them and raised them to their peak. Those who come later are wiser through the mistakes of their elders, and, lifted without great effort above that mass which exhausted the strength of the ancients, they build anew on their own foundations and see somewhat farther. It is therefore safer to entrust yourself to these observers, to whom it has been granted from such a height to look down, to block the arguments that oppose their opinions, and to bar the way against those who approach from afar. To this is added the great credulity of most of the ancients. They accepted tales of their own time, or drew them from nobody knows where, and gave them credence without mature examination. Anxiously trying to reconcile falsehoods with truths, which they often happily detected, they tortured their own wits in a wretched manner. From these they gathered an absurd doctrine and, as must happen, slid into more absurdities.

units.la: At recentium Scriptorum integra, regia, non astricta ingenia: quibus ardor est ad vivum resecare, quæ manifesta Ratio Experientiaque non pangunt, quantumvis ea Veterum superstitio coluerit: Et certè (quod à magnis nostrorum temporum Ingeniis admonemur) solum hoc filum est, quod Opinionum humanarum Labyrinthum ingredientibus, inter tortas errorum ambages, tutum promittat exitum, omnia non penitus ex-ploplorata certaque suspectare, quantumcumque plausibili veritatis specie se jactent. Accedit porro Veteribus affectata passim obscuritas, quae quaesitis saepe verborum involucris, plus loci sibi vindicat in eorum scriptis, quam sensus aut rationum momenta: Enimvero non nisi tenebrionum est, satis de se abstrusae, & mille modis intricatae perplexaeque Veritati, insuper noctem & latebras conciliare, & de suo ingenio caliginem offundere: Suspectumque id, cum aditum ad Naturae Arcana ducentem diuturnâ indagatione deprehendisse vis videri, eum posteris obserare, prementemque tua vestigia, nescio, quo sinuoso discursu deludere. Hinc non immeritò Recentium Scriptorum in hoc praecipuè desudat industria, ut distincta sint, dilucida, ordinataque que quæ tradunt: Dum operis suî Argumentum & artificium in libri vestibulo Lectori exhibent: dum illud scitè partinutur & diggerunt in Tractatus, in Sectiones, in Capita, Quæstiones, Articulos, Dubia, Paragraphos, Numeros, Puncta: nomina, quæ bonam partem, Antiquorum incondita confusio non novit! Dum ultimæ etiam subtilitatis argutias, quæ vulgi captum penitus effugiunt, pinguiâ aliquâ similitudine familiariter induunt, ut jam sub isto quasi amictu à quantumvis crasso ingenio hebetique palpentur.
units.tr: But the works of recent writers have free, royal minds, not bound by constraints. They are eager to cut away to the quick whatever clear reason and experience do not support, however much the superstition of the ancients may have cherished it. And indeed (as we are reminded by the great minds of our own times) this is the only thread that promises a safe exit to those who enter the labyrinth of human opinions, amid the twisted windings of error: to regard with suspicion everything that is not thoroughly explored and certain, however plausibly it may display the appearance of truth. Moreover, the ancients everywhere display a studied obscurity, which, by means of sought-after verbal wrappings, claims for itself more room in their writings than the substance of their meaning or the weight of their arguments. Truly, it is the work only of obscurantists, to add darkness and hiding places to a Truth already sufficiently abstruse and tangled and perplexed in a thousand ways, and to pour fog over it from their own wit. And when they seem to have discovered, after long investigation, a path leading to the secrets of nature, they bar it to posterity, and, pursuing their footsteps, mock them with I know not what devious wandering. Hence it is not without reason that the industry of recent writers labours especially to make what they deliver distinct, clear and orderly. They set out the argument and plan of their work in the vestibule of the book for the reader. They divide and arrange it cleverly into treatises, sections, chapters, questions, articles, doubts, paragraphs, numbers and points. These are names that the uncouth confusion of the ancients largely did not know! They also clothe the finest subtleties of argument, which wholly escape the grasp of the common people, in some homely comparison, so that even the dullest and thickest wit may grope at them, as if wrapped in such a cloak.

units.la: His tamen rationibus in occursum it Soliditas Antiquorum Scriptorum, nihil levi ac volante manu (ut effusus agilisque nostri sæculi genius est) sed plumbeo calamo omnia cautè ac maturè statuentium, nec quaslibet suas cogitata tationes, quæ inter calices forte, bene habitam jam & molliculam mentem dem ulcebant, in Publicu eructantium; sed duntaxat, quas momentis suis examinaverant, quas ad Rationis austeram trutinam discusserant, longa lucubratione, improbâ pertinaciâ. Certè major quondam erat Publici reverentia: Et quidquam huc adferre, nisi longa ruminatione digestum, nefas esse credebatur; Ubi hoc, quo vivimus ævum (quod cultum, quod expolitum, cum ludibrio Antiqui Rudimenti, Nostrates invidiosè jactant) quorumvis libidini frænum dedit, ut scribant, ut censeant, ut quidquid in buccam venerit, effutiant: Hoc solo fructu, quod ingenuam & in alta concitatam juventutem, nugis & gerris suis implicitam, remorentur & vilem faciant
units.tr: Yet against these methods stands the solidity of the ancient writers. They did not set down everything with a light and flying hand (as is the character of our own age, loose and nimble), but with a leaden pen, weighing all things cautiously and maturely. They did not belch out to the public every thought that happened to stir a mind, perhaps well settled and already soft, amid the cups; they published only those things which they had tested by their weight, and examined on the stern scales of reason, through long study and unrelenting perseverance. Certainly there was once a greater reverence for the public. To bring forward anything not digested by long rumination was believed to be a sin. But now this age in which we live (which the Moderns boastfully call cultivated and polished, mocking the ancient rudiments) has given the reins to anyone's whim, so that they write, so that they opine, so that they blurt out whatever comes into their mouths. The only fruit of this is that they hold back and make cheap the noble and eager youth, entangled in their trifles and chatter.

units.la: Atque has etiam nugas in limine speciosè inscribunt : Quæstio Curiosa, Quomodo Jupiter Junonem duxerit : Opus Aureum: Diu desideratum:
units.tr: And these trifles they inscribe on the title-page with showy titles: A Curious Question: How Jupiter Married Juno. A Golden Work, Long Desired.

units.la: Fortunam Priami cantabo & nobile bellum:
units.tr: I will sing of Priam's fortune and the noble war.

units.la: Quid dignum tanto feret hic promissor hiatu?
units.tr: What worthy thing will this promiser bring forth from such a gaping mouth?

units.la: Parturiunt montes; nascetur ridiculus mus.
units.tr: The mountains will be in labour; a ridiculous mouse will be born.

units.la: Patet etiam, si Veterum scripta diligenter pervolveris, nihil novi, quod tam anxiè deperiunt, hos Novos adferre; sed detractis sæpè quibusdam verborum fasciis, ipsissimum esse Antiquitatis fœtum, quem ut suum circumferunt: Quin etiam evulgati hodie prostant libri, jussi alienum Auctorem perfrictâ fronte mentiri, in quibus nihil aliud legas, quam Antiqui alicujus Scriptoris constipatam & contractam energiam, miserè distentam, & nescio quibus næniis ad fastidium intertextam: Futili laudis ambitu, ut nempe magnorum voluminum Auctores appareant, qui meri plagiarii, qui fures libellorum sunt:
units.tr: It is also evident, if you diligently turn over the writings of the ancients, that these moderns bring forth nothing new, the thing they so anxiously strive after. Rather, when certain bandages of words are removed, what they carry about as their own is the very offspring of Antiquity. Indeed, books are today published and put on sale, ordered with brazen face to lie about their author. In them you will read nothing but the cramped and contracted energy of some ancient writer, wretchedly stretched out and woven with I know not what nonsense to the point of tedium. This is done out of a vain ambition for praise, so that the authors of great volumes may appear, though they are mere plagiarists, the thieves of little books.

units.la: Quid mihi Celsus agit, monitus multumque monendus,
units.tr: What is Celsus doing for me, though warned, and much to be warned,

units.la: Privatas ut quærat opes, & tangere vitet
units.tr: that he should seek private wealth and avoid touching

units.la: Scripta, Palatinus quæcumque recepit Apollo:
units.tr: the writings that the Palatine Apollo has received, whatever they are;

units.la: Ne si forte suas repetitum venerit olim
units.tr: lest perhaps, if the flock of birds should one day come back

units.la: Grex avium plumas, moveat cornicula risum
units.tr: demanding its feathers, the little jackdaw

units.la: Furtivis nudata coloribus.
units.tr: stripped of its borrowed colours, should move them to laughter.

units.la: At ubi in diversas partes à Veteribus, non bene lectis, aut non bene intellectis abivêre, popularia quædam suis placitis appendunt argumentorum pondera, quæ jam pridem dem Veterum indefesso malleo ad exilem usque tenuitatem contusa sunt: ita ut vel solo spiritu ab Antiquitatis defensore difflentur, quibus totam Antiquitatem suppressum & suffocatum ire minabantur. Denique periculo non vacat, & religioni ac publicæ quieti palam noxium est, quod Recentiores non pauci frequentant: ut nimirum in rebus feriis, quinimmo & sacra concernentibus, ambigere, diversas ac pugnantes inter se sententias committere, ac utrimque rationibus instruere malint, quam solidè confutare alteram, alteram solidè stabilire: Ut hoc pacto Lectorem teneant, spectaculo & creperi certaminis eventu prurientem: doceantque posse se firma concutere & feria omnia ludibrio habere
units.tr: But when, having not read well or not understood well the ancients, some men have gone off in different directions, they attach to their opinions certain popular weights of argument, which have long since been battered down to thin dust by the tireless hammer of the ancients. So that the defender of Antiquity can scatter them with a single breath, when they threatened to suppress and smother all Antiquity. Finally, it is not without danger, and it is openly harmful to religion and public peace, that many of the more recent writers practise this: namely, that in matters of faith, and even in those touching what is sacred, they prefer to waver, to set against one another opposing and conflicting opinions, and to arm each side with arguments, rather than to refute one solidly and establish the other solidly. In this way they keep the reader in suspense, itching for the spectacle and the outcome of a doubtful contest, and they teach that they can shake all firm things and make a mockery of everything sacred.

units.la: Quæstio III.
units.tr: Question III.

units.la: An expediat virum doctum, Principum curis & curiùse interponere, an verò in musejo & inter Musas consenescere?
units.tr: Is it expedient for a learned man to meddle with the cares of princes and their affairs, or rather to grow old in the museum among the Muses?

units.la: Magnetica quædam in imperante virtus, eorum, qui imperantur, oculos pariter ac mentem in se convertendi defigendique: Hinc quo ille vel enititur prior vel delabitur, eò etiam hi trahuntur: Ad unius exemplum ac pene nutum, sive in præcipitium socordiæ proni, sive in arduum Virtutis erecti. Proinde non de cive aliquo, sed de Republica, non de homine, sed de Genere Humano bene merentur Sapientes illi, quibus id unum agitur, ut præsto sint imperanti: salutarium conconsiliorum face, viam prælucentes ad Templum illud Virtutis & Honoris. Abjectum autem perinde atque inhumanum est, ignavâ securitatis simulatione, in arido illo Scholæ pulvere sordescere, parumper à desidia & oblivionis sepulcro distantem; Ubi industriam tuam Patria postulat, ubi virtuti ac doctrinæ tuæ solium dignitatis Fortuna promittit. Quid quod hoc pacto Sapientiæ & Bonarum Artium candidatis accrescet animus & aviditas perrumpendi illa tædiorum ac laborum septa, quibus Natura Veritatem inclusit, ut Sapientiam viderint, non jam sub vili pallio latere, non intra humiles casas constringi (ut hodie res dant sese) sed amplis regum atriis, submissis fascibus suspici, sceptris assidentem: Quod enim alii, blandientis Fortunæ favor imperimpertiit, facile id sibi pollicetur humana credulitas: avidâ futuræ felicitatis imaginatione delusa, & ex paribus initiis, pares successus in præjudicium ambigui Casus compones. Ad hæc si vir doctus Aulam frequentet, ubi apud Principem, pro meritis auctoritate valuerit, facilè poterit pestes illas ab Aula profligare, quæ eam bonis omnibus infamem pariter atque exosam fecerunt: Frandibus larvam & fucum, ingenii dexteritate detrahere: adulationibus ambages, per quas se volvunt, obsepire: proterviam & lascivam comprimere ansterâ fronte & Sapientiæ conveniente supercilio: Adeo ut (quod decebat) Principis Palatium omnibus jam apareat delubrum quoddam beneficæ Majestatis, & afflictæ Innocentiæ tutissimum asylum.
units.tr: There is a certain magnetic power in a ruler, to draw and fix the eyes and minds of those he rules. So wherever he strives forward or slides back, they are dragged along too, at the example and almost the nod of one man, whether they are prone to the abyss of sloth or raised up to the steep path of virtue. Therefore those wise men deserve well not of one citizen but of the commonwealth, and not of one man but of the human race, whose sole aim is to be at hand for the ruler, carrying the torch of salutary counsels and lighting the way to that temple of virtue and honour. It is, however, base and inhuman, under the pretence of idle security, to grow filthy in the dry dust of the schoolroom, lying just a little short of the sepulchre of indolence and oblivion, when your country demands your industry, and when Fortune promises a throne of dignity to your virtue and learning. Moreover, by this course the candidates of wisdom and the liberal arts will gain courage and eagerness to break through those barriers of tedium and toil within which Nature has enclosed Truth, so that they may see Wisdom no longer lurking under a cheap cloak or confined within humble huts (as things now stand), but regarded in the spacious courts of kings, with lowered fasces, seated beside the sceptre. For what others have obtained through the favour of a flattering Fortune, human credulity readily promises to itself, deluded by the eager imagining of future happiness; and from like beginnings it will expect like successes, to its own harm when the outcome is uncertain. Besides, if a learned man frequents the court, where he may count for something with the Prince on account of his merits, he will easily be able to drive out from the court those plagues which have made it equally infamous and hateful to all good men: to strip off the mask and paint of frauds by the skill of his wit; to hem in with plain speech the windings by which flattery twists and turns; to restrain insolence and wantonness with a stern brow and a supercilious air befitting wisdom. So that (as is fitting) the Prince's palace may now appear to all as a kind of sanctuary of beneficent majesty, and the safest refuge of afflicted innocence.

units.la: His tamen obstat, quod ad Principem non pateat nisi per Ministros ejus aditus: major his quàm Principi arrogantia & impotentius fastidium: qui tunc demum egregiè se tutariDomini sui dignitatem arbitrantur, si quod ingenuum erat & non fictum, id omne tamquam læsæ majestatis suspectum represserint, si quod sine majorum imaginibus probum ac industrium, id omne tamquam plebeium & profanum à Principis sacrario repulerint: Hos sibi devinciat qui Deo vel notus esse voluerit: scis quo pacto? Assentationibus, servilibus blanditiis, donis, promissis, sordibus. Quod si hæc condicio minus æqua videatur & Philosophiæ legibus adversari, ævum teras necquicquam, atria quotidianis discursibus fatiges, & inter leviculam illam Aulæ juventutem exploexplosus oberres, sicut asinus inter simias. At finge primam illam sepem te perrupisse, nosci te à Principe, ad sermones ejus admitti, rebus seriis consilia tua postulari; scias aures hic esse teneras, asperum & inconditum sonare, si quid parumper ab adulationis concentu ad tenorem veritatis deflexit: admonitionem editum censeri, consilia ex eventibus æstimari, favores Domini ventorum in morem subinde reflare in diversum: & veteri adagio, Aulicos esse similes abaculorum calculis: hi enim secundùm computantis arbitrium, modò aurei sunt, modò æneí: & Aulici ad nutum Regis, nunc beati, nunc miseri. His adde factiones & dissidia potentum: Alteri parti te jungis? Periculum communicas: Ab utraque dissides? Vtrimque premeris. Adde & ingentem invidiæ fumum, quem nascens ille splen- dor excitat, eorum oculos intole- rabiliter exagitantem, quibus per- suasum est, stemmati & majorum ceris deberi cunêta, Virtuti nihil. Proinde si vir doctus intra privatos parietes se contineat, si chartis mandet, quæ Principem instru- ant, consulet & sibi & Principi: utilius Principi, & sibi tutius: ex- pedit illud calamo, quàm linguâ ducere: Umbra est vivorum dictis invidia; mortuorum scriptis reve- rentia.
units.tr: Yet this is hindered by the fact that access to the Prince lies open only through his ministers. Their arrogance and imperious disdain exceed that of the Prince himself; they think they then guard their lord's dignity most effectively when they repress everything that was honest and not feigned as suspect of treason, and when they thrust from the Prince's sanctuary everything upright and diligent that lacks ancestral images, as plebeian and profane. Whoever wishes to be known even to God must bind these men to himself. And how? You know how: by flattery, servile blandishments, gifts, promises, and sordid compliances. But if this condition seems less fair and at odds with the laws of philosophy, you will waste your life to no purpose, weary the courts with daily comings and goings, and wander about, lost and ridiculed, among that frivolous crowd of courtly youth, like an ass among apes. But suppose you have broken through that first hedge, are known to the Prince, admitted to his conversation, and your counsels sought in serious matters; know that here the ears are tender, and that anything which has turned a little from the harmony of flattery to the tone of truth sounds harsh and crude: it is taken for a rebuke, counsels are judged by their outcomes, the favours of the lord shift and blow back again in the opposite direction like the winds, and, as the old saying has it, courtiers are like the counters on an abacus: according to the reckoner's will they are now golden, now bronze; and courtiers, at the nod of the King, now happy, now wretched. Add to this the factions and quarrels of the powerful. Do you join one party? You share its danger. Do you dissent from both? You are pressed from every side. Add also the huge cloud of envy which that rising splendour stirs up, intolerably goading the eyes of those who are persuaded that everything is owed to pedigree and the wax of ancestors, and nothing to virtue. Therefore, if a learned man keeps within private walls, and commits to paper what may instruct the Prince, he will give counsel both to himself and to the Prince: more useful to the Prince, and safer for himself. It is better to lead by the pen than by the tongue. Envy is a shadow over the spoken words of the living; reverence is what is owed to the writings of the dead.

units.la: Quæstio IV.
units.tr: Question IV.

units.la: An virtuti expediat aperto marte cum invidia luctari, an vero tectis artibus eam declinare?
units.tr: Is it expedient for virtue to wrestle with envy in open combat, or rather to avoid it by hidden arts?

units.la: PEstilens Invidiæ venene- num in latus circum- quaque diffunditur & per æquales serpit: immunis est, & qui infra illam deprimitur ad contemptum, & qui supra illam erigitur ad dignitatem. Proinde si expandas Virtutis alas, & uno nisu in altum evoles, jam ultra Invidiæ fines penetraveris, antequam ad carpendum, dentes & morsum figere potuerit: Si vero dissimules, & in altum repas, & subinde à regia via declines, ne quo cautè tendis, ire videaris, ætatem teres & ingenium miseris consiliis: frustra inter dejectam plebem, Virtutem & Gloriam ex longinquo suspiciens.Quid quod sensim suffocetur Animus, in his tegnarum latibulis compressus & intortus? cui Natura infeverat igneum quiddam & amplum & angustiarum dedignans: Quid quod sensim in vitium degeneret? Ubi vix distant ab ignavia lenta consilia, à timiditate nimia cautela, à ferviservitute circumspectio, à fraude dissimulatio: Virtutibus enim propinqua vitia, facile ipsarum virtutum compellatione dignatur humanæ mentis effæminata indulgentia: deinceps speciosò nomine tam libenter se fallens, ac si Naturam ipsam & Supremam Regulam unà pervertat. Adde quod sit alto infractoque animo generosum & par exercitium, aperto campo in Invidiam ire, liventem ejus aciem irretortis oculis ferre, & impavidum subsistere, & pedem consefrere, & regio huic oneri æquos humeros supponere, quod est audire malè, cùm facias bene. Nec prætεriri debet, quod effrænis & implacabilis est Invidia, ubi locum tecedere, ubi declinari se sentit: ex tuo timore suas vires dimetiens, ex tua imbecillitate sibi feritatem & audaciam sumens: proinde ad-
units.tr: The pestilent venom of Envy spreads on every side and creeps along at the same level: whoever is pressed down beneath it into contempt is safe, and so is whoever is raised above it to dignity. Therefore, if you spread the wings of Virtue and rise to the heights in one effort, you will already have passed beyond the bounds of Envy before it can fix its teeth and bite. But if you dissemble, crawl upward, and keep turning aside from the king's highway, seeming to go by some cautious route, you waste your life and your talent on miserable schemes, looking up from afar at Virtue and Glory while the common crowd lies cast down beneath you. What if the mind is gradually stifled, cramped and twisted in these hiding-places of trickery, though Nature had endowed it with something fiery and generous that disdains narrow straits? What if it gradually degenerates into vice? For slow plans scarcely differ from sloth, excessive caution from timidity, circumspection from base servitude, and dissimulation from fraud. Vices lie close to the virtues, and the effeminate indulgence of the human mind readily clothes them with the very names of the virtues, and then gladly deceives itself under a fair name, as though it were overturning Nature herself and the Supreme Rule together. Add that it is a noble and fitting exercise for a lofty and unbroken spirit to go against Envy in the open field, to bear its malicious gaze with unflinching eyes, to stand fearless, to plant one's feet firmly, and to put shoulders equal to this royal burden under it: that is, to be ill spoken of while you do well. Nor should it be overlooked that Envy is unbridled and implacable, and that wherever it senses a place to retreat from or a place to be avoided, it measures its own strength by your fear and takes its savagery and boldness from your weakness. Therefore it rises up against every outstanding endeavour and leaps out unexpectedly, now daring not to gnaw from hiding but to tear openly.

units.la: ad omnem egregium conatum sese exeret, & ex improviso insiliet, au-sa jam, non tectim arrodere, sed aperte laniare. Vile est hoc vitium, si noveris, & debile, & tuo tantùm timore potens, si palam despicis, ringitur & crepat.
units.tr: ...to put itself forward at every noble endeavour and leap out unexpectedly, now bold enough not to gnaw at you covertly but to tear you openly. This vice is cheap and feeble, if you know it; it is powerful only through your own fear. If you openly despise it, it grinds its teeth and rattles.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod, hæc ad gloriam emergendi ratio, anceps & periculosa penitus, temeritate vix vacet: omnium oculos irritas, omnes ad invidiam & acerbitatem provocas, quisquis masculo illo & robusto passu vadis ad Virtutem & Honorem: Nec dumtaxat æqua-lium, quos præteris, allatratus & morsus; sed & præcedentium, quos premis, calces metuendi: Quin etiam qui longiùs evasêre, suffocari tamen cupiunt, quem ac-cedere & promicare vident, anti-cipantes æmulationem ante pari-tatem: Quin etiam ungues & ro-ftrum
units.tr: On the other hand, you do the opposite: this way of rising to glory is wholly hazardous and dangerous and scarcely free of rashness. You provoke the eyes of everyone and stir up envy and bitterness in all, whoever you are who strides with that manly, sturdy step towards Virtue and Honour. You must fear not only the barking and biting of the equals you pass by, but also the kicks of those ahead of you whom you press upon. Indeed, those who have got far away still wish to choke you when they see you approaching and pressing forward, anticipating rivalry before you are even equal. Indeed they sharpen their claws and beak

units.la: strum ad discerpendum acuunt, quos, ceu infaustas atræ noctis Striges, omnis feriæ ac manifestæ Virtutis exagitat spelendor; non equidem invidiâ, sed naturali odio & sævitiâ imbelle pectus armati. Enimvero ubi odia frendent, ubi minæ machinantur, ubi in caput tuum pericula conjurant, hîc tamen obniti, & contra fremere, & in manifestum interitum irruere, immane quiddam est & rabidum, à placido tranquilloque Virtutis in immensum aberrans. His adde quod naturalior Virtuti triumphus, qui arte, quàm qui vi paratur: Ars mitis illa & suavis ministra Virtutis, pariter cum Domina sua, pacis & quietis amica; Vis barbarus quidam satelles, contra incursum & ad extrema datus. Gratùm etiam & ingenuùm incidit imaginanti, Virtutem non illico totum impetum diffundere, & summe rigore discertare; sed cedere tantisper, & connivere, & impari adversario dare aliquid: & ad instar Solis in ortu suo, Invidiæ nebulæ nunc tegi, nunc livescere, nunc pallere, quousque meridiem scandat, & jam maturis radiis, tumultuantes illas infra se nubeculas discutiat & consumat.
units.tr: to tear you apart. They are like the ill-omened screech-owls of black night, harried by the splendour of open and manifest Virtue. They are driven not truly by envy but by natural hatred and savagery, their timid breasts armed against it. Indeed, when hatreds rage, when threats are plotted, when dangers conspire against your head, to resist here, to rage back and rush into manifest ruin, is something monstrous and frenzied, straying far from the calm and tranquil path of Virtue. Add to this that triumph comes more naturally to Virtue when won by art than by force. Art is the gentle and sweet handmaid of Virtue, a friend of peace and quiet like her mistress; force is a sort of barbarous henchman, given over for assault and extremity. It also pleases the imagining mind, and seems noble, that Virtue does not at once pour out its whole onslaught and contend with utmost rigour, but for a while gives way, and winks, and grants something to an unequal adversary. Like the sun at its rising, it is now covered by the clouds of envy, now grows dim, now pales, until it climbs to midday and, with its ripened rays, disperses and consumes those little clouds churning beneath it.

units.la: Quæstio V. An hodiernus mos, aliorum authoritates in dictis scriptisque citandi, sit approbandus?
units.tr: Question V. Whether the present custom of citing the authorities of others in discourses and writings should be approved?

units.la: OBstringimur à Natura religione quadam & reverentia vetustatis: anxii majorum dictis & sensis contrarie; his obsequi & consentire securi: Et jam tot labentibus annis
units.tr: By nature we are bound by a certain religious reverence for antiquity: anxious about what is said and thought by our elders, when it runs contrary to us, we feel safe in obeying and agreeing with them, and now with so many years gliding past

units.la: Tandem piaculum est concutere, quod cana Sæculorum sanxit authoritas : longâ serie post patres suos decurrentibus natis
units.tr: at last it is a sin to shake what the hoary authority of the ages has sanctioned, with sons running on in a long line after their fathers

units.la: Et natis natorum, & qui nascuntur ab illis.
units.tr: And to the sons of their sons, and to those who will be born from them.

units.la: Quid ni igitur pietatis & observantiæ laudem habeant, qui frequenti alienorum sensuum citatione profitentur, majorum se adorare vestigia, ab eâque, quam ipsi signauêre semitâ, ne latum quidem unguem velle declinare. Porro hac arte dictis tuis, si pulcra sunt, invidiam detrahis, dum ea non tibi sed mortuis ascribis, quos ab invidia Fatum semovit; si minus concinna sunt, nescio tamen quam gratiam concilias, dum in iis, quod antiqua putentur, semper quid abstrusum quæritur, semper quid amplius quam sonet intelligitur: ita Vetustatis Mystico Genio volente. Dum interea magnam dicenti scribentique commendationem parit, Antiquitatis monumenta perlustrasse, evolvisse libros, intellexisse sententias: Cana quædam & senilis sapientia est, quæ de isto fonte promanat, quæ non unius ævi limitibus constricta, præcedentia omnia complectitur, & ex his late se diffundit imposterum. Gratum etiam & peramænum Lectori spectaculum exhibetur, dum uno libello, quinimo unâ paginâ, ingens Sapientum chorus in Proscenium accitur, quasi super Quæstione, quæ decidenda proponitur, deliberaturus: dumque suo stylo declamantes inducuntur, suam singuli sententiam promunt, sed & genium suum produnt: ora ipsa mehercule, & lineamenta, non tam corporis, quam animi eorum, quos nunquam vi- dimus, videmur tamen quasi præ- sentes intueri. Denique dum hoc pacto majorum placitis suus honos vindicatur, compescitur effrænis illa novitatum cupiditas, cui Veri- tatis studium hodie prætexunt: quæ licet innoxia videri possit, quamdiu Physicarum speculatio- num cancellis circumscribitur; ubi tamen ulterius exemplo serpit, & ad Mores ac Religionem se transfert, turbulenta palam & exitia- lis est.
units.tr: Why should they not win praise for piety and deference, those who profess by frequent citation of other men's opinions that they worship the footsteps of their elders and will not turn aside so much as a nail's breadth from the path they themselves marked out? Moreover, by this art, if your sayings are fine, you escape envy, since you ascribe them not to yourself but to the dead, whom Fate has removed beyond envy; if they are not so elegant, you nonetheless win some favour, since in them whatever is thought ancient is always sought as something hidden, and always understood as meaning more than it says, the mystical genius of antiquity willing it so. Meanwhile it brings great commendation to the speaker or writer to have perused the monuments of antiquity, to have unrolled its books and understood its maxims: a certain hoary and senile wisdom flows from that fountain, which, bound by the limits of no single age, embraces all that went before and spreads widely from these into the future. A pleasing spectacle, too, is presented to the reader, when in one little book, indeed on one page, a vast chorus of sages is summoned onto the stage, as if to deliberate on the question proposed for decision; and while they are introduced declaiming in their own style, each puts forward his own opinion and at the same time reveals his own character: the very faces, by Hercules, and the outlines, not so much of the body as of the minds of men whom we never saw, we seem nevertheless to behold as if present. Finally, while in this way their due honour is vindicated for the opinions of our elders, that unbridled desire for novelties is restrained, which people today pretend to be the pursuit of truth. Though it may seem harmless so long as it is confined within the bounds of physical investigation, yet when it creeps further, by example, and transfers itself to morals and religion, it is openly turbulent and destructive.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod hæc in errores pronior, incautos à Ve- ritate seducat semita: Dum Au- thoritatibus illis & testimoniis un- dique corrasis hoc agitur, ut quid Authores dixerint, non quid di- cendum sit, quæratur: & qui in- dagandi rerum causas avidus ac- cesserat auditor, speciosis Scientiarum nominibus inductus, is ranci-dularum illarum Quæstionum, quid hic aut ille senserit, demitta-tur ad vomitum fatur. Certè his, ubi modum excesserè, inest manifesta vanitas, & abjectio, & quædam quasi servitus: Jam olim dictum volunt, & uberius dictum, quidquid omnino dici potest:gratis fatigari, nova molientem: Hinc & Libri, quibus nomen suum inscribunt, non nisi struem quandam continent hinc inde compilatam, & confusas diversorum Authorum faragines: Hoc Plato dixit, illud Ariftoteles, & istud Leucippus, aliique alia, & quod nemo dixit, ad minus Quidam dixit: In suis verò declamationibus, ubi ad Veterum scita, quibus passim intertextæ sunt, deventum est, hîc verò stylum abrumpunt, deniceps graviore tono verba singula gula inflantes & pausis morisque distrahentes: Horum aliquem fi audias, Rhadamanthum audire te putes jus dicentem apud manes;Et tamen quæ hoc apparatu dicuntur, sæpe nihil sacri sunt,
units.tr: Yet it works against this that this path, more prone to error, leads inquirers away from the truth: while by gathering authorities and testimonies from every side the aim is to seek what the authors have said, not what must be said; and the listener who came eager to investigate the causes of things, led on by the specious names of the sciences, is pushed down to vomit out, sated, those rancid questions about what this or that man thought. Certainly, where these practices exceed due measure, there is manifest vanity, abjection, and a kind of servitude: they insist that whatever can at all be said has been said long ago and said more fully, and that it is pointless to labour on new matters. Hence the books, to which they put their names, contain nothing but a heap compiled from here and there, and a jumbled hodgepodge of various authors: this Plato said, that Aristotle, and that Leucippus, and others other things; and what no one has said, at least someone has said. In their declamations, when they reach the maxims of the ancients, with which they are interwoven everywhere, they break off their style and then, with a heavier tone, puff up each word from the throat and drag them apart with pauses and affected mannerisms. If you listen to one of these, you would think you were hearing Rhadamanthus pronouncing judgement among the shades; and yet what is said with all this display is often worth nothing sacred.

units.la: Sunt apinæ tricæ que, & si quid vilius istis :
units.tr: They are trifles of chaff, and anything more worthless than these.

units.la: Quinimo, quæ sua faciunt, antiquis similiora credunt, si iis insipidum quid ac inolidum aspergant, quod intelligi facile non potest, quod longâ vetustate jam usque ad ossa macruit: Et tandem in cultum admirationemque rapiuntur, suspicientes Antiquitatis vegetum illud & felix ævum: cui puriore radio Veritas affulserit, & uberior scaturiverit ingenii vena; Arido hoc & fatiscentis Naturæ seculo, procul ad tenebras & barbariem relegato. Apage cum atra bile insomnia tua, quisquis hæc nobis morosò cerebro deliras: Ad plebem usque cultum est ævum hoc, & novis inventis insigne, & habet, si rectè ponderas, quod cum præcedentibus omnibus de nitore & festivitate contendat: Manum exere: aude aliquid,
units.tr: Indeed, they believe their own productions more akin to the ancients if they sprinkle on them something insipid and mouldy, something not easily understood, which has long since wasted away to the bone through age; and at last they are carried away to worship and admire, looking up to that vigorous and fortunate age of antiquity, on which truth shone with a purer ray and the vein of talent gushed more abundantly, while this dry age of failing nature is banished far off to darkness and barbarism. Away with your nightmares, black bile and all, you who rave to us with a morose brain! This age, notable for its new discoveries, is open to the common people, and, if you weigh it rightly, it has something to contend with all the preceding ages in polish and elegance. Stretch out your hand, dare something!

units.la: ——— Et te quoque dignum Finge Deo:
units.tr: ——— And fashion yourself also as worthy of a god.

units.la: Videbis minimum adhuc esse, quod majoribus nostris actum est, immensam esse segetem, in quam illi falcem non miserunt: Occupata non est, etiamnum maximâ parte latet Veritas: Communem illam viam aberrantium pedes triverunt; aliâ tendendum est.
units.tr: You will see that what our ancestors accomplished is still very little, that there is an immense harvest into which they did not put the sickle; it is not yet taken up, the truth lies for the most part still hidden. The feet of those going astray have worn down that common road; one must make for another way.

units.la: Quæstio VI. An mordacces, an vero edentulas expediat inter amicos esse facetias.
units.tr: Question VI. Whether it is expedient for friends to have jests that bite, or rather jests that are toothless.

units.la: VOluptatis excessum refugiunt Sensus, & ingrati alicujus gestiunt consortio: Acria, amara, salsa, quæ pungunt ac vellicant inter epulas amat Gustatus; saccharo ac bellariis semper vesci, etiam fæminæ puerique abnuunt: Et habet perpetuum illud ac exundans inter amicos obsequium, quo pertæsum sæpe faciat, quem nimium delinit: huic si de jocis acre quid & salsum asperseris, amicum nauseâ prohibuisti: officia tua sic condita, palatum semper irritant, salivam semper movent. Ingenium etiam, quod sine exercitio citio torpet & sopitum est, stimulis istis admotis, expergiscitur, agitque se & versat & omnes nervos intendit, ut, quibus perstringebatur, argutias, similibus refellat argutiis: nam paribus armis discertandum est: quod momordit, non nisi jocus erat, & non nisi joco remordendum est: Experimur equidem quotidie Musarum Curiales, adolescentulos eos, qui à patriis laribus obtusi & rudes, ad Academiam, studiorum caussâ concesserunt, ibidem æqualium suorum vexationibus, jocis & dicteriis dolari penitus & quasi ad cotem acui: mirantibus amicis ac notis, eos in patriam reduces, undique lepôrem jam & gratiam spirare, qui non ita pridem cubito emungebant. Potes etiam arte istâ, amicorum, quibus uteris, vitiis commodè mederi: dum prudenter ter aculeum tegis sub facetiâ, ut ulcus incîdas incauto: ferio reprehendere, hostem : serio monere, magistrum sapit : illud amicitiæ, hoc æqualitatis jura non ferunt: jocus, si recte uti noveris, quod in his tetricum est, præcîdit, quod fructuosum, servat. Denique popularem etiam & urbanum te reddes hac arte: Nam major pars hominum hac est indole, quâ catellus noster: qui eos colit impensius, à quibus irritatur magis : pedem ei trahunt, aurem vellunt, in tergum versant, divaricatos digitos intentant oculis: ipso interim blæso rictu infestam manum impetente, & frustratos dentes in dentes fatigante; Et his imposterum magis comis est, his in occursum pomptior, his cauda blanditur festivius: ad invidiam omnino & opprobrium eorum, qui sæpe sæpius pinguem ei offulam objecerunt.
units.tr: The senses shrink from an excess of pleasure and eagerly seek the company of what is unwelcome. The palate loves things that are sharp, bitter, and salty, which sting and tickle during a meal; women and children also refuse to eat nothing but sugar and sweetmeats. Among friends, constant and overflowing attentiveness can often weary the very person it too much soothes. If you sprinkle a little of something sharp and salty from jesting on that attentiveness, you have spared your friend from nausea. Your courtesies, seasoned in this way, always irritate the palate and always stir the saliva. The mind as well, which grows dull and drowsy without exercise, is roused when these goads are applied. It stirs itself, turns and wrestles, and strains every nerve so that it may answer with wit the wit that pricked it, for the contest must be fought with equal weapons. What has bitten was only a joke, and it must be bitten back with a joke. Indeed, we see it every day among the courtiers of the Muses: young men who came up to the Academy for their studies, dull and rough from their family hearths, are there thoroughly rubbed and, as it were, whetted on a whetstone by the teasing, jests and sayings of their peers. When they return home, friends and acquaintances are amazed to find them breathing wit and charm on every side, though not long before they had been wiping their noses on their elbows. By this same art you can also cure the faults of your friends, the ones you associate with, pleasantly enough: while you wisely hide the sting under a jest, you cut into a sore that the other does not guard. Seriousness is a hostile act, and a reproof given in earnest smacks of a teacher. Friendship and equality do not permit such things. A jest, if you know how to use it rightly, cuts away what is harsh in these matters and preserves what is useful. Finally, this art will make you agreeable and urbane. For most people have the disposition of our little dog, which courts most eagerly those who provoke it most. They pull its foot, tug its ear, turn it on its back, and thrust spread fingers at its eyes. Meanwhile, with its mouth wide open in a snarl, it attacks the hostile hand and wears out its teeth on teeth. And afterwards it is more fawning toward these people, more eager to run to meet them, and wags its tail more cheerfully at them. All of this is to the envy and disgrace of those who have often and repeatedly thrown it a fat morsel.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod dentatæ illæ facetiæ cuniculos agant ad arcem Amicitiæ demoliendam: Ex illis in convicia & jurgia facilis & trita semita : & ab his porro ad rixas, ad simultates, ad indictas & apertas inimicitias itur : & ut sit aliquid, quod præcipitem hunc cursum remoretur, ut ut sistant, antequam crebrius utrimque puncti exulcerentur animi; tamen Manet altâ mente repostum, & supra crudam injuriam, digestu malignum est, quod cum mordaci joco permiscetur ludibrium : Apertam contumeliam extenuat infe-rentis ira, concitatioque, & turbatæ mentis impotentia ; joco tectam, deliberati animi aggravat simulatio & perversitas : quæ sete-riò riò irrogatur, reconciliatione tollitur; hæret illa, quæ à joco lepôrem sumpsit, & narratur, & in vulgi fabulam abit. At apagesis intempestiva illa: Pone risus; non rictus: pone jocos non ad lanienam; sed ad mortiunculas duntaxat & pruriginem dentatos; Sed & hi sensim erodunt totum hoc, quod inter amicos candidum est & familiare: Dum incurioso esse non licet, dum cum amico aliter, quam tecum ipse loqueris, metuens sub facetia Censorem. Degenerat etiam animus, dum ad carpendum hinc inde coäctis fallaciis se intorquet, assuescitque tandem ad nugas se demittere, & plebeculæ in morem exquisitè cavillari: Certè serium quoddam & magnificum est, quod ei sapere, Natura voluit: frivolis abjectisque rebus inescari, affecti palati indicium cium est. His accedit, ita comparatum esse, ut acutuli illi, quibus fertilior semper excrescit ad velli-candum unguis, aliorum in se jocos plerumque non ferant, ut nescio quam in amicos & socios dominationem ac tyrannidem sibi sumere videantur: nam eorum non facetiis modò, verum etiam ineptiis applaudendum est; ni feceris, traheris in fabulam, ludibrio multandus.
units.tr: On the other hand, these toothed jests dig tunnels to undermine the citadel of friendship. From them the path to abuse and quarrels is easy and well trodden, and from these one goes on to rivalries, to feuds, and to declared and open enmity. And even if something checks this headlong course, so that the two sides stop before their minds are wounded too often on both sides, still it remains lodged deep in the mind. Beyond the raw injury, that mockery which is mixed with a biting joke festers. The anger and agitation of the one who inflicts an open insult lessen it; but when it is cloaked in a joke, the pretence and perversity of a deliberate mind make it heavier. What is inflicted in earnest is removed by reconciliation, but what took its charm from a joke clings on, is repeated, and passes into the gossip of the crowd. But that untimely prohibition, "Put away the laughter, not the sneer; put away jests not for mangling, but only for little bites and itches," comes too late. These toothed jests also gradually gnaw away everything that is open and familiar between friends. One is not free to be careless, and one speaks with a friend in a different way from how one speaks to oneself, fearing a critic hidden beneath the jest. The mind also degenerates when it twists itself to pick at others by forced deceits, and at last grows used to lowering itself to trifles and to carping in the manner of the common crowd. Surely nature meant us to have something serious and noble, and to be caught by frivolous and mean things is a sign of a depraved palate. To this must be added that it is so constituted that those clever fellows, in whom the nail for plucking at others grows ever more fertile, usually cannot bear jests aimed at themselves. They seem to claim for themselves a kind of domination and tyranny over friends and companions, for one must applaud not only their witticisms but also their silliness. If you fail to do so, you are dragged into gossip and must pay in mockery.

units.la: Quæstio VII.
units.tr: Question VII.

units.la: An deceat ingenuum adolescentem, vestem ad Novos Mores aptare?
units.tr: Whether it becomes a well-born young man to adapt his clothing to the New Manners.

units.la: Quod in vestium ritu Novi Mores ordinarunt, id protinus concinnum esse jubent elegans; quod abrogarunt, plebejum primò ac rusticum esto, deinde ineptum etiam ac riduculum: Sed exoletis quoque his, cum videtur, pristinam gratiam conciliant; & hæc, quæ nuper assumpserant,in contemptus barathrum abjiciunt: Arcano quodam fascino humanis sensibus illudentes. Qui igitur, o Adolescentes, refractarium hisce legibus indumentum habuerit, excidit jam nunc venustatis omnis ac elegantiæ commercio, suo ipse se calculo in ordinem redegit. Contra verò dici facile non potest, quantum honoris adolescenti conferat vestis illa, quam Novi Mores aptavêre: Nonne vulgi in se vertit ora? nonne æqualium prolicit officia? nonne, si majores suos salutaverit, resalutatur liberalius? Vult ea vestis in Academicis aliisque publicis Actibus demicis aliisque publicis Actibus ad confessum invitari, & perac̄tâ fabulâ sibi grates persolvi depo- scit: ambitur ejus in foro congres- sus, gaudet frequenti, eâque am- plâ ac magnificâ, etiam ignoto- rum salutatione. Auget etiam ve- stitus ille formam, perficitque & conspicuam ac illustrem reddit; hæc verò ubi hisce adminiculis fulcita est, nescio qua majestate intuentium animis dominatur, pellicitque, & in sui obsequium favoremque devincit. Habet in super hoc Novitas, ut qui ejusce cæremoniis ac superstitione re- guntur, eosdem inter se facilè con- greget & in mutuam consuetudi- nem familiaritatemque insinuet: Horum referti cœtus vicis vitam, foro pompam, templis solennita- tem faciunt: inter hos aptè loqui discès, lepidè confabulari, festivè salutare, deferre humaniter: hîc incefincessus, hîc obtutus, hîc etiam vocis stylus sonusque leges habent: hîc excutitur torpor & bar-baries; accersiuntur sales & gratiæ. Erigit denique juvenilem animum illustrium personarum ritu concinnatus habitus, ingeritque paria vesti studia, concitatque in Virtutis arduum: Splendorem & dignitatem, ad quam aspirat, anti-cipante fiduciâ.
units.tr: What the New Manners have ordained in the fashion of dress, they at once declare elegant and graceful. What they have abandoned, they call first common and rustic, and then awkward and even ridiculous. Yet when these things have grown obsolete, they again win back their former favour, and those things they had lately adopted they cast into the pit of contempt, bewitching human senses with a certain secret enchantment. Therefore whoever, young men, has a garment that refuses these laws has already fallen out of all commerce of charm and elegance, and by his own reckoning has put himself out of order. On the other hand, it cannot easily be said how much honour that garment which the New Manners have fitted confers on a young man. Does it not turn the eyes of the crowd toward him? Does it not invite the services of his peers? Does it not, if he greets his elders, bring a more generous greeting in return? That garment wishes to be invited to the gathering at the Academy and at other public occasions, and it demands thanks paid to it when the play is over. In the marketplace he is sought out for conversation; he delights in the crowd, and in the large and magnificent salutations even of strangers. That attire also enhances his appearance, perfects it, and makes it conspicuous and distinguished. When it is supported by these props, it rules the minds of onlookers with I know not what majesty, attracts them, and binds them to its service and favour. Moreover, the Novelty has this property: it easily gathers together those who are governed by its ceremonies and superstition, and insinuates them into mutual habit and familiarity. Crowded assemblies of these men make the streets lively, the marketplace splendid, and the churches solemn. Among them one learns to speak fittingly, to converse wittily, to greet gracefully, and to show courtesy. Here gait, here glance, here even the style and sound of the voice have their rules. Here torpor and barbarity are shaken off, and wit and charm are summoned. Finally, a habit fashioned after the manner of distinguished persons raises the young man's spirit, instils similar pursuits, and stirs him toward the steep ascent of virtue, with confidence anticipating the splendour and dignity to which he aspires.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod hęc in luxum & lasciviam, protervam juventutem dissolvat licentia: Dum animus ætate lubricus in vitium facilè diffluit, & quantumvis ca-stigatè coërceatur intra severitatis ac disciplinæ repagulum, ferocit tamen sæpiùs, & fremebundus obluctatur. Quid? nonne vestis illa sternit aditum, & incautum pu-gilem manu-ducit ad prostitutæ Veneris palestram? Salutat officio-sius, fiùs, applaudit festiviùs, Nymphis illis per vicos obviis, omni mundo muliebri venustis: nam favorem spondet habitus, & turpis repulsæ ac fastidii metum, quo inhiberetur, elidit: At quia studiosè resalutatur, placere se concludit, tremulo intus lenocinio solicitante præcordia: pergitque porrò ad vespertinum alloquium: & jam effari audet, quid petulantem animum excruciet, extenuatque vocem & blanditias miscet effæminatus, concinnâ simul veste patrocinante libidini. His adde deplorandum temporis, quod ad feria suppetebat dispendium: Quanta pars ejus tergendo, torquendo, pectendo, ligando, concinnando, reconcinnandoque consumitur! reliquū penè sibi vendicant crebri per templa plateasque discursus, etiam intempestivi: Ægrè enim vestis illa Musæis Scholisque continetur: videri gestit, & ad evolandum prurit. Adde porrò, supervacaneo sumptu bona patria lacerari, & sæpe alienum æs grande conflari: Dum in vestium formis quotidie novi quid effingitur, quod assumendum est, & vix assumptum antiquatur: Nec per se sola culpam habet vestis; Sunt hujus individui comites, qui plerumque lautius haberi volunt, quam ipsa: Quantum abliguriunt convivia! quantum expellunt Sphæristeria! quantum dilapidat phalerata per urbem obequitatio! quantum pessumdant vespertina tripudia! quantum ad Dominæ fores explodit noctura cum fulgetris musica!
units.tr: On the other hand, this fashion also works against us, since licence dissolves it into luxury and wantonness, and a headstrong youth. While the mind, slippery with age, easily flows away into vice, and however strictly it is restrained within the barrier of severity and discipline, it still often grows fierce and struggles, roaring in protest. What then? Does that garment not pave the way and lead the unwary young boxer by the hand to the wrestling ground of the prostitute Venus? He greets more obsequiously, and applauds more gaily, the Nymphs he meets along the streets, all of them lovely with every womanly adornment. For the habit promises favour, and it crushes the fear of a shameful rebuff and disdain, by which he would otherwise be held back. And because he is eagerly greeted in return, he concludes that he pleases, while a trembling pimp inside him solicits his heart. He presses on to an evening conversation, and now he dares to say what torments his wanton mind. His voice grows faint, and the effeminate man mixes in endearments, while the well-arranged clothing serves as patron to lust. To these add the deplorable loss of time that was available for study. How much of it is consumed in wiping, twisting, combing, tying, arranging, and rearranging! Frequent running about the churches and squares, even at untimely hours, claims almost all the rest for itself. For that garment is with difficulty kept within the Muses' and the Schools' bounds. It longs to be seen, and it itches to fly away. Add further that the goods of the fatherland are squandered on superfluous expense, and that a large debt is often incurred. For every day something new is devised in the shapes of clothes; what has just been adopted is hardly put on before it is out of date. Nor is the fault in the garment alone. It has companions which usually wish to be kept more lavishly than the garment itself. How much feasts consume in gluttony! How much the tennis courts drain! How much a horse-cavalcade in trappings squanders through the city! How much evening dances ruin! How much a serenade with flashing music spends at the lady's door at night!

units.la: Quæstio VIII.
units.tr: Question VIII.

units.la: An expediat virtuti clarìs, an obscuris natalibus edi?
units.tr: Whether it is expedient for virtue to be brought forth from illustrious birth or from obscure birth?

units.la: INest ut plurimum plebejis hominibus vile quid & sordidum, quod nec arte celari, nec dignitatum insigniis obrui facilè potest : quod quandoque per medios etiam splendores irrêpit, putetque, & fæcem suam titulis allinit : Honorum, quos gerunt, contaminatâ Majestate. Proinde non immeritò Virtuti, quæ humili tenuique de stirpe, ad amplitudinem sublimitatemque nititur, crebris repulsis obsepitur aditus, donec fæculentum illud, quod de plebe trahit, concoctum est. E contrario verò Virtus, quæ illustri exurgit prosapiâ, inter ipsos enutrita splendores, præcox sibi vindicat ex majorum meritis ad honores aditum : Fovet eam avitum familiæ decus, constipatque clientum turba, erigitque & affinis & consanguineus favor : non lassatur ambitu, non infringitur repulsâ; involant in eam congenitæ Mitræ, Dignitates & Sceptra. Ad hæc, subdunt facem generosæ menti monumenta exemplaque majorum : Urunt nepotem tot olim proavis exantlati labores, & quæ de tholis pendent spolia, & de altis montium jugis cladem hostibus exprobantia trophæa: Nam tacitè alloquitur cana parentum ac veneranda memoria, & inculcare videtur hoc sæpius :
units.tr: Most often there is something cheap and base in plebeian men, which cannot easily be hidden by skill or overwhelmed by the insignia of rank. It creeps in even amid the greatest splendour, and it stains its dregs with titles, tainting the majesty of the offices they hold. Hence it is not without reason that Virtue, which rises from a humble and slender stock and strives toward eminence and loftiness, has its approach hedged in by repeated rebuffs, until that filth which it draws from the common people has been digested. On the other hand, Virtue which springs from a famous lineage, nurtured amid splendours of its own, claims for itself an early access to honours on the strength of its ancestors' merits. The ancestral glory of the family cherishes it, a crowd of clients attends it, and the favour of both in-laws and kinsmen raises it up. It is not wearied by canvassing, nor broken by refusal; the hereditary mitres, dignities and sceptres fly to it. Besides, the memorials and examples of its forebears kindle a fire in the noble mind. The labours once endured by so many ancestors spur on the grandson, and so do the spoils hanging from the domes, and the trophies on the high mountain ridges that cast defeat in the faces of the enemy. For the venerable memory of the parents speaks to him in silence, and seems to impress this on him again and again:

units.la: Disce puer virtutem ex me, verumque laborem :
units.tr: Learn, boy, virtue from me, and true toil:

units.la: arguitque, & increpat, & pudoris ac verecundiæ fræno retrahit, si vel tantillùm ab eorum vestigiis degedegenerem pedem seducat licentia. Quid quod etiam ipsa Virtus, quae clarâ stirpe prodiit, magis conspicua est, magisque ad exemplum exposita? Nam facilè discutit invidiae nebulas, quibus emergentium Virtus pallescit, à stemmate mutuatus fulgor: & tum ipsa evibrat serenum illud jubar, quod aliunde non trahit, quod sibi proprium est, pacatque, & delinit intuentium animos: ad humani generis dignitatem & delitias.
units.tr: It admonishes and rebukes him, and holds him back with the bridle of shame and modesty, if licence should lead his foot even slightly away from their footsteps into degeneracy. What of the fact that Virtue itself, when it comes from a famous stock, is more conspicuous and more exposed as an example? For it easily dispels the clouds of envy under which the virtue of those who rise from nothing grows pale, since it borrows its brightness from its lineage. Then it itself gives out that serene radiance which it does not draw from elsewhere, which is its own, and it calms and soothes the minds of those who behold it, to the dignity and delight of the human race.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod magnam clari natales secum adducant exspectationem, cui non respondisse, degenerasse est: exspectantur autem majorum gestis gesta conformia; & ut praeclara quaedam praestiteris, possunt tamen illis comparata vilescere: Nam quae Fama benignior ad Applausus aram consecravit Immortalitati, eadem deindeinceps in tantum tumorem in-flat adulante tubâ, ut suspicienti Posteritati spes nulla relinquatur exæquandi; Contra verò novo-rum rectè facta, æquâ lance & suis ponderibus, non alienis examinantur. Quin etiam gratior est no-va Virtus, quæ jam primùm obscu-râ de plebe surgit: Dum ad instar exorientis sideris sensim emergit, & scandit horizontem illum, qui oblivionis ac silentii caliginem, à luce famæ & dignitatum fulgore discriminat: intuemur eam defixis oculis, & subinde miramur de cæ-ca nocte talem faculam prodire, & rapimur tacito quodam gaudio, & prosequimur votis, & favemus. Accedit robustum & par Virtuti exercitium esse, ab imo luctari: eni-ti & exerere sese per compressa an-gustæ fortunæ latibula: devorare malevolorum odia, æqualium in-vidias. vidias, potentum fastidia: perrum pere per obluctantes factiones, per insidiantes dolos, per insultante repulsas : & placido sibi semper constante vultu, nec frangi, nec etiam ferari : Atqui ex his crescit dein-ceps historiis ac theatris digna se-ges : Nam eorum præcipuè in annalibus gesta lectorem pascunt, quos in altum suus labor & sudor evexêre : Suspendit legentis animum conatus anceps, abripitque & obtutum defigit expectatio ; at heroicus vigor, & obstinatus per dedignans arduū ascensus, favorem prolicit : & tandem optatus exitus demulcet & plausum ciet : Erigi-turque in spem, atque ad audendum sollicitatur animus : dum in via illa, quæ à plebe ad decus est, confragosâ licet & difficultatum sentibus horridâ, signantur nihilominus antecedentium vestigia, quiquibus passum exæquare assuescas.
units.tr: Yet on the other hand it works against them, that a famous birth brings with it great expectation, and not to have met it is to have degenerated. Deeds are expected to match the deeds of ancestors; and even if you accomplish some outstanding things, they may nonetheless become cheap by comparison. For the kinder Fame that has consecrated to Immortality the altar of Applause then inflates them to such a swelling, with the trumpet of flattery, that no hope is left to Posterity, looking up, of equalling them. Whereas the deeds of new men are weighed on an even scale and by their own weights, not by those of others. Indeed, a new Virtue, which rises for the first time from obscure common stock, is more welcome: as it gradually emerges like a rising star and climbs that horizon which separates the darkness of oblivion and silence from the light of fame and the brilliance of dignities, we gaze at it with fixed eyes, and from time to time we marvel that such a torch should come forth from the blind night. We are carried away by a quiet joy, we accompany it with our prayers, and we favour it. In addition, it is a sturdy exercise, and one fitting for Virtue, to struggle up from the bottom: to strive and thrust oneself out through the cramped hiding-places of narrow fortune; to swallow down the hatreds of the ill-disposed, the envies of equals, the disdain of the powerful; to force a way through resisting factions, through lurking tricks, through insulting rebuffs; and always to keep a calm countenance, neither broken nor carried away. And from these things there grows afterwards a harvest worthy of histories and stages. For it is above all the deeds in the annals of those whom their own labour and sweat have raised on high that feed the reader. The uncertain struggle holds the mind of the reader in suspense, and expectation seizes and fixes his gaze. But heroic vigour, and the stubborn climb that disdains difficulty, draws out approval, and at last the longed-for outcome soothes and calls forth applause. The spirit is raised to hope and is stirred to dare; and on that path which leads from the common people to honour, however rough and bristling with the thorns of difficulties, the footprints of those who went before are nonetheless marked out, by which you may grow accustomed to matching their stride.

units.la: Quæstio IX.
units.tr: Question IX.

units.la: An deceat fervidas & clamosas in Academiis esse disputationes?
units.tr: Whether it befits disputations in the Academies to be heated and noisy?

units.la: Ingentem ac robustum planè spiritum sufficit Veritas iis omnibus, qui sub candido illius vexillo sacramentum dixêre: ejuratis, ceu insidiantibus hostibus, quibuscumque Præjudiciis, quantumcumque stabilitis hominum usu, authoritate, consensu: Qui verò adversa signa sequuntur, his angustus animus: & quamvis subinde in pervicaciam obstinatus; confoditur tandem liquidæ Veritatis spiculo, & succumbit. Quid ni igitur detur nobis entheum illum ardorem, quo congesta mens anheanhelat, ubi pro Veritate stamus despumare & effutire? & sublati clamoribus somnum illum ab rumpere, quo maxima pars hominum, quæ doctum nomen habet, tam altum indormiscit: quo vetustatis scrupulosa mysteria consopiunt, quos absorbent captiosæ vocum minutiæ, quibus unius Scriptoris sensum omnem sepelivit authoritas, quos superstitio fascinat, quos ut pueros à Veritatis tramite deterrent Mandu-cus &Lemures. Accedit,maximam partem auditorum, qui disputationes nostras avidè circumstant, vulgarem esse, & obtusam, nec quò per argutias subtiliter tendimus, comitari valentem: hi proinde certamina nostra ex ingenio suo metiuntur : apud hos detectam Veritatem,quæ paribus utrimque studiis inquirebatur, agnovisse proprobrum est; nitendum contra & obstrependum est, aut cadis: & mox agêris in triumphum
units.tr: Truth supplies a truly great and robust spirit to all those who have sworn allegiance under her white banner, who cast off, as treacherous enemies, whatever prejudices, however firmly fixed by the custom, authority and consensus of men. But those who follow the hostile standards have narrow minds; and although they are at times stubborn in obstinacy, they are at last pierced by the shaft of clear Truth and yield. Why, then, should we not be granted that divine ardour by which a mind drawn together gasps for breath when we stand for Truth, so that we may foam and babble? And, with shouts raised, we should break that sleep in which the greater part of men who hold the name of learned slumber so deeply: the sleep in which scrupulous mysteries of antiquity lull them to rest, in which the captious trifles of words absorb them, in which the authority of a single writer has buried all his meaning, which superstition bewitches, and which the bogeyman and the ghosts frighten, like children, from the path of Truth. Moreover, the greater part of the listeners, who eagerly crowd round our disputations, are common and dull, and not able to follow where we are led by subtle arguments. Such people therefore measure our contests by their own wit. Among them it is a disgrace to have recognised the Truth that was being sought with equal zeal on both sides; one must press on and shout down, or else give way, and soon you will be led in triumph.

units.la: — Manibus post terga re vinctus.
units.tr: — With hands bound behind the back.

units.la: Denique altercantibus istis clamoribus vigent & vivunt Scholæ: dum fervet opus, dum Doctorum dissidiis pulpita personant, & argumentorum sub pondere crepant cathedræ, scinditurque in diversa studia, infremitque pedum pulsu circumfusa juventus: Explorat omnem exitum coarctata Industria, & subinde elabitur per ignotas sibi ante semitas: insperato quodam per invium manu ducente genio: At in vestibulo stat attonitum ore patulo vulgus, reprimiturque profanum pedem horore sacro, & multa putat, effingitque sibi in caligante cerebro, de nostris contentionibus simulachra mira. Con-
units.tr: Finally, it is through these clamours in dispute that the schools flourish and live. While the work is in ferment, while the pulpits resound with the quarrels of the teachers and the chairs creak under the weight of arguments, while the young people are split into opposing camps and stamp their feet in a crowd, a cramped Industry searches every way out and slips away again by paths previously unknown to it, with some guiding spirit leading its hand unexpectedly through the trackless ground. But the common crowd stands in the vestibule, its mouth open in astonishment, and the profane foot is held back by a sacred dread. In its clouded brain it imagines and fashions many wonderful images of our contests.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod disputantium fervor ille, non leve sit vanitatis, & jactantiæ futilis argumentum: A rudibus gloriolam emendicat ille clamor, & in defici-entis ratiocinii locum sufficitur egregius vicarius: Quin etiam evocatam subinde rationibus Veritatem, rursum in latibula sua compellit profanus: & ne frustretur eo, quem effusæ mentis vanitate præsumpserat, triumpho, perturbat, & cahos ac caliginem rebus inducit: Præclarum enim verò Philosopho negotium, de palma certare, & oblatam Veritatem, quia reperit eam, alius, quia tu aberrabas inficiari: Procumben-dum illico & adorandum, ubi Titii Sejive operâ (nec interest) sanctum illud numen humano generi detegitur: Cur commune bonum invidetur uni? Accedit nostras illas las dissensiones indignè remorari avidum Scientiæ discipulum: ut qui Scholis docilem & attentum animum intulerat, nihilo excultior, domum reducat aures à vociferationibus tinnientes: Assuescitque tandem malo exemplo, non æquitate niti, non ratione stare & cadere; sed assumptam semel tenere mordicùs, & pugnis ac calcibus propugnare sententiam. Quid quod sæpè clamores illi, intumescente jam spititu, abeant in sibilos ac dicteria? Dum præcipitat, nec verba notat lubrica linguæ volubilitas & garrulitas: Concurritur elisis cornibus, & insultatur utrimque, & non jam argumenta probant, sed scommata cavillantur:contaminantur plebejo jurgio sacra Veritati certamina, & mendacem Philosophi frontem deridet inter irrumpendum muliebris impotentia. Denique ipsum Veritatis Numen, cujus nos Sacerdotes sumus, mite pacatumque est, & à turbis semotum: Non reperitur inter efferatos belli tumultus,procul est à forensi fumo & strepitu: comes ei & amica solitudo, nocturno gaudet & matutino silentio: Quid ad ejus sacra, rixosi isti Pertinaciæ Coribantes ?
units.tr: Yet that heat of the disputants is no slight proof of vanity and empty boasting. That clamour begs a little glory from the untrained, and an outstanding substitute is put in the place of failing reasoning. Indeed, the profane man, once Truth has been summoned forth by arguments, drives her back again into her hiding places. So that he may not be cheated of the triumph which he had presumed in the empty vanity of his overflowing mind, he disturbs things and brings chaos and darkness upon them. For it is a fine business for a philosopher to contend for the palm, and to deny that the Truth offered to him is Truth, because another found it and he himself was wandering. At once he must fall prostrate and worship, as soon as that holy divinity is revealed to the human race by the work of Titius or Seius (it makes no difference which). Why is the common good grudged to one man? Moreover, these our dissensions unworthily hold back the eager disciple of Knowledge: he who had brought a docile and attentive mind to the schools goes home no more cultivated, with ears ringing from the shouting. And at last he gets into the bad habit of relying not on fairness or on reason to stand or fall, but of holding fast whatever opinion he has once taken up, and defending it with fists and kicks. And what of the fact that often those shouts, as the spirit swells, turn into hisses and insults? While the slippery volubility and garrulousness of the tongue rushes headlong and does not weigh its words, they charge at each other with horns locked and insult each other on both sides; now arguments do not prove anything, but jests are bandied about. The sacred contests of Truth are polluted by plebeian wrangling, and the feminine impotence of those who break in mocks the lying brow of the philosopher. Finally, the very divinity of Truth, whose priests we are, is gentle and calm, and it stays away from the crowds. It is not found amid the savage tumults of war; it keeps far from the smoke and noise of the forum. Its companion and friend is solitude, which delights in the silence of night and morning. What have those quarrelsome Corybantes of Obstinacy to do with its rites?

units.la: Quæstio X. An mulieres ad Philosophicas Scholas admittendæ ?
units.tr: Question X. Whether women are to be admitted to philosophical schools?

units.la: Habet à natura muliebris sexus ingenium mite, inditasque, quæ deliniant & suavi filo in obsequium pertrahant, blanditias: Huic, si ad discendum Scholę, & ad docendum pateant Cathedræ, quanquantum accedet bonis artibus incrementum! Et ut periculum facias, age, finge animo, in Philosophico aliquo Gymnasio, è Magistri pulpito puellam differentem, & tenerâ voce moventem magnas rationum moles, & venusto ac facili ore implicitam humano sensui Naturam, enodantem:
units.tr: The female sex has by nature a gentle disposition, and the caresses implanted in it, which soothe and draw people by a sweet thread into compliance. If the schools were open to them for learning, and the chairs open to them for teaching, how great an addition would be made to the good arts! And to test this, come, imagine in your mind some philosophical academy, a girl speaking from the teacher's pulpit, moving us with a tender voice, unfolding great masses of reasons, and with a charming and easy mouth explaining Nature, which is entangled in human sense.

units.la: Quæ norma boni, quis limes honesti:
units.tr: What is the rule of good, what the boundary of honour?

units.la: Quid Deus: unde nubes, ventusque, & fulminis ignis:
units.tr: What is God; whence the clouds, the wind, and the fire of lightning?

units.la: Quid quatiat terras, qua sidera lege feruntur.
units.tr: What shakes the earth, by what law the stars are carried along.

units.la: Vidistin' quanta confluat ad audiendum turba? ut sub numeroso Discipulo subsellia laborent? ut compressæ circumstantium multitudini indignentur parietes? Quàm avidè dicta docentis excipiunt aures! hauriunt animi, & custodienda chartis tradunt calami;
units.tr: Have you seen how great a crowd flocks together to hear her? How the benches labour under the numerous students, how the walls, pressed in by the surrounding multitude, are indignant? How eagerly the ears take in what the teacher says! The minds drink it in, and the pens hand it over to be kept on paper.

units.la: At parte aliâ incomptum Sophi- stam destituit auditor: & vacuâ Scholâ boanti occlamat Echo, in asperitatis ac tetricæ frontis deri- sum: Abducente cunctos, & lenitati ac gratiæ ipsâ rerum faventeNatu- râ. Quid quod fæmineo in cor- pusculo sæpe habitet animus in- gens & erectus? qui indignè sta- minum & coli pensis exercetur, & humili ac impari negotio ringi- tur & contabescit. Et sanè, nescio qua fronte, tyrannidem usurpa- mus viri: & sexum illum, quia con- tra violentiam debilior est, sup- pressimus: Ab aris eum removimus, militiâ abarcuimus, à tribunali & magistratu rejecimus, à Schola de- nique, ne qua pateat ad splendo- rem rima, repulimus: Quid? u- nam aliquam gentem ad ignoran- tiam damnasse, eripuisse libros, ve- tuisse literarum studia, nefarium fit & inauditæ sævitiæ: Et eandem illam in mediam generis humani partem, qua quæso æquitatis specie tegimus injuriam? Nec intra limites istos statur : Sunt qui absentem adversarium in Scholis traducant, sunt qui mite subditumque ingenium, modo ut atrox, modo ut ambitiosum depingant: Nec falsâ perfuafione, quod ignosci poterat, aguntur, sed ambitu gloriolæ: & mulierum hostes libenter audiunt: Pol de sexu suo bene meriti mares! Denique ingenium fæminis, nostro nitidius est: & momentorum etiam, quæ rudes crassique negligimus, curiosum: Atqui à minimis illis tota pendet Philosophiæ messis : constat enim merentibus in hoc agro colonis, quod femen hîc jaciendum, fi fortè vel levi tantum falsitatis rubigine vitiatum fuerit, præposterâ fertilitate mox in infinita succrescat & luxuriet absurda.
units.tr: But in another part the listener deserts the uncouth sophist, and in the empty school the Echo, shouting back, cries out in mockery of his harshness and his gloomy brow, while nature itself, favouring gentleness and grace, draws everyone away. What of the fact that in that little feminine body there often dwells a lofty and elevated mind, which is unworthily exercised with spinning-wool and distaff, and frets and wastes away in a humble and unequal task? And truly, with what face I know not, we usurp the tyranny of men, and have suppressed that sex because it is weaker against violence.
