We have removed it from the altars, shut it out from military service, rejected it from the tribunal and from magistracy, and finally, lest any chink be open to its brightness, we have driven it from the school. What? To condemn a whole nation to ignorance, to snatch away its books, to forbid the pursuit of letters, is monstrous and of unheard-of cruelty. And that same wrong, inflicted upon the middle part of the human race, by what semblance of fairness, I ask, do we cover it? Nor does the matter stop at these limits. There are those who in the schools malign an absent opponent, there are those who depict a gentle and submissive disposition, now as savage, now as ambitious. And they are driven not by a false persuasion, which might be pardoned, but by the lure of a little glory; and men gladly listen to the enemies of women. By Pollux, how well the males have deserved of their own sex! Finally, the female mind is brighter than ours, and attentive even to those moments which we, rough and gross, neglect. Yet the whole harvest of philosophy depends on those smallest things; for it is agreed by the farmers who work this field that if the seed sown here is tainted even by a slight rust of falsehood, it soon grows up into an absurd luxuriance of infinite proportions.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod mulierum ad Scholas nostras admissio (si res caute & provide trutinetur) periculo nostro non vacet: Nam primo quidem sic statuo, acre & excultum artibus ingenium à publicis muniis repelli non debere; Si maligne obsistas, faciet sibi mille dolis & turbis aditum: Igitur si ad Scholas; & ad publica munia admittendae sunt feminae: Quid si nos collegas non ferant? quid si vices, ut meremur, rependant? Abigant nos ad culinam, ad ollas, ad scopas, ad colum, ad infantium pannos & fascias? Solae interim ipsae de summa Reip. consulant, solae arma tractent, solae in templis antistites, in foris judices, in Scholarum suggestibus magistrae: Nec juvat hic toros suos excutere & viriles lacertos minari: Numero incredibile est, quantum vincimur: longâ jam inter nos bellorum clade propemodum absumpti: Ad hæc, Natura nobis edendis avarior. Sed meticulosi hominis, si ita videatur, sint argumenta ista: Age, quantus cum novis istis ingeniis, novarum opinionum influet in Scholam gurges! qui deinceps, ut fit, ad mores & religionem derivatus, turbulentis tundet Remp. fluctibus: Quàm pertinaces exsurgent disputantium rixæ! Cùm nec inter nos conveniat, & videbitur indecorum fæminis cedere, & illis è contrario non ineptum ad contentiones ingenium: satis id probant domestica quotidie cum pueris ancillisque jurgia. Et subinde non parum angor, ne reseratis Philosophiæ scriniis, & perspectâ facultatum, quas conquisivimus mus tenuitate, expostulent ocyùs, & non è communi re gestum negotium, nobis improperent: qui jam à tot sæculis, ad mercandam publico bono Veritatem discurrimus, magno apparatu, exiguo huc usque quæstu & emolumento. Nec deerunt forte, quæ garrulâ, ut est illis, linguâ fucum nostrum plebi detegant, & meras nugas, quibus Schola tam sæpè fumat, exagitent. Deniq; muliebris sexus, sufficiendis in demigrantium loca inquilinis, nimis occupatur & insumitur: Videtur illis humani generis propaginem, nobis dignitatem Natura demandasse: illis ne intereat humanum genus; nobis ne degeneret, prospiciendum: Quantum melioris ætatis, gestandâ prole, pariendâ, fovendâ, lactandâ ablactandâque discedit! Si fæcundus in fœtum uterus, ad Sapientiæ studia vix supererit fracta senectus.
units.tr: Yet there are reasons against this, namely that the admission of women to our schools, if the matter is weighed cautiously and wisely, is not free of danger to us. For first, I maintain this: a keen mind, cultivated by the arts, ought not to be repelled from public offices. If you resist it spitefully, it will make for itself a way in by a thousand tricks and disturbances. Therefore, if women are to be admitted both to the schools and to public offices, what if they do not tolerate us as colleagues? What if they repay us in kind, as we deserve? Will they drive us off to the kitchen, to the pots, to the brooms, to the distaff, to the rags and swaddling of infants? Meanwhile they alone will deliberate on the highest affairs of the commonwealth, they alone will bear arms, they alone will be the priestesses in the temples, the judges in the courts, the mistresses on the platforms of the schools. Nor does it help here to shake out our own couches and threaten with manly brawn; in number it is incredible how greatly we are outnumbered, having been almost wiped out by the long slaughter of wars among ourselves. Besides, Nature has been more greedy in giving us to be born. But if these arguments seem to be the fears of a timid man, well then: consider what a flood of new opinions will pour into the school along with these new minds! Then, as usually happens, it will be carried over into morals and religion, and will batter the commonwealth with turbulent waves. How obstinate the quarrels of the disputants will rise up! Since we do not agree among ourselves, it will seem unbecoming for women to yield, and on the other hand their disposition is not unfit for contention; the daily domestic quarrels with boys and maidservants prove this well enough. And from time to time I am not a little anxious lest, once the coffers of philosophy are unlocked and the poverty of the faculties we have gathered is seen, they will quickly demand an account and reproach us with an enterprise not conducted for the common good: we who for so many centuries have been running about, with great display and little profit or gain so far, trading in Truth for the public good. Nor will there perhaps be lacking those who, with that chattering tongue which is theirs, expose our trickery to the common people and tear apart the mere trifles with which the school so often smokes. Finally, the female sex is too much occupied and taken up with supplying the tenants for those who are leaving their places. It seems to them that Nature has entrusted to them the propagation of the human race, and to us its dignity: they must see to it that the human race does not perish, we that it does not degenerate. How much of the better part of life is spent in carrying, bearing, fostering, nursing and weaning offspring! If the womb is fruitful for bearing children, scarcely any broken old age will be left over for the studies of wisdom.

units.la: Quæstio XI. An laudabile diversarum gen-tium idiomata perdiscendi studium?
units.tr: Question XI. Is the study of learning the languages of various peoples commendable?

units.la: Magna generis humani calamitas, linguarum, quibus scinditur in varias gentes diversitas: Nam quos in unum similis ratio conciliat, eosdem inter se dissimilis oratio separat: Indeque fit, ut ad dissitas forte regiones proficiscentes, videamur nobis inter mille tædia, non à domo & Patria, sed ab humana societate discessisse: Adeo ad crebra quæsita, quæ fertilis in interpellationes solicitudo progenerat, alibi taciturnitas reddитur, ditur, alibi risus, alibi disparata nec intellecta responsio. Videtur proinde communem illam calamitatem, in qua cuncti nascimur, feliciter à se depulisse, qui in capaci memoriâ plurimarum gentium repositit idiomata: Ubique inter suos est, omne solum ei patria: nusquam familiaribus intercænam sermonibus accumbit caperatâ fronte mutus auditor : nusquam viam sciscitaturus, mutilis mixtisque vocabulis cachinnum movet accolæ: nusquam inter ridentium sales suspiciosus,quid sibi velint, in aurem insusurrat interpreti. Ad hæc, magnum omnino confert bene regendæ Reipublicæ momentum, confinium populorum, sociorum, hostium novisse mores & genium; Atqui ista ex solo etiam idiomate non vanè conjiciet peritus rerum æstimator: tor : ita produnt gentis indolem ac studia linguæ stylus, & sermonis rigor aut lenitas. Hoc amplius, dispersa per Nationum libros arcana in unum thesaurum facile corradit linguarum peritia, & bene merità manu conquisitas ab extetis Scientiarum divitias profundit in patriam. Denique venustus est, & circumstantes mire detinet familiaris sermo diversorum populorum interpolatus adagiis: dum illa præsertim suis linguis, non alienâ, quam sæpe non bene callent, effantur: Et quasi Proscenium panditur, quo diversæ Nationes in spectaculum prodeant suâ linguâ declamantes: Suâ garrit Gallus, suâ lascivit Hispanus, suâ sibilat aspiratque & gargarizat Germanus, & subinde etiam barbarum quiddam ac exoticum adjiciunt Turcus & Arabs: Suspendit ininterim audientium animos interpres, & amænâ deludit ambage.
units.tr: The great calamity of the human race is the diversity of languages by which it is split into various nations. For those whom a like reason joins together, a dissimilar speech separates from one another. Hence it happens that when we set out for regions perhaps far away, we seem to ourselves, amid a thousand annoyances, to have departed not from home and country but from human society. So often, when a questioner's restless anxiety produces its many inquiries, the answer is silence in one place, laughter in another, and a garbled reply that is not understood in a third. He therefore seems to have happily driven off that common calamity into which we are all born, who has stored the idioms of very many nations in a capacious memory. Everywhere he is among his own; every land is his fatherland. Nowhere at a shared dinner, among familiar talk, does he sit as a silent listener with a furrowed brow; nowhere, when he asks his way, does a local raise a laugh at his broken and mixed-up words; nowhere, suspicious amid the jests of those who laugh, does he have to whisper to an interpreter what they mean. Besides, it contributes greatly to the well-ordered government of a commonwealth to know the manners and temper of neighbouring peoples, allies and enemies. Yet a skilled judge of affairs will not rashly infer these things from language alone: the style of a language, and the harshness or gentleness of its speech, reveal the character and pursuits of a nation. Furthermore, skill in languages easily gathers into one treasury the secrets scattered through the books of the nations, and pours into one's own country the riches of learning drawn from abroad by a well-earned hand. Lastly, it is charming, and a familiar conversation of diverse peoples, spiced with proverbs, holds the listeners wonderfully: especially when they utter those sayings in their own tongues rather than a foreign one, which they often do not speak well. And a kind of stage is opened, on which the different nations come forward as a spectacle, declaiming in their own language. The Frenchman chatters in his, the Spaniard prattles in his, the German hisses, breathes hard and gargles in his, and now and then the Turk and the Arab add something barbarous and exotic. Meanwhile the interpreter holds the minds of the hearers in suspense and beguiles them with a pleasant circumlocution.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod melior vitæ portio in linguis addiscendis prodigenda sit, si satis multas ad ostentationem memoriâ tenere, easque tibi familiares, & ad nutum promptas esse volueris: Tetricus qui hic desudat aridusque labor est, sine succo qui pascat animum, tricarum plenus, ingenii vacuus: quantum ei temporis adjicis, tantum Sapientiæ studio detrahis: Et forte ubi multa didiceris, vicina confundes, illaqueatus in ridiculum cahos, ægrè admodum expediendus, & jam etiam in materno idiomate balbus: Sed etsi rete istud operosè devites, aut obstinatè perrumpas; post laborem tamen nulla quies: fastigium hic non nisi iisdem, quibus ad id scanditur, nisibus ærumnisque tenetur: si vel tantillum remittas, mox in antiquum rudimentum devolutus, senties te cum Sisypho lapidem rotare. Accedit tot idiomatum congeriem, qua quidam obruunt memoriam, nulli plerumque bono usui parari; sed Vanitati dumtaxat in theatrum, quo se jactet subdi: Sufficit nobis cum vernaculâ, Latina lingua: hanc discipulis, illam popello damus: cur ad supervacua sudatur? Non mendicanda nobis à peregrinis linguis artium præcepta: totus in Latium concessit Scientiarum chorus, totus illi linguæ creditur hodie doctrinæ thesaurus: sola hæc è Magistri cathedrâ tonat, sola Discipulorum calamos exercet, sola replet voluminibus Musæa: hujus commercio in unam Remp. coëunt, quotquot per Europam & ultra disperguntur docti: cum hac, ubi tantantum extra vilissimam plebem sumus, ubique in patria, sumus. Denique in ipsis exterorum linguis, nescio quo contagio, eorundem vitia sunt: Alia loquax, alia salax, alia in supervacaneas cæremonias pomposa, alia in serviles Principum adulationes projecta: Candidus his, ô Belgæ, quia colorem facile bibit, inquinatur animus.
units.tr: On the other hand, it is against the case that the better part of life should be spent on learning languages, if you want to keep so many in memory for show, and to have them familiar and ready at your beck. That dry and grim labour, which toils here without juice to feed the mind, full of trifles and empty of wit: as much time as you add to it, so much you subtract from the pursuit of wisdom. And perhaps, when you have learned many, you will confuse those that are close to one another, entangled in a ridiculous chaos, very hard to extricate yourself from, and by then stammering even in your mother tongue. But even if you carefully avoid that snare, or obstinately break through it, there is no rest after the labour: this summit is held only by the same efforts and toils by which one climbs to it. If you relax even a little, you will soon slide back to the old rudiments and feel yourself rolling a stone like Sisyphus. Add to this that the heap of so many idioms, which some crush their memory with, is mostly acquired for no good use, but only to be displayed on the stage of Vanity so that one may show off. Latin suffices for us along with our vernacular: we give the one to students, the other to the common people. Why are we toiling over superfluous things? We need not beg the precepts of the arts from foreign tongues: the whole chorus of the sciences has retreated into Latium, and today the whole treasury of learning is entrusted to that language alone. It alone thunders from the teacher's chair, it alone exercises the pens of pupils, it alone fills the Muses' shelves with volumes. By its commerce all the learned who are scattered through Europe and beyond come together into one commonwealth; with it, where we are only the most worthless of the common people, we are at home everywhere. Lastly, in the very languages of foreigners, by some contagion, their vices are present: one is talkative, another lewd, another pompous over superfluous ceremonies, another prostrate in servile flattery of princes. A candid mind, O Belgians, is easily stained, because it readily drinks in the colour of these things.

units.la: Quæstio XII.
units.tr: Question XII.

units.la: An inter amicos conveniat Nova, quæ Remp. concernunt, narrare?
units.tr: Is it fitting for friends to relate news concerning the commonwealth?

units.la: HOdiernis moribus opportunè decretum est, ut à bonis malisvè Novis, in familiaribus colloquiis ducatur exordium : Nam & ea statim in plurimos divesissimosque discursus, uberi se venâ diffundunt, & scitè abigunt rancidos illos miserosque prologos, qui præmissâ salutatione, non nisi de præsentis auræ temperie, vel inclementiâ præfari didicêre. Adde quod exercitio isto intellectus plurimum in Politica Scientia proficiat: Dum bellicos Ducum æstus cum eventibus componit, suæ Reipublicæ statum cum hostium opibus trutinat, sociorum ex indiciis fidem probat aut suspectat: Et alibi inter calices etiam de Summa rei deliberat cum amicorum lepido Senatu: Quo pacto novis pecuniis exhaustum ærarium infarciri queat, unde auxilia conquirenda, quò mittendus ad hiberna miles, ubi debeant nova munimenta exstrui, ubi collapsa restitui: Et sunt quæ hic promuntur, inefficaces quiquidem; tamen sine partium studio, sine Principum adulatione sententiæ. Adde porrò, quòd jucundè pascatut animus, ambiguis rerum eventibus, inter hastam & caduceum, inter spem metumque suspensus: Nam subinde profugam jam nimium pacem intercipit alicubi ancipiti fiduciâ, & futuram securitatem delibat inter præsentes tumultus: Et modò insidias, excursiones ac stragem præsagit, & inter amicos præscire vult videri: Et subdit tamen hoc suspirium
units.tr: By the custom of our times it has been rightly decided that conversation among friends should begin with good or bad news. For such news at once spreads out into many and very rich digressions, pours forth in a copious stream, and wisely drives away those stale and wretched preambles which, after a greeting, have learned to say nothing but a word about the present weather, whether mild or harsh. Add that this exercise of the mind contributes greatly to political science: while it weighs the warlike exploits of generals against their outcomes, weighs the state of one's own commonwealth against the resources of the enemy, and tests or doubts the loyalty of allies from the signs given, and elsewhere, over cups, deliberates on the chief matter with the witty senate of friends: how the treasury drained by new expenses may be refilled, whence auxiliaries are to be sought, where a soldier is to be sent into winter quarters, where new fortifications should be built, and where collapsed ones restored. Though what is put forward here is, to be sure, ineffectual, yet the opinions are free of partisan zeal and of flattery of princes. Add further that the mind is pleasantly fed by the ambiguous outcomes of events, hung between spear and herald's staff, between hope and fear. For at one moment it seizes a peace already fled too far with an uncertain confidence, and anticipates a future security amid the present tumults; and now it foretells ambushes, sallies and slaughter, and wishes to seem to know them beforehand among friends. And yet it adds this sigh: "Would that I were a vain soothsayer for my country!"

units.la: — Utinam Patriæ sim vanus haruspex!
units.tr: — Would that I were a vain soothsayer for my country!

units.la: Et modò segnes increpat Ducum cunctationes, & indignatur elapsam incautis inter dentes & ungues victoriam: Nec mora, ipse belli ducem induitur, castra metatur, urbes obsidet, militem in mœnia subigit, & instat opeoperi, & à tergo premit, & perrumpit, & vincit: In amabilem insaniam semper ultrà & ultrà effræni se concitante mente: Dantque isthæc luculentum indicium, licet bene merendi occasionem iniqua Fortuna semoverit, cordati tamen & unicè Patriam amantis animi. Denique debita militibus impenditur Imperatoribusq; merces, quorum devota Patriæ pectora, exponunt se graßantibus hostium furiis gloriosum obicem: Dum hesternam victoriam, & abacta⁠m nuper ab hostibus prædam, mille modis Fama sedula propalat: In epistolis scribit, ad prelum imprimit, per Tabellarios defert: in foris legit, in templis murmurat, in vicis cantat, in tabernis divulgat: alibi exaggerat, alibi dubitat, alibi certat: Et tandem bene meritum facinus in historiarum monunumentis tradit immortalirati.
units.tr: And now it rebukes the sluggish hesitations of the generals and is indignant at a victory let slip from careless teeth and claws. Straightway the mind itself dons the role of war-leader, pitches camp, besieges cities, drives the soldier against the walls, presses hard on the enemy, attacks from the rear, breaks through, and conquers. The mind, unbridled, is always carried further and further in a lovable madness. These things give a clear sign of a mind wise and loving only its country, even if an unfair Fortune has removed the occasion of deserving well. Lastly, the wages due are paid to soldiers and generals, whose devoted hearts expose themselves as a glorious barrier to the raging fury of the enemy. Meanwhile busy Rumour spreads yesterday's victory and the booty lately snatched from the enemy in a thousand ways: she writes in letters, sends to the press, carries by couriers; she reads in the marketplaces, murmurs in the temples, sings in the streets, spreads abroad in the taverns; here she exaggerates, there she doubts, there she disputes. And at last she hands the well-deserved deed down to immortality in the monuments of history.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod sua quemque curare æquum est; aliena verò iniquum:
units.tr: On the other hand, it is against the case, because it is right for each to attend to his own affairs, and wrong to attend to another's:

units.la: Navita de ventis, de tauris narret arator:
units.tr: The sailor should speak of the winds, the ploughman of the bulls.

units.la: Quo ausu stolidum illud vulgus ingerit se in arcanas Principum curas, & circumspecta ac desudata consilia, temerariæ subjicit censuræ? Solo nimirum ista successu plebejum ingenium metitur; à quibus hunc Fortnna rescidit, iniqua sunt illis, vesana sunt illis, & perfida consilia: & hinc dilacerant maledicâ linguâ, concitantque se insulso rumultu in optimum sæpenumero ac Patriæ benevolentissimum Principem. At inter Philosophos (licet à profanis istis plebeculæ moribus, supientiâ secretos) exilis ille nimium, qui de Novis instituitur, sermo est: Indignum num quippe eos inter formicarum ossas constringere, & civitatum, quas in hoc terrestri puncto distinguì rident, obsidionibus detinere, quibus à vasta corporum cælestium mole, non minùs turget cognatus astris & familiaris animus. Adde quod Nova renarrantes, confictis plerumque nescio pro cujus libidine nugis occupemur: tot ista scatent mendaciis, ut ipsamet fidem, quam creduli adhibemus, irridere videantur: Sunt qui inter nocturna insomnia lucubratam fabulam, manè decantent facilibus illis & ad novum quemque tinnitum arrectis auribus: Quæ ab his porrò ad alios it ac alios, agglutinatque sibi à singulorum ingeniis partem aliquam,
units.tr: With what daring does that foolish crowd thrust itself into the secret cares of princes, and subject their circumspect and laboured counsels to rash censure? Undoubtedly the plebeian mind measures these things only by success: whatever Fortune has cut off from them, they judge unfair, mad and treacherous counsels; and so they tear at them with a slanderous tongue, and rush with senseless uproar against the best, and often most patriotic, of princes. But among philosophers (though secluded from the profane manners of the common crowd by their wisdom), that talk about news is too paltry. Is it not unworthy to confine them among the bones of ants, and to hold them under siege in those cities which they laugh at as divided in this little earthly point, when a kindred and familiar mind, swollen by the vast mass of the heavenly bodies, is no less akin to the stars? Add that in relating news we are mostly occupied with fictions, invented for the sake of I know not whose whim: such things teem with lies, so that they seem to mock the very trust which we credulous people give them. There are those who, during sleepless nights, compose a fable and at morning recite it to ears that are ready for every new jingle. From these it passes on to others and others, and gathers to itself some part from the talents of each,

units.la: Et vires acquirit eundo: Et subinde vesperi domum devolvitur, per omnium ora volutalutatum phantasma , tot additis circumstantiis oblitum, tot accersitis in munimen figmentorum figmentis, ut jam etiam Authori suo non difficulter imponat : Atqui ista sunt, quibus vicissim dolemus ac lætamur, angimur, speramus, desperamusque ridiculi: Et elusi hactenus, credulam etiamnum præbebimus aurem : ad primum rumorem excîti, forum petemus ocyùs, & in circulum pressi, auscultabimus impostorem : mox audita domum conferemus avidi: & subinde interpellabimur in viis, & renarrabimus scitè , & subinde sponte spargemus in obvios: Ita urimur mortales , ita juvat decipi.
units.tr: And it gathers strength as it goes: And later in the evening it rolls home, a phantom passed from mouth to mouth, so many circumstances added and so many fictions piled up in its defence that it easily imposes even on its own author. Yet these are the things by which, in turn, we grieve and rejoice, are troubled, hope and despair, ridiculous as we are. Though we have been fooled so far, we will still offer a credulous ear: roused by the first rumour, we will hasten to the marketplace, and pressed into the crowd we will listen to the impostor; soon, having heard him, we will eagerly carry it home; and afterwards we will be stopped in the streets, and will retell it cleverly, and then of our own accord we will spread it on to whoever we meet. Thus we mortals are set on fire, and thus it pleases us to be deceived.

units.la: Quæstio XIII.
units.tr: Question XIII.

units.la: An suam Patriam suosque cives, apud exteros laudare conveniat?
units.tr: Whether it is fitting to praise one's own country and fellow citizens before foreigners?

units.la: G Estat pietatis indubitatam tesseram, quem suorum tangit honos, quem Patriæ suæ decus irrequietis adurget stimulis, ut impatiens moræ, involet in munia Famæ non satis officiosæ, & meritam suis pompam apud exteros ducat zelosus apparitor: Atque interim arctas ipse sibi leges dictat, paria iis, quæ laudat, præstandi: turpe enim erit, si degener, si indignus laudatâ patriâ judicetur ipse laudator. Adde præconium istud, quod plenis buccis in Patriam difflamus, in nos ipsos provolvi latente ductu: Et cùm alibi suasuarum laudum invidiosus fit encomiasta, hîc jactantiam celat artificium, & prætensa pietas geminat honorem. Enimvero gloriosum est, in ea urbe infantem vagiisse, hîc hausisse spiritum, hîc indolem suxisse, ubi rerum nitor, ubi morum candor, & ad justum pondus temperata cum gravitate comitas: ubi inter sumptuosas ædium structuras ingeniosa ludit artificum industria, & inter opulentum apparatum augusta consternat intuentes amplitudo: Credibile quippe fit, illapsam aliquam istius aurę particulam, & cum rudi adhuc animulo permixtā, conformasse eum ad decus & sublimitatem. Quid quod prædicatio illa ad referendum gratias alliciat, & totam Patriam benevolo devinciat alumno? Alibi scitè laudasse, unius alicujus popularis amicitiam parit; hîc feliciori proventu, omnium: Et hinc distribuendis Magistratuum officiis intento populo, magnâ jure merito valet prærogativâ, quem constat oblatis occasionibus, è dignitate Civium solitum censerere; Sicut è contrario non nisi repulsam apud suos ambit execrabilis candidatus, cui quondam inter pocula soluto, temerè excidit, quæ Reipublicæ Majestatem violabat, calumnia.
units.tr: Surely it is an unmistakable mark of piety when the honour of one's own people touches a man, and the glory of his country spurs him on with restless goads, so that, impatient of delay, he rushes into the duties of a not very dutiful Fame and, as a zealous attendant, leads the deserved procession of praise among foreigners. Meanwhile he lays down strict laws for himself: he must do the very things he praises. For it would be shameful if the one who praises his country were judged degenerate and unworthy of it. Add that this boasting, which we puff out with full cheeks on behalf of our homeland, rolls back upon ourselves by a hidden leading. While elsewhere the self-praiser becomes hateful for his own praises, here the pretence of piety hides the vanity and doubles the honour. Indeed it is glorious to have wailed as an infant in that city, to have drawn breath and sucked in one's character there, where there is splendour of affairs, candour of manners, and courtesy tempered to just weight with gravity; where the ingenious industry of craftsmen plays among sumptuous building works, and the majesty of the place astonishes onlookers amid rich furnishings. It is credible that some particle of that breeze, mingled with the still rude little soul, shaped him to dignity and loftiness. What of the fact that such praise wins people to giving thanks and binds the whole country to a benevolent foster-child? To praise well elsewhere gains the friendship of one fellow countryman; here, with a happier outcome, it gains the friendship of all. And hence, when the people is intent on distributing the offices of the magistracy, he rightly and justly enjoys a great prerogative, since it is well known that on offered occasions citizens are wont to rate a man by his dignity. Just as, on the contrary, the detestable candidate, whom a slander against the majesty of the Republic once rashly slipped out over his cups, seeks nothing but rejection from his own people.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod illa Patriæ & civium assentatrix laudatio, difficulter occulat perorantis jactantiam, alienas laudes sibi arrogantem: nam quantumvis illa speciosum prætendat; hæc tamen à peritis rerum deprehenditur sub fuco, & inter candestinas ambages intercipitur: hîc verò dum patet, tum ipsa præter eam, quæ sibi propria est, quam de se progignit ama-
units.tr: Yet on the other side it counts against him that such flattering praise of country and citizens can hardly conceal the boasting of the speaker, who arrogates to himself the praise of others. However specious a pretext it puts forward, it is detected under the veneer by those skilled in affairs and is caught in secret circumlocutions. Here, moreover, when it is exposed, the thing itself, apart from the self-love that is its own and that it begets concerning itself,

units.la: amarulentam invidiam, nescio quid malignum de fraude trahit, quod non nisi obtortis oculis aspici potest. Quin huc etiam opprobrii contemptusque speciem ad acerbitatis summam accersit: Dum namque suorum decora clangit sublatâ tubâ, aut his imparia Exteris improperat, aut paribus insolenter obstrepit: Donec assidentium turba, diuturno jam lacessita fastidio, mordaces hinc inde regerit facetias, & tandem inter irridentium sibilos demittit confusum praeconem: Et verò si pretio isto aliquantus Patriæ veniret homnos, non essent detrectanda ludibria; Scomma est, quod illi emi tanto, & eodem nobiscum Patriam involvimus convitio: Gravitatem fastui, splendorem luxu vertunt interpretes peverfissimi. Ajunt comem illū, qui nobis prio priu orius est, officiosumque sermonem, nil esse præter marsupium palpantes blanditias, & sub composita larva inhiantem lucro cupidine: Quin fuerunt, qui improbo spiritu fanatici, lividum calamum listrinxêre in Dithyrambū: & laudibus, quibus nos gentilis alicujus pietas irradiaverat, diras opposuerunt: Adeò tenebriones istos exagitat, quod se non celat decus. Expedit ergo quam suos laudare, cum suis laudanda facere: & Exteros tacito illo ac suavi filo obsequentes, in venerationem Patriæ pertrahere, quàm intempestivo laudum crepitaculo, quasi vis inferretur, obluctantes experiri.
units.tr: bitter envy, and it draws from fraud something malicious that can be looked at only with sidelong eyes. Indeed it also summons to the highest bitterness the appearance of disgrace and contempt. For while he trumpets the glories of his own people with raised trumpet, he either reproaches foreigners as unequal to them or insolently clamours over equals; until the crowd of bystanders, already provoked by a long-lasting weariness, returns biting jokes from every side and at last, amid the hisses of the mockers, lets the confused herald down. And indeed, if the country came to us at this price, such mockeries should not be shunned; but it is a joke, because we buy it so dearly and involve our country in the same reproach as ourselves. The most perverse interpreters turn gravity into arrogance and splendour into luxury. They say that the courteous man who is most devoted to us and his obliging speech are nothing but flattering caresses patting the purse, and a greed gaping for gain under a composed mask. There have been some who, with the wicked spirit of fanatics, have sharpened a malignant pen into a dithyramb and opposed dire curses to the praises with which the piety of some gentleman had lit us up; so much does the glory that does not hide itself torment those scoundrels. It is therefore more expedient to praise one's own people by making them worthy of praise, and to draw foreigners, yielding to that quiet and sweet thread, into veneration of the homeland, than to test them by resisting, with an untimely rattle of praise, as if violence were being applied.

units.la: Quæstio XIV.
units.tr: Question XIV.

units.la: An in Theatralibus spectaculis exercenda juventus?
units.tr: Whether young people should be trained in theatrical spectacles?

units.la: ORbis terræ, Theatrum est: in hoc personam agimus omnes: Et adoratas regum majestates, pariter cum ludicro Tyranno, sæpè circumscripsit hora una. Quid ni igitur, ô juvenes, optabile sit in Scenam quandoque prodire? id est gratâ vicissitudine, à magno illo Theatro, in parvum quoddam secedere: ac ibidem exutâ plebis quam inviti geritis, personâ, parserè cum Mundi Monarchis, momento debacchari. Adde, Proceres & Satrapas & circumfusum incurvo poplite Satellitium, quæ in vasto illo Proscenio perduellis est hîc esse tutam turbam: Conspiren- quamquamvis; innoxia est eorum in ca-put tuum conjuratio, sine cede re-bellio: Nec magè lædit, quæ fabu-lam claudet, funesta catastrophe. Sed etsi triumphales tibi pompas, & supplices ad nutum accursus, ex æquo ludat simuletque Scena, ne cede tamen, ne cede parte ista Cæ-saribus: Feres etiam hic, judice me, palmam: Horum honores assenta-tor; tuos histrio mentitur: Dic quid interest? Tibi inter festivas acclamationes securo esse licet; his sub blandiente palpo insidiatur jugulaturus mucro: Quantum in-terest! At nos qui Orchestram pre-mimus Spectatores, suspicimus in plebejo juvene, dignam diademate frontem, & obtutum Solio ac Fas-cibus parem: Et subinde colligi-mus tantillum esse, quod humili-tatem inter & majestatem est: Et deturbamus tandem ex animo peftiferum illud Idolum, quod Principatui tam magnificum effinxerat Superstitio, & cui tot anhela suspiria necquicquam immolaverat Ambitio: nec desunt de circumfusa plebe, qui nobiscum sentiant, extemporales Philosophi. Videtur etiam exercitio hoc, violentos illos spiritus sedari posse, qui quandoque intra depressæ & angustæ sortis cavernas indignantes, moliuntur irruptionem cum strage, & ad invertendum Reipublicæ statum, turbulento feruntur impetu: His si detur in Cothurnum erigere se, & in Heroica quædam crepitacula effutire, videntur sibi inani istâ specie, naturalem amplitudinem consecuti: Et tantisper laxati, imposterum concutiunt & quassant mitiùs.
units.tr: The whole world is a theatre: in it we all play a part, and the revered majesties of kings are often reduced, within a single hour, to the level of a comic tyrant. Why then, young men, should it not be desirable now and then to step onto the stage? That is, by a welcome change, to withdraw from that great theatre into a small one, and there, having put off the commoner's mask you wear against your will, to rage for a moment on nearly equal terms with the monarchs of the world. Add that on that vast stage it is safe to be a rebel among nobles and satraps and the attendant crowd bowing low: the conspiracy they form against your head is harmless, and rebellion without bloodshed. Nor does the fatal catastrophe that closes the play harm anyone more. But even if the stage gives you triumphal processions and suppliant crowds running at your nod, do not give up, do not give up that part to the Caesars. In my judgement you will carry off the palm here too. The actor lies with honours for them; for you he merely pretends. Tell me, what is the difference? Among festive acclamations you may be safe; for them, a dagger lies in wait under a flattering pat. How great the difference! But we spectators, crowded into the pit, look up at a young man of common birth whose brow is worthy of a diadem and whose bearing matches a throne and the fasces. And thereupon we gather that there is only a tiny gap between humility and majesty. At last we cast out of our minds that pestilent idol which superstition had moulded so grandly for sovereignty, and to which ambition had sacrificed so many panting sighs in vain. Nor are there lacking, among the crowd around, impromptu philosophers who agree with us. This exercise also seems able to calm those violent spirits which, sometimes indignant within the caverns of a low and narrow lot, plan an irruption with slaughter and rush with a turbulent impetus to overturn the state of the commonwealth. If these are allowed to raise themselves onto the buskin and to spout heroic bombast, they seem to themselves to have gained their natural greatness by that empty show; and, relaxed for the time being, they shake and batter less fiercely afterwards.

units.la: Contrà. Compendiosus ad insaniam juventuti trames, exercitatio tio ista: Animus ætate fervet, & agili implexus spiritu, salit & extuberat suâpte naturâ: Ad quid adventitio isto instigatur impulsu, nisi ut exorbitet toto cælo? & jam res ipsas hyperbolico pede transgressus, imaginariis implicetur deliriis, Fabulosorum Heroum ridiculus æmulator: Ita nempe perstringitur ludicris illis Paludamentorum Sceptrorumque fulgoribus, ut ad seria caliget: ita clamosis obtunditur Tragœdiæ metris, ut verum moderatumque non capiat: Mox ad id omne, quod jambico tonitru non immugit, surdaster. Quin hæc in scelus, si cautè pensites, via lubricat: Et quandoque revera sævus est, qui decernit simulata supplicia, qui inocentum sanguine & favillâ gestit Mimus: & fermè sacrilegus, dum Superos seque execratur, dum frendet & furit, & fas nefasque miscet: Non totum illud hæret in alienis exuviis; Sine sensu liquescit aliquid, & distillat in animum: Distat Serium à Ficto, non ita magno, ut rudes putant, intervallo: Aut sanè ab hoc, in illud pronus est & lubricus, discensus. Ut ut est, candidum animum non bene stringunt artæ illæ & infauste larvæ: nec decet ingenuum adolescentem, Sceleris alicujus, quod detestamur, quodque humano generi tam diram inussit notam, tam aptè repræsentare personam: Eum ego hominem suspicio, qui nefanda ista (ut sunt) non effatur, qui nescit ista describere, cui displicent non scelera modò, sed & scelerum umbræ: qui vellet fœdum illud pus, quod virulento contactu refugientem exulcerat memoriam, Nerones, inquam, & Heliogabalos, los, quod unum possumus, in æ-terno silentio defodi: Cur cloa-cam moves? cur portentis illis cor-tinam aperis ? Impius in genus tuum quisquis es nugator.
units.tr: On the contrary: this exercise is a short road to madness for young people. The mind boils with age and, entangled in an agile spirit, leaps and swells of its own nature. To what end is it stirred by this outside impulse, unless to go astray by the whole heaven? And once it has crossed the boundaries of reality with a hyperbolic step, it is entangled in imaginary delusions, a ridiculous imitator of the heroes of fable. Thus it is so dazzled by the showy glitter of military cloaks and sceptres that it grows blind to serious matters; so deafened by the noisy metres of tragedy that it cannot grasp what is true and measured; and soon it becomes deaf to everything that does not roar with iambic thunder. Indeed, if you consider carefully, this path slides toward crime. And sometimes the one who decrees feigned punishments is truly cruel, the mime who delights in the blood and ashes of the innocent; he is almost a sacrilegious man, while he curses the gods above and himself, rages and storms, and mingles right and wrong. Not all of that clings to foreign cast-off garments; something dissolves without sense and trickles into the mind. The serious differs from the feigned by no great interval, as the untrained think, or at least the descent from one to the other is sloped and slippery. However that may be, those narrow and ill-omened masks do not bind a candid mind well, nor does it become a well-born young man to represent so aptly the character of some crime, which we detest and which has stamped so dire a mark upon the human race. I suspect that man who does not utter those wicked deeds (as they are), who does not know how to describe them, who dislikes not only crimes but even the shadows of crimes: the man who would wish that foul pus, which with its poisonous touch ulcerates the memory that recoils from it, to be buried in eternal silence, since we can do only this with Neros and Heliogabaluses. Why do you stir up the sewer? Why do you open the curtain on those monsters? Whoever you are, you impious trifler against your own kind.

units.la: Quæstio XV.
units.tr: Question XV.

units.la: An expediat viros doctos, divi-tes, an, ut sit, pauperes esse?
units.tr: Whether it is advantageous for learned men to be rich, or, as is the case, poor?

units.la: NAturalis amplitudinis Doctrinæ vindices Divitiæ: Alioqui ad po-stem Egestatis alligata, necquicquam in valvis ejus pro-micat, & indignans lora tendit, ad sui fermè strangulatum. O si Musarum Mystæ: ô si Aureum illud Numen, propitiâ manu laxet il-lam, quæ tam malè nos habet, re-stim! Quàm grata foret inassuetis pedibus, patens in excursum a-rea! rea! ut juvaret in aperto sole apricari, longo situ jam senta membra! Nec tamen in effrænem proterviam dissolveremur cum Vulgo, cui Dea illa ( quod pace ejus dixerim ) nimium indulsit: Alias nobis leges præscribunt modestæ illæ & placidæ, quas amamus, quas deperimus Musæ. Sed profecto, quæ facies rerum! quantus inesset officio nostro splendor, si iidem essemus, & Musarum Antistites, & Mecœnates! Quanta se castris nostris agglomeraret turba! Ut sub opulentis ex stipendio veteranis, æmularentur indefessa tyrocinia! Jam, incredibile est, quantum Virtuti conferrent, crebræ, quas illi de more consecramus, disputationes & honorificæ censuræ: Quantum haberet Sententia nostra pondus, si audientes pariter, & ratio convinceret, & fulgor perstrinstringeret ! si aurata dicentem ful-cirent pulvinaria, & longo in ter-ram syrmate deflueret è cathedra murex, astaret pedibus discolor famulitium. At nunc sub detrita palla, & nudo è pulpito, quod u-num superest, Numini tuo lita-mus, ô Virtus: æqui boniqueconsule , ô Virtus : Magnificè de te censemus, amplum subitò stylum adhibemus , sonora verba conge-rimus , ubi incidis in mentionem: Nec desunt de numero nostro, qui promissam barbam& impexum ca-pillitium afferant austeri: ut splen-dorem , quem majestati tuæ con-ciliare non possunt , sacro quem à profanis mentibus extorquent, horrore compensent. Sed hoc ta-citus nullo modo præterire pos-sum , Philosophus qui sim : In Physicis summa regula : Explora naturam experimentis: suntque hæc tum propriis impendiis, tum aliorum, ut necesse est fieri, conductis operis sumptuosa; Hoc admiculo destituti nostrates Philosophi, risum non teneas, ita suspicantur & hariolantur variè: Et tandem id statuunt plerumque, quod speciosum, quod Mundi harmoniam ornatumque commendet: Salvete ô bene meriti de Natura rerum Errones: Quin ridiculo isto, quo nitimini principio, Philosophos omnes divites asseritis? Et, ut video, assereretis profecto, nisi Sensus tam vivaci ferulâ doceret contrarium.
units.tr: Riches are the champions of learning in its natural greatness. Otherwise, bound to the doorpost of Want, it strives in vain to get out through its doors, and, indignant, strains its reins until it nearly strangles itself. O if the initiate of the Muses, O if that golden deity with a propitious hand would loosen that cord which treats us so badly! How welcome would an open area be to our unaccustomed feet, for basking in the open sun, our limbs long stiff with neglect! Yet we would not dissolve into unbridled impudence along with the crowd, to which that goddess (with her pardon be it said) has been too indulgent. Otherwise those modest and gentle Muses, whom we love and whom we dote upon, prescribe other laws for us. But truly, what a state of affairs! How much splendour would our office have, if we were both the priests of the Muses and their patrons! How large a crowd would gather in our camp! How the untiring apprentices would vie with one another under veterans paid from rich stipends! Indeed, it is incredible how much frequent disputations and honourable assessments, which we in our customary way dedicate to them, would contribute to virtue. How much weight our opinion would have if, while the listeners were equally moved, reason convinced them and brilliance dazzled them; if gilded cushions propped up the speaker, and a purple robe of many colours trailed in a long train down from the chair, and a varied retinue stood at his feet! But now, under a worn cloak and from a bare pulpit, we offer only what remains, to your divinity, O Virtue: you are pleased with what is equitable and good, O Virtue. We think highly of you, we at once adopt a grand style and heap up sonorous words whenever your name comes up. Nor are there lacking, among our number, austere men who bring a promised beard and unkempt hair, so that they may compensate with the sacred horror they wrest from profane minds for the splendour they cannot win for your majesty. But I cannot pass over this in silence, of what sort of philosopher I am: the highest rule in physics is, "Test nature by experiments." These, whether at one's own expense or at the expense of hired workers, as must be done, are costly undertakings. Our native philosophers, deprived of this aid, guess and divine in various ways, so that one can hardly keep from laughing. And at last they mostly settle on whatever is showy and commends the harmony and ornament of the world. Greetings, O wanderers who have deserved well of the nature of things! Indeed, do you not, by that ridiculous principle you rely on, declare all philosophers rich? And, as I see it, you would surely declare so, were it not that experience taught the contrary with a very lively rod.

units.la: Contrà. Esset doctorum hominum nimis invidenda felicitas; & aliorum deplorata calamitas, si illos & Opes erigerent & Scientiæ; hos Paupertas deprimeret & Insci-tia: Cur cum tantis montibus voragines tantæ? Nimias illas asperitates tates exosa, planitie gaudet æquabilis Natura: & liberali fluxu profusa, distribuit se potius in omnes, quam avarâ manu, in unum congerat, quod cæteris detrahat: Et hinc aliis quidem Musas, aliis Fortunas elargita, videtur istâ compensatione reperisse paritatem; Quia tamen varietate capitur, montes etiam subinde quosdam attollit, in quos conglobatâ mole, & Scientias pariter & Divitias, & Dignitates accumulat: Non invidemus; Sed in subjectum pavimentum cum plebe librati, suspicimus: & si modo licet, enitimur, & assurgimus exemplo. Sed mafte, ô quisquis es Musarum Patrone: Colliga, si lubet, intra scamna nostra Doctrinam & Quæstum: Et ecce quæ species! Mox sartores, sutores, fabros, cerdones: totum illum Diti ac Lucro initiatum gregem, gem, abjectis forcipibus & subulis & incudibus & ferris & trullis, intra Scholas nostras compactum videbis: Quænam illa confusio? Interitus rerum paratur isto molimine: Nihil exaggerandi gratiâ dico: Quid? Nympha nostra, nullâ penè dote propositâ, formâ tantum & augusta specie, innumeras illas Studiosorum classes pellexit in amorem: Et inter hos quibus interdum feliciori radio, Dominæ blanditur oculus, pertinaci ad fores ejus statione, perdios & pernoctes videbis, ad siccam usque tussim ac tabem: Dentur divinæ isti pulchritudini census & divitiæ: & desipio, nisi totus Mundus, relictis necessariis ministeriis abeat in corrivales. Quod si ista non tenent, sed obluctamur, & porro ad divitias pergimus avidi, Saltem hic in diverticulo tantisper subsistendum cencenseo, donec divitum leges nobiscum ipsi revoluerimus; ne forte castris illis nomen dedisse poeniteat, dum serius est: Eorum hæc sunt officia: interdiu sæpius loculos invisere, summam recensere, ratiunculam subducere: subinde etiam sperisis hinc inde de industria nummulis, domesticorum fidem tentare: vesperi universam domum obire, ceras, vectes, & pessulum explorare: nocte aliquoties lecto exilire, sedes & scamna infestare, angulos incursare, & vociferari, ne forte celent alicubi illud revellens claustra, illud effringens fores, quod somnum expulit somnium. O bona Minerva! quàm belle dorso nostro quadraret ista sarcina! qui quovis negotio interpellati, morosi sumus & inviti: & interdum vel levi tantum strepitu inter sacra tua disturbati, excandesci-
units.tr: On the contrary: the good fortune of learned men would be too much to envy, and the wretched lot of others too much to lament, if wealth and learning raised the former, while poverty and ignorance kept the latter down. Why such abysses alongside such mountains? Nature, which hates excessive roughness, delights in an even plain, and pouring herself out in a generous flow, she distributes herself among all rather than gathering in a grasping hand what she takes from the rest. Thus, granting the Muses to some and fortune to others, she seems to have found equality by this balance. Yet because variety delights, she also raises up certain mountains now and then, upon which she piles, in a massed heap, learning, riches and dignities alike. We do not envy; but, balanced with the common people on the level floor below, we look up, and if we may, we strive and rise by example. But come, O whoever you are, patron of the Muses: gather, if you like, within our benches, learning and gain. And see what a sight! Soon you will see tailors, cobblers, smiths, butchers, the whole crowd initiated into Pluto and Lucre, with tongs, awls, anvils, iron tools and trowels cast aside, crowded together inside our schools. What a confusion! The ruin of things is being prepared by this effort. I say nothing by way of exaggeration. What? Our nymph, offering almost no dowry but only her form and noble appearance, has enticed innumerable classes of students into love. Among these, on whom at times her eye smiles with a more fortunate ray, you will see them keeping a persistent watch at her doors by day and by night, until they are worn down by a dry cough and wasting. Let riches and wealth be given to that divine beauty, and I am a fool unless the whole world, abandoning its necessary services, goes over to her rivals. But if these things do not hold, and we struggle on and keep greedily pressing toward riches, I think we should at least stay for a while in this inn, until we have turned over the laws of the rich with ourselves, lest perhaps we regret having enlisted in those camps when it is too late. Their duties are these: during the day to visit the purses often, to review the sum, to work out a little reckoning; and now and then, having deliberately scattered small coins here and there, to test the loyalty of the servants; in the evening to go round the whole house, inspecting the wax seals, bars and bolts; at night to leap from bed several times, to molest the chairs and benches, to run through the corners and shout, lest perhaps somewhere someone is hiding who, by pulling out the bolts or breaking through the doors, has driven out sleep with a dream. O good Minerva! How well would this burden fit our back! We who, whenever interrupted by any business, are peevish and unwilling; and who, sometimes disturbed even by a slight noise amid your sacred rites, grow angry.

units.la: Quæstio XVI.
units.tr: Question XVI.

units.la: An officii gratia, invisentem amicum, geniali potione accipere conveniat.
units.tr: Whether, as a matter of courtesy, it is fitting to take a convivial drink when visiting a friend.

units.la: TArdum ac austerum, etiam inter familiarissimos sermonis initium: Nam is depulso necdum lentore, quem à præcedente silentio trahit, laborat in vestibulo, & duriusculè, quasi remorantes inter asperitates, provolvitur: Si proinde limen istud geniali liquore proluimus, salva res est: lubricâ jam semitâ, fertur ocyùs in consuetas fabulas, quæ horas devorant & diem: & ne sic quidem expletæ, ad seram noctem abrumpuntur veriùs, quàm finiuntur. Ad hæc, laxat ille succus & emollit arcanas curas, quas sobria nimis verecundia constrinxerat in obstinatam sub pectore duritiem : Hæ uno jam alterove haustu conspersæ, macerantur & liquescunt sensim, & solutæ pertentant exitum; Sæpiusque repelluntur, & detinentur dentibus, & in summis labiis reperiunt obicem; At charo sinui, dum se offert, dum probatam toties fidem, & spondet, & exprobat, denique committitur depositum : Et ecce ! jam generosus eructat singultus compactam illam, quæ immeritum cor, suffocatum ibat, massam : Subit interim partitum onus amicus, extenuatque verbis: Tum ultro citroque consultant: Et montes Ætnæ omnes atque asperos Athones, quos atra bilis, & silentium, & solitudo aggeaggeraverant, tandem in plani-tiem diffundit irriguum de majori Dyòta profluvium. Quin falsos amicos eâdem operâ detegimus: Nam reperto alicubi per larvam spiraculo, exhalat sæpenumerò cum fumis Lyæi, indoles quædam humilis & prava, inimica candori, probum illud ac industrium indignè exagitans; vafro tamen, quamdiu excubabat, ingenio dissimulata: Et qui terga latenter infestaverat Susurro, formam immutante Libero, faciem non reveretur Contumeliosus: Ridemus dum se prodit: & miseret nos, tantum antehac calamistris & fuco deformem impendisse Momum.
units.tr: Conversation is harsh and austere at the start, even between the closest friends. Speech, not yet freed from the sluggishness that the previous silence imposes, struggles on the threshold and rolls out rather stiffly, as if snagged on roughnesses. If we wet that threshold with a convivial liquor, all is well. The path now slippery, talk runs more quickly into its customary chatter, which devours the hours and the day; and even so, unsatisfied, it is broken off late at night rather than ended. Besides, that juice relaxes and softens the hidden cares which excessive sober modesty had bound into a stubborn hardness beneath the breast. Sprinkled with one or two draughts, these cares soak and gradually melt, and once loosened they press towards the exit. Often they are pushed back and held by the teeth, and find a barrier at the very lips. But when they are offered to a dear bosom, when the faith so often tried is pledged and urged, the deposit is at last entrusted. And behold! Now the noble friend belches out sobs, that compacted mass which was choking the undeserving heart. Meanwhile the friend takes up part of the burden and lightens it with words. Then they consult back and forth, and all the Etnas and rough Athoses which black bile, silence and solitude had piled up are at last spread over the plain by a copious flood of greater Dyota (wine). Indeed, by the same means we also uncover false friends. For when some vent is found through the mask, there often breathes out with the fumes of Lyaeus a certain base and wicked disposition, hostile to candour, unworthily harassing the upright and diligent man, yet concealed by cunning while it kept watch. And one who had secretly attacked the back with whispering, now with Liber changing his form, the insulter feels no shame at his face. We laugh while he betrays himself, and we pity Momus for having spent so much until now on a face deformed by curling-irons and rouge.

units.la: Contrà tamen facit, quòd propinatio ista frequentior, amicos dolio tuo pariat, non tibi: Donec huic vena fluet, adhærebunt lateri Achates isti: Nutus observant obvii, num fortè in pomeridianum adesse jubeas; Si jusseris, præsto sunt cum umbris: Sedetur, bibitur: Et ut propensi cujusque animi certa sit tibi fides, illicò salutí tuæ consulunt, non sine cæremoniis: Nam Salius ingentem gutturi devovet, ad ultimam usque stillam, quæ unguiculo excipienda est, cratherem: Et Sospes, ait, sit hospes: Circuit porrò per confodalium orbem Amystis: atque in caput iterum iterumque redit. Sed explora, si lubet, officiosò istos, invisentes siccos habe: Caussaberis exanime jam ferè vasculum tuum, ad pulsum digiti, miserum in modum bombilare: Ecce, demittunt auriculas, medios fermè sermones abrumpunt, &
units.tr: On the other hand, this frequent drinking has the effect that such friends are born to your cask, not to you. As long as the vein flows, those Achates cling to your side. Attendants watch your nods, to see whether perhaps you bid them come in the afternoon; if you order, they are at hand with their shadows. They sit, they drink. And so that you may be sure of the loyalty of each one's inclined mind, they at once look after your health, not without ceremonies. Salius vows a huge cup to his throat, down to the last drop, which must be caught on a fingernail, and says, "Safe be the guest!" Then Amystis goes round the circle of fellow-drinkers and comes back to your head again and again. But test these obliging visitors, if you like: go dry. You will pretend your little vessel is almost empty, and at the tap of a finger it gurgles pitifully. Behold, they droop their ears, break off the conversation halfway, and

units.la: diffugiunt cadis Cum fæce siccatis amici, Ferre jugum pariter dolosi.
units.tr: "the friends scatter from the casks, dried of their dregs, unwilling to bear the yoke together with a deceiver."

units.la: Quid? Nònne grave omne & solidum, quod in Virtutis fundamentum corraserat Sobrietas, emolliunt illa stillicidia, & dissolvunt in inutile lutum? Tum animus à subjecto limo flaccidus, cedit arduo, contra difficilia fugax, subjici & componi promptus, languet ad perrumpendum: Sanè experimento discimus, raro versari serium inter pocula sermonem, qui honestati vim & decus addat: Frivolum, & de lana caprina est, quidquid hîc garrulas exercet linguas: Et quæ diductis leviter labiis, modico vix risu dignaremur jejuni, illa, & vix illa sunt, quæ effusos hîc cient cum temulentia cachinnos: Quin ibidem sæpè manum fatigat alea, & intentum cerebrum vertigine corripiunt scrupi, & chartulæ lusoriæ: turpiter ille quæstuosus cum jurgiis labor. abor. Quod si incommoda ista ab invisentium cœtu, rariore scy- pho propellas, patieris alia non ninora: Charum inter cætera ca- put, & meliora meritum, quem obliviosa præterierit propinatio, neglectus suspicione confusum, & vultu luctantem cum indigno pudore.
units.tr: What then? Do not those drops soften everything solid which temperance had hardened as the foundation of virtue, and dissolve it into useless mud? Then the mind, flabby from the soft mud, yields to what is arduous, flees from difficulties, and is ready to be bent and arranged, but grows languid at breaking through. Indeed, by experience we learn that serious conversation, the kind that would add force and dignity to honour, rarely takes place over the cups. Frivolous is whatever chatter exercises the garrulous tongues here. What we, fasting, would scarcely deem worthy of a slight smile with lips barely parted, those, or scarcely those, are what raise loud guffaws here amid drunkenness. Indeed, in the same place dice often tire the hand, and dice-boxes and gaming-cards seize the intent brain with dizziness, and the shameful labour of gain comes together with quarrels. But if you ward off these inconveniences from the company of visitors by a rarer cup, you will suffer others no less: a dear head, deserving of better things, whom the forgetful toast has passed over, is embarrassed by the suspicion of being neglected, and struggles with an unworthy shame in his face.

units.la: Quæstio XVII.
units.tr: Question XVII.

units.la: An meridianis præstent vespertina convivia?
units.tr: Do evening banquets surpass midday ones?

units.la: AUgustum quid & magnificum habent nocturna solennia: Nam languida funalium lumina, nævos & inconcinna celant, & rei speciem vicinitate suâ commendant, ac ultra verum distendunt laterales umbræ: Insuper Nox ipsa, quæ fores obsidet cui alto Silentio, quo Majestatem Æ&tui conciliet, circumfundit ali quid de superstitioso Terrore. Quin igitur in seram vesperam differas Convivium, si tantus luxus, tantillo parari possit impendio. Tunc etiam animus noster qui interdiu in diversa dispergitur, curis jam defunctus, conferet se totum intra triclinium: retrahensque se ab atra illa, quæ terras undique cælumque tenet solitudine, gestiet ad candelarum facu-las, insolitâ quadam, quæ meridiem non novit, ac titillante lætitiâ: Intempestâ ceu fortè nocte Insomnes pueri, mille timent lemurum ludibria, donec correptâ stragulâ obvolvant caput, tremulo jam gaudio sollicitante corculum, quod confusum illud Silentum chaos, qui minitabant straragem, & excidium & his pe-ora centuplo, egregius iste pro-ulset agger. Si genio indultum uberius, si plus æquo compota-um fuerit, semotis arbitris indi-ium omne sepelitur in caligine: Nec titubantem in reditu pedem otant cum falsâ irrisione, latè de-populata jam & cæca fora: At an-eambuloni suspicionem eximit ncrepatio : Nam accelerat cum ucerna, retardàtve nimium: Et vicinior radius perstringit ocu-um; remotior absorbetur ab o-paco; Ambo mali duces: Quid mi-rum si herus cespitet? Domum am reversum, quantocyùs exci-pit cubile : Tum vapido, qui ce-rebrum circumvolat, fumo, spon-te sociat se Somnus: à subsidio jam intrepidus, jam curarum, quas ante fugiebat, incuriosus: Et illabens deciduo cum rore, mul-cet cet artus in tenacem quietem: qu[?] nil galliciniis, nil languido mo[?] crepusculo, abrumpitur demu[?] valido jam Sole, & altùm tumu[?] tuante cum vehiculis equisqu[?] plebe.
units.tr: Nocturnal festivities have something august and magnificent. The feeble lights of the torches hide blemishes and awkward things and lend the scene an appearance by their proximity, and the side shadows stretch it beyond the truth. Besides, Night herself, who besieges the doors, surrounds the whole with a deep Silence by which she lends the feast majesty, and something of superstitious Terror. Why then do you not defer the banquet to late evening, if such luxury can be provided at such small expense? Then also our mind, which during the day is scattered in diverse directions, now freed from its cares, will betake itself wholly within the dining-room. Withdrawing from that black solitude which holds lands and sky on every side, it will delight in the candle-flames with a strange joy unknown at midday, and a tickling pleasure. As boys, sleepless on some untimely night, fear a thousand mockeries of ghosts, until, seizing a blanket, they wrap their heads, with trembling joy now stirring their little hearts, so that the confused chaos of those Silences, which threatened slaughter and destruction and horrors a hundredfold, is kept far off by that remarkable rampart. If more than enough indulgence is given to the genius, if more than is right is drunk, then with the witnesses removed all decency is buried in darkness. Nor do the empty streets, now deserted and blind, mock the staggering foot on the way back with false derision. The echo of the walker's step removes suspicion, for it hurries with the torch-bearer or lags too far behind; and the nearer ray dazzles the eye, while the more distant one is swallowed by the darkness. Both are bad guides. What wonder if the master stumbles? Once home, the bed quickly receives him. Then, as the vapid smoke circles his brain, sleep joins itself to him of its own accord, now fearless of help, now careless of the cares he had fled before. Gliding down with the falling dew, it soothes his limbs into a tenacious rest, until nothing from the cock-crow, nothing from the faint twilight, breaks it off at last, when the sun is strong and the street roars with carts, horsemen and the common people.

units.la: Contrà. Meditaris vespertinu[?] epulum ? Ne dubites: Aderit cu[?] convivis, Propterviæ Genius in[?] solens, Heris invisus ille parasitu[?] Nam qui januam observat Pu[?] dor, cum admittendi excludend[?] que Discretione, Cereris parite[?] ac Bacchi largitionibus, impor[?] tunè sollicitatus, corrumpitur ta[?] dem: Tum sensim à poste reduct[?] januâ, finit intrudi petulcun[?] quiddam; Adhuc exile tamen, & [?] non nisi facetiæ festivâ veste com[?] positum: At fuscâ, quæ super[?] venit Nocte, quo ruborem tega[?] janitor, promittente velamen, fa[?] cessit ille penitus: Jamque bipaten[?]
units.tr: On the contrary: are you planning an evening feast? Do not doubt that the Genius of the Forum, that parasite always hateful to masters, will be present with the guests. For Shame, who watches the door, is importunately worn down by the Discretion of admitting and excluding, and by the largesses of Ceres and Bacchus, and at last is corrupted. Then the door is gradually drawn back from its post, and allows some impudent thing to be thrust in: still slight, and dressed only in the festive garb of wit. But when the dusky night comes on, that doorkeeper who was to cover the blush with a veil withdraws entirely. Now, both leaves of the door being open, Impudence rushes into the dining-room with the Crowds and disordered Neglect,

units.la: tibu[?] ibus foribus, irruit in cœnacu-lum Petulantia cum Turbis & confuso Neglectu: Et inter accumbentes vagabunda discurrens, alibi temeraria manu evertit cum poculis calices, alibi miscet disputantium jurgia, alibi armisono tinnitu lances collidit & patellas, alibi reducto in angulo delibat osculum cum lucerna præstolantis ancillæ: in herilis severitatis turpe detrimentum. Interea fervet opus, & subinde temulentum attollitur, quod laquearia feriat Evohe: Fugatur è vicinia Somnus: & fessos oculos perosa Vigilia, mille diris devovet intempestivum cum helluonibus hospitem. Post hæc discceditur, sed sinuoso, & subinde tibias decussante passu: Donec opportunum nactus, exilit ex insidiis lavernio: & direptâ fugit cum chlamyde: Tum Fures! Fures! Sed frustrà: Nam priusquam foribus alicujus efferatur Pharus, tuta jam dudum subiit cum spoliis pirata. Domum veni‐tur tandem: Impatiens moræ lassitudo, oblatum fortè circa fo‐cum procumbit in sedile: Et pro‐tinus alto sepulta somno crapula, aperit sibi ructibus & runcis spi‐raculum, crastinis demum ac pe‐rendinis medenda repotiis.
units.tr: and wandering among the reclining guests, here with a reckless hand overturns cups with goblets, there mixes in the quarrels of the disputants, there clashes dishes and plates with an armed clatter, and there in a corner steals a kiss from a maid waiting with a lamp, a disgraceful loss to the master's severity. Meanwhile the work boils, and now and then a drunken cry rises to strike the ceilings: "Evohe!" Sleep flees from the neighbourhood, and Wakefulness, hating the tired eyes, curses the untimely guest with the gluttons a thousand times. Afterwards they depart, but with a winding step, now and then crossing their legs, until, finding a chance, a cutpurse leaps out of ambush and flees with the stripped cloak. Then the cry: "Thieves! Thieves!" But in vain, for before a lantern is raised at anyone's doors, the pirate has long since got away safe with the spoils. At last they come home. Weariness, impatient of delay, throws itself down on a seat by the hearth, and at once the indigestion, buried in deep sleep, opens for itself a vent with belches and snores, to be cured by the feasts of the following days.

units.la: Quæstio XVIII.
units.tr: Question XVIII.

units.la: An indoles agilis & popularis, an sedata &, ut vocant, Stoi‐ca sit præoptanda?
units.tr: Whether a nimble and sociable disposition, or a calm one, which they call Stoic, is to be preferred?

units.la: IN motu, in strepitu, in celebritate Vita est: Mortis imaginem habent Torpor & Sopor & deserta Silentia: Et verò Mors ipsa ex his unum est, si modò falcem seponat, si sternat tantùm, non metat etiam, si perinde atque assines sui, vicissitudinem admittat cum Vita. Excitet se igitur, versetque, & irrequietum sit ingenium, ut angustum illud spatium, quod cunis ac feretro, ortu ac obitu Natura definivit, nullo vacuo intervallo, redundet ubique vitâ: Huc Alacritas, Sedulitasque, & vigiles Industriæ: Abarcete exiguis hisce mœniis, quantum potestis de Morte: Satis illi juris est in immensum illud ac æviternum, quod hæc circumjacet, Nihil: Cur per otium & desidiam in alienum fundum irrepit insatiabile Monstrum? Sic etiam vicinis excutitur veternus, & animantur exemplo, & nostris impulsibus experrecti reviviscunt: Tum specie rerum tenemus, & novitate sussuspendimus: Et varietas agili per diversa discursu, temperat rancidum illud, quod res omnes infi-cit, fastidium: Interdum etiam fallimus longum iter, & impo-nimus horis: Et forte navis alvo recepti cum plebe, multa commi-niscimur, & cum linguâ nutus pariter gestusque vivunt: Mixtas inter seria facetias, avidis bibunt auribus assidentes: Et arrepto ali-quis per humerum puero, furtim digito nos monstrat: Et talem, ait, te praestes aliquando:
units.tr: Life consists in movement, in noise, in crowds. Torpor, drowsiness and deserted silence bear the likeness of death. Indeed Death itself is one of these, if only it lays down its scythe, merely lays people low without even reaping them, and, like a close relation, admits an exchange with Life. So let the mind rouse itself, turn about, and be restless, so that the narrow span which Nature has marked out between the cradle and the bier overflows everywhere with life, with no empty gap left. Here come briskness, diligence and watchful industry. Drive Death back from these small walls as far as you can. Nothing has enough right over that vast and everlasting expanse which surrounds this little space. Why should the insatiable Monster creep onto another's land through idleness and sloth? So too drowsiness is shaken off by one's neighbours, they are roused by example, and awakened by our impulses they come back to life. Then we hold the attention by the look of things, and keep it suspended by novelty; and the variety of a nimble run through diverse matters tempers that rancid weariness which infects all things. Sometimes we even beguile a long journey and make the hours pass. And perhaps, when we are packed into a ship's belly with the common people, we contrive many things, and our tongues and nods and gestures are busy together. Mixing jokes among serious matters, those who sit beside us drink it in with eager ears. And someone, taking a boy by the shoulder, points us out with a sly finger and says, "Be such a one yourself, sometime":

units.la: Omnis Aristippum decuit status & color & res:
units.tr: Every condition, every complexion and every circumstance became Aristippus:

units.la: Tentantem majora ferè; praesenti-bus æquum.
units.tr: Aiming mostly at greater things, yet content with the present.

units.la: Denique ingenium illud ig-neum & à natura facilè, fertur in-defesso per Scientias omnes vola-tu: Nunc in sublime nititur, mox media perlabitur, mox ima legit: Et excerpit humanis usibus apta, & accommodat se vulgarium captui: Ubi indoles illa durior, sedentario & cunctante labore compingit illiberale quiddam & exoticum, importunum commercio, nisi boni judicii discerniculo, atræbilis integram libram excribaveris & quincuncem.
units.tr: Finally, that fiery mind, which by nature is quick, is said to fly without fatigue through all the sciences: now it strives on high, soon it glides through the middle, soon it gathers from the lowest things, and it picks out what is suited to human uses and adapts itself to the grasp of ordinary people. Where a harder disposition, by slow and hesitant labour sitting at its desk, piles up something illiberal and outlandish, unsuited to ordinary intercourse, unless with the fine sieve of sound judgment you have sifted out a full pound and five-twelfths of black bile.

units.la: Pro opposita parte. Regalis illa indoles & imperio nata, quæ torvo venerabilis silentio, virilem præfert sine nutu vultum, sine gesticulatione manum, quæ specie ipsâ proscribit è vicinia sua proterviam, & pudore multat levitatem, & suo se tuetur contra contemptum pondere: At indoles illa tractabilis & benignior (iniquum hoc quidem, ita tamen est, ô Superi) ipsis displicet obsequiis, ipsâ sui copiâ & suavitate vilescit: Non indignatur & cedit: Facilis præpræteriri, & computari cum ple-be. Tutior etiam contra malevo-lorum odia, genius ille durior: Nam si foribus alicubi se prodat, & allatret dicacitas, nec subsistit turpi duello, nec gradum concitat molossus; sed nequam ac præva-lidâ virtute compescit adversa-riorum animos, & elidit contu-maciæ laqueo; Si tamen temera-rior quispiam perrumpat & insul-tet, districto unico ac dedignante rictu, blæsum catellum abigit in-ter ejulatus. Adde quod ærum-nas ferat, & adversis perduret illa indoles: Nam prosperis non ener-vatur, nihil remittit austera; sed collecto compacto semper sem-perque robore, perstat obstinata, & riget instar cautis contra sæ-vientem Fortunam: Ubi indoles illa lenior, furentibus illis pro-cellis non est ferendo: Tum quod effueffusa sit benignitas, & affectu in diversa partito debilior: tum quod incautam, ac meliora de Diis, & sperantem pariter, & merentem, duplicatis ictibus, adversarum rerum truculentia tundat & indignitas. Denique Scientiis aptius est ingenium illud lentum & consultum: Non vagatur in incertum, nec temere desistit incepto; Sed quod semel congerit in rudimentum, hoc digerit: Uni, uni, noctu incubando diuque, nec deserit ante complementum: Non seducitur verbis, non hæret in rerum superficie; Sed pertinaci ad puteum Democriti ligone, fundum everrit: & eruit callosis manibus, altè defossam sub hominum delicata desidia Veritatem.
units.tr: On the opposite side: that royal disposition, born to command, which by its grim and venerable silence shows a manly face without nods and a hand without gesticulation, which by its very appearance drives impudence from its neighbourhood and punishes levity with shame, and defends itself against contempt by its own weight. But that gentler and more pliant disposition (unfair as this is, yet so it is, O gods) is despised for its very compliance, and grows cheap through its own abundance and sweetness. It does not feel indignation and gives way; it is easily passed over and reckoned with the common crowd. That harder genius is also safer against the hatred of ill-wishers. For if wit shows itself at some door and begins to bark, it neither stands up to a shameful brawl nor hurries its step like a mastiff; rather, by a strong and unyielding virtue, it restrains the spirits of its opponents and snares them in the noose of its stubbornness. Yet if some more reckless fellow breaks in and insults it, with a single disdainful snarl it drives off the lisping puppy amid its yelps. Add that such a disposition bears hardships, and endures adversity. It is not weakened by prosperity; the austere nature relaxes nothing, but, with its strength always gathered and compacted, it persists obstinate, and stands stiff like a rock against a raging Fortune. Where the gentler disposition cannot bear those storms: partly because its kindness is poured out and, being divided among many objects, is weaker in feeling; partly because the harsh cruelty and indignity of adversity strikes it, unguarded and hoping for better things from the gods, and deserving them, with doubled blows. Finally, that slow and deliberate disposition is better suited to the sciences. It does not wander into the uncertain, nor rashly abandons what it has begun. Whatever it first piles up as a foundation, it arranges in order. It works on one thing, one thing, brooding over it by night and by day, and does not desert it before it is complete. It is not led astray by words, nor does it cling to the surface of things; but with the stubborn pickaxe of Democritus it sweeps the bottom of the well and with calloused hands digs out the Truth that lies buried deep beneath men's soft indolence.

units.la: Quæstio XIX.
units.tr: Question XIX.

units.la: An legitimum sit judicium, quod de ignotis, ex incidente fortè cum iis colloquio, formamus?
units.tr: Whether the judgment we form about strangers from a conversation that happens to arise with them is legitimate.

units.la: SErmo dum animo consonat, interpres ejus, dum dissonat, plerumque proditor est: Nam si animi sensa, os inficiari audeat, statim ad equuleum ruboris à conscientia protractum, ipsis se accusat indiciis: quin etiam alia quædam à re, fatetur sæpenumerò, confusionis tormento perplexum, quæ nisi in fraudis odium fuissent extorta, puro puto silentio concessum erat occulere: Adeo commercium istud, quod Natura nobis sanxit, non impunè rescindicindimus mortales. Cur igitur non liceat loquentis animum ex sermone suo conjicere, præsertim primo? Qui quo studiosior esse solet, ut se commendet novis auribus, eo etiam mentem ex qua nascitur, refert vivaciùs: Suis nempe motibus dignoscitur animus, & agitatione fragrat aut fœtet: Ab omni parte patet, qui cum contentione loquitur: Et facilè minimum inter ea quæ dicit, est id quod lingua dicit: Frons, oculi, nutus, gestus, tonus ipse & modulatio, ipsa per intervalla taciturnitas, nihil horum mutum est, omnia diserta: quàm multa excidunt inconsideranti! sed & quam sæpe revelat cautela, quod tutiùs dissimulasset incuria! Adde quod præproperâ de aliis sententiâ, nobis ipsi tempestivè consulimus: Dum adulatorem ab ipso profproscribimus vestibulo: & ante contagium abarcemus, quod abjectum est, quod serpit, quod desidiâ torpet, & languore sopit industriam, quod obtrectat & sanie pascitur invidiosum, quod attactu conspurcat lutulentum: Matura vocentur ista, quantumvis accelerent, quantumvis præcipitent consilia, quæ prospiciunt integritati, quæ non vulnus modo cavent, sed affrictum, nec uri tantum ab incendio, sed afflari etiam timent: Ne cunctEris hîc, ô judex: Periculum in mora: Ne dubites: In promptu est, quo lis deciditur experimentum: Tenta pulsu:
units.tr: Speech is the interpreter of the mind when it agrees with it, and it is usually the mind's betrayer when it disagrees. For if a man dares to deny his thoughts with his mouth, his own conscience, dragged to the rack of blushing, straightaway accuses him by the signs it gives. Indeed, he often confesses other things, tormented by the rack of confusion, which, had they not been wrung out of him by hatred of deceit, he could have kept hidden in plain, quiet silence. So much does that intercourse which Nature has ordained for us, we mortals cannot break off without penalty. Why, then, should it not be allowed to infer a speaker's mind from his speech, especially at first meeting? The more eagerly a man usually strives to recommend himself to new ears, the more vividly he also reveals the mind from which his speech springs. A mind is recognised by its own movements; it gives off a scent of liveliness or of stench. Everything lies open in one who speaks with earnestness. And among the things he says, it is easy to see that the tongue is not the only thing speaking. The forehead, the eyes, nods, gestures, the very tone and modulation of the voice, even silence in the pauses: none of these is mute, all are eloquent. How many things slip out of the careless man! And how often does caution betray what carelessness would have concealed more safely! Add that by forming a hasty opinion of others we give ourselves timely advice: we thrust out the flatterer right from the threshold, and we keep away before the contagion whatever is base, whatever creeps, whatever is numbed with idleness and lulled to sleep by languor, whatever backbites, feeds on rottenness and envy, whatever befouls by its touch and is muddy. Let those counsels be called ripe, however quickly and headlong they act, which look out for integrity, which guard not only against a wound but against a rub, and fear not only being burned by the fire but even being breathed upon. Do not hesitate here, O judge: there is danger in delay. Do not doubt: the test by which the case is decided is at hand. Feel the pulse:

units.la: —— sonat vitium, percussa maligne
units.tr: —— it rings with a fault when struck in an ill-natured way

units.la: Respondet, viridi non cocta fidelia limo.
units.tr: It answers: an unbaked pot of green clay.
