units.la: Facilem etiam bonis ad nos aditum tum referamus: Dum parvo admittuntur examine, & extemplo amicos inter recensentur; eosdem fortassis averterent dilata judicia, saltem morosa suspicio exerceret immerito: Probitas & industria, vitio manifestiores sunt: Datâ per os viâ, statim alacres exiliunt ad auras: quia publicam lucem non metuunt, fucum non morantur ut prodeant, sciunt se placere genuinâ fronte: Et ut cætera lateant, certè candor loquentis latere non potest: conspicuus ei nitor: etiam cum reliquos
units.tr: Let us also count among the good men an easy way to us: when they are admitted after a slight examination and are at once reckoned among friends. Delayed judgments would perhaps turn those very men away, or at least a morose suspicion would wrongly torment them. Uprightness and industry are more evident than vice. Once an opening is given through the mouth, they leap out at once, eager, into the air. Because they do not fear the public light, they do not waste time on paint before they come forward; they know they please with a genuine brow. And if other things lie hidden, the candour of the speaker certainly cannot lie hidden: its brightness is conspicuous to him, even when the black night

units.la: nox atra colores
units.tr: has stolen the colours

units.la: Abstulit; ——— micat ille tamen, & inditâ sibi scintillâ vivit.
units.tr: Has taken away; ——— yet he shines, and lives with a spark kindled within him.

units.la: Contrà. Temeritas vocatur hodie, quæ fidit humanæ linguæ, levitas vocatur hodie, quæ tam imbelli nititur conjecturâ, aut insscitia: scitia: quæ non redarguit, quæ fallaci frontis argumento dat vi-ĉtas manus: Sermo, nutus, ge-stus,dolis ubique ac mendaciis infames: Inusta est, ô pudor! detergi non potest illa nota: Palam est, celari non potest: Perfricuerunt jam sæpiùs homines, & ingenuam frontem triverunt: Superest servilis, quæ adversum Conscientiæ carnificinam induruit callo: Et sub verbere negat & pejerat obstinata: Si tempestate hac, vultu ducimur & linguâ, faveamus ergo vasramento, & repulso candore, suffragio nostro gaudeat indignus competitor, amicorum larvas numeremus imposterum, non amicos: Fidem & officiosam sollicitudinem ad vivum imitantur inanes rugæ & inquies & crebra sciscitatio: Benevolentiam simulant obsequia, ne simulationem nimia prodat affectatio, fraudem fraude temperat versipellis simplicitas, & prætenta libertas inter increpandum adulatur: Hæ olim Aulis principum vix notæ, nunc plebi quoque familiares artes; ambitionis tunc quidem ministræ, lucro nunc etiam serviunt, donationes captant & hæreditates. Adde præmatura illa judicia, bonis viris ut plurimum male cedere: Quid usitatius quam primos eorum affatus ad expectationem non esse? Frontem plerumque negligit Soliditas, & quo in secessu fruitur, contenta est: Eliciendum, & sensim se exerit, quodcumque re ipsâ magis, quam specie bonum est: Primum oculum quilibet è vulgo pictor rapit in suam tabulam: Levis tantum variusque color est, quo ille rapitur; Si Zeuxis pinxepinxerit, aut Apelles: Defige te ex adverso, attende animum, intuere singula: Quid ais jam? Miraculum penicilli! Spirat ad invidiam Naturæ, & vivit imago ista: Atqui item, bonum virum non nosti, quisquis eum in fronte legis: Intus ille est, retraxit se, & seposuit in arduos casus: Non vacat ei, ad passim occurrentia depromere sese, majoribus intentum: Amicitiam ejus promerere, insinua te in ejus familiaritatem: Usu deprehendes illum & probabis.
units.tr: On the contrary. Today rashness is the name given to one who trusts a human tongue; levity is the name given to one who relies on such feeble conjecture, or on ignorance, which does not refute, which gives up its hands to the deceitful evidence of the brow. Speech, nods and gestures, everywhere notorious for tricks and lies: that brand is branded in, O shame, and cannot be wiped clean! It is plain, and it cannot be concealed. Men have now rubbed their faces many times and worn away the honest brow. What remains is the servile sort, who has hardened against the torture-chamber of conscience with a callus, and who, under the lash, obstinately denies and perjures himself. If in this age we are led by face and tongue, then let us favour the cunning, let candour be rejected, and let the unworthy rival rejoice in our vote. Henceforth let us count the masks of friends, not friends. Empty wrinkles, a restless brow and frequent enquiry imitate faithful and dutiful concern to the life. Compliances feign goodwill, lest excessive affectation betray the pretence; a slippery simplicity tempers fraud with fraud, and a feigned frankness flatters even while it rebukes. These arts were once hardly known in the courts of princes; now they are familiar even to the common people. They once served ambition; now they serve profit too, hunting for gifts and inheritances. Add that those premature judgments usually turn out badly for good men. What is more common than that their first words do not meet expectation? Solidity mostly neglects the forehead, and is content with the retreat it enjoys. Whatever is good in fact rather than in appearance must be drawn out, and it shows itself gradually. Any painter from the crowd snatches the first eye for his picture: only a light and changing colour is what catches him, whether Zeuxis or Apelles has painted. Fix yourself opposite it, attend to the spirit, look at each detail. What do you say now? A miracle of the brush! That image breathes in rivalry with nature and lives! Yet likewise, you do not know the good man if you read him only in his forehead. He is within: he has withdrawn himself and secluded himself in difficult circumstances. He has no leisure to bring himself forward into what meets the eye everywhere, being intent on greater things. Earn his friendship, insinuate yourself into his familiarity: you will discover him by experience and prove him.

units.la: Quæstio XX.
units.tr: Question XX.

units.la: An levando vitæ tædio, varia magis, quàm stabilis vitæ ratio conducat?
units.tr: Whether, to relieve the weariness of life, a varied way of living serves better than a steady one.

units.la: QUid homini tædiosius quam vivere! Vitæ moram lusu, jocis, somno fallit: vitæ sensum, legum solennitatibus, superstitionum cæremoniis, inutilium Scientiarum tricis obruit & obtundit: Vitam ipsam, præsentium impatiens, futuri spe & aviditate præcipitat. Triste quoddam & fatale est sub quo gemimus onus: graves ipsi nobis & intolerabiles sumus: nec quid discruciet, dici potest; & non dici, videtur expedire: Tabem illam melius effugies, si non noveris: incrementum sumit, dum correptum te fateris: Ne scrutêre, vulgavulgaris esto: Sanari potes, si decipi potes, si fidem habes amuleto. Principia rerum recenti succo esculenta, acrimonia sua palatum vellicant & salivam cient: decocto novitatis condimento, arescunt & insipida sunt media: quod deinceps ad finem vergit, nauseâ fœtet & vomitu: Vides brevi compendio, quam partem in rebus Vigor habeat, quam partem occupet Fastidium: Hanc devites, istam tene. Uni te mancipat, quæ in futurum prospicit anxiè, quæ momenta perpendit deliberatio: In arena consilium, quod de vitæ conditione statuat: Hanc cape vel illam: Non tantum interest, quantum suspicantur morosæ curæ: Qualis qualis ista sit, quam seligis, novitate placet, fastidium exclusit à vestibulo: Per principium ejus decurre, meta figatur ante
units.tr: What is more wearisome to a man than living! He beguiles the delay of life with play, jests and sleep. He buries and wearies the sense of life with the solemnities of laws, the ceremonies of superstitions, and the trifles of useless sciences. Life itself, impatient of the present, he hurries on with hope and eagerness for the future. It is a certain sad and fatal thing, under which we groan as under a burden. We are heavy and intolerable to ourselves, and it can be said neither what it is that torments us, nor does it seem expedient to say it. You will escape that wasting better if you do not know it; it grows while you confess yourself seized by it. Do not inquire; be a common man. You can be healed if you can be deceived, if you have faith in an amulet. The beginnings of things, like fresh food full of juice, tickle the palate with their sharpness and stir the saliva; once the seasoning of novelty has been boiled away, the middles grow dry and insipid, and what tends toward the end stinks with nausea and vomiting. You see in a brief summary what part of things belongs to Vigour and what part is taken over by Weariness. Avoid this, hold to that. Deliberation, which looks anxiously into the future and weighs each moment, binds you to one thing: the plan that settles the condition of your life is written in sand. Take this one or that one; it does not matter as much as anxious cares suppose. Whatever kind of life you choose, it pleases by its novelty, and it has shut weariness out of the vestibule. Run through its beginning, and fix the goal before the middle. From there you will bounce back, and soon you will turn aside to another wrestling-ground, with no less eagerness.

units.la: medium : hinc resilies: & ad aliam mox ac aliam divertes te palæstram,non dissimili intentione: Nulla vita vivacior, quam varia: quæ irritato leviter appetitu, mox delibat aliud, nec satietate, sed aviditate pascitur. Cur inchoanti lex est ut perficiat? Quis hoc decernit? Atra bilis: Ut habeat nempe quas Fastidio mactet victimas, & Pertinaciæ, & Desperationi: ut sensim nos astringat & exsiccet: & amandet extra rerum Universitatem, quidquid fluidum, solutum, liberale: Non feremus: dentibus & unguibus rescindimus importunum decretum: Loquere: Te audimus, ô Vigor, tibi paremus:
units.tr: No life is more lively than a varied one, which, its appetite lightly irritated, soon tastes something else, and is fed not by satiety but by eagerness. Why is it the law of a thing that begins that it should be finished? Who decrees this? Black bile does, so that it may have victims to sacrifice to Weariness, to Obstinacy and to Despair; so that it may gradually bind and dry us up, and banish from the universe of things whatever is fluid, loose and free. We will not bear it. With teeth and nails we tear away this troublesome decree. Speak: we hear you, O Vigour; we obey you.

units.la: Dimidium facti, qui bene cœpit, habet,
units.tr: He who has well begun has half of the deed done,

units.la: & ultra finem est, qui mediis appropinquat alacriter: Larga regula; Sed la; Sed tamen te limitat Solertia: Vive, glisce; sed Principium inter & Medium: si proserpis ultra, si rerum arcana penetres penitius, mox amisso formoso nomine, verteris in anile delirium: hallucinaris: in prunis castra vides & lucos in nubibus.
units.tr: and he is beyond the end who approaches the middle eagerly. The rule is broad; yet Skill limits you. Live, press on; but keep within the bounds between beginning and middle. If you creep beyond them, if you penetrate the secrets of things too deeply, soon the fair name is lost and you turn into old women's delirium: you hallucinate, and see camps in the embers and groves in the clouds.

units.la: Pro opposita parte. Tædia circumfert instabilis & vaga vita; non aufert: Si palaris, & in devium aberres, plus lassabere, quàm si directo calle, finem premas incessanter. Est & ipsius Varietatis ac Inconstantiæ fastidium: Gravissimum id quidem: & quod ex ipsis nascatur remediis, insanabile: Dum nulli stabilis insistit, inter divertendum se perdit animus: dispergitur, & irretitur hinc inde, nec colligere se potest attonitus: Ut quondam pueri, crepundiis insani, à paternis laribus abscedunt lonlongiusculè : pavent experrecti derepentè, circumspiciunt ignota majoribus ocellis, hiant, sudant, & incerta discursatio expedire niº titur illud insuperabile chaos: Ita vagus animus domestico, quem solita familiariaque pandunt, de- stitutus secessu, vacillat inter alie- na, impos sui: & hinc rerum pe- regrinâ facie percellitur, illinc ob- ruitur indigestâ multitudine: Sci- licet ut harmoniâ rerum, & ritè dispositis pacatur animus, ita di- sturbant illum, quæ temerè con- gesta, quæ confusa sunt: angi- mur subinde, & exercet nos mi- nutum quiddam, quod immo- rigerum est, nec ordini concor- dat, quem imaginatio præscripse- rat. Unam aliquam vivendi nor- mam præscribe tibi, non specio- sam; Duram, rationi magis, quàm opinioni consentaneam: in hanc jura: Quas hic generosus Ardor rogaverit leges, nunquam illas abroget Desidia, nunquam in dissuetudinem trahat Intermissio, nihil immutet Inconstantia, nihil in favorabilem partem interpretetur Indulgentia: Rigidus ipse tibi exactor esto. Ut multa libenter facias, illa saepè fac, quae non lubenter facis: Solidissima voluptas, quam ipse rebus, quibus derat, assuetudine paraveris: tua est, tu illam rebus, non res tibi contulere: totam tibi vindices jure meritissimo. Quo eminus allicere specie, Virtutem gaudio tinxit Natura; Sed tinxit tantum: haec eadem, bonae mentis exercitio delibuitur penitus & exsaturatur jubilis. Si taedium creat assiduitas; & taedium terit assiduitas: Consto in sententia: amarulenta potio uno bibenda est spiritu: Cur abnuam bnuam pueriliter ? cur differam? ur sorbillem modò, & modò remittam, duplicatâ nauseâ repe-endum Decoctum?
units.tr: On the opposite side: an unstable and wandering life brings weariness around; it does not remove it. If you wander and stray off the path, you will be more worn out than if you pressed on to the end without stopping along a straight track. There is also a weariness of variety and inconstancy itself. It is indeed a most grievous one, and, arising from the very remedies, it is incurable. While the mind settles on nothing steady, it loses itself in turning aside; it is scattered and entangled this way and that, and, dazed, cannot gather itself together. As children once, mad with their rattles, wander away from the home hearth, a little too far: on waking suddenly they grow afraid, look around at unknown things with wider eyes, gape and sweat, and their uncertain running about strives to escape that insuperable chaos. So the wandering mind, deprived of the domestic retreat which familiar and customary things offer, wavers among foreign things, not master of itself. On one side it is struck by the strange face of things, on the other it is overwhelmed by an undigested multitude. Surely, as the mind is calmed by the harmony of things and their rightly ordered arrangement, so it is disturbed by what is carelessly heaped together and confused. We are troubled from time to time, and some small thing vexes us, which is unruly and does not agree with the order that imagination had prescribed. Prescribe for yourself some one norm of living, not showy, but harsh and agreeing more with reason than with opinion, and swear by it. Whatever laws this generous Ardour has asked for, let Idleness never abrogate them, let Intermission never bring them into disuse, let Inconstancy change nothing, and let Indulgence interpret nothing in a favourable sense. Be a strict exactor to yourself. That you may do many things willingly, often do those things which you do not do willingly. The most solid pleasure is the one you have prepared for yourself by habit in things that were lacking; it is yours. You have given it to things, not things to you, so claim it entirely for yourself by the most deserved right. Nature has tinged Virtue with joy so that it may attract from afar by its appearance; yet she tinged it only on the surface. This same virtue, by the exercise of a good mind, is thoroughly imbued and saturated with joy. If constant repetition creates weariness, constant repetition also wears weariness away. I stand by my opinion: the bitter potion must be drunk in one gulp. Why should I refuse it childishly? Why should I put it off? Why should I sip it now and then, and set it aside, and take up the boiled-down draught again with doubled nausea?

units.la: Quæstio XXI. An probabilis affectatio, quæ aliorum mores assumendo, nativam indolem corrigere studet.
units.tr: Question XXI. Whether a probable affectation, which tries to correct one's native disposition by taking on the manners of others, is right.

units.la: UNdi potest Humanus Animus: Et typi, cui se ingerit, lineamenta consequitur facilè: ab illo lævis est aut asper: Nil scalpro, durâ nil opus incude, nec friante malleo, ut demissâ veteri, aliâ circumscribatur figurâ: Dum alienos ritus inspicit attentiùs, eodem quo capitur, liquescit radio: Et in cavum devolutus, influit angulis, circumcircumfluit tuberculis : Et indu[?] & to coagulo, novus derepent[?] prodit è nova forma. Oportunur[?] igitur fuerit, ad boni alicujus vir[?] cujus copiam nacti simus, ir[?] genium nos confingere : More[?] ejus notet Observantia, & in nc[?] stros transscribat Exercitium : Nu[?] tus etiam gestusque, & quæ vulg[?] captum effugiunt minutias, im[?] tabimur studiosè : His, si nescis[?] arctissimè signum suum impress[?] Animus : Conformemur, ut pul[?] chrâ metamorphosi, boni simu[?] imposterum : Dura nobis indo[?] les & morosa ? Lenior aliquis in[?] quirendus in exemplar: Tenerio[?] res ex illo erimus & mites: Si con[?] tra soluti sumus & effæminati[?] severiore quopiam proposito, r[?] formabimur in viros : Si torpe[?] genius & desidet, excitabimur a[?] gili: Si fervet & ebullit, compesce[?] [?]édatus. Quam vecors pertinacia! quæ totâ vitâ ratum id habet, quod è prava nutrice suxit infans, quod quondam puero persuasit pappus, quod imposuerunt nocturna terricula, quod inflixit sub ferula magister: Hæc sunt, quæ primam indolem formavêre, hæc congenita nobiscum, hæc ipsa Natura videtur insevisse: religioni ducimus ea concutere: Stramine ligatur Stultitia: Cur caput non exerimus è turbâ? quid hîc periculi, ô miselli? Fidite: pacatiora sunt hîc omnia: Inscitia vulgi, fulminum ictibus infamat superiora: Quia nubes æquat sideribus, putat fumis nostris involvi Solem: Imum est, insani, quod elusis oculis suspicitis inter altissima: Si assurgere non piget, si æquo animo dissentimus à plebe, jam crepundia rejecimus, jam prætexprætextam exuimus, & pari passi gradimur cum viris. Divinum quid habet, Philosophi in moribus à plebe dissensio, non ægra illa & astricta; sed exercitio multo liberalis jam & robusta: Audeamus modo: Priscam cum negleCtu gravitatem præferemus redivivi Catones.
units.tr: The human mind can be moulded. It readily takes on the outlines of the die pressed upon it, and is smooth or rough according to that die. It needs no chisel, no hard anvil, no hammer blows, so that the old shape is let down and another figure is cut around it. While it examines foreign customs more closely, it melts under the same ray by which it was captured. It rolls down into the hollow, flows into the corners and around the bumps, and, once hardened and set, it suddenly emerges in a new form. It is therefore fitting, when we have gained the company of some good man, that we shape our disposition on his. Let observation note his manner, and let practice transfer it into our own. We shall also imitate studiously his nods and gestures, and the small details that escape the common understanding. If the mind has impressed its mark on us very tightly through these, let us be conformed, by a fine metamorphosis, to a good model for the future. Is our disposition hard and peevish? Then we must seek some gentler man as our exemplar, and from him we shall become more tender and mild. If, on the contrary, we are lax and effeminate, we shall be reformed into men by some stricter pattern. If our genius is sluggish and idle, we shall be roused by a nimble one. If it boils over and bubbles, we shall be checked by a calm one. What a senseless obstinacy! It holds for life as settled whatever the infant sucked from a bad nurse, whatever the grandfather once persuaded the boy of, whatever nocturnal bugbears imposed, whatever the master inflicted under the ferule. These are what formed our first disposition; these are born with us; nature itself seems to have sown them. We think it a matter of conscience to shake them. Folly is tied with straw. Why do we not raise our heads out of the crowd? What danger is there here, you poor wretches? Trust me: everything here is more peaceful. The ignorance of the crowd slanders what is higher with its thunderbolts; because it puts clouds level with the stars, it thinks the sun is wrapped in our smoke. It is the lowest thing, you madmen, that you look up at among the highest, with deluded eyes. If it does not shame us to rise, if we dissent from the common people with equanimity, then we have already cast off the baby's rattles, already stripped off the boy's purple-bordered toga, and walk with men at an equal pace. There is something divine in a philosopher's dissent from the common people in conduct. It is not that sickly, constrained kind, but one made far more free and robust by practice. Let us dare: we shall display ancient gravity, disregarding the crowd, like Catos brought back to life.

units.la: Contrà.
units.tr: On the contrary.

units.la: Naturam expellas furcâ, tamen usque recurret.
units.tr: Drive out nature with a pitchfork, and she will still keep coming back.

units.la: Frustrà cespitem dimoveas, & fundum pertentes ligone Rationis: Numquam erues annosum illud robur, quod tam alte demisit intricatam radicem; sin relictâ stirpe, sarmentum putes, mox pertinaciori frutice repullulat, & jacturam sui compensat cum fœnore: Non nisi sarcophago deponeS, quod sub fasciis commiserunt incunabula: tecum coaluit, non diveldivelles : tecum ascendet in cathedram, tecum sedebit in tribunali, sub toga tecum erit & sub saga, tecum deportabitur ad Sarmatas, tecum revertetur in Patriam. Dum nativam indolem recudere studet Exercitium, inanem pascit fine successu Credulitatem : periculum faciente, & profectus speci-men requirente Casu, non respondebit Eventus: multa præmeditatum, multa consultum destituet in arena Fiducia ; Huic tamen abeunti, si vicariam feceris Pertinaciam, depromet hæc de duro penu tetricum quiddam & invitum, quod adstringit astantium Ingenuitatem, & tædio vexat, & mille modis importunum est : Mussitanus, caput scalpimus impatientes, & inter abeundum oggerimus illud Poëtæ.
units.tr: In vain you shift the turf and probe the bottom with the mattock of Reason. You will never uproot that ancient oak which has sent so deep and intricate a root. But if, leaving the stump, you think you have cut off a mere shoot, it soon sprouts again as a more stubborn bush and makes up its loss with interest. You will lay this aside only with the coffin, the thing the cradle committed to us under our swaddling bands. It has grown together with you, and you will not tear it away. It will climb into the chair with you, sit on the tribunal with you, be with you under the toga and under the soldier's cloak, be carried with you to the Sarmatians, and return with you to the homeland. While practice strives to refashion one's native disposition, it feeds a vain credulity without success. When Chance makes the trial and demands a proof of progress, the outcome will not answer. Confidence, though much premeditated and much considered, will desert you in the arena. Yet when this departs, if you have put obstinacy in its place, that obstinacy will bring out from its hard store something gloomy and unwilling. It constrains the free bearing of bystanders, vexes them with tedium, and is in a thousand ways troublesome. We mutter, scratch our heads impatiently, and as we leave we throw back at it that line of the poet: O imitators, a servile herd!

units.la: O imitatores servum pecus! Scilicet genuino capimur, fictum & affectatum non ferimus: Humile est, quod emendicat: quod aliena sibi miscuit, adulteratum est, & descivit à germano. Sed cur inquietamur queruli? cur ista tam speciosa sunt, quæ nostra non sunt? In aliena te concitas, & si æstimare modò nosses, tua, quæ tibi viluerunt, sunt optima: Sortitus es rudem indolem & severam? Gaude, Virtuti debetur ista: cur emasculatum te vadas futilibus gratiis, & lacertis istis non conveniente cultu? Si remissa, si faceta sit indoles, Euge! gratus eris, amabere: cur serenitatem istam obnubiles supercilio? cur explicatam à natura frontem, deturpent adscititiæ rugæ? Si lentus sit genius, constans hic idem erit & solidus: Si excitatus, duplicabit tibi vitam: Pia mater Natura, dum singula mortalibus dispensat, compensat tamen omnia: Pauca consideranti, enormis se ingerit asperitas; cuncta comparanti pa-rescit lenis æqualitas: Quam asper videtur ille nobis quem incolimus Globus: hîc sidera feriunt turres & alpes, illic in tartarum dehi-scunt voragines; si tamen de cælo prospiciat Jupiter, totum unico dimensus obtutu, glabrum hunc dicat & concinnatissimum.
units.tr: Of course we are captivated by the genuine; we cannot bear the feigned and affected. What begs for its living is humble. What mixes in other people's things is adulterated and has departed from the genuine. But why do we fret and complain? Why are those things so attractive which are not ours? You rouse yourself over others' things, and if only you knew how to value them, your own, which have become cheap in your eyes, are the best. Have you been allotted a rough and severe disposition? Rejoice; that is owed to virtue. Why would you go about unmanned by frivolous graces, and wear that dress which does not suit those arms? If your disposition is easy and witty, bravo! You will be pleasing and loved. Why cloud that serenity with a frown? Why should borrowed wrinkles disfigure a brow that nature made smooth? If the temperament is slow, this same temperament will be steady and solid. If it is lively, it will double your life. Kindly mother Nature, while she dispenses single gifts to mortals, nonetheless balances all things. To one who considers few things, enormous roughness forces itself upon him; to one who compares all things, a gentle evenness appears. How rough that globe we inhabit seems to us: here towers and Alps strike the stars, there chasms gape into Tartarus. Yet if Jupiter looked down from heaven and took in the whole with a single glance, he would call it smooth and most well-ordered.

units.la: Quaestio XXII.
units.tr: Question XXII.

units.la: An animi & exercitii gratiâ, procum agere conveniat ingenuo adolescenti.
units.tr: Whether it befits a well-born young man to woo a woman, for the sake of recreation and exercise.

units.la: ARcanâ pollet energiâ puellaris spiritus, dum teneris evibratus oculis pertenat juvenile præ-corcordium : de statu dejicit animum, ubi incidit ex improviso, consternat & percellit, & sponte sequacem,pellicit in lasciviam, aut ægrè sub luƈta sibi constante pugili, ovat interim invidendâ facilitate: Agnosceres hîc imperium simile Virtutis imperio:blandum est utrumque, sed potens, suave, non violentum, utrumque confusione plecƈit rebelles. Concessisse proinde nonnihil,& paruisse satius est, ò Ingenuitas, quam indigno rubore palloreque vapulari refractariam: Obsequio devincîtur illa potentia, congressu, colloquio, familiaritate cicuratur : Exteros attonitos habet Majestas, non suos: Noƈturni Manium bombi non terrent vespillones : Quidquid ad cotem Panici pavoris acuitur, hoc aciem perdit & hebescit usu. Est & ingenio perutilis labor, quem ista suppeditat exercitatio: Dominam sermone detineas necesse est : disertum te faciet hæc Schola: Sed ecce quæ Rhetorica: Sacros de religione, Philosophicos de Natura, forenses de Republica, familiares de œconomia sermones, ab elegantiis proscripsit magister Amor : Tetricos hos vocat aut frivolos: inter Myoses ei & Battologias recensentur: Si aliquam ex his phrasim dictis tuis aspergis, ad manum ei vibratæ ferula facetiæ, & ni ocyus desistas, turpis scutica repulsæ: Sit geniale, festivum, & cum cæremoniis officiosum, quidquid huc adsertur ; Est tamen & in parte ista, quod evites: Si exquiras nimium, & è libello dicas, irridebere Pomphologus. Adde quod ad venustatem efflorescit animus, qui subinde reficitur arrisione, & benigno Dominæ radiatur diatur oculo : crudus ille est in juvene & acidus, & non nisi influxu hoc maturescit in dulcorem: Ut se effert ! quantum sibi sumit fiduciæ! si longo in Ecclesiis atrio, conspecta forte Phyllis, protinus assurgat inclinanti, & decorâ poplitum bis terve subsidat inflexione, hinc interea pedis in aversum ductu, stridente pavimento : erigit se exeritque Puber, circumspicit astantes, & tacitè scîscitatur super prærogativa sententiam, & serenatâ fronte præjudicat: Post hæc, recipit se,& Dominæ præstolatur egressum: Si non gravetur illa, si admittat oblatam inter officiosas mussitationes dexteram: Tum verò! Vix è templi vestibulo solvit; & singultit, & in acutos cachinnos crepat lætitia : Secu-rior jam à fulcro, concitat se puel-laris greßus : Præter volantes excipiunt piunt officiosâ salutatione noti, ignoti, majores pariter ac æquales; At retro Corrivalium zelus, longo cum suspicionibus prosequitur obtutu.
units.tr: A girl's spirit is powerful with a hidden energy when, darted through tender eyes, it pierces the young man's inmost heart. When it strikes unexpectedly, it unsettles the mind, dismays and overthrows it, and, if the man yields willingly, it lures him into wantonness. If he is a wrestler who holds his ground, it struggles with him only with difficulty, and meanwhile it exults with an enviable ease. Here you would recognise a rule like the rule of Virtue: both are gentle yet powerful, sweet and not violent, and both overcome rebels by confusion. It is therefore better to yield a little and obey, O Gentility, than to be beaten by unworthy blushing and paleness for being stubborn. That power is subdued by obedience and tamed by meeting, conversation and familiarity. Majesty astonishes strangers, not its own. The buzzing of the night-time Manes does not frighten the gravediggers. Whatever is sharpened on the whetstone of Panic fear loses its edge and grows dull with use. The labour this practice supplies is also very useful for the mind: you must keep the lady engaged in talk, and this school will make you eloquent. But see what rhetoric Love the master has banished from elegance! Sermons on religion, philosophical talk about Nature, forensic talk about the State, and domestic talk about household management, he calls grave or frivolous; they are counted among Myoses and Battologies. If you sprinkle any such phrase into your speech, the ferule of wit is at hand, raised to strike, and unless you stop more quickly, the shameful whip of rejection. Whatever is put forward here should be lively, festive and dutifully ceremonious. Yet in this part there is also something to avoid: if you seek too much and recite from a little book, you will be laughed at as a Pomphologus. Add that the mind blossoms into charm, refreshed from time to time by a smile and lit by the kind eye of the lady. In a young man that mind is raw and sour, and it ripens into sweetness only by this influence. How he puffs himself up! How much confidence he takes to himself! If, in the long forecourt of a church, he happens to catch sight of Phyllis, he at once rises to bow to her, sinks twice or thrice in a graceful bending of the knees, and meanwhile draws back his foot with a scraping on the pavement. The youth straightens and puffs himself up, looks around at those standing near, and quietly asks about the prerogative vote, and with a serene brow he pronounces his judgment. After this he withdraws and waits for the lady to leave. If she does not object, if she accepts his offered right hand amid courteous murmurs, then indeed! Scarcely has he left the vestibule of the temple before he gasps and bursts into shrill laughter with joy. Now bolder, away from his support, his stride quickens with girlish flightiness. Acquaintances, strangers, elders and equals alike greet him with dutiful salutations as he flies past; but behind him the jealousy of rivals follows him with a long, suspicious gaze.

units.la: Contra. Muliebrem sexum Natura fecit sequiorem : Imbellis est, quisquis nostrum cedit, & herilem nescit obfirmare vultum : Obsequeris partim, & partim obniteris lenocinio, diversum te faciunt intestina dissidia : Sed collige te, & in unum corrade vires : totus obluctare, vinces: infra iram deinceps infraque negotium habiturus hostem ; Si tamen ab improviso fecerit impressionem, consta qua potes, meliore parte : nil deprecare : cladis notam non penitus effugit, qui cum hoste cogitur pacisci : erubescat sub lucta vultus & palleat: tanti sanè est, asseruisse libertatem, & ingenuâ cervice recusasse
units.tr: On the contrary: Nature made the female sex the weaker. Whoever of us yields is unwarlike and does not know how to set a masterful face. You are partly compliant and partly struggle against her enticements, and your inner divisions make you divided. But collect yourself and gather your strength into one: wrestle with your whole being and you will conquer, and thereafter you will have as an enemy something beneath anger and beneath your concern. If, however, she has made an unexpected attack, hold your ground as well as you can, with your better part, and deprecate nothing. One who is forced to bargain with the enemy does not entirely escape the mark of defeat; let the face blush and turn pale in the struggle. It is certainly worth it to have asserted liberty and to have refused, with a free neck,

units.la: fasse jugum, nec ad unguem discessisse propositio: Nihil animo par est, ubi nosse se cæpit: & prelucente ratione, debitum sibi Sceptrum capescivit imperii. Ad hæc, periculosa juveni cum puella familiaritas: & non nisi robusti illius ac incuriosi, quod in nobis pulcherrimum est, mercanda dispendio: Exile quiddam & minutum, paullulum supra crepundia est, quo tota distinetur & capitur mulier: Si placere vis, descende, vocem extrenua, parvus semper sit tuus pullus: Superi! quam bene quadrant Herculi colus & pensa! Gradu scilicet inter nos & pueros, medius est ille Sexus; ambitiosus tamen, fuco rerum & ementitis blanditiis inescatur; ferium omne & quod res est, infirmo nauseante stomacho: Restat igitur ut insuper Proco serviliter sit aduadulandum : Sideribus assimilet quædam, quædam Cynosuræ: & Allegoriæ non minima pars sit benignus ille Solis, qui inferiora vegetat, influxus: de aris interdum & sacrariis despiciat, interdum ceu alter quidam Briareus,congerat Hyperbolum montes, & cælo inferat, Dominæ suæ divinitatem. Ludicra videantur ista; Ecce syrtes! ecce brevia! Sua deinceps credit commenta; & quod fecit, adorat Numen: Jam demulcet eum fractus Puellæ incessus & affectata deliquia: nutus unus, gestusque, certus tussendi modus languentem habet: Quinimò Turpia decipiunt cæcum vitia, aut etiam ipsa Delectant: veluti Balbinum polypus Agnæ:
units.tr: to shake off the yoke, and to have held firm to the resolution not to depart from it by a hair's breadth. Nothing is equal to the spirit once it has begun to know itself, and with reason shining forth it has seized the sceptre of rule that is its due. Besides, a girl's familiarity is dangerous for a young man, and it must be bought at the cost of that robust and careless quality which is most beautiful in us. A slight, small thing, a little above rattles, is what captures and distracts the whole woman. If you wish to please, stoop down, lower your voice, and let your little chick always be small! Gods above! How well distaff and spindle suit Hercules! Evidently, in rank, that middle sex stands between us and boys. Yet it is ambitious, and it is enticed by the paint of appearances and by feigned flatteries; everything plain and true makes it queasy, like a weak stomach. It remains, therefore, that the suitor must be servilely flattered above all: she must be likened to certain things, such as the stars, and to others, such as the Cynosure. A great part of the allegory must be that kindly influence of the Sun which quickens lower things. Sometimes he must look down from altars and shrines; sometimes, like another Briareus, he must heap mountain upon mountain in hyperbole and set her divinity against heaven. These things may seem playful; behold the quicksands! behold the shallows! Then he trusts his own inventions, and what he has made, he worships as a god. Now the girl's affected gait and feigned swoons soothe him; a single nod, a gesture, a certain practised way of coughing holds the languishing man. Indeed, base vices deceive a blind man, or even delight him, as the polyp did to Balbinus' Agna.

units.la: & ad hæc desigit interdum scintillantillantes oculos: molli quadam teneritudine, cordis sauciante meditulliū: Totus deditítius, totus impensus, diffluit inter deperiendū, & perit. Adeò præcipitat hic semita, malè cauti Puberes, quæ de FiGto vergit in Serium: Et ut alibi sit latum satis, Genuinum inter & Simulata discrimen; certè mimesis amoris, amor est.
units.tr: And at times she fixes her sparkling eyes on him with a soft tenderness that wounds the very middle of his heart. Wholly surrendered, wholly devoted, he melts away in love and perishes. So steeply does this path slope for young men who are badly on their guard, a path that leads from the feigned toward the serious. And, as is said elsewhere, the distinction between genuine and simulated is wide enough; certainly the mimicry of love is love.

units.la: Quæstio XXIII. An, quod illustres quidam Auctores fecerunt, commentitias Historias edere conveniat.
units.tr: Question XXIII. Whether it is fitting to publish fictitious histories, as certain illustrious authors have done.

units.la: Soror historiæ, fabula: Magis arctum est inter illas, quàm imperiti putent contubernium: Fidelissimus etiam Commentator multum habet de Poëta: Extemporales inter gesta fuerunt Principum Ducumque sermones; eosdem habet Historia compositos à disertissimis hominibus, elaboratos cunctante stylo, & exoticam istam imaginationem, qua quondam Heroës effinximus, exæquantes: Insuper quæ vulgaribus circumstantiis immixta, latebant partim, & partim communione viluerant, juxta regulam Historiæ præcisa, jam omnino sunt alia, jam ad oculati quoque testis suspensionem insolescunt, rara penitus & augusta sunt: Speculum Veritatis est Historia; sed auget formam: textrix est; & telam, cui Natura cum auro fortè & bysso, vilem lanam & canabim interneverat, rudi glomo rejecto, retexit in Attalicum Paludamentum. Quid juvat ergo se constringere, & arctam Veritatis sepem circumdare, si transiliendum sit alialicubi ? Latus & pulcherrimus in procursum campus, si maceriam illam tollas: Quid juvat proplasma praefigere tabulæ, si evagetur generosior penicillus, si imitari dedignetur,& superet propositi speciem ? Euge ! ista colorum temperies, liberalis ille dutus, istud lineamentum tam decens, tam vivax, in hanc aut illam Nympham non quadrant; Summæ sunt ista reservanda Pandoræ: Bonæ mentis adhuc illa labes est, ut Virtutem, quod eam quamplurimis optet esse communem, affingat immeritis: probrum adulationis sibi conscisci incauta Pietas:Nulli formam istam astringe materiæ:Divina est:Exhibe nobis boni Principis Notionem: dic licet in scemate quid egerit: dic justitiam clementiâ,dic potentiam temperasse modestiâ, dic terribilem lem hostibus, mitem devictis, Patrem inter suos magis audivisse quàm Dominum: cur hunc Alexandrum appelles? faceßat.
units.tr: Fable is history's sister. The bond between them is closer than the unskilled suppose, and even the most faithful commentator has much in common with the poet. The speeches of princes and generals were, in fact, extempore, yet historians give us them composed by the most eloquent men, polished with a deliberate pen, and so they rival that exotic imagination by which we once fashioned our heroes. Moreover, the things that were hidden, mixed in with ordinary circumstances, or grown cheap through common talk, and which history had cut down to its rules, are now entirely different. Some have become so striking that they swell even the wonder of an eyewitness, and they are wholly rare and grand. History is a mirror of truth, but it enhances the image. It is a weaver. Nature had woven ordinary wool and hemp into the cloth, perhaps with gold and fine linen, and the weaver, having cast aside the rough skein, unravels it and reweaves it into a Pergamene purple cloak. What good is it, then, to confine oneself and surround truth with a narrow hedge, if one may leap over it elsewhere? The field is wide and beautiful for the running, if you take away that wall. What good is it to set a model before the panel, if a more generous brush wanders off, disdains to imitate, and surpasses the appearance of the subject? Ah! That blending of colours, that generous outline, that graceful and lively form does not suit this or that nymph. Such things must be kept for Pandora's sum. It is still a blemish of a good mind that, wishing virtue to be shared by as many as possible, it ascribes it to the undeserving; an unwary piety incurs on itself the reproach of flattery. Bind that form to no matter. It is divine. Show us the notion of a good prince. Say, if you like, what he did in the scheme of things; say that he tempered justice with clemency and power with moderation; say that he was terrible to enemies, gentle to the conquered, and heard more as a father among his own than as a lord. Why would you call him Alexander? Away with it!

units.la: Fœlix regnorum prædo, non utile Mundo
units.tr: Fortunate plunderer of kingdoms, of no use to the world

units.la: Editus exemplum:
units.tr: Set forth as an example:

units.la: Cur Cæsarem voces? Impotens ille est, dominatus libidini fas omne prostituit; Anonymum vocabis eum: Si suspensum desideras & avidum lectorem, ab humili Principem tuum deduces in fastigium, infractum repulsis, adulationum negligentem ambages, pulchrâ per invium eluctantem incuriâ: Narrabis, ut insidias eluserit sine dolo, ut fraudes Aulæ sine fraude devicerit: Turpes illas Machiavelli Noctuas, simplici semper excæcante Candore: Ah quomodo nos rapit robustum illud & liberale! quantum ei decus!
units.tr: Why do you call him Caesar? He was powerless, a slave to lust, who prostituted all that is lawful. You will call him Anonymous. If you want an attentive and eager reader, you will lead your prince from humble beginnings up to the summit, unbroken by rebuffs, careless of flattery's detours, struggling through the trackless ways with a fine indifference. You will relate how he eluded plots without deceit, how he overcame the frauds of the court without fraud. Those foul Machiavellian owls are always blinded by simple candour. Ah, how that strong and generous quality carries us away! What glory is his!

units.la: Hoc sanè, si quidquam, humanis mentibus inditum, vocabimus divinæ particulam auræ. Tandem, ævi nostri vitia insectabere liberrius: Queri licebit exulem ab animo pietatem, & ad externos ritus proscriptam: Serium omne nugi[?] & argutiis contaminatum: Præclusum generosis ingeniis ad amplitudinem iter, vafris & humilibus patulum: Credulos gubernatores, Reipublicæ clavum piratis cedentes, non secundùm immobilem justitiæ Cynosuram, seprivati quæstus & ambitionis Erraticam velificantibus: Si hæc au[toribus?] thoribus suis subscribas vitia,
units.tr: If anything has been implanted in human minds, we shall surely call this a particle of divine breath. At last you will attack the vices of our age more freely. It will be permitted to complain that piety has been exiled from the mind and banished to outward rites; that all seriousness is tainted with trifling and wit-games; that the road to greatness is closed to noble talents and open only to the crafty and the lowly; that credulous governors, yielding the helm of the commonwealth to pirates, sail not by the unmoving Cynosure of justice but by the wandering star of private gain and ambition. If you subscribe these vices to your authors...

units.la: Periculosæ plenum opus aleæ Tractas :
units.tr: You are handling a work full of perilous dice.

units.la: Sub Patria potestate sunt, non i[rritabis] ritabis impunè; Ubi larvis quibusdam & fictis nominibus emancipantur, tutum est ea, prout m[?] rentur, traducere: Posteri, sic hodie sunt Candor & Veritas.
units.tr: They are under paternal authority, and you will not provoke them with impunity. Where they are emancipated under certain masks and fictitious names, it is safe to portray them as they deserve. Such, nowadays, are candour and truth, as far as posterity is concerned.

units.la: Contra tamen facit, quod Commentitiæ istæ Historiæ, frænum paulatim laxent calumniis: Dum satyricis ingeniis in latibulis suis spondent impunitatem: Vix carceribus & lictore coërcetur ille furor, quin œstro suo percitus erumpat aliquando, & Principum virorum famam sugillet, & optimi cujusque verecundiam proterat sub pedibus: Dexteram ei præcîdas, maledicam linguam evellas è faucibus; non desistet: Minatur etiam sic, immurmuraturum se terræ, ut isto femine surgant arundines Midæ, quæ ad venti flatum resonent occulta vitia, quæ te toto Mundo traducant, & infament,
units.tr: On the other hand, these fictitious histories work against us, since they gradually loosen the reins for slander. While they promise impunity to satirical wits hiding in their lairs, that rage can scarcely be restrained by prisons and the lictor. Stirred by its gadfly, it will sooner or later break out, tarnish the fame of men in power, and trample the modesty of every good man underfoot. If you cut off its right hand and tear out its slanderous tongue from its jaws, it will not desist. It even threatens to whisper into the earth, so that reeds like those of Midas may spring up from that seed and, rustling in the breath of the wind, reveal hidden vices that will drag you through the whole world and defame you.

units.la: Et misero socient Lycambi: Sic debacchatur intra clathros suos ista rabies: Quid futurum existi- mamus, si quovis prætextu, fores habeat reseratas? Sed esto: Scri- ptor Commenti, vir bonus sit: Candidum sit ei pectus, & à furia- libus istis facibus non suffumiga- tum: nosti Sæculum hoc quale sit? Callidis scatet & acutilis: & (si ullum anterius) in exoticas inter- pretationes effusum est: Verba singula percolant, syllabas omnes ad vivum discutiunt: Et quod Pappo accidit, dum forte sub se- ram vesperam, ad focum garrit cum nepotulo: Nam in semisopi- tis prunis castra vident, & reges, & si Dis placet, Belluam Lernæ: Ita & hi delirant: Legunt in Au- thore, quæ non scripsit, quæ ne per somnium quidem cogitavit: Futile vitium, nec tamen magnis caret exemplis: Audi Lipsium no- strum de hoc hominum genere conconquerentem: Quæ nos, inquit, communiter diximus, sic volunt accipi, quasi in Titium aut Seium dicta, imò Vates etiam agunt, non lectores, nec sumunt à nobis sensum, sed adferunt, & mentem aliquam affingunt ex sua mente: Si in Doctorem hæc audent, qui non gesta narrat, sed gerenda præcipit, vitia damnat non homines: Quid in Historiam? præsertim ubi personarum rerumque fictio, superstitiosis ingeniis auguria suppeditat, allegorias ingerit & mysteria. Ecce! Nasutior iste Sybillam interpretabitur: Sensum tuum odoratus est, rem acutetigit: Nega, clama; Secus non credent, ne jurato quidem: Adde fieri facile posse, ut Fabulæ istæ, veris nostri temporis Historiis fidem derogent: Caduca res est testimoniorum religio, dum vacillat evertitur: suspecta res est, dum in uno fefellisse deprehenditur, tota rejicitur: Periculum sanè, ne ubi verissima etiam in Annales contulerimus, Græcæ tamen fidei insimulent ævum nostrum feri nepotes: Adeo sunt ad Scenam pleraque, sed heu funestam! Si autem historicam fidem à posteris non requiras, fi perspicaci lectori satis innuas Ideam te scribere voluisse, non Historiam, steriliter sanè te fatigas: Surculus ille quem pangis, eodem penè quo Historia labore rigari & coli postulat; præ-cipuum tamen Historiæ fructum, studium, inquam, imitandi non profert: Exempla nos docent, non commenta: Quia homines, pedum post se vestigia relinquunt, quæ viam signent; non inanes umbræ: Flosculum fortè delectationis progignet ille frutex; sed vanum & brevi deciduum: Nec solidè, nec diu delectat, quod tantùm delectat: Natura voluit voluptatem condimentum esse; non cibum: Pernici semel oculo lustrasse Fabulam, avidæ curiositati sat est: Imò subinde sistimus in medio: conscii nimirum, earum apud nos imaginum innumerabilem esse copiam, quas exponimus obtutui, dum volumus, nec ad sculpendum, alieno nos indigere cælo.
units.tr: And join the wretched Lycambes. Thus this madness rages within its bars. What do we suppose will happen if it has its doors thrown open on any pretext? But grant that the writer of the fiction is a good man, with a candid breast, not smoked by those furious torches. Do you know what kind of age this is? It is full of cunning and sharpness, and (if ever there was one) it has poured itself into exotic interpretations. They sift every single word and examine every syllable to the quick. It happens to them as it did to Pappus, who, when by chance in the evening he was chatting by the hearth with his little grandson, saw camps and kings in the half-dead embers, and, heaven help us, the Beast of Lerna. So these people rave. They read into an author what he did not write, what he never even dreamed of. It is a trivial fault, yet it lacks no great examples. Hear our Lipsius complaining about this sort of man: What we have said in common, they want to be understood as if said against Titius or Seius; indeed, they even act as seers, not as readers. They do not take their sense from us, but bring their own and fasten onto us some meaning out of their own minds. If they dare to do this to a teacher who does not narrate deeds but prescribes what is to be done, they condemn vices, not men. What will they do with history, especially where the fiction of persons and things supplies superstitious wits with omens, and heaps on allegories and mysteries? See! That sharper fellow will interpret the Sibyl. He has smelled out your meaning and touched the matter to the quick. Deny it, cry out; otherwise they will not believe you, not even under oath. Add that it could easily happen that these fables cast doubt on true histories of our own time. Belief in testimony is a fragile thing: when it wavers, it falls; when it is caught deceiving in one point, it is rejected entirely. There is real danger that, even when we have committed the most true things to the annals, our savage descendants may charge our age with Greek unreliability. So much of the stage is in most of these works, and alas, a fatal one! If, however, you do not demand historical credibility from posterity, and you sufficiently hint to the discerning reader that you meant to write an Idea and not a History, you are indeed wearing yourself out to no purpose. That little shoot you plant needs almost the same labour of watering and tending as history does, yet it does not yield the chief fruit of history, I mean the zeal for imitation. Examples teach us, not inventions, because men leave footprints behind them that mark the way, not empty shadows. That shrub may put forth a small flower of delight, but a vain one that soon falls. What delights only, neither solidly nor for long delights. Nature willed pleasure to be a seasoning, not food. To have glanced over a fable with a quick eye is enough for eager curiosity. Indeed, we sometimes stop in the middle, aware that there is an endless supply of such images, which we set before the gaze whenever we wish, and that for carving them we have no need of another sky.

units.la: Quæstio XXIV.
units.tr: Question XXIV.

units.la: Vtra præstantior, Belgica, an Latina lingua?
units.tr: Which is the more excellent language, Belgic or Latin?

units.la: ACris sæpenumerò in sympofiis, aliisque amicorum cœtibus, Idiomatum inter se digladiatio: Nos Latium huc & Belgium produximus in Palæstram stram, induimus Cæstus, & concitamus in Luctam: Rident quidam, ut video : Herculen ex nunc distinguunt & Antæum; Sed præoccupati sunt : Homines præjudiciis hic fermè laborant omnes : Æquitas sola Brabeutes esto. Primùm igitur pro Latina lingua est, quod latissimè per Orbem dispersa, in Sacris ritibus, in Scholarum pulpitis, in doctorum libris penè sola sit: Belgis etiam ac Germanis, nescio quo fato, plusquam Italis suis placuit: lippi callent hic illam & tonsores, & penè dixeram, mulierculæ: Certè quod olim de Romano Imperio cecinit Poeta, hodieque id obtinet in Lingua: Gentibus est aliis tellus data limite certo ; Romanæ spatium est urbis & orbis idem.
units.tr: I have often heard, at dinners and other gatherings of friends, a wrangling between the two languages. We have brought Latium and Belgium into the arena, put on the boxing gloves and joined battle. Some laugh, as I see, and say that we are already distinguishing Hercules from Antaeus. But they are prejudging the matter, as almost everyone does in these disputes. Let fair play alone be the umpire [βραβευτής]. First, then, in favour of Latin: it is spread very widely through the world, and it is almost the only language used in sacred rites, in the pulpits of schools and in the books of scholars. For some reason or other, the Belgians and Germans have taken to it more than the Italians themselves. Blear-eyed men and barbers speak it well here, and I was almost going to say little women too. What the poet once sang of the Roman Empire is still true of the language today: "To other nations land is given within fixed bounds; for Rome, the space of the city and of the world is the same."

units.la: At Belgica lingua ubi est ? In hoc terræ angulo, in hac gleba: & ibidem non nisi verna & famula, per culinas strepit & popelli tabernas: Aulam frequentat Gallica, Academiam Latina, mercatorum Basilicas Lusitana, inter elegantiorum subinde cœtus Itala lascivit & Castellana. Quam sonat iste cæstus, ô Belgica! Nil miror, si diro verbere dentes aliquos excusserit tibi: quod si ita est, degluti & absorbe protinus, ne advertat Antagonista: Ridet indignans: & quod nos exitialem interpretabamur ictum, testatur inanem esse dumtaxat inter cæstus complodentes crepitum: Et caput quassans cum generoso fastu: Vices suas habent res quæque: Erit, inquit, cum fucum pertæsus, adorabit Candorem, & Belgarum imperio colla lubens submittet Orbis: Tunc non unius victrix certaminis, sed Penthala ferar: Sic ait, & protinus in mediam se proripit arenam : ingruitque Latio prior, agitque hoc argument pondere : Belgas, quibuslibet peregrinis linguis addiscendis, sua lingua promptissimos reddit : Itaque est : Idipsum exteris frequens jam comprobavit experientia : Paucorum mensium exercitio, Italis Italum, aut ipsis etiam Hispanis mentimur Hispanum ; nisi subinde conspicua magis cutis celare nolit : Vocis accentum, quin etiam crebriores in isto populo nutus ac gestus ( quorum quidem nos sincerior Natura fecit expertes) animi tamen gratiâ, dum lubet, imitamur ad vivum : In ipsa etiam Romana lingua, quibus cedunt Belgæ ? imò qui non cedunt Belgis ? Unde depulsâ nuper præcedentium sæculorum barbarie, priscus illuxit Orbi Latino nitor, nisi
units.tr: But where is the Belgic language? In this corner of the earth, in this clod, and here it rattles only among servants and maids, in kitchens and the taverns of the common people. French frequents the court, Latin the academy, Portuguese the merchants' exchanges, and Italian and Spanish now and then play their wanton part in the gatherings of the more refined. What a sound that glove makes, O Belgic! I am not surprised if it has knocked some of your teeth out. If so, swallow them and gulp them down at once, lest your opponent notice. Latin laughs, indignant, and shaking its head with noble scorn, testifies that what we took for a deadly blow is only an empty crack of gloves striking together. "Things have their turns," it says. "There will come a time when the world, tired of the dark, will worship the Bright One, and will gladly bow its neck to the rule of the Belgians. Then I shall be carried off not as victor in a single contest but as winner of the pentathlon." So saying, it hurls itself straight into the middle of the sand and attacks Belgic first, pressing this argument with weight. Belgic, it says, makes its speakers very quick to learn any foreign tongue. And so it is: experience has already shown this to foreigners many times. After a few months of practice, we pass for Italians among Italians, or even for Spaniards among Spaniards, unless our too-conspicuous skin refuses to hide us. We copy the accent of the voice, and even the more frequent nods and gestures of that people (from which our plainer nature has kept us free), lively and to the life, whenever we like, for the sake of amusement. And in the Roman language itself, to whom do the Belgians yield? Or rather, who does not yield to the Belgians? Since the barbarism of the preceding centuries was lately driven out, the old brightness of Latin has shone again upon the world.

units.la: Quæst. Cisi è nostro hoc Belgio? Erasmi, Ipsii, Grotii, Puteani nostri sunt: a Latium adhuc viros, quibus desunt tantum: At vero qui aliud in unis idioma suxerunt, mirum est quam exterorum linguis deinceps addiscendis sint inhabiles: quocumque devenerint, semper tolent maternas cæpas: Et ne longius excurram, res patet in vicinis nostris Walonibus: Qui vixdum ex ephebis egressi, & huc forte translati, dum idioma nostrum affectant, oleum & operam perdunt: Curvilingues (sic Belgis vocantur) degunt inter nos ad capularem usque senectutem: Eandem difficultatem Itali experiuntur & Hispani, tum in mutuis linguis ac Latinâ, quas confundunt, tum in Germanica ac Belgica, quas miserè mactant, addiscendis: Et id ipsum procul dubio notaremus etiam in Latinis, si alicubi restarent indigenæ, si non tempestiv[?] totos se abscondissent in libris Hæc pro Belgio; At intentatum ictum retundit hoc umbone La-tium: Egregiam verò laudem ć[?] Belgica: Quid hoc, quo ita tur-ges, est aliud, quàm cæteris idio-matibus ancillari? Nam quemad-modum Ludiones & Pyrrhicha-rii, plumbum circumferunt in fo-leis, quo pes ab onere solutus in Scena, cum levi socco saltet agi-lius: Ita Belgica lingua gentiles suos asperè habet: Duriuscula est & barbarizat: Vox utplurimum non nisi syllba: Et in unam sylla-bam, integrum aliquando plau-strum exonerat Aspirationum & Consonantum: Hinc dum Belgæ nitidis exterorum ac fa-cilibus se addicunt linguis, vel manumissi à rigida pædagoga, lu-xuriant, xuriant, plusquam ipsi indigenæ in eloquium effrænes. Honora-rium est istud verber, mi Belgica: Pectore excipias aut cavo latere, ut sonet, & testetur sub artubus robur: Ne te pudeat, ne diffiteare: Virago es pariter cum Germanica lingua; sed tamen sofrore, vel (ut quidam volunt) matre tuâ placidior: Admittit, ut suademus: & ultro insultans: At Latina lingua, inquit, mollis & effæminata: Vix ultra duas Consonantes proferre valet sine fulcro Vocalis: Blæsa etiam est, & balbutit, frequenti ejusdem syllabæ geminatione: audi balbutiem in exemplo: Quid de re mererere? Quid de re rere rara? jactat faber fecisse sese securim: Hoc amplius, quia ultimam syllabam Latina lingua non producit, in qua tamen Nominum ac Verborum Declinationes constituit,
units.tr: Who from our Belgium? Erasmus, Lipsius, Grotius and Puteanus are ours. Still, Latium has men who lack only this: those who have sucked in some other language from the cradle are strangely unfit to learn foreign tongues afterwards. Wherever they go, they always carry their mother's tongue with them. Not to go on at length, the thing is plain in our neighbours the Walloons. They have scarcely left school and have been brought here by chance; while they try to master our language, they lose their oil and their labour. The Curvilingues (that is what the Belgians call them) live among us until a senility fit for the coffin. The Italians and Spaniards experience the same difficulty, both in learning Latin, which they confuse with their own tongues, and in German and Belgic, which they cruelly murder. Without doubt we would note the same thing in Latin too, if any native speakers were still left anywhere, if they had not in good time buried themselves altogether in books. So much for Belgium. But Latium turns aside the threatened blow with this shield. And what great praise is this, O Belgic, in which you swell up? What is it but to serve as a handmaid to the other languages? For just as dancers and pyrrhic performers carry lead about in their shoes, so that the foot, freed from the weight on the stage, leaps more nimbly in light slippers, so the Belgic language keeps its own people hard and rough. It is somewhat stiff and barbarous. Its word is for the most part only a syllable, and into a single syllable it sometimes unloads a whole cartload of aspirates and consonants. Hence, when Belgians give themselves over to the neat and easy tongues of foreigners, or, freed from the stiff schoolmistress, run riot, they become more unbridled in speech than the natives themselves. That is a fine whipping for you, my Belgic: take it on the chest or the flank, so that it resounds and shows that your strength lies in your limbs. Do not be ashamed, do not deny it. You are a virago, equal in kind to the German language, though perhaps gentler than your sister, or (as some would have it) your mother. Let it be admitted, as we advise. And Latin, leaping up again, says: "But Latin is soft and effeminate. It can scarcely pronounce more than two consonants without the support of a vowel. It is also stammering and babbles, with the frequent doubling of the same syllable. Hear the stammering in an example: Quid de re mererere? Quid de re rere rara? jactat faber fecisse sese securim." Moreover, since Latin does not lengthen its final syllable, although it forms the declensions of nouns and the conjugations of verbs in it,

units.la: stituit, hinc eminùs per clamores non intelligitur:Ex Theatro etiam ac Suggestu non percipitur, nisi ab exercitatis pronuncietur, qui usu didicerunt vim aliquam ultimis syllabis, licet eas corripiant, impartiri. Excandescit crebris his lacessitum ictibus Latium: & cum convitio: Da, si potes, exlex & barbara Regulas quæ te dirigunt: etiamnum in incude Grammatica tua, nec prodit: & ut vides, desperant, qui in hoc unum tam impensè desudant artifices: Quid exteros invidiosè traducis? quid miri, nunquam bene disci, quod doceri non potest? Irrumpit adversùm istæc cum furore Belgium: Quid? Sed ne ludrica vertantur in serium, finis esto Luctæ. Ecce quia Gymnasta sum, deponunt cæstus,& obediunt.
units.tr: it follows that it is not understood from a distance by shouts. Nor is it heard from the theatre or the pulpit unless it is pronounced by practised speakers, who have learned by use to give some force to the last syllables even though they shorten them. Latium, provoked by these repeated blows, flares up and cries out with abuse: "Give me, if you can, the rules that guide you, you lawless and barbarous thing! Your grammar is still on the anvil and does not come forth. And as you see, those craftsmen who sweat so hard at this one thing despair." "Why do you so spitefully disparage foreigners? What wonder is it that what cannot be taught is never well learned?" Against these words Belgium rushes in with fury. "What? But lest our playful bout turn into earnest, let it end. Look, because I am the trainer, they put down their gloves and obey."

units.la: Quæstio XXV.
units.tr: Question XXV.

units.la: An furor Principis, an populi magis exitialis sit?
units.tr: Whether the rage of a prince or of the people is the more destructive?

units.la: ATrocior est noster quam Jovis ignis: Alpes hic ferit & turrium apices, securæ valles humilesque casæ; Ille dum furit, ventorum forte flatibus irritatus, tecta, templa, sylvas, segetes, ima pariter ac summa, nullo corripit discrimine: Sic dum Principis aliquantisper simultate pressa intumuit ira, crepat illa cominùs, & stragem edit in Satrapas: tutum est eminùs Terræ Filiis spectaculum; At si vulgi turbulenta rabies, Legis excusserit capistrum, contumaci ungulâ Ruit omnia latè: Fas, nefas, sacra, profana susque deque O deque habet: Inter balistas & fra-gores, inter sudes & saxa, inter fa-ces & incendia grassatur in Princi-pem ac Optimates, etiam per suum latus. Theatrum est Mos-cua, Moscoviæ metropolis, in qua trux Erynnis, lugubrem nuper exhibuit Tragœdiam, quæ locu-ples testimonium faciat meæ Sen-tentiæ. Res ita se habet. An-no 1648. 1. Mai., Moscoviæ & Russiæ Imperator, cum Patriar-cha & Clero, ac præcipuis regni proceribus (Bojardos vocant) ad solennem, quæ quotannis isto die peragisolet, Supplicationem accin-gitur: Cives Moscuenses, oportu-num rati, querimoniam scripto ediderant, eam ad Imperatoris genua, dum pietati vacaret, dela-turi: querebantur immensis se ve-Etigalibus[?], quæ aliquot jam annos pendebant, exhaustos: quod miseris à duro isto torculari supererat sangui-nis, id Bojardorum prædam esse: Quapropter malle se semel cum con-jugibus ac charißimis pignoribus, ju-gulum lictori præbere, quam infelicem vitam tamdiu trahere per tot ærum-nas: Hoc instructi libello, accur-runt ad Cæsarem: Densa stipabat illum Bojardorum corona: hi a-barcebant ingruentem populum & prohibebant aditu: Quidam etiam è Bojardis videntes libellum, quem unus supplicum prætendebat, di-ripiunt eum è manibus, perlectum lacerant, de cætero mandant fa-mulis, fustibus egregié multent in-solentes illos vappas, & abigant in malam crucem: Probrum hoc, & mistum cum sævitia ludibrium, multitudinis animum, gravissime jam ante afflictum, incredibile est quantum exulceraverit; Dissimu-lant tamen, quoad Sacrorum cære-moniæ moniæ finiantur : interea mutuo fremitu, & summi Numinis obte-statione, justas iras exacuunt. A meridie cum turbis confertim ad-sunt ad Cæsareum Palatium : hic plebi junguntur Imperatoris præ-sidiarii, & ipsi propter imminuta nuper stipendia desperabundi, qui accessione suâ seditiosum illum numerum auxerunt ad aliquot millia. Hinc factâ manu concur-ritur ad palatium Borysii, summi totius Russiæ Gubernatoris, qui ab aliquot jam ante mensibus, Imperatricis germanam duxerat in uxorem : Irruunt diffractis portarum ceris ac vectibus, momento diffunduntur intus per omnes aulas & atria: & non invento Borysio (nam is clancu-lum per posticam evaserat ad Cæ-sarem) immensam auri ac argen-ti supellectilem pretiosissimasque mar-
units.tr: Our rage is more savage than the fire of Jupiter. That fire strikes the Alps and the tops of towers, but spares the sheltered valleys and humble cottages. When it rages, roused perhaps by gusts of wind, it seizes roofs, temples, woods and crops, low and high alike, without any distinction. So when a prince's anger has been held back for a while under pretence, it bursts out at close quarters and makes slaughter among the nobles. Its spectacle is safe to watch from a distance for the sons of the earth. But if the turbulent fury of the common people has shaken off the bridle of the law, then, with a stubborn hoof, it overturns everything far and wide. Right and wrong, sacred and profane, it holds all of them of no account. Amid crossbows and crashing stones, amid stakes and rocks, amid torches and conflagrations, it rages against the prince and the nobles, even at its own side. Moscow, the capital of Muscovy, is a theatre in which a fierce Fury lately put on a mournful tragedy, which will amply bear witness to my opinion. The matter stood thus. In the year 1648, on 1 May, the Emperor of Moscow and Russia, together with the Patriarch, the clergy and the chief nobles of the realm (whom they call Boyars), was preparing for the solemn supplication that is held every year on that day. The citizens of Moscow, thinking it fitting, had drawn up a written complaint, intending to bring it to the Emperor's feet while he was occupied with piety. They complained that they were drained by the immense taxes that they had been paying for some years now; that whatever blood was left to the wretched people after this harsh press was the prey of the Boyars. For this reason they would rather once for all offer their throats to the executioner, together with their wives and dearest children, than drag out an unhappy life through so many hardships. Armed with this petition they ran to the Caesar. A dense crowd of Boyars surrounded him. These men held back the pressing people and kept them from approaching. Some of the Boyars, seeing the petition that one of the supplicants was holding out, snatched it from his hands, tore it up after reading it, and then ordered their servants to punish those insolent scoundrels thoroughly with clubs, and drive them off to the devil. This insult, mixed with cruel mockery, cut the feelings of the multitude, already deeply afflicted, to an incredible degree. Yet they dissembled, until the ceremonies of the sacred rites were finished. In the meantime they sharpened their just anger by mutual muttering and by calling on the name of the highest Deity. From midday they gathered in crowds at the Imperial Palace. Here the Emperor's guards joined the common people. They too were desperate because their pay had recently been cut, and by their joining they swelled that seditious throng to some thousands. Then, forming a band, they made for the palace of Borysius, the chief Governor of all Russia, who for some months had married the Empress's sister. They burst in, breaking the wax seals and bars of the gates, and in a moment spread through all the halls and courts inside. Borysius was not found, for he had slipped out by a back door to the Caesar. They threw out of the windows into the public square a huge store of gold and silver plate and the most precious pearls. No one touched them, and they shouted eagerly: [Toot nassi kroof]! that is, Behold our blood! The rest of the things to which art had given value, such as paintings, carpets and statues, they hacked with swords and trampled under foot. Then they turned to the house of Tsiftesius, who was the chief Chancellor of the Empire. They found him in bed (for he was lying ill from a bad wound to the back of the head, which he had got not long before by falling from his horse). They dragged him naked from his bed, head first, across the floor, and then hauled him into the garden to the dunghill. Here he was beaten with fists, stones and clubs, and a deadly blow was struck at him with an axe. [Ismeenic toot pro sol], that is, Traitor, this for salt. For that unhappy Tsiftesius had recently imposed a great tax on salt, not knowing, fool that he was, that soon he would have to pay that tax with his head to these unbending collectors.

units.la: (Notes in the right margin are cut off and only partly legible; they are not transcribed.) margaritas, per fenestras undique conjiciunt in publicū : nemine eas deinceps manu contingente, certa-tim clamabant: Toot nassi kroof! id est, Ecce noster sanguis ! Reliqua quibus ars pretium fecerat, velut picturas, tapetes, & statuas, gladiis conscindunt, & proterunt pedibus. Hinc vertunt se ad domum Tsi-ftesii, qui erat summus imperii Cancellarius: Et offendentes eum in lecto (decumbebat enim ex malè ominato vulnere, quod non ita pridem ex equo prolapsus accepe-rat in occipite) nudum eripiunt cubili, capite prostratum, per pavi-mentum raptant : dein in hortum trahunt ad sterquilinium: hîc pug-nis, saxis, stipitibus vapulat : qui-que letalem ei ictum securi im-pertitur : Ismeenic toot pro sol, id est Proditor, hoc pro sale : sali e-nim infelix iste Tsiftesius grande vecti-
units.tr: pearls, and flung them out through the windows into the street on every side. No one touched them afterwards, and they shouted eagerly: Toot nassi kroof! that is, "Behold our blood!" The remaining things on which art had set a price, such as pictures, carpets and statues, they slashed with swords and trampled underfoot. Then they turned to the house of Tsiftesius, who was chief Chancellor of the empire. They found him in bed, for he was lying ill from an ill-omened wound in the back of the head, which he had received not long before when he fell from his horse. They dragged him naked from his bed, head-first, across the floor, then into the garden to the dunghill. There he was beaten with fists, stones and clubs, and an axe-blow was dealt him that proved fatal. Ismeenic toot pro sol, that is, "Traitor, this is for the salt": this unhappy Tsiftesius had lately imposed a heavy tax (vectigal) on salt, not knowing, the fool, that the tax would soon have to be paid with his head to these hard tax-collectors.

units.la: { vectigal nuper constituerat, nescius ah demens! brevi id sibi capitis tributo, apud rigidos hos telones solvendum restare. Ast illi occiso hero, nihilo segnius domum ejus impetere, obvia quaeque prosternere, secare, demoliri, vastare: inter pulveres & rudera, inter fumum & ruinas, consuetum hoc rugire: Hic est noster sanguis.
units.tr: But their master slain, they attacked his house no less fiercely, overthrowing, cutting down, demolishing and laying waste everything in their path. Amid dust and rubble, amid smoke and ruins, they kept up their customary roar: Hic est noster sanguis.

units.la: Mox domus Pretoris urbani, ac plurium aliorum Bojardorum similli gaudent forte; ipsi tempestivè se subduxerant, & ad vicina monasteria confugerant. His gestis nox supervenit, & exasperatos leniturus videbatur sopor; Cum postero die, orto vix Sole, recrudescit hesternum ulcus: Confluunt iterum ad Imperatoris Palatium, postulantes ocyus sibi sisti ad manus Plesseophum, qui unus præ cæteris, civium omnium flagraflagrabrat odiis & execrationi-bus: item etiam Borysium Rufsiæ Gubernatorem, qui pridie è manibus eorum elapsus fuerat: item etiam Troghniotophum. Imperator sperans unâ victimâ paccandum populi furorem, Plesseophum emittit cum Lictore, qui ad conspectū securi cædat infelicem: Vix prodierat, involant: ad forum pellunt, raptant: huc ubi deventum, sudibus contunduut, secant securibus, confodiunt gladiis, nudum ac discerptum cadaver spectaculo relinquunt: Et rursus ad Palatium pro Borysio jam: Videt Imperator, rabiem illam, dum sanguinem lingit, efferari magis magisque: Prodiens igitur cum plangtu, quem res fictum esse non sinebat: Amici, inquit, & cives mei, biduum concedite, ut consulam de duobus istis, quos tradi vobis petitis: respondebo voluntati vestræ, quantum fas est: Et nihil de his, quæ impresentiarum gerebantur, conquestus, subtrahit se cum gemitu: Humilis ista Majestatis species & abrupta, cunctorum animos emollivit pariter ac perculsit: Altum subito silentium: nec ultra quidquam: domum abeunt sedati & mæsti. Sed ecce tibi inopinatum quiddam, & his quæ hactenus præcesserunt atrocius: Eodem die sub meridiem, incendium ingens, nec unicum, variis dissitisque locis dispersum, quod ventis instigatum, & his qui ad extinguendum accurrebant, quod in diversa tenderent, in se mutuo impactis & confusis, grassabatur impunè: Adeò ut spatio quatuordecim fermè horarum, tertiam magnæ illius urbis partem redegerit in cineres. Qui interfuêre, ajunt incendio illo absumptas esse domos ultra quinquaginta millia: inter quas etiam Palatium Nikitzii, Imperatoris avunculi, quod inæstimabilis pretii fuisse perhibetur: structurâ pariter, ac sumptuosâ, qua refertum erat, supellectili stupendum: Cùmq; incendium istud inciderit in meridiem, perierunt tamen homines, sive flammis impliciti, sive fumo præfocati, mille septingenti. Hoc tunc etiam accidit memorabile: Sub mediam noctem, cum flamma jam perrexisset ad forum, ubi cella vinaria Imperatoris, in qua vinum adustum, cujus apud gentem istam creber potus, maximâ asservatur copiâ: cùmque periculum esset, ne si flammam concepisset, pereundem esset omnibus: ajunt Monachum quendam adfuisse, stricto gladio: quantum. tum poterat cœtum populi coë-gisse: & protinus: Nisi caput hujus Sceleris (monstrabat autem cadaver Plesfeophi, quod nnper per lanienam exanimatum, nudum etiamnum jacebat in foro) nisi, inquit, caput hujus Sceleris ultricibus istis flammis devovemus, actum est de nobis omnibus: Nec plura, ipse caput cadaveri amputat, & vino adusto intinctum, conjicit in medias flammas: Res miraculo similis: nam in foro sedatur incendium: Extemplo consequitur vulgi superstitio, & truncum cadaver in partes concisum, variis locis, flammis propitiandis objectant. Inter hæc, quidam ex Incendiariis deprehensi, & in carceres detrusi; postridie vero in quæstionem postulati,& torti, fatebantur diserte, ad facinus pecuniâ emptos se à Boryfio Russiæ Gubernatore, qui suasuavi hoc diverticulo populum detinere, & à conceptæ in eum sententiæ exsecutione avocare studuerat: Tùm verò frendere omnes & disrumpi: ad Palatium irruere: sublatis vociferationibus, Scelus istud & Patriæ bustum deposcere ad sævam necem, sine mora, jam, jam: Contrà Imperator laborare, viri salutem humiliter deprecari, instare, & quæ antehac bene gesserat, apud populum exaggerare: ad hæc Nikitzium avunculum suum, deprecatorem facere: erat is populo perquam charus: tum ob recentem ac communem in incendio isto jacturam, amabatur tenerius. His tandem flexi, descendunt in hanc sententiam: ut prædictus Borysius, Russiæ Gubernator, muniis omnibus ac fortunis exutus, insuper tonsus & cucullum indutus, initietur in Monachum, chum, ablegeturque in Monasterium Kiriliense, quod centum miliaribus distat à Moscua, situm ad ripam Sochinæ: & sententia hæc executionem sortitur duodecimâ Junii, eodem anno 1648.
units.tr: The houses of the city praetor and of several other boyars probably suffered the same fate, though they themselves had withdrawn in good time and fled to the nearby monasteries. After these events night came on, and sleep seemed likely to soothe their angry minds. But the next day, scarcely after sunrise, yesterday's sore broke out again. They flocked once more to the Emperor's palace, demanding that Plesseophus be handed over to them at once. He, more than any other, was burning with the hatred and curses of all the citizens. They also demanded Borysius, governor of Russia, who had slipped from their hands the day before, and Troghniotophus too. The Emperor, hoping to appease the people's fury with a single victim, sent out Plesseophus with a lictor, to be struck down with the axe in their sight. He had scarcely come out before they swooped down on him and dragged him off to the marketplace. There they beat him with clubs, cut him with axes and stabbed him with swords, and left the naked, mangled corpse as a spectacle. Then they returned to the palace and demanded Borysius now. The Emperor saw that their rage grew more and more savage as they licked up the blood. So he came out with a show of grief, which the situation did not allow to be feigned, and said: Friends and citizens of mine, grant me two days, so that I may consider these two men whom you ask me to hand over to you. I will meet your wishes as far as is right. He made no complaint about what was going on at the time, and withdrew with a groan. This humble and broken appearance of majesty softened and at the same time struck the hearts of all. There was a sudden deep silence, and nothing more; they went home calmed and sorrowful. But behold something unexpected and more atrocious than what had gone before. That same day, about noon, a huge fire broke out, not a single one but scattered over various and widely separated places. Driven by the winds, and with those who ran to put it out rushing in different directions and colliding and mixing with one another, it raged unchecked. So much so that in about fourteen hours it reduced a third of that great city to ashes. Those who were there say that more than fifty thousand houses were consumed by that fire, among them the palace of Nikitzius, the Emperor's uncle, said to be of inestimable value, remarkable both for its structure and its costly furnishings. Although the fire broke out at noon, nevertheless seventeen hundred people perished, either caught in the flames or suffocated by smoke.
