This also happened, worth recording: after midnight, when the flames had already reached the marketplace, where the Emperor's wine cellar was, in which burnt wine, the frequent drink of that people, is stored in great quantity, and when there was danger that if it caught fire everyone would perish, they say a certain monk was present with a drawn sword, and gathered as large a crowd of people as he could. Immediately he said: Unless we devote the head of this crime (he was pointing to the corpse of Plesseophus, which had lately been butchered and still lay naked in the marketplace) unless, he said, we devote the head of this crime to these avenging flames, we are all undone. Saying no more, he cut off the head of the corpse himself, dipped it in burnt wine and threw it into the middle of the flames. The thing was like a miracle, for the fire in the marketplace was quelled. At once the superstition of the crowd followed, and they threw the trunk, cut into pieces, to various places to appease the flames. Meanwhile some of the arsonists who had been caught were thrown into prison; but the next day they were brought before the court and put to torture, and they openly confessed that they had been hired for the deed with money by Borysius, governor of Russia, who had tried to keep the people occupied with this pleasant diversion and to divert them from carrying out the sentence they had conceived against him. Then indeed all of them roared and seethed; they rushed at the Palace, and with shouts raised they demanded that this crime and the burning of their country be given over to a savage death, without delay, now, now. The Emperor, on the other hand, laboured: he humbly begged for the man's life, pressed his case, and reminded the people of what he had done well before. To this end he made his uncle Nikitzius an intercessor, and he was very dear to the people, both because of the recent loss they all shared in the fire and because he was loved more tenderly. At last they gave way to these entreaties and agreed on this sentence: that the aforesaid Borysius, governor of Russia, stripped of all his offices and fortunes, and moreover shaven and dressed in a cowl, should be initiated as a monk and sent away to the monastery of Kirillov, which lies on the bank of the Sukhona, a hundred miles from Moscow. This sentence was carried out on the twelfth of June, in the same year 1648.

units.la: Mitior est naturalis quàm artificiosus ignis: Nam si intempestâ forte noê‑te, non ritè sopitus focus, alicubi fecerit incendium, exciti ad pulsum Feralis Nolæ, concurrimus protinus cum scalis & hamis: & hinc detractis, qui suppetebant in pabulum, titionibus, depluentibus illinc syphonibus & situlis, tandem abigimus indi‑gnan‑ gnantem inter stridores Vulcanum; At si is pyrio conceptus pulvere, latentes devolvitur per cuniculos: premant eum gravia murorum mœnia, & incumbentes cum turribus arces; non suppriment: Onere lacessitus, elucta-bitur, & perrumpet in stragem horribiliorem. Sic etiam populi furor apertâ nititur viâ: Non te-ctæ, non repentinæ machinationes: Maturâ seditiosi capitis suppressione, incussâ superstitione, vanâ spe, aliisque, quibus mancipatus est affectibus, terretur, circumvenitur, sedatur facilè. At Principum Tyrannis, ambage tectâ molitur excidium: Non probitas illam, non dignitas, non merita compescunt: Quin insimulet, & subornet, & omnem lapidem moveat, quo tandem, ceu perduellem feriat, quem obstare libidibidini suæ suspiciosa dictat ambi-tio. Adsit Sophy Cha-abas, Persa-rum nuper Tyrannus, & effuso à se, innocuo ac Regio sanguine, obsignet meam Sententiam cru-deli litura: cui sanctos denique ci-neres, & Martyris favillam insper-gat. Sophy Cha-abas, Persarum Rex, missis Legatis ad Alexan-drum Georgiæ Regem, Christia-num Principem, qui pridem, ita cogente necessitate, sub Persarum protectione se dederat, petit fidei obsidem Constantinum, filium ejusdem Alexandri natu majo-rem: Mittitur: Tyrannus ubi ju-venem recepit, complectitur, fo-vet blanditiis, maria montesque pollicetur: His tandem assequitur, ut Constantinus Christum ejuret, & nomen det Mahometi. Sceleris rumor, pios Principes, Constan-tini parentes, incredibile est, quan-tum tum afflixerit : Execrantur sacrilegum transfugam, nec jam amplius inter suos numerant , qui sub Christi signis non censeretur : Tota jam iis prosapiæ spes in Davide suo , natu minore recumbit: Cui proinde principem & leétissimam virginem desponsant, nomine Catharinam : Quæ & filium ei peperit , qui vocatus est Tamaras Myrsa: Hunc Myrsam, tenerum adhuc ( quod videretur hæres regni, excluso Constantino ad Davidem jam devoluti ) etiam deposcit Persarum Rex in fidei obsidem , & quia non tutum videbatur tergiversari , confestim mittitur. Myrsam ad se delatum, Rex iisdem aggreditur blanditiis, quibus antè Patruum ejus Constantinum pellexerat in suam se-ctam; Necquidquam: Nam adversus nefandæ Sirenis cantum, nimis
units.tr: Natural fire is gentler than artificial fire. For if, on a dark night, a hearth not properly banked has started a blaze somewhere, we rush out at once, roused by the peal of the death bell, with ladders and hooks. We pull down whatever is at hand to feed it, drench it with water from the syringes and buckets, and at last drive out the angry Vulcan amid hissing. But if the fire has been kindled by gunpowder and rolls through hidden tunnels, heavy city walls and citadels with their towers piled on top will not suppress it. Provoked by the weight, it will struggle free and break out in a more dreadful slaughter. So too the fury of a people forces its way along an open path. Its plots are neither hidden nor sudden. By prompt suppression of the seditious leader, by instilling superstition, by empty hope, and by the other passions to which the crowd is enslaved, it is frightened, circumvented and easily calmed. But the tyranny of princes works its ruin by a hidden and roundabout route. Neither uprightness, nor rank, nor merit restrains it. Rather, it will falsely accuse, suborn witnesses, and move every stone, so that at last it may strike down, as though he were a traitor, the man whom its suspicious ambition declares to stand in the way of its lust. Let Sophy Chaabas, the lately reigning tyrant of the Persians, be present, and with the innocent royal blood he has spilled let him seal my sentence with cruel erasure. Let him finally scatter over me the holy ashes and the dust of a martyr. Sophy Chaabas, King of the Persians, sent envoys to Alexander, King of Georgia, a Christian prince who had earlier, under compulsion of necessity, placed himself under Persian protection, and demanded as a pledge of his faith Constantine, the elder son of the same Alexander. He was sent. When the tyrant had received the young man, he embraced him, cherished him with flatteries, and promised him seas and mountains. By these means at last he brought it about that Constantine renounced Christ and took the name of Muhammad. The rumour of this crime afflicted the pious princes, Constantine's parents, beyond belief. They cursed the sacrilegious deserter and no longer counted him among their own, since he was not reckoned under the standards of Christ. All their hope of family now rested on David, their younger son. To him they betrothed a princess, a most chaste virgin named Catherine, who bore him a son called Tamaras Myrsa. The King of Persia demanded this Myrsa, still tender in years (since he seemed to be the heir of the kingdom, Constantine being excluded and the succession having already passed to David), as a pledge of faith. Because it seemed unsafe to refuse, he was sent at once. When Myrsa was brought to him, the King approached him with the same flatteries with which he had earlier enticed his uncle Constantine into his sect. In vain: the noble boy had stopped his mind's ear too firmly against the song of that unspeakable Siren. So the King turned back to his Constantine, since he now seemed cast down to every crime, having once trampled underfoot the Christian, that is, that gentle and tender piety. Fawning on him, he said:

units.la: altè mentis aurem obturaverat generosus Puer. Igitur Rex ad Constantinum suum revertitur ( quia jam ad omne scelus projectus videbatur, qui nuper Christianam, id est mitem illam & teneram pietatem, protritum iverat sub pedibus ) & palpans : Constantine, inquit, tempus jam dudum & res ipsa postulant, ut stem promissis, & obsequiis in me tuis aliquando respondeam. Sed non sentis alienatos à te tuorum animos? Quò res vergat, non percipis ? Sceptrum quod jus & natura tibi dederant, excussum de manibus non vides ? Primus ego rebus tuis consulam : Dic age: si patrem tuum hujus in te consilii architectum, fratremque qui te supplantavit, tibi sisterem: Tantùmne animi, ut acinacem strinxeris, & iniquum illud filum, quo corona perduellionis immi- net vertici, recideris ? Exercitu mea stipastipatum & tutum, reponam te paterno solio. Tyranni mentem percepit Constantinus, & inhorruit: pallet, hæret: Tandem ira, & dolor, & indignatio, & sibi debiti, (sic censebat) Sceptri cupido, effrænem jam excusså Religione animum concitarunt in facinus: Annuit: Et tuis, inquit, ô magne Sophy, ut æquum semper duxi, parebo jussis & consiliis. Nec mora, mittit Rex, qui suo nomine præsto esse jubeant Alexandrum & Davidem Georgiæ Reges, cum manu quatuor millium è suis: Ita regni sui negotia postulare. Ubi advenêre, convivio eos accipit Constantinus lauto, Regio; Sed demum inter bellaria, quàm funestum apophoretum! Ex improviso consurgit horridus: Momento citius, & sicam stringit, & recondit eam in patris sui pectore, & rursum sum in auras librat, & adigit per fraternum latus. Extemplò volare fama execrabilis parricidii, & Georgianorum castra tremulo tumultu miscere. Adest Rex Persarum: Voce, gestu levat consternatos: Facinus adscribit temulentiæ, contentionibus, jurgiis, quibus dum cognatus ac familiaris sanguis colluctatur, sævius utplurimùm in mutuam perniciem ebullit, quàm ignotus : cæterum cùm tristis casus ita tulerit, nolle se in illam impotentiam severius animadvertere ; Sed pacandis Georgianis rebus intentum se & sollicitum, dare iis Constantinum in Regem: Utpote Regiæ familiæ germen, cui jam antè hæreditario jure sceptrum deberetur. His Parricidæ munita via : qui protinus ad suorum castra tetendit : & auctus insuper manu quatuordecim millium Persarum, abitum tum maturabat in patriam. Sed jam nuncius horribilis parricidii, ferenissimam fœminam Cathari- nam perculerat, ac tantum non exanimaverat, simul instare sacrilegum parricidam cum infidelium exercitu detulerat. Quid agat? colligit se: & sexum egressa, altâ simulatione premit dolorem pariter & consilium: Interea militem in insidiis locat ad montium, quæ Georgiam à Persŧde discriminant, angustias, obviàm ipsa procedit Constantino: ubi ad prædictos montes deventum, mittit, qui Constantino dicant: Lugere se, ut par erat, mariti ac soceri sui triste letum; cæterum jam antè è Persarum Rege didicisse, id non Constantino, sed repentinæ cuidam iræ, cujus compotes non sumus mortales, imputandum. Ad regni limites in occursum se adesse: & porrò perrecturam fuisse, fuisse, nisi suorum consilio, quibus id praeter sexus pudorem videbatur, obsequendum judicasseт: quapropter rogare se, ultrò ipse veniat: esse quod conferat de terrore, quem externus miles, civibus ejus, nihil nisi Constantini adventum anhelantibus incuteret, deque aliis, quæ coram commodius, quam per legatos agenda differret. Accepto nuncio, exultat Parricida: & jam etiam fratris à se mactati thalamum cogitare audet incestus. Paucis comitantibus domesticis, per montium fauces ad Reginam pergit: cumque jam cassès effugere non posset, exilit ex insidiis miles, circumveniunt incautum: trucidant: & generosus aštus vices rependit sceleri: Nec satis: per montium juga effunduntur, & suis aggregati, numerum cum Persis æquant, quos confusos ac ignaros cædunt, uno fermè ac altero. tero, qui cladis nuncium deferrent, elapsis. His inauditis Persarum Rex ad interiores artes se convertere, & fraudem jam fraude temperare: Myrsam matri suæ remittere cum literis: Quibus primò quidem heroicam illam parricidii vindictam extollebat, & dignam immortalitate censebat: dein mandabat unicum hunc regiæ stirpis surculum, sollicitè à se hactenus fotum, quamprimùm pangeret, ut Georgiæ sceptrum constaret, quæ ceteroqui regiâ deficiente propagine, Perfidis accederet coronæ. Ubi matri redditus adolescens, prudentissimæ fæminæ summæ curæ erat, non quidem compositis Tyranni consiliis, quæ alium scopum spectabant, parere; sed quod res ipsa postulabat, exsequi. Igitur principem puellam è vicino regno Tessliensi, Myrsæ suo in matrimonium petit; tit; At Persarum Rex corrivalem tempestivè subornat Alovaffam Tefflis regem: Et zelo ac invidiâ horum Christianorum Principum opportunè abusus, datis clam ad utrumque literis, alterum in alterius necem instigabat; Sed utrique suspectum negotium, quod tam sedulò Veterator urgeret, cujus perfidiam, quidquid ipse praetexeret, satis jam prodebat eventus. Igitur suspicio ad colloquium eos excivit, colloquio veritas detecta est: Tum verò indignitate moti, statuunt se Persarum tyrannidi subtrahere, & Turcorum protectioni regna sua transcribere: Reseiit Persa, quantumvis tecta consilia, & ingentibus copiis vicinam sibi Georgiam inundat. At Catharina pro suorum salute obicem se positura, pergit in occursum Tyranni: Excipit ille genibus suis advoluvolutam, nec asperum quidquam præ se ferens, abducit Catharinam in Persidem. Sæpiùs scribenti Myrsæ, & matris reditum obnixè efflagitanti, nihil: Donec Muscoviæ Legatus, qui illac forte cum muneribus ad Persarum Regem tendebat, precibus & pietate flexus, Myrsæ patronum se fecit: Hîc enim constrictum se sensit Tyrannus, & ultra impatiens simulatio crepuit in apertam rabiem: Mandat ocyùs Catharinam deferri ad civitatem Chyram:Gubernatori literas ipse destinat, quarum hæc summa: Velle se ut ad manus ejus, Catharina renunciet Christo, & Mahometi nomen det: Addit promissa quæ pelliciant, inter quæ consortium tori & regni: Addit minas quæ compellant, non unam per laniatus & suppli-cia mortem. Hæc ubi Catharinæ exhi-
units.tr: Constantine, the time and the situation itself have long demanded that you keep your promises and at last repay my favours with your service. But do you not see that the minds of your people have turned away from you? Do you not perceive where the matter is tending? Do you not see the sceptre, which right and nature gave you, shaken from your hands? I will be the first to look after your affairs. Come, tell me: if I were to hand over to you your father, the architect of this plot against you, and your brother, who supplanted you, would you have the spirit to draw the dagger, and cut that unjust thread by which the crown of treason hangs over your head? Guarded by my army, I will restore you to your father's throne. Constantine understood the tyrant's mind and shuddered. He turned pale and froze. At last anger, grief and indignation, together with a desire for the sceptre that he thought was owed to him (so he judged), drove his spirit, now unbridled after casting off religion, into the crime. He nodded assent: And, great Sophy, as I have always thought right, I will obey your commands and counsels. Without delay the King sent men to order, in his name, Alexander and David, Kings of Georgia, to be present, together with a force of four thousand of their men, since the affairs of his kingdom demanded this. When they arrived, Constantine received them at a lavish royal banquet. But at last, among the sweetmeats, what a deadly dessert! He suddenly rose up, bristling. In an instant he drew a dagger, plunged it into his father's breast, then lifted it again into the air and drove it through his brother's side. At once the report of the accursed parricide flew abroad and threw the Georgian camp into trembling tumult. The King of the Persians arrived. With voice and gesture he calmed the dismayed men, and laid the deed to drunkenness, quarrels and brawls: where, while kindred and familiar blood wrestles together, it usually boils over into mutual destruction more savagely than blood that is unknown. However, since this sad event has turned out so, he would not punish that frenzy more severely; but being intent and anxious to calm Georgian affairs, he would give them Constantine as king, since he was a scion of the royal family, to whom the sceptre was already owed by hereditary right. The way was thus paved for the parricide, who immediately made for the camp of his own people. Reinforced besides by fourteen thousand Persians, he now hastened his departure for his homeland. But news of the horrible parricide had already struck the most gentle lady, Catherine, and had almost stunned her; at the same time it had reported that the sacrilegious parricide was approaching with an army of unbelievers. What was she to do? She gathered herself, and, going beyond her sex, she concealed both her grief and her plan under a deep pretence. Meanwhile she posted soldiers in ambush at the narrow passes of the mountains that separate Georgia from Persia, and she herself went out to meet Constantine. When they reached the aforesaid mountains, she sent messengers to tell Constantine that she grieved, as was fitting, over the sad death of her husband and father-in-law; but she had already learned from the King of Persia that this had been committed not by Constantine but by a sudden anger, over which we mortals have no control. She had come to meet him at the borders of the kingdom, and she would have pressed on further had she not judged, on the advice of her counsellors, that she should yield to them, since this seemed to them to go beyond the modesty of her sex. Therefore she asked him to come to her, since she had something to discuss with him about the terror which foreign soldiers were striking into her citizens, who longed for nothing but Constantine's arrival, and about other matters which she preferred to deal with in person rather than through envoys. On receiving the message, the parricide exulted, and the incestuous man now dared even to contemplate the bed of the brother he had slaughtered. With a few household attendants he went through the gorge of the mountains to the Queen. But when he could no longer escape the snare, soldiers leapt out of the ambush and surrounded the unsuspecting man, and slaughtered him; and the noble army paid back crime in kind. Nor was this enough: they poured over the mountain ridges, joined their own men, and equalled the number of the Persians, whom they cut down in confusion and ignorance, except for one or two who escaped to carry the news of the defeat. When the Persian King heard of these events, he turned to subtler arts and began to temper fraud with fraud. He sent Myrsa back to his mother with a letter. In it he first extolled that heroic revenge for the parricide and declared it worthy of immortality; then he ordered that this sole shoot of the royal stock, which he had carefully cherished until now, should be sent back as quickly as possible, so that the sceptre of Georgia might be secure, since otherwise, with no royal line left, it would fall to the Persian crown. When the young man was restored to his mother, that most prudent lady, who had the greatest care for him, did not obey the tyrant's designs, which aimed at another goal; but she carried out what the situation itself demanded. Therefore she asked for a princess from the neighbouring kingdom of Tiflis for her Myrsa's marriage. But the King of Persia promptly suborned a rival, Alovassa, King of Tiflis. Abusing the zeal and envy of these Christian princes to his advantage, he secretly wrote to each of them and urged one against the other's death. But both found the business suspicious, since the schemer was pressing it so eagerly; whatever pretext he offered, the outcome was already revealing his treachery well enough. So suspicion drew them to a conference, and at the conference the truth was uncovered. Then, moved by the indignity, they resolved to withdraw from the Persian tyranny and to hand over their kingdoms to the protection of the Turks. The Persian was enraged, and, however carefully they had concealed their plans, he flooded Georgia, which lay next to him, with great forces. But Catherine, to secure the safety of her people, set herself as a barrier and went out to meet the tyrant. He received her, flung down at his knees, and, showing nothing harsh, led Catherine away into Persia. Though Myrsa wrote often and earnestly begged his mother's return, there was no answer, until an envoy of Muscovy, who was passing that way with gifts to the King of Persia, moved by her prayers and by his own piety, became Myrsa's patron. For the tyrant felt himself hemmed in by this, and his pretence, no longer able to endure, burst into open rage. He at once ordered Catherine to be taken to the city of Chyra. He wrote the letter to the governor himself, and its substance was this: that he wished her to be brought into his hands, so that she might renounce Christ and take the name of Muhammad. He added promises to entice, among which were the partnership of his bed and kingdom; he added threats to compel, not just one death by mutilation and torture. When these were presented to Catherine,

units.la: exhibita, vultum attollit animosa: Terror nihil, & minus, si fieri possit, profecêre blanditiæ: In jubilum effusa, suspicit Divina Consilia, quibus visum esset Sanctam suam Legem, tot olim heroum oppigneratam sanguine, nunc etiam vilis (sic aiebat) mulierculæ signo firmare. Igitur ubi à sententia non dimovetur, ex præscripto Regiarum literarum, tortoribus traditur: Qui innocuam hanc Christi oviculam, vestibus exuunt ad summam nuditatem: Ad palum ligant: Ac primò quidem ubera, dein brachiorum ac tibiarum suras candentibus avellunt forcipibus: Et purpurâ suâ jam ritè ornatam, jam speciosam divinis oculis sponsam, in ardentem rogum conjiciunt: Nunquam ante hac in Solio suo tam formosa. Unicum hoc ei inter tormenta suspirium: ium: Exile, nihil, Iesu, quod pro te vatior. O non degenerem Christi obolem post tot sæcula! ô invi-diendam (aude pietas) ipsis etiam Ecclesiæ primordiis Heroinam!
units.tr: ...lifted her face, full of courage. Terror achieved nothing, and flattery achieved even less, if that were possible. Breaking into songs of joy, she looked up to the divine counsels, by which it had seemed good to confirm his holy Law, once sealed with the blood of so many heroes, now also with the sign of a mere (as she put it) low-born woman. So when she could not be moved from her decision, she was handed over to the torturers, as the royal letter had ordered. They stripped this innocent little lamb of Christ to utter nakedness, bound her to a stake, and first tore off her breasts, then the calves of her arms and legs, with red-hot pincers. Then they threw into a blazing pyre the bride, already duly adorned in her purple, already lovely in the eyes of God, more beautiful than ever before on her throne. Her only sigh amid the torments was: Nothing is hard, Jesus, that I suffer for you. O what a worthy offspring of Christ after so many ages! O heroine (dare I say it, piety) to be envied even in the earliest days of the Church!

units.la: Quæstio XXVII. An hodie non sit periculosissi-mum, ad magnas in Republica dignitates evehi.
units.tr: Question XXVII. Whether today it is not most dangerous to be raised to high dignities in the Commonwealth.

units.la: Vidi concitato nimis cer-tantem cursu, impa-ctum in metas, ad letale asthma contudisse pe-ctus: vidi violentâ ruentes in re-pagulum trabe, super ipsum præ-cipites, dirâ plagâ cruentasse vul-tum: Et Emblema vidi ingentis cujusdam ac immanis animi, quem iniqua paupertas coarctat, & ge-neris pesùm premit humilitas:
units.tr: I have seen a man who, racing too fiercely, struck the turning posts and crushed his chest with a deadly gasping. I have seen men rushing headlong against a barrier beam, and falling forward, bloodying their faces with a dreadful wound. And I have seen an emblem of a huge and savage spirit, which unfair poverty confines and lowly birth presses down most cruelly.

units.la: Tantum ei roboris coäcervavit angustia, tantum irritavit indignitas, tantum stimulavit conscientia, ut effuso derepentè in primum illud ac iners obstaculum impetu, concidat cum ipso in ruinam: aut elugtatus, & jam etiam victoriâ ferocior, sui, viriumque suarum impotem se, ad illos ipsos honorum titulos allidat, in quos tam pernici & invidendo pede contendebat. Horum ætas nostra ferax Exemplorum: Tot una suppetit, quot multa simul juncta majorum sæcula non colligunt: Bassam Nasus in Turcia, Miersam Tachi in Perside, in Germania Albertum Walstenium Ducem Fridlandiæ, Rodericum Calderonem Comitem de Oliva in Hispania, Conchinum Concini Marchionem d' Ancre in Gallia, & ibidem ac alibi plures. Ex quibus omnibus visum est unum num istum Conchinum, quod magis ad manum sit, in Scenam producere. Hic igitur ex Italia, in Franciam tendens, Irus quidam in patrio etiam solo non notus, vix tantum in Fortunæ castris merebat, quantum vili lixæ sufficeret ad victum: Ubi in Aulam se intrusit, nescio quo genio aspirante, favorem Reginæ Mariæ de Medices, quæ per id tempus, demortuo marito clavum tenebat, tam dexterè captavit, & ceu proprium sibi vendicavit, ut primò quidem uxorem ab ea impetraverit Eleonoram Dori (hæc fabri cujusdam Florentini filia, ob acre ingenium Reginæ intima) dein etiam ad Marchionatum d'Ancre, & inter Franciæ Pares evectus sit. Tum verò campum nactus, & pueritiâ Regis opportunè abusus, res novas moliri, ærarium expilare, exteros acci-
units.tr: Such is the strength that distress has piled up in him, such the anger stirred by indignity, such the goad of conscience, that, rushing out in a sudden onslaught against that first and inert obstacle, he either collapses with it into ruin, or, grown bold and even fiercer from victory, forgets himself and his own weakness and dashes himself against those very titles of honour which he was striving for with such headlong and envied speed. Our age is rich in examples of these: one life alone supplies as many as many centuries taken together would not gather. Bassa Nasuh in Turkey, Mirza Taqi in Persia, in Germany Albrecht Wallenstein, Duke of Friedland, Rodrigo Calderón, Count of Oliva, in Spain, Concino Concini, Marquis d'Ancre, in France, and many more there and elsewhere. Of all these, it seemed best to bring forward on the stage this Concino, as he lies nearest to hand. He, then, coming from Italy into France, a beggar who was not even known in his native land, could scarcely earn in the camps of Fortune enough to keep himself as a cheap camp-follower. When he had worked his way into the court, by some genius (I know not which) inspiring him, he so skilfully won the favour of Queen Marie de' Medici, who at that time held the helm after her husband's death, and so claimed it as his own, that first he obtained from her a wife, Eleonora Dori (the daughter of a certain Florentine smith, and a close confidante of the Queen, a woman of sharp wit), and then he was raised to the Marquisate d'Ancre and among the peers of France. Then, having found the field open, and having taken advantage of the boy-king's youth at the right moment, he began to launch new schemes, to plunder the treasury, to bring in foreigners,

units.la: cire, usurpatâ sibi authoritate militem conscribere, inexpertum Regis animum à proceribus alienare, illos vicissim in Principem suum concitare: his denique luxum ad invidiæ summam conjungere, unâ subinde noctè aureorum trecenta, & amplius miilia per aleam & convivia prodigere. Horum jam sæpiùs criminum coram Rege à Dynastis insimulatus, qui, ut optimus etiam fuisset, zelo tamen frendebant hominis & peregrini & novi; sciverat nihilominus callidum & vivax ingenium, speciosis erga Regem suum obsequiis, criminationes istas diluere. Sed invalescentibus adversariis, & indies invidiâ crescente, ajunt tandem sensisse Regem, ab insidiis irrequieti hominis, ne capiti quidem suo satis tutum esse: Proinde Vitrio præsidiariorum suorum duci mandat, Marchionem d'Ancre sibi sistat, vivum, mortuum; non interesse : Nec multò pòst prædictus Marchio, fati impendentis ignarus, Parisios contendit, Regem officii gratiâ conventurus: cumque insolitâ pompâ stipatus, Palatio appropinquaret, majores etiam valvas, honoris ergò reseratas habuit. Sed mox in interiore area à Vitrii militibus aliquot sclopetorum glandibus trajicitur, & sine voce aut ejulatu concidit 24. Maji anno 1617. Ubi rumor cædis increbuit, tanta populi exultatio, tantus ad Palatium confluxus, cespitantium hinc inde, & mutuis recursibus turmatim labentium, ut insanire præ gaudio tota simul multitudo videretur. Rex aderat è superiori fenestra civium studia despiciens: Illi festivas non voces, sed vociferationes tollere : Vive le Roy: Roy: Et Rex quidem caput honoris ergò populo detegere cernebatur; sed liberale istud Le Roy vous remercie, quod per suos identidem responderi jubebat, exaudire per immanes strepitus & clamores non licebat. Interea cadaver Marchionis in cubiculum janitoris protractum; postridie verò sine funeris apparatu elatum, in D. Germani, sub organo forte, in fossam abjicitur, ore pronum, capulo in dorsum illiso; Sed à plebeja rabie mox effosum, ad patibulum raptatur: Et ubi ex pedibus aliquantisper suspensum fuerat, comburitur: cineres in profluentem sparguntur: Hæc in irritum & ridicula sævitia, quæ larvas impetit, & dentem fatigat in exuviis; istud commiserationem jure habeat: Uxor occisi Marchionis Eleonora Dori, in carceres detrusa, exquisitis sitis insimulabatur criminibus læsæ Majestatis, & magicarum artium, ac etiam cædis cujusdam Proüille: Ex his morti addicitur: Cumque uterum gestare se proclamasset, obstetricum brevi examine præmisso (quod nudum sine re prætextum arguissent) jubetur collum lictori porrigere: Ausa etiam tunc sub umbra collimantis in cervicem gladii, ad districtum Dei tribunal, judicem suum citare: Truncus ad extremum, & caput infelicis Marchionissæ, flammis data.
units.tr: to usurp authority for himself and enrol soldiers, to alienate the untried mind of the King from the nobles and in turn to stir those nobles against their own Prince, and finally to join luxury to the highest pitch of hatred, squandering three hundred thousand gold pieces and more in a single night on dice and feasting. Although he was often accused of these crimes before the King by the great lords, who raged with jealousy at a man who was a foreigner and a newcomer, however good he might be, he nonetheless knew that his shrewd and lively wit could wipe away those charges by splendid displays of devotion to his King. But as his enemies grew stronger and the hatred against him increased day by day, they say the King at last felt that he was not safe even from his own head, given the plots of this restless man. Therefore he ordered Vitry, the captain of his guards, to bring the Marquis d'Ancre before him, alive or dead; it made no difference. Not long afterwards the said Marquis, ignorant of the fate hanging over him, hastened to Paris to meet the King out of a sense of duty; and when, attended by unusual pomp, he approached the Palace, the great doors were opened wide in his honour. But soon, in the inner courtyard, he was pierced by the balls of several muskets from Vitry's soldiers, and fell without a cry or a groan, on 24 May 1617. When the rumour of the killing spread, such was the rejoicing of the people, such the crowd rushing to the Palace, stumbling here and there and falling in heaps as they ran back and forth, that the whole multitude seemed to have gone mad with joy. The King was present, looking down from an upper window on the enthusiasm of his citizens. They raised not festive voices but shouts: Long live the King! The King! And the King was seen to uncover his head out of respect for the people; but that gracious reply, The King thanks you, which he kept ordering his men to repeat, could not be heard amid the huge din and clamour. Meanwhile the Marquis's corpse was dragged into the porter's room; but the next day it was carried out without any funeral display and thrown, face down, with the head struck against the back, into a ditch by the organ at Saint-Germain. But it was soon dug up by the rage of the common people and dragged to the gallows, and after hanging there from its feet for a while, it was burned, and the ashes were scattered into the river. This is a vain and ridiculous cruelty, which attacks masks and gnaws at the remains; it may well deserve pity. The wife of the slain Marquis, Eleonora Dori, was thrown into prison and accused of manifold charges of treason, of magic arts, and also of the murder of a certain Proüille. On these charges she was condemned to death; and when she declared that she was pregnant, a brief examination by midwives was ordered first (which, when they found it to be a bare pretext without substance, showed it to be empty), and she was ordered to offer her neck to the executioner. Even then she dared, under the shadow of the sword aimed at her neck, to summon her judge before the strict tribunal of God. Finally the trunk, and the head of the unhappy Marchioness, were given to the flames.

units.la: Quæstio XXVIII.
units.tr: Question XXVIII.

units.la: An frigidæ plagæ ferociores incolas habeant quàm calidæ?
units.tr: Do cold regions have fiercer inhabitants than warm ones?

units.la: IMmite cælum, & hujus socii labor, nuditas, egestas, ubi conglobatâ incubuêre mole, animos efferant humanum omne exutos & ulcerant: At exulceratos deglubit census, & apparatus Barbarorum Principum, & immanitas, vectigalium omnium ac tributorum inexplebile barathrum: Grassantur interim in populo per fraudes furta, per violentiam rapinę, per famem rabies, per tenebras confusio, membrorum per frigora sideraciones, mutuæ per furorem cædes, reorum per deteriores leges supplicia, & indomita, dum lubuit Tyrannis, spectaculo dumtaxat, taxat, & gratis ludit in humano sanguine. Solum iter Legatorum Belgii, per Moscoviam anno 1616. institutum, sufficiet huic confirmandæ Sententiæ. Rem Belgico stylo describit Antonius Goeterus, qui & ipse in eorum comitatu aderat. Cùm, ait, Novogroodtæ in castro versamur, & emendi gratiâ sæpiùs in civitatem excurrimus, luctuosum memoratu, qualia per plateas passim se ingerrent spectacula: Hic hominum conglaciata cadavera, & stipitum instar indurata funestabant publicum: Illic mutuis brachiis implicìti, discurrebant cum uxoribus & infantibus viri, pannosi omnes, aut nudi verius inter sævissima frigora, fame tabidi, stipem & opem aliquam tam miserabili ejulatu implorantes, ut ferrea etiam suorum civium corda emollire potuissent, si tantum fuissent ferrea: Ast illi frustum panis, juglandis magnitudne interdum porrigebant: Currebant porrò miseri, unicum hoc domando frigori solatium nacti, donec moribundi concidèrent; Etiam tunc neglecti: & inter irrita lamenta exhalabant animam in publico conspectu: Circuibant manè, qui sparsa cadavera in feretrum accumulabant, & in domum aliquam comportabant: Inde statis temporibus, integræ per plaustra strues efferebantur, in puteos extra civitatem ad hoc effosos. Et subdit idem Gœterus: Hieme istâ, quâ nostri legatione funguntur, atroci isto mortis genere absumpta sunt octodecim millia hominum, in sola civitate Novogroodtensi: Quid in pagis? Deus bone! Sepulta per octiduum cadavera, rursum in nefandas epulas exhumata:
units.tr: A harsh sky, and its companion labour, nakedness and want, when they settle on people in a compact mass, brutalise their spirits, strip them of all humanity and wound them. The wounded are then flayed by the wealth and display of barbarian princes, and by their savagery, the insatiable abyss of every tax and tribute. Meanwhile there rage among the people: through fraud, theft; through violence, robbery; through famine, frenzy; through darkness, confusion; in the limbs, frostbite from the cold; among one another, slaughter from fury; among the condemned, punishments under harsher laws. And tyranny, unbridled whenever it pleases, plays with human blood merely for the spectacle, for a price, and for nothing. The journey of the Dutch envoys through Muscovy, undertaken in 1616, will suffice to confirm this opinion. Antonius Goeterus describes the matter in Dutch style; he was himself in their company. "When," he says, "we were staying in the castle at Novgorod and often went out into the town to buy things, it is sad to recall what sights presented themselves everywhere in the streets. Here frozen corpses of men, hardened like stakes, defiled the public square. There husbands, linked arm in arm with their wives and infants, ran about, all in rags, or rather naked amid the most savage cold, wasted with hunger, begging for alms and some help with such a pitiful wailing that they could have softened even the iron hearts of their fellow citizens, if only those hearts had been iron. But those people offered a morsel of bread, sometimes the size of a walnut. The wretches ran on, having found this single consolation against the cold, until they collapsed dying. Even then they were neglected, and amid useless laments they breathed out their souls in full public view. Each morning men went round gathering the scattered corpses onto a bier and carrying them into some house. Then at fixed times whole piles were carried off on wagons to pits dug for this purpose outside the city." And Goeterus adds: "In this winter, during which we are engaged on our embassy, eighteen thousand people were carried off by this dreadful kind of death in the city of Novgorod alone. What of the villages? Good God! Corpses buried for eight days were dug up again for unspeakable feasts:

units.la: Quest. mata: mactantes invicem, & devorantes homines:imò viscera sua, in viscera sua regerentes matres: Quæ cursim transeo,enecant enim immorantem:Cuncta interim hæc iisdem Legatis, per Starram Russam iter suum prosequentibus, tum oculis, tum fide dignis testibus comperta. Pergit porrò Gœterus, & aliam tragœdiam adjungit: Irrepserant, inquit, Novogroodtæ in culinam nostram tres Russi juvenes, qui coquo spe micarum ministrabant: Horum unus cum infirmari cæpisset, noćte quadam ab aliis duobus in focum conjectus est: Invidiâ scilicet, quod offæ inter tres partitæ,minor portio veniret ad singulos: Postridie semitoftum cadaver, cum nidore in licibus repertum: quod hospes, nihil casu consternatus,forcipibus detulit in sterquilinium. Sed quod ibiibidem de Basilio Moscovitarum Imperatore, ex eorundem relatione subdit, quàm horrendum! Hic Basilius anno 1569. cum esset Novogroodtæ, ex ponte quo fluvius Wolgada instratus est, dejecit in profluentem mille septingentos cives, & multos insuper monachos & sacerdotes: nullâ nisi spectaculi caussâ: pastus natantium confusione, & cum fluctibus ac morte luctâ: Cumque post alios, prædivitem quemdam mercatorem, fune ad lumbos accinctum, in flumen demisisset, & immergi crebrò ac vicissim extrahi jussisset: tandem restituto in pontem homine, petiit per ludibrium: Si miri quiddam in fluvio speculatus fuisset (otium etenim habuerat) enarraret: Ego verò, inquit mercator, per fluvium & fundum fluvii, in Infernum & Gehennam usq; prospexi, pexi: & vidi ardens inter picem & sulphura, quod te manet, Solium Tyranne: Ast ego, inquit Basilius, tibi, cui faceto etiamnum esse non piget, de calidiore balneo prospiciam, ubi commodiùs, quàm in frigida, lasci-vias & argutère.: Et protinus virum corripiens, ac in lebetem olei conjectum, admoto sensim igne lixavit.
units.tr: killing one another and devouring men; indeed mothers feeding their own entrails back into their own entrails. These things I pass over quickly, for they kill whoever lingers. Meanwhile all of this was ascertained by the same envoys, who pursued their journey through Staraya Russa, by their own eyes and by trustworthy witnesses." Goeterus goes on and adds another tragedy: "Three young Russians, who served our cook in hope of scraps, had crept into our kitchen at Novgorod. When one of them began to fall ill, one night the other two threw him into the fire, out of jealousy, because a morsel divided among three meant a smaller portion for each. Next day a half-roasted corpse was found in the pots with the broth, and our host, not at all dismayed by the chance, carried it out with tongs to the dung heap." But what the same writer adds, on the report of the same people, about Basil, Emperor of the Muscovites, is no less horrible! This Basil, in 1569, when he was at Novgorod, threw 1,700 citizens from the bridge across which the river Volkhov is spanned into the stream, along with many monks and priests besides, for no cause but the spectacle, feeding on the struggle of the swimmers with the waves and with death. When, after the others, he had lowered a very rich merchant, girt at the loins with a rope, into the river and ordered him to be dipped again and again and drawn out in turn, he finally had the man restored to the bridge and asked him in mockery whether he had seen anything marvellous in the river (for he had leisure) and would tell him. "But I," said the merchant, "looked through the river and the bed of the river, down into Hell and Gehenna, and I saw burning amid pitch and sulphur what awaits you, Tyrant, on your throne." "But I," said Basil, "will provide for you, who are still not ashamed to be witty, a place in a warmer bath, where you can more conveniently indulge your wanton and clever talk than in cold water." And at once seizing the man, he threw him into a cauldron of oil and boiled him over a fire gently applied.

units.la: ORATIO DE REMOVENDIS PARERGIS ET NITORE CONCILIANDO DISCIPLINIS.
units.tr: ORATION ON REMOVING SIDE-ISSUES AND ON WINNING OVER THE DISCIPLINES TO BRIGHTNESS.

units.la: Quam dixit Lugduni Batav., cum Lectiones publicas in Logicam auspicaretur.
units.tr: Delivered at Leiden, when he began his public lectures on Logic.

units.la: Nitor & intaminata puritas, Charitum prima gratia est: hic Achelojus ille fons est, quo illæ lavantur: Sordent Gratiæ sine hac gratia. Ornatus cum Nitore non est quod se conferat: Ante omnem comparationem, primas ei debet: Nitor ingenuus est, & sui juris; Ornatus servit, & fingit refingitque se ad mores ac rumores: Illi nativa venustas est; huic varie conquisita, & velut ostiatim emendicata lenocinia: Diffluit hic, totus in pompis, in bullis, in calamistris & phaleris; continet ille, & rejectis omnibus supervacaneis, redigit se intra gyrum necessarii & decori: Hic lascivit; ille viget: Hic adulteratus; ille genuinus: Hic effæminatus; ille totus masculus est: Hic nimis habet; ille satis: Hic redundat; ille sufficit. Sentio equidem mihi Belgæ, ad vos Belgas dicenti, promptum & facile Nitoris encomium esse. Mundus quidem est ipsum Belgium, si à munditia, quod volunt, Mun-
units.tr: Brightness and unstained purity are the first of the Graces' gifts. This is the Achelous spring in which they bathe, and without this grace the Graces are squalid. Ornament cannot be compared with brightness; before any comparison, it must give brightness the first place. Brightness is free-born and answerable to no one. Ornament is a servant, shaping and reshaping itself to fashions and gossip. Brightness has a natural charm; ornament has charms sought out with effort and begged from door to door. Ornament pours itself out in display, in frills, in curling-irons and trappings. Brightness restrains itself and, rejecting all that is superfluous, keeps itself within the bounds of what is necessary and seemly. Ornament wantons; brightness flourishes. Ornament is adulterated; brightness is genuine. Ornament is effeminate; brightness is wholly manly. Ornament has too much; brightness has enough. Ornament overflows; brightness suffices. I feel, indeed, that when I speak to you Belgians, a ready and easy eulogy of brightness lies to hand. Belgium itself is clean, if it is called "clean" from cleanliness, as they would have it, Mun-

units.la: Note: the catchword "Mun-" is at the foot of the page, below the last line.
