units.la: Mundus dicitur: ita hic nitorem spirant, ad amussim, & affabrè se habent omnia: Nitor in ædium structuris, nitor in stratis platea-rum, in vallorum & portarum munimentis, in pomœriorum hortis, in aquæ ductibus, in na-vigiorum apparatu: Nitor in mec-hanicis instrumentis, nitor in do-mestica supellectile, nitor in vesti-bus, nitor in ipsis hominum cor-poribus: Et candor in animis nostris, quotquot non degenera-vimus, o Belgæ! Hîc à domorum reductis angulis, hîc à reconditis sub terra caveis, hîc ab editis sub tecti fastigio tabulatis, ab horreis, ab ipsis haris, à pecorum caulis & stabulis fimus, strigmenta, suli-gines, araneæ, mucor, uligo, & denique quidquid in sordium fa-milia est, studiosè discutitur, au-sterè proscribitur: Repetitis lava-cris, cris, indefessis setarum, scoparum, peniculorumque detersionibus, pellucent in fenestris vitra, relucent in lacunaribus robora, in pavimentis marmora, in parietibus dolata quercuum, in picturis ebena marginum, æs in pessulis, in seris chalybs: Verbo dicam: Nitor natales suos debet Belgio: Alibi subinde peregrinatur; hoc ei patria est, hîc sedem fixit, hîc habitat. Sed si Nitor, quocum Belgis tanta necessitudo, quorum animos totus incessit, quibus jam, quod dici solet, in succum & in sanguinem abivit: Si, inquam, formosus ille Nitor exularet à Scholis? (Scholas non intelligo, sicut vulgus, parietes aliquos, aut pluteos, aut cathedras, aut subsellia; sed tenorem docendi, methodum tradendi Scientias, castam cum Musis nostris consuetudinem illo nomine defigdesigno)Nonne indignum hoc foret, si domi quidem limpidi, foris nitidi; volutaremur autem in Schola? Huc centones conferremus,& farragines, &
units.tr: clean it is called. So here they breathe brightness, and everything is done with precision and skill. There is brightness in the building of houses, brightness in the paving of streets, in the fortifications of ramparts and gates, in the gardens within the city walls, in the water conduits, and in the fitting out of ships. There is brightness in mechanical instruments, brightness in household furnishings, brightness in clothing, brightness in the very bodies of people, and candour in our minds, all of us who have not degenerated, O Belgians! Here, from the recessed corners of houses, here from the storage vaults beneath the ground, here from the floors raised beneath the roof-ridge, from the granaries, from the very farmyards, from the sheepfolds and stalls of the cattle, dung, scrapings, filth, cobwebs, mould, damp, and in short whatever belongs to the whole family of dirt, is carefully searched out and sternly banished. With repeated washings and tireless scrubbings with bristles, brooms and mops, the glass in the windows shines, the oak in the ceilings gleams, the floors are marble, the walls are planed oak, the ebony frames the pictures, bronze is on the bolts and steel on the locks. In a word, brightness owes its birth to Belgium. Elsewhere it travels now and then; here is its homeland, here it has fixed its seat, here it dwells. But if brightness, with which the Belgians have so close a bond, which has taken hold of all their minds, and which, as the saying goes, has passed into their juice and blood, if, I say, that lovely brightness were exiled from the schools? (I do not mean by "schools", as the common people do, certain walls, or desks, or chairs, or benches, but the manner of teaching, the method of handing on the sciences, and the chaste practice of our Muses, which I designate by that name.) Would it not be shameful if we were clean at home and bright abroad, but wallowed in the school? We would bring here patchwork and hotchpotch, and

units.la: ——— Crispini scrinia lippi?
units.tr: ——— the chests of bleary-eyed Crispinus?

units.la: Rem ita se habere, non ajo, non nego; sed tantùm, si ita se haberet, quam iniquum hoc foret, perpendo: Et sanè hujus turpitudinis vel solam suspicionem, si quæ esset, nonne deceret Belgas tam amantes elegantiæ, tam nitoris cupidos, omni conatu, summis viribus à se quantocyus amoliri? Existimemus verò rem non ita se habere; occurrere tamen & cavere licet, & excludere tempestivè,quod nondum irrepsit. Ego igitur limum illum, illud cœnum designabo, quod imperitâ si fortè manu commotum fuerit, fundo absistat, & sacra Hippocrenes fluenta, colluvioluvione sua conspurcet: Ut si fieri potest, maturè subducatur ex alveo; sin minus, & fundo quandoque se tollet, subsidere sensim sinamus, ne turbato fonte potemus avidam & Scientiæ sitibundam juventutem. Hæc, cum paucis exsequor & cursim perstringo, tum id obnixè deprecor, quæ communiter dico, ne sic accipiatis, quasi in Cajum aut Sejum dicta sint: Indole sum alienissimus à faciendo conuicio: tum etiam particulatim ignarus, ut qui me nunquam interponam rei ad me non pertinenti.
units.tr: I do not say, and I do not deny, that things are so; I only weigh how unfair it would be if they were. And indeed, should even the mere suspicion of this disgrace exist, would it not behoove Belgians, who love elegance so much and desire brightness so much, to remove it from themselves as quickly as possible, with every effort and all their strength? Let us, however, suppose that things are not so; still, it is allowed to meet and guard against it, and to exclude in time what has not yet crept in. I therefore point out that mud, that filth, which, if it is stirred up by an unskilled hand, will rise from the bottom and pollute the sacred streams of Hippocrene with its muck. So, if it can be done, let it be drawn out of the channel early; but if not, and it rises at some point from the bottom, let us not allow it to settle back down, lest with the water stirred up we poison eager youth thirsting for knowledge. I set this out briefly and touch on it hastily, and I earnestly beg that what I say in general terms not be taken as if said against Gaius or Seius. By disposition I am most averse to abusing anyone, and I am also personally ignorant of particulars, since I never insert myself into a matter that does not concern me.

units.la: Parergon illud, illuviem, inquam, Scientiarum nitidas lymphas inquinantem, eructant hæ quatuor potissimùm Cloacæ, PROLOGUS, PROGNOSIS, RHAPSODIA, & ANOMALIA. Ad PROLOGUM spectant étant Quæstiones, ut vocant, Proœ-miales, prolixæ illæ, centum ar-gumentationibus, earumque rur-sum refutationibus, centum plicis ac replicis exaggeratæ, quibus antequam datâ operâ Scientiam aliquam tractent, de ipsa illa Scien-tia diffusè tractant: Et ut uno velut exemplo complectar omnia, Logicam tradituri, quærunt, quid sit Logica, An sit pars Philosophiæ, an Instrumentum, An sit Ars, an Scientia, Quid Logica docens, quid utens, Quid naturalis, quid artificialis, Quod objectum ejus, quis finis, An ad alias Scientias adipiscendas sit necessaria, In quot partes ac tractatus dispesci debeat, & id genus alia quamplurima. Quidàm adhuc altius rem ab exordio repetunt: Et Logicam (ut in eodem exemplo persistamus) tractaturi, non tantùm de Logica tractant, sed universerverfim de Philosophia: transcribentes huc Nani & Langii, & nescio cujus adhuc similis convafatoris integras Polyantheas. Inepta sunt hæc, quod vel me tacente, res ipsa loquitur : Quid enim ? quæris quid sit, quod ipse traditurus es? Eja trade, & videbimus: Nunquam melius hoc docebis, quam tradendo: Quæris num sit Scientia, quam traditurus es? Id tu videris: Si enim bonâ & rectâ ratione subnixum est, quod disseris, certè Scientiam præstabit tua dissertatio;Si vero conjecturas tantum accumules & harioleris, si controverseris tantum, & argumentorum laqueos vicissim nectas ac solvas, si quod aliorum testimonio cæcus imbibisti, rursum tuo testimonio propines, scrupulos, opiniones, confusiones, imposturas, & quidvis potius quam Scientiam tiam conferet tractatio tua: Sed quid opus est ea te disceptando præfari? Age quod agis, dic quod dicendum habes, & litem istam satis dirimet eventus. Quod si tamen disputatio illa non de tuo sit instituta discursu, nec quæras quis aut qualis ille sit; sed quem & qualem res, quæ præ manibus est, vel admittat, vel deposcat, hanc fateor ex genere suo non esse supervacuam disquisitionem; quin potius utilem in Prologo, velut legem aliquam operi subsequenti, quam cum ipse præscripseris, æquum est ut rigidè serves; Sed arctandam illam disquisitionem, cum ibi non sit proprius locus ejus, & obiter habendam esse contendo: Siquidem alterius longè naturæ est, & spectat ad Disciplinas toto cælo diversas, Scientiam aliquam tractare, & de Scientia illa tractare: re : Logicus aliquis aut Physicus tractatus, ad Logicam pariter aut Physicam pertinet: Sed quæ sunt de Logica vel Physica Disputationes, non his Scientiis, sed Metaphysicæ, aut, quod malo, Disciplinæ cuidam, cui nomen non est, quæque de ipsis Disciplinis agit, debentur: Sed & hisce legibus circumscriptam ac ita contractam Præfationem, in libris quidem perito & exercitato Lectori facile crediderim; sed eâ rudem in Scholis Discipulum non interturbem: Non distraham in sublime, demissum & etiamnum fundamenta molientem: Non raptem in penetralia, laborantem adhuc in vestibulo: Non distineam Metaphysicâ subtilitate, Logica rudimenta requirentem: Discat hic Logicam per partes, etiam ignarus, quid sit Logica: Quid illa præpræstet, & quorsum tendat, quis eam inter & alias Artes ordo, quod commercium, quæ necessi-tudo, hæc & his quæcumque si-milia, tyro quilibet tutus ignorat.
units.tr: Those four cesspits chiefly belch out that side-issue, I say, which pollutes the bright waters of the sciences: PROLOGUE, PROGNOSIS, RHAPSODY, and ANOMALY. To the PROLOGUE belong what they call Quæstiones, Proœmiales, those lengthy questions, elaborated with a hundred arguments and their refutations in turn, a hundred plicæ and replicæ, with which, before they deliberately take up any science, they discuss at length that very science. And to sum up all of them in a single example: when they are about to teach Logic, they ask what Logic is, whether it is part of philosophy, or an instrument, whether it is an art, whether it is a science, what Logic is when teaching, what when used, what is natural, what is artificial, what is its object, what is its end, whether it is necessary for acquiring other sciences, into how many parts and treatises it ought to be divided, and very many other things of this kind. Some go back even further, to the beginning of the matter. And when they are going to treat Logic (to keep to the same example), they treat not only Logic but, in a word, philosophy in general, copying here whole polyanthea of Nanus and Langius and of I know not what other similar compiler. These things are silly, and even without my speaking, the matter itself makes this clear. For what? Do you ask what it is that you yourself are about to teach? Come on, teach it, and we shall see. You will never show this better than by teaching it. Do you ask whether it is a science that you are about to teach? That is for you to see. For if what you set forth rests on sound and right reasoning, your discourse will certainly produce a science. But if you merely pile up conjectures and dabble, if you only dispute, and by turns tie and untie the snares of arguments, if what you have blindly soaked up from others' testimony you again pass on on your own testimony, your treatment will produce doubts, opinions, confusions, deceptions, and anything rather than science. But why is there any need to preface things with such disputation? Get on with what you are doing; say what you have to say, and the outcome will settle the quarrel well enough. Yet if that discussion has not been undertaken as part of your own argument, and one does not ask who or of what sort that person is, but what sort of person the subject at hand either admits or demands, I admit that this is by its nature not a superfluous inquiry. Indeed it is useful in a Prologue, as a kind of law for the work that follows; once you have prescribed it yourself, it is only fair that you keep it strictly. But I maintain that such an inquiry, when there is no proper place for it there, should be confined and treated in passing. For it is of a wholly different nature, and belongs to disciplines utterly different from one another, to treat a science and to treat of that science. A Logical or Physical treatise belongs equally to Logic or Physics. But disputations about Logic or Physics are owed not to these sciences but to Metaphysics, or, as I prefer to say, to some discipline without a name, which deals with the disciplines themselves. Yet I could easily believe that a Preface so bounded and so contracted by these rules is fitting in books for a learned and practised reader; but I would not disturb a beginner in the schools with it. I will not drag him aloft while he is still laying his foundations low down; I will not snatch him into the inner sanctuary while he is still struggling in the entrance hall; I will not distract with metaphysical subtlety a student who still needs the rudiments of Logic. Let him learn Logic part by part, even though he does not yet know what Logic is. What it is good for, and where it tends, what order it holds among the other arts, what dealings and what bond it has with them, and whatever else is similar to these things, any novice may safely remain ignorant of.

units.la: Hæc de Prologo: Proxi-ma Sentina Prognosis est: Nam amplis illis, quos commemoravi Prologis, tum ipsi, qui docent, dilassati ac ferè viribus defecti, tum confusione perditum, & enectum ipsius rei, quæ semper differtur, exspectatione Discipulum, deducunt ad Præcognita, ut passim vocant: Et hic iterum gurges, & iterum obruuntur: Nam fortè in Logica, quod eâ Mentem in operationibus suis dirigi demonstraverint in Prologo, non dubitabunt ab ipsa Mente tractationem suam auspicari: De intellectu ejusque caussis ac origine, ejus operaperationibus & effectis, ejus, cum à voluntate, tum à sensibus distinctione, fusa,confusa commini-scentes : Ita præoccupantibus omnia,&in caput ac primam partem suorum commentariorū attrahentibus,præter jejuna quædam & rancida, vix suppetit in progressu, quod dicant, tamquam exhausti jam & marcidi : Edentes profecto fungis quibusdā quam simillimos tractatus : Quibus amplus quidem pro capite bulbus obtigit; cæterum exiguus caudex & nulla radix.
units.tr: This is what I have to say about the Prologue. The next sink is the Prognosis. The authors of those large prologues I mentioned, worn out and almost exhausted, lead the student, who is left confused and worn down by waiting for the subject itself, which is always postponed, on to what they commonly call the Præcognita. Here again the student is swallowed up, and again overwhelmed. Having shown in the Prologue that logic directs the mind in its operations, they do not hesitate to begin their treatment with the mind itself. They invent long, rambling discussions of the intellect, its causes and origin, its operations and effects, and its distinction from both the will and the senses. Since they have used up everything at the start and at the head of their commentaries, little is left for the body of the work except some dry and stale material, and they have nothing more to say, as though already drained and withered. Clearly they are producing treatises very like mushrooms: they have a large bulb for a head, but a thin stalk and no root.

units.la: Quidam, ut id incommodi devitent, infestant tertiam Cloacam, ad Rhapsodias, inquam, se conferunt, & ex his affatim hauriunt, quo res suas, alioqui tenues & exiles infarciant. Hi pro re nata, varias Historias narrant, lepidas Fabellas admiscent, Versus etiam sæpe citant è Poë-
units.tr: Some, to avoid this inconvenience, invade the third sink and turn to the Rhapsodies, I mean, and draw from them freely, so that they can stuff out their own thin and meagre matter. As the occasion arises, these writers tell various stories, mix in pleasant little fables, and often quote verses from

units.la: Poëtarum aliquo, & Sententias ex Oratoribus, intertexunt & Adagia: Ubicumque, etiam ex rebus levissimis captant occasionem hæc in medium producendi: Imo non sumunt occasionem ex rebus, sed adferunt: Verbi gratia, in Logica de-Individuo forte agentes, in Exemplum adducent Alexandrum & Bucephalum, quasi Petrus & Paulus, qui ad pedes eorum assident, illi muneri obeundo non sint pares: Et mox (quasi reseratâ jam in RHAPSODIAM fenestrâ) hic, inquiunt, est ille Alexander Philippi, qui tot Persarum exercitus delevit, & totum Orientem suo subjugavit imperio: Bucephalus autem est equus ferocissimus, quem ille puer etiamnum domuit, quo facto Philippus ei, præsagiendo spoponderat Orbis imperium: Atque ita passim corradunt ex Veterum rum Annalibus, imo etiam ex Sacris Paginis, & ex cunctis angulis Exempla: quasi in summa penuria; cum tamen eorum plena sint fora, & quotidie versentur ante omnium ora manusque. Alii ex eadem RHAPSODORUM familia, citandis Auctoribus, præsertim veteribus (quod illis obsoleti plus inesse credant) gnaviter incumbunt: Et quid Zeno, quid Leucippus dixerit, quid contra Parmenides & Melissus censuerint, quid Pythagoras & Empedocles, quid Democritus & Epicurus statuerint, imo statuere debuerint, multis exponunt: His Auctoribus, velut in Theatrum quoddam & Proscenium accitis, tum verò Versibus & Adagiis Fabula peragitur: Nam Zeno rem acu tetigit: & Leucippus in Sententiam ejus manibus pedibusque concessit: Parmenides &
units.tr: some poet, and weave in sayings from the orators and proverbs. Wherever they can, they seize any occasion, even from the most trivial matters, to bring these things forward. Indeed they do not take their occasion from the matter at hand but bring it in from outside. For example, when they are discussing the Individual in logic, they will cite Alexander and Bucephalus, as though Peter and Paul, who sit at their feet, were not equal to the task. Then, as if the window of the RHAPSODY had now been thrown open, they say: this is that Alexander, son of Philip, who destroyed so many Persian armies, and subjected the whole East to his empire. Bucephalus, they add, is a most fiery horse, which that boy tamed while still a child, and by this deed Philip, foreseeing it, had promised him dominion over the world. And so they gather examples everywhere, from the annals of the ancients, indeed even from the Sacred Pages, and from every corner, as though in great want, when in fact the forums are full of such things and they are talked about daily before everyone's eyes and hands. Others of the same family of RHAPSODISTS apply themselves vigorously to citing authors, especially the ancient ones, because they believe that obsolete authors have more weight. They set out at length what Zeno said, what Leucippus said, what Parmenides and Melissus held in opposition, what Pythagoras and Empedocles thought, what Democritus and Epicurus laid down, or rather ought to have laid down. With these authors brought on as if to a kind of stage and proscenium, the play is then carried on with verses and proverbs. For Zeno hit the nail exactly on the head, and Leucippus gave way to his opinion with hands and feet. Parmenides and

units.la: Melissus extra chorum saltant: Epicurus!
units.tr: Melissus dance outside the chorus. Epicurus!

units.la: Spectatum admissi, risum teneatis amici:
units.tr: You were admitted as spectators, friends; keep your laughter in check.

units.la: Et tandem Aristoteles Solus habet mentem, reliquis errantibus umbris:
units.tr: And at last Aristotle: He alone has a mind; the rest are wandering shadows.

units.la: Affingunt iis Sententias, quas nunquam senserunt, de quibus fortè ne per somnium quidem cogitaverunt: Si monstrari tibi petas, ubi tandem, ubi Veteres illa dixerint, Respondent, quod res est, Eorum plerorumque commentarios, injuriâ temporis intercidisse: ut nempe vel hoc solo indicio clarè intelligas, totum hoc fermè commentum, imaginariis eorum conjecturis deberi.
units.tr: They attribute to these men opinions they never held, about which they perhaps never even dreamed. If you ask them where, where the ancients said those things, they answer, as is the case, that most of their commentaries have perished through the injury of time. So that you may clearly understand, from this sign alone, that almost this whole fiction is owed to their own imaginary conjectures.

units.la: Restat ANOMALIA, congeries immensa sordium: Augiæ stabulum dixeris: & Herculeus profectò labor est illud expurgare: gare : Ita profundè subsîdit, & per cuniculos in purissima quæ-que surrepit illa colluvio : A N O-MALIAM in Scientiis voco, cum Objectum uni, & tractandi modus alteri cuidam Disciplinæ accom-modatus est : ut si res Logicas Physicè, aut Physicas Logicè con-templemur. Plerumque, qui in hac Sentina volutantur, Objectum ex quavis Disciplina nacti, mo-dum tractandi mutuantur ex Grammatica & Metaphysica: quod hæ duæ Disciplinæ generales sint, & omnium quodammo-do, Metaphysica quidem rerum; Grammatica verò nominum: Ex Grammatica hos præcipuè Typos desumunt: Etymologiam, Conjugationem, Homonymiam, Synonymiam; Ex Metaphysica Causas, Effecta, Genus, Species, Conspecies, Subjecta, Adjuncta &c. Penes has NorNormas expendunt, quidquid inciderit, cujusvis illud naturæ, & ad quamcumque pertineat Disciplinam: Verbi gratia de Argumentis acturi (lubens enim Exemplis Logicis insisto, quod in his invidiæ minus sit) Argumentum, inquiunt, ab arguendo dicitur, quod est alterius dicta refellere & rationibus allegatis confutare: Alii (etiamsi forte nemo alius hoc dixerit) Etymon istius nominis deducunt, ab Ergo, quod est præcipua pars & velut anima quædam Argumenti. Ubi dicendo exhaustum est, quidquid Etymologiæ lacuna continebat, conferunt se ad secundum Typum, nempe ad Conjugationem: Argumentatur, inquiunt, is qui alterum Argumentis aggreditur, ut Thesim ab eo propositam evertat, eique Respondens seu Defendens opponitur: Atque ibi, si modo velint, ingens excursus de antiquis ac hodiernis Disputantium ritibus se pindit. Ubi jam etiam exaruit ista vena, Synonymiam consulunt: Argumentum, inquiunt, etiam Argumentatio dicitur, item Ratiocinatio, à Ratione, quæ in ea maxime conspicua est; Græcè vero Syllogismus dici potest, de quo Aristoteles tam multa scripsit, & inter cetera præclaram scilicet illam Definitionem: Syllogismus est oratio, in qua quibusdam positis, aliud quid à positis, præter ea quæ posita sunt, necessariò sequitur: Nunquid appositè? Ubi etiam ex hoc penu, quidquid suppetebat, depromptum est, convertunt se ad Homonymiam: Argumentum, inquiunt, subinde etiam dicitur de Indicio: Ut cum Seneca dicit, Primum Argumentum bene compositæ mentis existimo posse subsistere & secum morari: rari:ibi Argumentum idem est ac Indicium: Argumentum subinde etiam capitur pro Materia scribendi vel dicendi, &c. apud Calepinum. His tandem, quæ Grammatica suggerebat, belle defuncti, reliquum est, ut Metaphysicas considerationes eâdem aviditate depascantur: & primùm quidem de Caussis Argumenti despiciant: Efficiens & Prima Caussa Argumenti, inquiunt, Deus est: & quamvis ille Argumentum efficiat, non dicitur tamen argumentari: Atque ibi ingeritur Locus ex Theologia, cur Deus non argumentetur: cui scitè subnectent, ubi & quomodo Christus aliquando fuerit argumentatus: Caussa secunda Argumenti est homo, qui Argumentum animo concipit, & ore veluti parit ac in lucem edit: Atque ibi rursum nascitur controversia; an Angeli etiam etiam & Mentes nostræ, dum à corporeis vinculis solutæ sunt, argumententur : Caussa finalis Argumenti. Sed abrumpo : Vereor enim jam dudum, Auditores humanissimi, ne patientiam vestram næniis istis, licet susurratis tantum & summatim propositis, plus æquô fatigem : Antequam sane, reliquos Typos Mimesis mea percurrisset, jam vos per Theologorum arcana Mysteria, per Pandectas Jure Consultorum, per Medicorum Aphorismos, Astrologorum Horoscopos, Chymicorum Chrysulcas, Poëtarum Fabulas, Annalium Historias, ac nescio per quas non ambages, & in se subinde recurrentes Labyrinthos circumduxissem : Horas & diem absumpsissem capitibus materiæ duntaxat enarrandis, ne dixerim, pertractandis, & ea, quam imp immensa rerum multitudo postulat, oratione deducendis. O miscella rerum! ô confusio! Hæc, quæ in Argumentationem tam prolixa, tam ultro citroque conquisita commentus es, ANOMALE, cui bono sunt? si quis illa studiose pervolverit, quid inde reportabit emolumenti? promptior erit ad Argumentandum qui ista sciverit, hebetior qui nesciverit? Ratio dictat & suffragatur Experientia, obesse quidem illa sæpe, ut quæ distrahant, quæ sensum obtundant & mentem obruant; prodesse nunquam: Quid enim? Nos, qui venam illam tuam exploravimus, ANOMALE, nos qui illud tuum Cornucopiæ deteximus, putasne tam abjectè de te sentire, ut Argumento cuiquam imparem te esse suspicemur? Dices si voles de gerris & lyris,
units.tr: What remains is ANOMALY, a huge heap of filth. You might call it the stable of Augeas, and cleaning it out is truly a labour worthy of Hercules. It sinks so deeply and creeps through underground channels into the purest things, this filthy flood. I call it ANOMALY in the sciences when the Object belongs to one discipline and the mode of treatment to another, as when we consider logical matters physically, or physical matters logically. Most of those who wallow in this sink, having got hold of an Object from some discipline, borrow their mode of treatment from grammar and metaphysics, because these two disciplines are general and in a sense belong to all: metaphysics to things, grammar to words. From grammar they chiefly take these types: Etymology, Conjugation, Homonymy, Synonymy. From metaphysics: Causes, Effects, Genus, Species, Subspecies, Subjects, Adjuncts, etc. By these norms they weigh whatever comes up, whatever its nature and whatever discipline it belongs to. For example, when they are going to treat of Arguments (I gladly dwell on logical examples, since they arouse less ill will), they say: Argument is derived from arguing, which means refuting another's assertions and confuting them by alleged reasons. Others (though perhaps no one else has said this) derive the etymology of this word from ergo, which is the chief part and, as it were, the soul of an argument. When they have exhausted everything that the gap in etymology contained, they turn to the second type, namely conjugation: he who attacks another with arguments, they say, in order to overturn the thesis put forward by him, is said to argue; and he is opposed to him as the respondent or defender. And there, if they like, they pour out a vast digression on the ancient and modern customs of disputants. When this vein too has run dry, they consult synonymy: Argument, they say, is also called argumentation, also reasoning, from reason, which is most conspicuous in it; in Greek it can be called syllogism, on which Aristotle wrote so much, and among other things that famous definition: a syllogism is a discourse in which, certain things being laid down, something other than these follows of necessity. Is that not apt? When they have drawn out of this storehouse whatever was available, they turn to homonymy: Argument, they say, is sometimes also used of evidence, as when Seneca says: I think the first argument of a well-ordered mind can stand on its own and abide with itself; there argument means the same as evidence. Argument is sometimes also taken for the matter of writing or speaking, etc., according to Calepinus. Having finished off, with some success, what grammar suggested, they have only to devour metaphysical considerations with the same eagerness. First, they look into the causes of argument: The efficient and first cause of argument, they say, is God; and although he produces arguments, he is not said to argue. And here they bring in a topic from theology: why God does not argue. To this they cleverly add where and how Christ once argued. The second cause of argument is man, who conceives the argument in his mind and, as it were, brings it forth with his mouth and puts it into the light. And here again a controversy arises: whether angels and our minds, when they are released from bodily bonds, also argue. The final cause of argument. But I break off. For I have long feared, most gentle listeners, that I may tire your patience too much with these trifles, though they are only whispered and summarily proposed. Before I had run through the remaining types of my mimesis, I would have led you through the secret mysteries of the theologians, through the Pandects of the jurists, the aphorisms of the physicians, the horoscopes of the astrologers, the gold-making of the chemists, the fables of the poets, the histories of the annals, and I know not through what other endless detours and labyrinths that keep turning back on themselves. I would have spent the hours and the day merely in describing the heads of the matter, not to say treating them, and in setting them out in the discourse that the immense multitude of things demands. O medley of things! O confusion! These things, which you have contrived to bring together into such a long argument, so eagerly sought out from every side, ANOMALY, to what good are they? If someone should diligently read them through, what profit will he gain from them? Will the man who knows these things be readier to argue, and the man who does not know them be duller? Reason dictates, and experience confirms, that these things often do harm, since they distract, dull the sense, and overwhelm the mind; they never help. For what? We who have tested your vein, ANOMALY, we who have uncovered your Cornucopia, do you think we have such a low opinion of you that we suspect you are unequal to any argument? You will say, if you like, about gnats and lyres,

units.la: de luto dices, de quisquiliis, de calceis & caligis: & de quovis horum diffusè dices ac tomis integris: Ars id tua promittit, promittunt illi Typi, quos consuetus aspectas, velut totidem semitas in amplissimos dicendi campos excurrentes; Sed fi de calceis(ut hos duntaxat in Exemplum affumamus ) more tuo scripseris, per Etymologiam, Conjugationem, Homonymiam, Synonymiam, Causas, Effecta, Species & reliquos Typos discurrendo (ut liberrimos hîc discursus offerunt isti Typi) non unum tamen sutorem formet commentatio tua: ipse etiam à lucubratione ista nihil instructior, calceum non conficias, imo ne resarcias quidem, qua parte detritus est aut rimam agit. Vides igitur omissâ totâ aliquâ Difcipli-nâ, de Objecto tamen istius Disci-pliplinæ, diffusissimam institui posse tractationem: adeo ut res Logicæ sine Logica, Physicæ sine Physica, Ethicæ sine Ethica, & ita deinceps, tradi facilè possint & soleant. Qui igitur Scientiam aliquam ritè excolet, is Objectum abstrahat necesse est, & separet ab omni materia, & id modò, quod ex intima illius natura dimanat, amplectatur; cætera tamquam spuria removeat, omnem iis illabendi rimam occludat; tantum abest, ut aucupetur, & intrudat etiam reluctantia; Qui secus fecerit, sciat se in hoc, quod ad Sapientiam est itinere, non progredi; sed vagari, & circuire Delubrum illud Musarum; non adire. Tetrum etiam præ reliquis exhalat hæc Cloaca, & mephitim sub auras spergit: Afflat accolis suis garrulitatem, fastum, & desidiam:
units.tr: of mud you will speak, of trifles, of shoes and boots. And on any of these you will speak at length, in whole volumes. Your art promises this, and so do those Types that you are used to gazing upon, like so many paths running out into the broadest fields of discourse. But if you write about shoes (let us take these alone as an example) in your usual manner, running through Etymology, Conjugation, Homonymy, Synonymy, Causes, Effects, Species and the rest of the Types (which those Types offer for wonderfully free wanderings), your treatise will still not make a single cobbler. You yourself will be no better equipped by that midnight labour: you will not make a shoe, nor even mend one where it is worn or split. You see, then, that with some whole Discipline left out, a very extended treatment can still be made of that Discipline's Object. So it is that the matters of Logic can easily be taught without Logic, those of Physics without Physics, those of Ethics without Ethics, and so on, as such things are easily and commonly taught. Whoever cultivates any Science properly must therefore abstract its Object, separate it from all matter, and embrace only what flows from the inner nature of that Object. Everything else he must cast off as spurious, and close every crack through which it might slip in. He must not so much as go hunting for such things or force them in, even when they resist. Whoever does otherwise should know that he is not advancing on the road that leads to Wisdom, but wandering and circling around the shrine of the Muses, not approaching it. This Cesspool also gives off a fouler stench than the rest, and spreads its mephitic vapour into the air. It breathes garrulousness, arrogance and idleness upon its inhabitants.

units.la: Et esse quidem garrulos hujus stagni colonos necessum est, nam propositâ quacumque materiâ, etiam eâ, quam profundissimè nesciunt, ex Typis tamen illis, quos sibi jugiter præfixos habent, nunquam deest, quod coäxent. Tumidi sunt etiam, & multo spiritu distenti: ut qui persuasum habeant scire se cûncta, de quibus dicunt, & quanto liberalius de illis dicunt, tanto melius scire: Cum vero, & per plurima passim oratione divagentur, & facile perspiciant, nihil esse, in quo tali methodo non possint quam latissimè palari; etiamsi aliam ab ea, qua jam instructi sunt, scientiam sibi non conquirant, huc nullo negotio seducuntur, ut se tamquam omnia mente complexos, & Pandoræ cujusdam aut Deæ Copiæ gratiosos sponsos circumspiciant ac mirentur; Cæteros autem, quos sæpe non latet quidem ars eorum, sed pudet artis eorum, despiciant, velut aridos, siccos, exsangues, & Minervæ (crassæ scilicet illius) turpe repudium. Faštum desidia sequitur: cur enim studeant, qui sibi satis superque docti sunt? cur anxiè quærant, quod consecutos se credunt? quo scandant, quos jam in culmen evexit sua persua-sio? Lexica modò sint ad manum, Indices, Analecta, Polyantheæ, Theatra Mundi, & similes ad omnem pedem facti cothurni: his freti, securè stertunt, & dormiunt, quod dici solet, in utramq; aurem. Quin etiam farragines illas (ita frontem perfricuêre) subinde non verentur palam hoc Titulo notare venditare, Dormi securè: Erubescit ad hoc probrum, Diligentiæ præses Aurora, ejulant antelucana galligallicinia, obmutescunt nocturna conticinia, tam amica Philomusis, tam familiaris societas: Dum interim Anomali Collectaneis illis & Elenchis suis, ceu baculis quibusdam & crucibus axillas subnixi, librant se sat belle, & assultim prodeunt; iisdem forte destituti, haesitant ubique, ubique cespitant, & humi repunt potius, quam gradiuntur deformes Empusæ.
units.tr: The inhabitants of this pool must indeed be garrulous, for whatever subject is set before them, even one they know least about, there is never a shortage of something to chatter about, drawn from those Types which they keep constantly fixed before them. They are also puffed up and swollen with great conceit, as men who are persuaded that they know everything they talk about, and who think that the more freely they talk, the better they know. Since they range about in their speech in countless places, and easily see that there is nothing on which they cannot display themselves at full length by such a method, they are, even without acquiring any other knowledge than the one they already possess, effortlessly led to look around themselves, admiring as if they had grasped everything in their minds, and as favoured suitors of some Pandora or goddess Copia. They despise the others, whose art is often not hidden from them but whose lack of art shames them, as dry, arid, bloodless men, and as the shameful divorce of Minerva (that thick Minerva, of course). Arrogance is followed by idleness: why should they study, who are learned enough and more than enough for themselves? Why anxiously seek what they believe they have already attained? Where should they climb, when their own persuasion has already lifted them to the summit? Let there only be Lexica at hand, Indexes, Analecta, Polyanthea, Theatres of the World, and similar buskins made for every foot. Relying on these, they snore in safety and sleep, as the saying goes, on both ears. Indeed, having rubbed their brows raw, they do not hesitate to advertise those medleys openly under this title: Sleep Securely. Dawn, the president of diligence, blushes at this disgrace; the pre-dawn cockcrows wail, the nocturnal stillness of midnight falls silent, so friendly a company is it to the Muses' lovers, so familiar a fellowship. Meanwhile the Anomali, propped on their collections and Elenchi as on certain crutches and crosses, balance themselves fairly well and advance with mincing steps. Perhaps deprived of these supports, they stumble everywhere and stagger everywhere, and crawl on the ground rather than walk, like deformed Empusae.

units.la: Hisce PROLOGIS & PRÆ-NOTIONIBUS, hisce RHAP-SODIIS & ANOMALIIS, cum omnes propè Disciplinæ foedum in modum inquinatæ sint, tum vel maximè Logices contemeratus est decor & polluta gratia: Purissimus ille latex versus est in obscoenam paludem, unde jugiter in alias Scientias restagnent Parerga, & ANOMALORUM RHAPSODORUMQUE recremen-ta: Sita: Siquidem in Logica nunc, præ-ter Anomaliæ Typos,quos paulo ante commemoravi, nihil ferió tractatur : hi soli præcipuè spectantur ibi, explicantur ibi, inculcantur ibi,& in usum,in habilitatem ac Naturam quodammodo crebris exercitiis deducuntur;Cætera tantum incidunt, tamquam præludia, tamquam antecœnia, & quod eo conferre aliquid, aliquid eam in rem facere quoquo modo videantur. Res igitur in Parergon, Discursus in excursum , Logica in Paralogismum conversa est ; Sed heus erro ! Metamorphosim non patitur illa Forma, Divina est : Et homines quidem in alias formas mutatos, in Poëtis legimus ; non Deos : illud volui dicere, Paralo-gismum ab ignaris coli pro Logica, illum hujus loco suffectum ab incautis ; Logicam illibatâ gratiâ & inconcnssâ majestate discessisse, e-vasisse, subduxisse se ab indignis: Nam quæ splendorem illum præ-focet confusio? quæ nitorem illum polluat impietas? quæ vigorem il-lum lacessat temeritas? qui pari fe-rè cum alma Ratione, qua Deum ipsum referimus ad vivum, digni-tate præpollens, quo supra tumul-tum & injurias efferatur altius, vix habet: Ita est: Divinæ illi Particu-læ tam similis est Logica, ita ma-trissat, tam undiquaque refert & spirat Rationem, ut eodem & no-mine & vultu, non peregrinis modo; sed familiaribus suis sæpius imponant: Qua specie, quidam è Philosophiæ non infimis proceri-bus delusi, & longius, quam par erat, quasi reverentiâ seducti, Lo-gicam à Scholis submovendam esse decreverunt, quod eam cum In-tellectu confundentes, Disciplinâ non opus esse judicarent, ubi doceret Natura ; Sed nempe seducti sunt & errant illi : Quamvis enim Logica suas inter sororesⓢ(reliquas, inquam, Scientias) natu maxima sit, non est tamen ipsa Ratio, sed Rationem ex æquo cum sororibus suis, ut matrem agnoscit: Nec enim Principia tantum (quod Rationis officium est) & Communes Notiones perhibet Logica; sed Theoremata, quæ ex Principiis elicienda sunt legitimâ & catenatâ Demonstratione: Exempli gratia : Quod dicitur de Prædicato, dicitur etiam de Subjecto:Ex quo non sequitur Consequens, ex eo non sequitur Antecedens, &c. non sunt Principia, nec simpliciter sumi possunt; sed probari debent; citra Demonstrationem suspecta sunt; Ea verò sine Demonstratione recipere, quod Exemplis quibusdam confirmari videantur, temetemerarium est & cæcum & infi-nitis erroribus obnoxium : quia sæpe, quod in quamplurimis Ex-emplis obtinet , eo ipso tamen corruit, quod fallat in uno: Et hinc Sapientum Oraculo sanci-tum est, Scire est per Definitionem cognoscere; non vero per Exempla, quæ quotquot numero producan-tur ; quamdiu tamen non constat omnia produci, non figunt men-tem, sed suspendunt, anxiam an a-libi forte non lateat aliquis error. Cum igitur Logica non sit ipsa Ratio; sed partus quidam Ratio-nis , primùm quidem hisce cunis, & cum adoleverit illi gynæceo: Scholis, inquam, & Academiæ de-betur. Nec faciem tantum & exter-na lineamenta Rationis æmulatur Logica; sed multo magis indolem, affectus ac munia: Matris quodam-modo partes circa germanas suas explet hæc soror natu grandior: sinu fovet eas & bajulat in ulnis: Hoc ajo, Scientias omnes Logicis Theorematibus ceu fundamentis suis incumbere: His non probè jactis vacillare, his quassis collabi necesse est, quidquid in reliquis Disciplinis extructum est molis: Hæc Theoremata: Ex vero nil nisi verum, Ex quo Antecedens, ex eo Consequens, & cætera, quæ Cubo Logico à me nuper edito continentur, substrata sunt omnibus Disciplinis: Toti Scientiarum machinæ suppositi arduos humeros Atlantes isti: sine fulcris illis in Scientiis non unus discursus, vix unus passus. Igitur imago Divinitatis est Ratio (hoc ipsa Ratio clamat, hoc in confesso est apud omnes) Imago Rationis est Logica (hoc ne quidem adversarii ejus negant, qui eam ideo Scholis interdixerunt) runt) Quid ad dignitatem præcla-rius, quid ad majestatem sublimius in Logicam dici poterat? Imago enim quodammodo est res illa, quam repræsentat: Imo imago à materia, quam insidet, mente cogitationeque separata, non est jam amplius imago, sed res expressa: Sicuti, si posthabitis lineamentis ac maculis, quas tabulæ penicillus aspersit, totus in rei, quæ ad vivum exhibetur, contemplatione defigare, jam non Artem, sed Artis exemplar, non effigiem, sed effictum, non picturam, sed Naturam vides. Quæ cum ita sint, mirari profectò subit, ecquid caussæ sit, quod Humanus Intellectus Physicis, quam Logicis considerationibus inhiet avidius: quin imo in his plerumque tædio quodam torpeat, quod non nisi alacritas oppugnet, & non nisi assiduitas averuncet: Non est mihi anianimus classicum canere, & bellum inter Scientias seminare: sacrum hoc inter sorores contubernium, importunâ nolim æmulatione discindere: Dicam tamen, ô Naturalis Minerva, dicam pace tua, quod res est, & fidens animi dicam: memor cum Scientiis, id est cum ipsis Gratiis mihi esse negotium, quæ arctis benevolentię brachiis inter se complexæ, mutuas prærogativas libenter agnoscunt, iisque subinde gaudent impensius, quam suis: Igitur à Corpore, quod contemplatur, suas Physica mutuatur illecebras: easdem fermè blanditias edocta Mathematica, addictiores procos habet, quam Logica; Magis tamen adhuc, quam Mathematica, Physica pellicit: quia non Corpus tantum, ut illa, sed & motum ejus, qui Mentis nostræ cum Corpore vinculum est, consideratur: Constat autem tem Mentem hîc inescatam carne, ergastulum hoc & compedes suas, non ferre jam æquo animo ( quod Ratio jusserat ) sed perditè amare, & indole degeneri frui servitute, differre libertatem : Hæc est illa Humanæ Mentis ad Corpus agglutinatio,& totis affectuum uncis adhæsio: Et hinc,ut plurimum ille à Physica, in juveniles præsertim animos, quos carnis ille limus altius absorpsit, pruritus & irritamentum. Logica verò Mentem nostram considerat, ejus Motum seu Discursus contemplatur: Et, quod mirêre, Discursus illos, recursus esse videt, repetitiones, & Idearum miro ordine in se remeantium gyros & flexus: Adeo ut nullus ( quod alibi demonstravi ) legitimus sit Discursus, nulla bona Consequentia, quæ non Repetitione, geminatione, & aliquo ex Antecetecedente in Conclusionem resump-nitatur: Non gaudet hisce, non c-pitur Mens, à Corpore, cum qu-tota consuevit & ferme coalui-obesa, obtusa, hebes: Nam ipsa si-non sapit, quæ à se exulat, & def-derium pulcherrimæ illius Patri-jam dudum exuit: & ordinatas illi-Repetitiones ac Rhytmos, ceu r-coctam crambem detestatur: nih-præter nauseam & vomitum ad is-parat: & Meandros illos, ingenu-suos lusus, ut tricas, ut spinas asp-cit, imo ut Maleam quamdam su-pectat: nihil præter tædia, fastidi-formidines ad ista gerit. Sed gene-rosæ Mentes exsolvunt se istis Pra-judiciis: malunt secum, quam cu-corpore versari: Et hisce Logicat-placere necessum est; Sed genu-nam Logicam: nam in spuriam i-lam merito debacchantur: illa m-hi juxta ac illis, invisa semper eri-
units.tr: With these PROLEGOMENA and preliminary remarks, these RHAPSODIES and ANOMALIES, since almost all the disciplines have been foully defiled, and Logic above all has had its beauty tarnished and its grace polluted, that purest stream has run into a filthy swamp, from which by-products and the dregs of anomalous rhapsodies constantly stagnate in the other sciences. For now in Logic, apart from the types of anomaly I mentioned a little earlier, scarcely anything else is treated. These alone are chiefly considered there, explained there and drummed in there, and by frequent exercises they are brought into use, into habit and, as it were, into nature. Other things only creep in, like preludes and appetisers, and are thought to contribute something to that end in some way. So the thing has become a by-product, the discourse a digression, and Logic a paralogism. But hold on, I am mistaken! That Form does not suffer metamorphosis; it is divine. In the poets we read of men changed into other shapes, not of gods. What I meant was this: paralogism is worshipped by the ignorant in place of logic, and it has been substituted for logic by the incautious. Logic has departed, escaped and withdrawn from the unworthy, its grace unblemished and its majesty undisturbed. For what confusion could smother that splendour? What impiety could pollute that lustre? What rashness could assail that vigour? Logic is nearly equal in dignity to kindly Reason, by which we portray God himself to the life, and it has scarcely anything that could be raised higher above tumult and injury. So it is: Logic is so like that divine particle, so closely does it mirror and breathe Reason on every side, that it often deceives not only strangers but its own familiars, with the same name and the same face. It was by this appearance that certain leaders of philosophy, not the lowest, were deceived and, led astray by a reverence greater than was fitting, decided that Logic should be removed from the schools, because by confusing it with Intellect they judged it unnecessary where Nature teaches. But those men were misled and in error. For although Logic is the eldest of its sisters (I mean the other sciences), it is not Reason itself; it acknowledges Reason as its mother, on an equal footing with its sisters. For Logic teaches not only principles (which is the office of Reason) and common notions, but also theorems, which are to be drawn from the principles by lawful and linked demonstration. For example: What is said of the predicate is said also of the subject; from what the consequent does not follow, the antecedent does not follow from it, and so on. These are not principles, nor can they be taken simply as such; they must be proved, and without demonstration they are open to suspicion. To accept them without demonstration merely because they seem confirmed by certain examples is rash, blind and liable to endless errors, because often what holds in very many examples nevertheless collapses for the very reason that it fails in one. Hence the oracle of the wise has been sanctioned: to know is to recognise through definition, not through examples, however many are produced. As long as it is not established that all cases have been produced, examples do not fix the mind but keep it in suspense, anxious lest some error lurk somewhere else. Since Logic, then, is not Reason itself but a certain offspring of Reason, it is owed first indeed to these cradles, and when it has grown up, to the schools and the Academy, I mean. Nor does Logic merely imitate the face and outward lineaments of Reason; it imitates its nature, its affections and its duties much more. This elder sister in a way plays the mother's part towards her younger sisters: she cherishes them in her bosom and carries them in her arms. I say that all the sciences rest on the logical theorems as on their foundations. If these are not well laid, whatever mass has been built in the other disciplines must totter, and if they are shaken, it must collapse. These theorems: from the true nothing but the true follows; from what the antecedent is, the consequent follows; and the other things contained in the Logical Cube I lately published are the supports on which all disciplines rest. These Atlases, who bear the heavy shoulders of the whole machine of the sciences, without these props there is no single line of reasoning in the sciences, scarcely a single step. Therefore Reason is the image of Divinity (Reason itself cries this out, and it is admitted by all), and Logic is the image of Reason (even its opponents, who for that reason have banned it from the schools, do not deny this). What more illustrious thing, what more sublime thing, could be said of Logic in terms of dignity and majesty? For an image is in a way the thing it represents. Indeed, an image separated in mind and thought from the matter it inheres in is no longer an image but the thing expressed. Just as, if you set aside the lines and blots that the painter's brush has spread on the panel, and fix your whole gaze on the thing displayed to the life, you see no longer the art but the model of art, no longer a likeness but the thing likened, no longer a picture but Nature. Since these things are so, it truly makes one wonder why the human intellect pants more eagerly after physical than logical considerations, and indeed why it commonly grows sluggish in these with a certain weariness, which only eagerness can attack and only constant application can avert. I have no intention of sounding the trumpet and sowing war among the sciences; I do not wish to tear apart this sacred fellowship of sisters with unseemly rivalry. Still, I shall say, O Natural Minerva, I shall say with your leave, what is the case, and say it with a confident mind: I know I have to do with the sciences, that is, with the very Graces themselves, who, embracing one another in close arms of goodwill, gladly acknowledge one another's privileges and rejoice in them more eagerly than in their own. Thus Physics borrows its allurements from the body it contemplates. Mathematics, taught much the same flatteries, has more ardent suitors than Logic. Yet Physics attracts still more than Mathematics, because it considers not only the body, as the latter does, but also its motion, which is the bond between our mind and the body. It is clear, then, that the mind, here enticed by the flesh, no longer bears its prison and fetters with an even temper, as Reason had ordered, but loves them to ruin and, with a degenerate nature, enjoys servitude and puts off freedom. This is that clinging of the human mind to the body and its adhesion with all the hooks of the passions. And hence Physics is for the most part a stimulus and an irritant, especially to young minds, which that clay of the flesh has sucked deeper in. Logic, however, considers our mind and contemplates its motion or discourse. And, what is strange, it sees those discourses to be recurrences, repetitions, and whirls and windings of ideas returning into themselves in a wonderful order. So much so that (as I have shown elsewhere) there is no lawful discourse, no sound consequence, that is not renewed by repetition, duplication, and a resumption of the conclusion from some antecedent. The mind does not delight in these things and does not grasp them, because it has long been accustomed to be wholly bound and almost grown together with the body, and has become gross, dull and blunt. For the mind that is cut off from itself does not taste what it has long since lost the desire for that most beautiful Father, and it loathes ordered repetitions and rhythms as cold cabbage reheated. It prepares nothing but nausea and vomiting at such things, and it regards those meanders, the proper play of intelligence, as thorns and briars, even suspects them as some Medea. It bears towards them nothing but tedium, disgust and dread. But noble minds free themselves from these prejudices: they prefer to dwell with themselves rather than with the body. And these are the people who must please Logic. But they must rightly rage against the spurious Logic, for that one, equally hateful to them as to the others, will always be hated.

units.la: DIXI.
units.tr: I HAVE SPOKEN.
